Various related notes:

- PDF 2.0 now requires annot appearance streams (as per Table 166) except for 2 very specific cases which does not include custom annots. So custom/unknown annots still need to have appearance streams.

- Table 167, Bit 1, Invisible says "Applies only to annotations which do not belong to one of the standard annotation types and for which no annotation handler is available. If set, do not render the unknown annotation and do not print it even if the Print flag is set. If clear, render such an unknown annotation using an appearance stream specified by its appearance dictionary, if any (see 12.5.5, "Appearance streams")."

- Table 167, Bit 2, Hidden says "If set, do not render the annotation or allow it to interact with the user, regardless of its annotation type or whether an annotation handler is available."

> So custom/unknown annots still need to have appearance streams
>
that is correct - as far as it goes.  But is that then the only "expected behavior" that is mentioned by 12.5.1?

> and for which no annotation handler is available
>
And a processor is only required to have them for the standard types (as defined in 12.5.1, P4) - so yes, we're saying that Invisible has to be handled.
And same with Hidden, OK - that works.

But what about Actions on the annotation?  What about trigger events?

You make a really good point - what does "expected behaviour" mean for both non-interactive and interactive viewers, for renderers, for other types of PDF processor (e.g. text extractors, imposition/page extraction engines, etc etc)?

The required Appearance streams in PDF 2.0 only simplifies things and doesn't fully resolve...

I also found this in clause 12.5.5:

"If a PDF processor does not have native support for a particular annotation type, the PDF processor shall render the annotation with its normal (**N**) appearance. PDF processors shall also attempt to provide reasonable behaviour (such as displaying nothing) if an annotation’s **AS** entry designates an appearance state for which no appearance is defined in the appearance dictionary."

Trying to progress this forward (in very small steps!)...

Proposal: correct Section 12.5.1, paragraph 4:

> An interactive PDF processor shall provide certain expected behaviour for all annotation types that it does not recognise, as documented in 12.5.2, "Annotation dictionaries".

to:

A PDF processor shall provide certain expected behaviour for all annotation types that it does not recognise, as documented in 12.5.5, "Appearance streams" and "Table 167 - Annotation flags" (bit positions 1 and 2).

@lrosenthol - do you think that is sufficient for what is currently already documented in ISO 32000-2?
PDF TWG agree

Looking at the implementation of a well known PDF processor...

We always look for the short form/abbreviation first.  If not present, then we look for the full name.

Proposed solution: prioritize abbreviated keys first, then use full key names.

Proposed additional sentence: "In the situation where both an abbreviated key name and the corresponding full key name from Table 91 are present, the abbreviated key name shall take precedence."

Appended to this paragraph "The key-value pairs appearing between the **BI** and **ID** operators (as listed in "Table 91 — Entries in an inline image object") are analogous to their respective key-value pairs in an image XObject dictionary (see "Table 87 — Additional entries specific to an image dictionary") or a stream dictionary (see "Table 5 — Entries common to all stream dictionaries"). For convenience, the abbreviations shown in "Table 91 — Entries in an inline image object" and "Table 92 — Additional abbreviations in an inline image object" may be used in place of the full names. Entries other than those listed shall be ignored."

+1 for the proposal. 

But every time I re-read a section I find some more niggles. So here are a few minor tweaks in the related text; feel free to split into separate stories if you think these are worth following up:

•	There a striking contrast between the text in the 1st para after Table 90: “Unless the image uses ASCIIHexDecode or ASCII85Decode as one of its filters” and in Note 2: “if the final or only filter is ASCIIHexDecode or ASCII85Decode”. Shouldn’t the first of those also talk about “if the final or only filter” rather than ASCII~ being “one of its filters”? I realise you’d need to have done something very odd if you’re using ASCII~ and something else, and the ASCII~ is not last, but …

•	Note 1 carefully mentions both Length and L, but Note 2 only mentions L, which seems inconsistent. Note 2 should identify both as well.

•	Note 3 says that various colour space names don’t refer to resources in the ColorSpace subdictionary; all well and good. But it starts by saying that they identify the corresponding colour spaces directly. Hmmm, don’t DefaultGray, DefaultRGB and DefaultCMYK kick in here?

Could you please make a new Issue for your 2 new points above?
This issue is about the behaviour for logically-duplicated-but-not-actually-duplicated keys in inline images, whereas your new issues are about special handling rules for ASCII* filters in inline images. Same clause but different core issues. Thanks.
Done, thanks
I believe that is correct as well.
Proposed solution as per above

Technical questions:   
- Is Table 120 **CharSet** key permitted or not? (it’s not “metric information only”) 
- Are the required keys **Type** and **FontName** from Table 120 also required in this case? (Type and FontName are both not “metric information only” but they are required – or are they?)   
- Is Table 120 **FontFamily** key permitted? (it’s also not “metric information only” but descriptive)

Here is one proposed new wording:

The key for each entry in an **FD** dictionary shall be the name of a class of glyphs as defined in “Table 123 - Glyph classes in CJK fonts” — that is, a particular subset of the CIDFont’s character collection. The entry’s value shall be a font descriptor whose contents shall be a subset of the keys defined in “Table 120 — Entries common to all font descriptors” that override the font-wide attributes for that class only. This font descriptor shall contain entries for metric information only; it shall not include **FontFile**, **FontFile2**, **FontFile3**, _xxxx see above - anything else?? xxxx_ or any of the entries listed in “Table 122 Additional font descriptor entries for CIDFonts”.

What is the "_anything else_"?

Looking at well known implementation, the following keys in a font descriptor are processed:

**Required**
- Flags
- FontBBox
- StemV
- CapHeight
- Ascent
- Descent
- ItalicAngle

**Optional** (aka read if present)
- MissingWidth
- StemH
- XHeight
- Leading
- MaxWidth
- AvgWidth
- Style/Panose

Just confirming - are you saying that your logic does **NOT** require the FontDescriptor required keys (**Type** and **FontName** from Table 120) as well?
If not, then they shouldn't be specified as required back in Table 120!

That is correct concerning that implementation not looking at those keys.

However, they are required for other reasons.  (remember, said implementation is *not* a validation tool...just a processor)

Understood. So the solution will state that all required keys from Table 120 are required, as well as then explicitly listing various other keys from Table 120. The starting point for said "other keys list" is _both_ your lists from above - subject to further suggestions or modifications by others.

I'm assuming Leonard missed anything obviously not a metric off his list (FontFile etc and everything that's better described as designers' metadata such as FontStretch). If so then I can confirm the same set here.

I think "X, meaningful only if Y" means:
- key X must be optional - makes no sense if X is always required 
- if Y is false, then X is completely ignored and, for example, if it had the wrong value or a wrong type then it would not be an error
- if Y is true, then X might be required or optional (depends on each usage??) but it must have the correct type and value
- Y cannot refer back to key X directly or indirectly with “meaningful” statements (circular confusion!)
- in each case, is Y fully sufficient or insufficient? 

ISO 32000 also uses "required when ..." style statements so how is "meaningful when ..." different? Should any occurrences be "required when ..."?

Anything else??

From looking over the spreadsheet, I agree that most of them are of the form "X is optional and/or ignored unless key Y meets some criteria" (where _some criteria_ is usually either present and/or true, though may also be of a certain type).

There are a few where it is used in a more "editorial" fashion (eg. 14.5 NOTE) but a better word would suffice.

Leaping into a solution rather than further problem analysis, would it work to replace "X is only meaningful if Y" with "X shall be ignored unless Y"?

That would retain the existing additional semantics around being optional if Y etc.

That doesn't help with ArtBox and "the page's meaningful content" of course ..., or the various statements along the lines of "operators shall be meaningful only inside a content stream". I'm not convinced that most of the latter are ... meaningful? useful? anyway!

I interpret "... shall be ignored if ..." as a clearer statement since this also implies that validators shall(!) not report the key or key value under the stated condition (so even if it was invalid it is technically not a reportable error because of the presence of the other key). Of course "... shall not be present ..." is an even stronger statement.

I also agree a number of uses of the word "meaningful" are also more casual/editorial but I'm not so concerned with them.

I believe this is correct, in that this is starting from the `Link` element and not the content element.   A content element could have many `Link` children, but a `Link` can only bind back to a single content element.

Since annotations are bound to pages, it would be problematic to start thinking about them outside that context.  This is why block level elements that span pages, such as a paragraph are broken into inline elements (eg. Spans) for each page.  And if you needed to duplicate the Link, that would be OK.

Actually, this doesn't sound right to me.  There's no reason that a single Link can't have content that spans pages and then OBRJs gathering the related annotations for that link.  However, when I read this, I don't see the prohibition that is being stated. 

14.7.5.3 is simply stating the mechanism for referencing an object, in this case a link annotation.  14.8.4.7.2 is just talking generally about how a Link element links content to annotations, since that is how links work.  The wording is a little sloppy, in that it implies there is only one, but it doesn't state that anywhere.

Annex L doesn't try to limit this and even the 2017 edition clearly allowed multiple OBJRs in a Link.  I'd say we can close this or make a small editorial change.

> Since annotations are bound to pages, it would be problematic to start thinking about them outside that context. This is why block level elements that span pages, such as a paragraph are broken into inline elements (eg. Spans) for each page. And if you needed to duplicate the Link, that would be OK.

To be clear about this, there's no requirement (that I am aware of) for **Span** elements when a **P** includes content that occurs on >1 page, and it's common practice to omit such **Span** elements in this case.
@DuffJohnson totally agreed.  Spans can be used to separate them, but certainly aren't in any way required.

@mrbhardy @DuffJohnson while I agree that 32K itself has no requirements on the `Span` elements - we should most certainly ensure that it is part of "advanced tagging" work such as PDF/UA or related documents.

I agree that prescriptions for "good tagging", including PDF/UA, should include a requirement for use of a <Span> or similar in these cases (note taken), but the implied need for a <Span> or similar to contain a page-spanning <Link>'s respective OBJRs (as they cannot themselves span pages) is clear enough from the existing text, IMO.
I would actually disagree with that position.  I believe that any element name that is not in the SST *shall* be in a namespace.

@lrosenthol for backwards compatibility with documents being upgraded from PDF 1.7, if an element is in the standard namespace (i.e. no namespace is defined), then it needs to be processed through the global RoleMap (just as it would in 1.7).  So in principle, you can still have an undefined namespace, but it has to meet the requirements of tagged PDF (i.e. be role mapped to something in the standard).  The preference is that all custom tags have a well-defined namespace so they can be used more broadly, but this isn't mandated any more than it was in 1.7.
@mrbhardy You are correct about the current state of things - however, I am suggesting that in future "advanced tagging" work that we *require* the namespace.
@mrbhardy Is your comment above worthy of an informative note? I think it is. Care to draft one (pretty please)?

Proposal is to add a note in 14.8.6.1:

NOTE Namespaces are designed to provide greater interchange of PDFs including logical structure, providing a means to identify the custom namespace for each element, if appropriate.  However, structure elements types in undefined namespaces continue to be permitted.

There are multiple references to a "page's content stream" throughout the text. Removing the parenthetical text would clarify those greatly as well. 

As an example, that would mean that 8.11.3.2 para 1 would clearly say that BMC, the optional content itsent and EMC could appear in up to three separate elements in a Contents array.
Proposed solution: removing the text in parentheses in clause 7.8.3
Agreed. `Length` is always required and should->shall
Proposed solution: reword second sentence as "However, the **Length** entry shall still specify the number of those bytes (usually, there are no bytes and Length is 0)."
I wonder how many files out there will be invalidated by this ... but you could make a good case that they're already invalid anyway, so I'm not going to lose sleep. +1
Then how would you know the name of the font, such as for display in a processor's UX?

So are you saying "Table 110 — Entries in a Type 3 font dictionary" is incorrect then and needs **BaseFont**?
Or that "Table 120 — Entries common to all font descriptors" **FontName** description is incorrect/incomplete for Type3?

did some reading of code and here is the situation...

For Type 3 fonts, the name comes from the `Name` key (if present) in the Type 3 font dictionary. For all other font types, it comes from the `BaseFont` key of the relevant subtype's font dictionary (eg. T1, TTF, etc.).

The `FontName` key in the font descriptor dictionary is used primarily for the purpose of determining if a font has been subset, based on the requirements of 9.9.2 (Font subsets).  

Since Type 3 fonts are either always subset or never subset (depending on how you look at it), there is never a need to have the `FontName` key present in the font descriptor dictionary.  Accordingly, I'd change Table 120 to make it "(Required for non-Type 3 fonts)".

Proposed solution: change Table 120 — Entries common to all font descriptors, FontName to say:

(_Required for non-Type 3 fonts_)

Just saying "Required for non-Type 3 fonts" doesn't say it shall not be there for Type 3, which leads to two problems:
* the rest of the text doesn't make any sense for t3 fonts
* it doesn't make any statement about it having to match anything else for a T3 font.

It may be going a bit overboard, but:

_(Required for fonts other than Type 3)_ The PostScript name of the font. For Type 3 fonts that include a **Name** entry in the Type 3 font dictionary, this name shall match the value of that key. For all fonts other than Type 3 this name shall be the same as the value of **BaseFont** in the font or CIDFont dictionary that refers to this font descriptor.
Proposed solution: replace sentence "The value shall not be 5" with ""The halftone may be of any Type other than 5."

PDF TWG would like wording to be use ISO terminology ("shall"/"shall not").
This needs to be consistently applied to the other tables describing halftone dicts.
I'd tend to favor the second suggestion since it's normative and makes it more clear which keys are impacted.

Proposed solution: add the sentence "Additional limitations also apply to this key when used in soft-mask image dictionaries - see clause 11.6.5.2 Soft-mask images." to the description for each of the Table 87 keys: Intent, Alternates, Name, ID, StructParent, and SMask.

Agreed.

Other formatting issues: 

- Table 147 Viewer Preferences, ViewArea, ViewClip, PrintArea and PrintClip keys - CropBox shouldn't be bold as it is not the key name, but a name value. They should be italic. I also note that for these cases there is not a definitive list of all the permitted CamelCase values - the references describe what they are, but don't enumerate the name values. Easiest solution is to to describe the list of values as matching the key names in Table 396 — Entries in a box colour information dictionary - or we can list them out fully in Table 147 for each key.

- Table 87 Image Dictionary, ImageMask description: the Mask key name in "... the Mask and ColorSpace shall not..." needs to be bold
Proposed solution: all of the above

Also Table 8: Columns (positive)?

It doesn't make any sense to allow a value of 0 here, does it? FWIW, I'll come out to admit that I managed to produce a segfault if 0 was given.

Similarly for the Columns entry in Table 11 (you wrote non-negative above)?

Re Columns in Tables 8 and 11 possibly being zero: I was half thinking about the highly degenerate corner case situation where there is no data in the compressed images, in which case Columns being zero might be equally pointless/degenerate. But if we assume images always have at least 1 pixel then yes, Columns would be strictly greater than zero.

How many rows of width zero does a zero-pixel image have?
Allowing Columns = 0 begs the age-old question of what is 0 divided by 0.

However, a zero-pixel image with Columns any positive integer is perfectly possible. It simply has 0 rows of that size.

(I'm assuming this data is always stored in row-major order... is it?)

Yes - I believe these compressors require row-major order.
As I said I only half thought about it 😀... so maybe Columns should be defined to always be strictly greater than zero.

BTW based on a recent PDF TWG discussion, we will switch to avoid the use of terms such as "positive", "negative" or "non-negative" because of regional differences of interpretation as to whether each of these includes or excludes zero. We'll go with explicit wording w.r.t to zero.

More:
* Table 337, PlayCount - does 0 make any sense?
Recommend that it should be byte string to match

Proposed solutions:

1. "If the crypt filter is referenced from **StmF** or **StrF** in the encryption dictionary, this entry shall be an array of byte strings, where each _byte_ string shall be a binary-encoded CMS object that shall ..."
2. change the Type column to say "_byte_ string or array"
3. "... this entry shall be a _byte_ string that shall be a binary-encoded CMS object that shall contain a list of all recipients ..."

I would actually go further to say that the bigger picture here is that the algorithm for generation of an annotation's appearance is undocumented/implementation specific.  There is guidance given in some cases, such as this example, but many of the keys are not (fully) specified as to how to use them.  This is especially true for anything related to text & fonts.

Whether we wish to attempt to tackle this holistically is worthy of some discussion...

"Table 176 — Additional entries specific to a link annotation" clearly states that **QuadPoints** is only about _activation_, not _appearance_: "An array of 8×𝑛 numbers specifying the coordinates of n quadrilaterals in default user space that comprise the region in which the link should be activated" and "If this entry is not present, or the PDF processor does not recognise it, or if any coordinates in the **QuadPoints** array lie outside the region specified by **Rect** then the activation region for the link annotation shall be defined by its **Rect** entry."

Furthermore below "Table 166 — Entries common to all annotation dictionaries" is the normative statement:
"A PDF reader shall render the appearance dictionary without regard to any other keys and values in the annotation dictionary and shall ignore the values of the **C, IC, Border, BS, BE, BM, CA, ca, H, DA, Q, DS, LE, LL, LLE,** and **Sy** keys."

Considering also the description of **Border** in Table 166, it's clearly the definition of a visual appearance of a rounded rectangle that's included in the appearance stream whereas **QuadPoints** in Table 176 is about activation areas. 

So a key question from all this: is the annotation border the same as the link activation area?  
Definitely not when **QuadPoints** is used. But if **QuadPoints** is not present, then **Rect** gets used instead and the answer just so happens to be yes. But I think that is just coincidental...
 
I thus think there is an unstated assumption in your question that **QuadPoints** relates to the visual appearance. I don't believe that's correct as it clearly states activation multiple times. And, yes, that makes it very difficult to regenerate appearance streams (especially if the activation area is desired to have a visible stroked outline as the activation path will not be the same as the centre path of the stroke by half the stroke width!).
And let's not forget that we have the "NonRectangular Links" document in review that will now add `Path` - though that is only valid on a Link annotation (which can have an AP).

Without attempting to solve the very large issue of appearance stream regeneration, but trying to address @MPBailey's original question...

Proposed solution: add the following note (informative, stated as factual) to both the **QuadPoints** and **Border** cells in Table 176:

Note: When **QuadPoints** is used, the activation area and the visual appearance (including border) of the link annotation are not required to be the same. This is because **Border** always uses the annotation **Rect** entry.

PDF TWG - concern that Border description in Note is not aligned with wording in Table 166.
Pending

Further research about the definition of annotation borders: clause 12.5.4 Border styles only says "_An annotation may optionally be surrounded by a border when displayed or printed. If present, the border shall be drawn completely inside the annotation rectangle_". This definition also supports the additional behaviour described in Tables 177 and 180 which can use a different rectangle for drawing borders (the **RD** key).

Easiest solution is to remove the offending sentence from the proposed note:

Note: When **QuadPoints** is used, the activation area and the visual appearance (including border) of the link annotation are not required to be the same.
Approved by PDF TWG.

Proposed solution: add a new 2nd sentence:

If the name is **DeviceRGB** and the page where the annotation referencing the 3D stream is used has a **DefaultRGB** color space, then the **DefaultRGB** color space shall be used (see 8.6.5.6 Default colour spaces).
PDF TWG also identified typo "If this key is not present, the colour space for the 3D artwork colour values are considered undefined..." --> "... is considered..."
This is also related to #34
Tripped up by an error 404 from GitHub; closing

PDF TWG request wording change to: "_(Required except for conditions listed below...)_"

(PDF TWG would like more specific information instead of just "usually"...)

Some comments:

- Table 166 possibly already defines what you call a "zero-size annotation": "Annotations where the value of the **Rect** key consists of an array where the value at index 1 is equal to the value at index 3 and the value at index 2 is equal to the value at index 4. NOTE (2020) The bullet point above was changed from “or” to “and” in this document to match requirements in other published ISO PDF standards (such as PDF/A)." - however the choice of "AND" means that a zero-wdith-only or zero-height-only annot would still paint a pixel thin line (thanks to the scan conversion rules). 

- I agree that the description wording choice in Table 166 de-emphasises the newly stated importance of **AP** in PDF 2.0 and changing to something like "_(Usually required, PDF 1.2)_" would be much better.

- for the para after Table 166 I do not think "For all annotations containing an AP entry, a PDF reader ..." is what is meant. To me, the current wording says that PDF readers shall _always_ ignore all the appearance description keys and thus shall not try and simulate any appearance streams. ISO 32K is written from a compliance point of view so since AP shall always be present excepting for the few cases stated then that is what shall be used. However a PDF _writer_ will need to use those keys to create or regenerate AP appearance streams using their own implementation-dependent algorithms.

> PDF readers shall always ignore all the appearance description keys and thus shall not try and simulate any appearance streams

Correct.

> However a PDF writer will need to use those keys to create or regenerate AP appearance streams using their own implementation-dependent algorithms

Correct.

Thanks, so we have concensus on what a renderer should do, but what we don't yet have is some text that says that. So I'm going to suggest:
* Amending the AP entry to say "usually required", as discussed above.
* Amending the 1st para after the table to: “_For all annotations containing an AP entry,_ a PDF reader shall render the appearance dictionary without regard to any other keys and values in the annotation dictionary. _If no AP entry is present the annotation shall not be rendered. When rendering the annotation a PDF reader_ shall ignore the values of the C, IC, Border, BS, BE, BM, CA, ca, H, DA, Q, DS, LE, LL, LLE, and Sy keys.”

The "when rendering an annotation" bit is because a reader that is doing something other than rendering should NOT ignore those keys, of course.
Isn't the point of `BM, CA and ca` to specify how to composite the appearance onto the page?   If that's true, then those keys (if present) *shall* be used for rendering the AP/annotation.

@lrosenthol you are correct for `BM`, but not for `ca` or `CA` as they are both currently explicitly specified to be the content stream and exclude themselves for when AP streams are present. 

But having **BM** including in the list of keys in the 1st para after Table 166 is incorrect! 

Quoting Table 166:

- **BM**: (_Optional; PDF 2.0_) The blend mode that shall be used when painting the annotation onto the page ...

- **ca** : (_Optional; PDF 2.0_) When regenerating the annotation's appearance stream, this is the opacity value (11.2, "Overview of transparency") that shall be used for all nonstroking operations on all visible elements of the annotation in its closed state (including its background and border) but not the popup window that appears when the annotation is opened.
Default value: 1.0
The specified value shall not be used if the annotation has an appearance stream (see 12.5.5, "Appearance streams"); in that case, the appearance stream shall specify any transparency.
If no explicit appearance stream is defined for the annotation, and the processor is not able to regenerate the appearance, the annotation may be painted by implementation-dependent means that do not necessarily conform to the PDF imaging model; in this case, the effect of this entry is implementation-dependent as well.

- **CA**: (_Optional; PDF 1.4, PDF 2.0 for non-markup annotations_) When regenerating the annotation's appearance stream, this is the opacity value (11.2, "Overview of transparency") that shall be used for stroking all visible elements of the annotation in its closed state, including its background and border, but not the popup window that appears when the annotation is opened.
If a ca entry is not present in this dictionary, then the value of this CA entry shall also be used for nonstroking operations as well. Default Value: 1.0
The specified value shall not be used if the annotation has an appearance stream (12.5.5, "Appearance streams"); in that case, the appearance stream shall specify any transparency.
If no explicit appearance stream is defined for the annotation, and the processor is not able to regenerate the appearance, the annotation may be painted by implementation-dependent means that do not necessarily conform to the PDF imaging model; in this case, the effect of this entry is implementation-dependent as well

**6.12.3 Annotation appearances**
For all annotation dictionaries containing an AP key, the appearance dictionary that it defines as its
value shall contain only the N key. If an annotation dictionary’s Subtype key has a value of Widget and

field will have multiple appearance states, each one associated with the specific values that the button can take.

Referring to ISO/IEC 15444-2:2004:

* Table 190 - Additional entries specific to a screen annotation: **MK** key: (_Optional_) An appearance characteristics dictionary (see "Table 192 — Entries in an appearance characteristics dictionary"). The **I** entry of this dictionary provides the icon used in generating the appearance referred to by the screen annotation’s **AP** entry.

* Table 191 - Additional entries specific to a widget annotation, **MK** key: (_Optional_) An appearance characteristics dictionary (see "Table 192 — Entries in an appearance characteristics dictionary") that shall be used in constructing a dynamic appearance stream specifying the annotation’s visual presentation on the page. ...

* Para below Table 191:
> The **MK** entry may be used to provide an appearance characteristics dictionary containing additional information for constructing the annotation’s appearance stream. "Table 192 — Entries in an appearance characteristics dictionary" shows the contents of this dictionary.

A misc change for the bullet below Table 190 - PDF 2.0 now requires AP appearance streams for screen annotations so the sentence "If **AP** is not present, the screen annotation shall not have a default visual appearance and shall not be printed." is meaningless in PDF 2.0 and can be deleted.

Another somewhat relevant statement:

* clause 12.11.6. Note 2: "Other common fallbacks can include presenting a static annotation appearance in place of a dynamic annotation."

So I believe the intention of all the words is trying to distinguish between a "static appearance model" defined by **AP** appearance streams in almost all annots and always used by non-interactive processors (such as print RIPs) vs a "dynamic appearance" that might be used by certain interactive processors such as when users are interacting with form widgets. However the dynamic appearance aspects are not standardized or defined as PDF is the definition of a file format, not a software product spec - and vendors/implementors can make their own decisions/innovations. 

Note that the terms "static appearance model" and "dynamic appearance" are not official ISO 32000-2 T&Ds.

Note also that ISO 32000 is silent on how to construct/re-construct appearance streams from all the various dict keys, etc. - again, there is currently no expectation that all PDF processors would construct visually identical appearance streams.

Related discussions are also in Issues #1, #17, #23, #42.

So, to summarize for the question actually asked, I therefore think **MK** does **_not_** belong in the list of keys below Table 166 as that list is related to "static appearance" streams.

As a PDF 2.0 writer you must provide AP appearance streams for your annots, and you can optionally provide **MK** to influence interactive processors if/when they allow dynamic user interaction with your widgets.

> So I believe the intention of all the words is trying to distinguish between a "static appearance model" defined by AP appearance streams in almost all annots and always used by non-interactive processors (such as print RIPs) vs a "dynamic appearance" that might be used by certain interactive processors such as when users are interacting with form widgets.

I can't believe this. The AP appearance stream encodes  various "dynamic" states like rollover and down, /Yes, /Off.  I have code for checkboxes which use on AP for the various states and work fine.

In my opinion the difference is not a difference from user interaction, but how a PDF processor/viewer create the rendering: AP describes the appearance and so the rendering fully by  pointing  to an form Xobject, while MK gives a set of rules (like the text of the caption) and allows the renderer to create something on the fly.

I mean that the AP appearance streams are "static" in that a processor just selects the appropriate stream they want (On, Off, Up, Down, etc) and renders it directly without changing it or attempting to reverse engineer how it was constructed to change it. However when a user does data entry into a widget/field, a GUI often needs to be dynamic in the sense that it changes on each keypress and UX designers may want other visual elements to assist/highlight - and this is what the optional MK provides. So I think we are agreeing.

Given other proposed solutions in #94 and #42, adding **MK** to the list below Table 166 **as well as** the new wording in those solutions is OK (since the new wording highlights this "ignoring" is only when rendering appearance streams and PDF processors should not intermix keys and appearance streams when rendering). 

Note that the Table 190 description for MK explicitly refers to "... provides the icon used in generating the appearance referred to by the screen annotation’s **AP** entry" - and PDF remains silent on ways and means of regenerating appearance streams. That is a far bigger issue!

PDF TWG: OK to ignore MK for Widget. Screen annots require AP therefore OK to ignore.

Feedback from ISO JTC 1 SC 29 experts:

* PDF spec should probably reference ISO/IEC 14496-22 generically (non-dated) form (and also generically refer to amendments)

ISO TC 171 SC 2 also hopes that ISO JTC 1 SC 29 can clarify their meaning of "deprecation" in a future ISO 14496-22.

Here is some further textual analysis related to this possible confusion, with some suggestions for improvement of the language used. 

I understand the reluctance to change any of the existing text, so maybe an extra informative and clarifying paragraph could be added that explains in one place (using straightforward and consistent language) the correct interpretation of all the relevant phrases and sentences (see below for details of which these are).

--
As Matthew explained, the problems stem from the usage 
in these clauses of the word “substitution”, which occurs 
only in the following three sentences (plus NOTE 2 itself):

A:
“the alternate description text . . . is a complete (or whole) word or phrase substitution for the current element.”

B:
“The value of ActualText is a character substitution for the content enclosed by the structure element . . .”

C:
“The E value (a text string) is a word or phrase substitution for the tagged text . . .”

In all these three cases it would be much better 
(correct, even!) English to not use the word 
“substitution” but instead to write: 
“to be substituted”    
or maybe just   
“substitute”. 

Notes/Reasoning:  The word “substitution” is normally 
understood to refer to the act of substituting/replacing
 (a player in a soccer team, for example) rather than 
to the material (the new player) that gets used as the substitute/replacement.

Additionally -- There are other problems with the above sentences:
1.  the phrase “a character substitution” is very misleading as 
it suggests just a single character!   
This would be better as follows:
“The value of ActualText is a string of characters to be substituted . . .”
or even better (as in the E case):
“The value (a text string) of ActualText is a string of characters to be substituted . . .”
2.  in the sentence concerning Alt, the phrase “complete (or whole) word or phrase” is again misleading (and why does it 
need the alternate for “complete”?) since Alt can contain 
whole paragraphs of (natural language) text, so long as it 
is presented as a pure ‘text string’ with no formatting, 
mark-up, tags etc.

--
Following this route we would get the following more complete and consistent version of  NOTE 2 (I prefer the use of “replacement” to “substitute” here):

﻿”The treatment of ActualText, in which the substitute (replacement) text is simply a string of characters, is different from the treatment of Alt, in which the substitute (replacement) text consists of whole words, phrases or more, including multiple sentences and paragraphs, that form a complete description.”

There are two things we ARE trying to say here.  The first is that ActualText represents a text equivalent for content and that Alt provides a description of the content to which it applies.  The second is that when consuming elements where ActualText or Alt text is provided, a processor may choose to substitute that element's content with the text provided in the ActualText or Alt entries.

with

"The treatment of ActualText, in which the substitute (replacement) text is simply a string of characters, is different from the treatment of Alt, in which the _intended_ substitute (replacement) text consists of whole words, phrases or more, including multiple sentences and paragraphs, that form a complete description _of the item_.”

I just don’t think we should change this text as described. This has nothing to do with author intent. It is the specification’s intent to provide two different (three if you count E) methods to provide alternative information for content. 

One mechanism is a means of providing a textual equivalent to content that would be visibly understood to be text by a sighted user or consumed as text (ActualText). 

One provides a description of a unit of content that is intended to be complete in its own right (Alt). 

One provides an expansion for an abbreviation if a user requires it (E). 

None of the above describe how these should be presented or used and there is no control of that by the author. It is just whether they are provided and then what action is being taken by the processor (e.g. text extraction might use ActualText, whereas a screen reader might use Alt). They could both be present on the same node. 

The proposed text doesn’t clarify any of this that I can see and it is wrong to say that it is intended to replace or do something. That is up to the processor.

>the signing application should create two signature reference dictionaries here: a FieldMDP SigRef dictionary ... and a DocMDP SigRef dictionary

No. Indeed, a **FieldMDP** transform shall be created based on the **SigFieldLock** dictionary. But creating a **DocMDP** transform is not required.

* First of all creating a **DocMDP** transform when signing a signature field with a **P** entry in its signature field lock dictionary is actually _forbidden_ if there already is a certification or approval signature in the document. Thus, creating a **DocMDP** transform cannot be required.
* Also the description of the **P** value in the signature field lock dictionary conveys that it *updates* the MDP settings from a *previous author signature*, and if there is no such author signature, assumes initial permissions to be based on the value 3. This in particular implies that this lock dictionary entry does not request that the signature to put into the field shall be an author signature (which a **DocMDP** transform would imply).

One might even discuss whether a signature with both a **FieldMDP** and a **DocMDP** transform is allowed at all. (I only have the ISO 32000-2:2017 version yet, so I cannot be sure whether this question is decided in the current format.)

----

That being said there indeed are some peculiarities in how Acrobat signed your document:

* As you already remarked yourself, Acrobat seems to have copied the **P** entry along from the signature field lock dictionary to the **FieldMDP** transform. This is peculiar as the **P** entry is neither mentioned as possible **FieldMDP** transform parameter nor as an entry a signing application is expected to copy there from the lock dictionary.
  (On the other hand the note under that copying instruction claims that _copying is done because all objects in a signature dictionary are direct objects if the dictionary contains a byte range signature._ If otherwise referencing was ok, this would at least _allow_ the presence of any lock dictionary values in the transform parameters, in particular the **P**.)
* That note mentioned above makes it quite peculiar that in Acrobat's signature the transform parameters actually are copied into a separate indirect object. Here apparently Acrobat only loosely follows the specification.

Thank you, @mkl-public , apparently I was wrong about the semantics of **Lock**, and I misinterpreted the meaning of the **P** key in **Lock** as a requirement on the signer to create a **DocMDP** entry in the signature. I rationalised that as OK, because I (also mistakenly) believed that the certification signature was identified by the pointer in **Perms** in the document catalog, rather than by the mere presence of a **DocMDP** signature reference dictionary. Thanks a lot for helping me realise what the source of my confusion was!

Nonetheless, we seem to be in agreement about **P** in **FieldMDP**.

Coming back to this issue after sitting on it for some time, I'm still not sure what the right thing to do here would be. Does the following sound reasonable?

Add a note (perhaps at the end of clause 12.8.2.4?) clarifying how to compute the DocMDP permission level that is currently in effect, making reference to the relevant clauses describing Lock and DocMDP. This would still ensure that all validation-related information for implementers (to the extend defined by ISO 32000) can be found in clause 12.8. If people agree with this approach, I'll draft some words.


I'm less sure what we should (or even can) say about **P** in **FieldMDP** in such a note.

The discussion in the DigSig TWG today ended up addressing the remaining open points here:

 - It affirmed that the **P** key in a field lock dictionary is indeed the intended way to apply DocMDP-like locking to a signature that is not the first one in the file.
 - As a suggestion out of the DigSig TWG to make this a bit less confusing, we suggest adding the **P** key from Table 236 (Entries in a signature field lock dictionary) to Table 259 (Entries in the FieldMDP transform parameters dictionary) as well. In addition, the text below Table 259 should be modified accordingly (details below). Like this, the signature reference dictionary/dictionaries canonically define the MDP level.


## Proposed changes

Add a **P** entry to Table 259 of type _number_ with the following description:

> _(PDF 2.0; optional)_ An integer value describing the access permissions for this document. This entry shall have the same restrictions and semantics as the **P** entry defined in Table 236 (Entries in a signature field lock dictionary).

Modify the 3rd bullet point in the para below Table 259 as follows:

> The Action,  Fields entries in the transform parameters dictionary shall be copied from the corresponding fields in the signature field lock dictionary.

to 

> The Action, Fields, and P entries in the transform parameters dictionary shall be copied from the corresponding fields in the signature field lock dictionary.

(side note: several implementations that I am aware of already do this)

Wordsmithing welcome.

Strictly speaking this changes the (_documented!_) way the **P** works in this context, originally having the **P** entry in the **Lock** dictionary was the single documented way to lock the document.

After the proposed change, what is the expected behavior of a PDF processor confronted with a signed PDF having the **P** entry only in the **Lock** dictionary? Or only in the **FieldMDP** transform parameters? Or having different values in those locations?

MDP all along (with the lock dictionary only serving as a hint for downstream signers, i.e. communicating _author_ intent). This issue was discussed during the virtual meeting of ISO TC 171 SC 2 WG 7 (PDF/Engineering) last night.

To summarize for others:
* earlier versions of PDF actively used E4X for use-cases such as using embedded XML inside PDFs as a data source for AcroForms (XML data would be a PDF attachment); prior to AcroForm submission, pre-processing submitted data as XML (when not using XFDF); and processing XMP and XFA via E4X.
* existing files with a dependency on E4X from earlier versions of PDF still exist so PDF 1.x processors still need to support E4X
* popular open-source JavaScript engines have removed E4X support in line with modern JavaScript changes
* WG9 agreed that PDF 2.0 should **not** depend on E4X as the JavaScript landscape has significantly changed
* WG9 also acknowledged that such a decision means that "upgrading" PDF 1.x files that rely on E4X to PDF 2.0 is no longer trivial/possible. This creates a forward-compatibility issue that is acknowledged and accepted.

The agreed solution is for WG7 to update [ISO 21757-1:2020 "Document management — ECMAScript for PDF — Part 1: Use of ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0)"](https://www.iso.org/standard/71559.html) at some time in the future. No changes are needed to ISO 32000-2:2020 (PDF 2.0) as it does not mention or refer directly to E4X - it 'inherits' the reference via an undated normative reference to ISO 21757-1. Until such time, this proposed resolution will be recorded here and at [https://www.pdfa.org/pdf-issues/](https://www.pdfa.org/pdf-issues/) once the PDFa PDF TWG agree.

Note also that ISO 32000-1:2008 (PDF 1.7) is unaffected as it does not reference ISO 21757-1 - and the title of ISO 21757-1 clearly indicates it is for PDF 2.0 only anyway. So ISO 32000-1:2008 (PDF 1.7) will continue to depend on E4X.

Re. the point that Table is not a _block-level element_, I was stumbling over my words on the call the other day but what I was trying to get at is that these terms are, unfortunately, hugely overloaded.

CSS (my other working group) has the concept of an "outer" and "inner" layout model: how an element appears to its parent, and how it lays out its children. The table in my example above is an "block table" - externally it's a block, laid out full width below its previous sibling, but internally a table with children in rows/columns. And as Chris said, it's equally possible to put a table on the same line as surrounding text, making it an "inline table".

HTML+CSS need this distinction for layout, and the term _block-level element_ in CSS is specifically describing the outer display aspect. So yes, tables are _block-level elements_ by default, but `<table style="display:inline-table">` is not - it's a _flow_ (aka _inline_) level element.

TL;DR is that we need to be careful comparing the word "block" between HTML and PDF.

PDF doesn't care about layout, so any distinction between group, block and inline feels arbitrary to me. In fact, on this topic I'd like to make an argument for `aside` to be allowed as a valid child of `p` as well, for the same reason we allow tables, figures, formulae and lists.

Having multiple password-based (standard) crypt filters is not something that makes sense in PDF right now, that's right. However, you can have PDFs where embedded files are encrypted but the rest of the document is not, or PDFs where all strings/streams are encrypted but metadata is not. This is achieved by combining the **Identity** crypt filter with a regular **StdCF** one (again, assuming that we're using the standard security handler).

In a document protected by a public key security handler (as opposed to the standard one), it's not so hard to imagine a situation where different embedded files are encrypted using different keys, and hence different crypt filters, for example. The standard allows for that kind of thing (that's why **Recipients** is a crypt filter property, not a security handler property for public key security handlers). That being said, I'm sure that very few viewers, if any, would support it. You could go even more wild with custom security handlers & crypt filters if your use case requires it.

Long story short, the crypt filter mechanism is very flexible, but for interoperability reasons, only a very specific set of configurations is actually practical to use for public workflows.

EDIT: Is your question about why "filters" is plural in "crypt filters named **StdCF**"? I think that's just a generic plural; at least in my view, it doesn't imply the potential presence of multiple StdCF filters in a single document---that would be impossible anyway, since crypt filters are in a document-wide namespace.

Our parser is designed to only expect to find indirect references in certain places (i.e. as entries in an array and as the values of dictionary entries). Proposed solution (for 7.5.7):

> NOTE: Including the document catalog in an object stream has interoperability implications, particularly for encrypted documents. If the catalog dictionary is part of an object stream, a PDF processor reading the document must first process that object stream before it can access potentially relevant document metadata, including the declared PDF version, developer extensions and XMP metadata.

IIRC "must" is informative in ISO-ese, and I don't think this sounds normative, but feel free to wordsmith as appropriate.

As to why I wrote "process" instead of "decrypt" in the second sentence: encryption is the only case where any of that currently matters (hence why it's called out explicitly), but this wording would also cover potential future extension TSes that define new compression algorithms, for example. Not that that's particularly likely to happen, but it doesn't hurt to make the phrasing a little more inclusive, IMO.

> There are technical reasons why the Catalog must not be stored in an ObjStm:

I'm not sure that these are actually technical reasons but rather reasons caused by a certain policy.

> * it would potentially hide the version number of the PDF

There's no reason why someone needs to know the version number of an encrypted PDF file unless the file can be decrypted by the user.

> * it would hide the /Metadata for the PDF if the PDF was encrypted.

Same argument as above: Why should someone get access to the Metadata of an encrypted PDF file unless the file can be decrypted by the user. Compare that to a Document Information dictionary: The entries in a Document Information dictionary are encrypted if the file is encrypted.

Please correct me if I'm wrong, but according to my understanding the /Encrypt dictionary is self-contained, and it isn't necessary to know the concrete PDF version for being able to determine the key to decrypt a file. If that is correct, then a PDF processor can first determine the decryption key, then decrypt the catalog to determine the PDF version, and then act appropriately depending on the PDF version.

Yes, that's true, and in fact it's exactly what our library (iText) does. But I can see why you might want to access information about developer extensions & version info prior to attempting authentication & decryption in an interactive viewer. For example, ISO 32003 defines a new security handler with an encryption algorithm that is incompatible with any of the existing ones. A viewer that doesn't support ISO 32003 wouldn't be able to infer that it was missing a developer extension; all it would see is crypt filter definitions that it doesn't recognise.

As for XMP metadata: there's an option to leave metadata unencrypted for indexation purposes. In such cases, you presumably want to make sure that a PDF processor can still reliably locate the metadata stream without requiring authentication. That doesn't apply universally, obviously, but it's still an edge case worthy of consideration IMO.

That said, I think you have a point in that this is probably a matter of policy, and better left up to the implementation to decide. I think adding a note calling out the potential interoperability issue would still be valuable, though.

> As for XMP metadata: there's an option to leave metadata unencrypted for indexation purposes. In such cases, you presumably want to make sure that a PDF processor can still reliably locate the metadata stream without requiring authentication. ISO 32000-1:2008 Annex C (normative) also has this statement with "should" requirements:

> When a conforming reader reads a PDF file with a damaged or missing cross-reference table, it may
attempt to rebuild the table by scanning all the objects in the file. However, the generation numbers of
deleted entries are lost if the cross-reference table is missing or severely damaged. To facilitate such
reconstruction, object identifiers, the **endobj** keyword, and the **endstream** keyword should appear at the
start of a line. Also, the data within a stream should not contain a line beginning with the word **endstream**,
aside from the required **endstream** that delimits the end of the stream.

For consistency it would be best if all those cases were considered equal. That is an end of file is causing many real world problems by NOT having the same status at real EOF as anywhere else in a file.

Explanation of what I mean, There are many PDF writers that will consider that the %%EOF at the end of a /Linearized section MUST follow the rule ALL lines are terminated thus %%EOF is automatically followed by implied mandatory EOL. HOWEVER when it comes to "current" final %%EOF the old guides and current standards only mention a need for "optional" EOL after an EOF and worst of all encourage no EOL by the statement in 7.5.5 
> ...The last line of the file shall contain
only the end-of-file marker, %%EOF....

 Hence often a file that is to be signed or edited has no REAL physical EOF marker simply an "F" in placement 

Why does this matter is because the next appendage often starts without an EOL, thus we constantly find in the real word examples such as `%%EOF1000 0 Obj<EOL>` clearly a problem for parsing signatures and annotations.

Signature failure and annotation failure are often undetected until a later stage.

Proposal remove the optional use of EOL and ensure
- require EOL before and after %%EOF comment keywordS anywhere in the file including the last.

>Why does this matter is because the next appendage often starts without an EOL, thus we constantly find in the real word examples such as `%%EOF1000 0 Obj<EOL>` clearly a problem for parsing signatures and annotations.

PDF processors can prevent creating such problems by starting an incremental update with an EOL, at least if they find no EOL at the current end of the PDF. 

Admittedly, depending on your choice of EOL this can make Adobe Acrobat unhappy when validating changes in incremental updates to signed PDFs, see [this stack overflow q&a](https://stackoverflow.com/q/77743967/1729265). But on one hand this can be considered an Acrobat bug and on the other there is a clear work-around, using a different EOL, 

Thus, I'd consider clarifying this merely a nice-to-have.

Also I'd propose to implement the clarification not by a specific requirement for **%%EOF** but instead by defining the term _line_ (as in _line in the file_, not as in _line in a path_). If I recall correctly, there is no real definition thereof in the spec.

Let's clarify a few things here.

1 - ISO standards, such as ISO 32000-2:2020, are just that - standards.  There is no source code, closed or otherwise, involved.

After discussion on this thread it seems that the consensus is converging on requiring a Resources dictionary in a Type 3 font. To do that, and to respond to Thomas’ comments on strange constructions, I propose replacing the 2nd bullet in 7.8.3 with the following, adopting wording based on the previous bullet (for resources on Page objects):

> - For a content stream that defines a glyph description of a Type 3 font the resource dictionary shall be designated by a Resources entry in the Type 3 font dictionary that shall specify all the resources used by all the content streams in the CharProcs dictionary of the font.

There’s also been a discussion around whether Resources is allowed in each CharProcs stream. I haven’t found anywhere in the current text that says what you’d do with it if it were present (as Peter says, any generic statements about Resources in arbitrary streams are pretty vague, especially if the list at the end of the 3rd bullet in 7.8.3 is taken as an exclusive list). Leonard says that a well-known implementation would use one, but that’s not sufficient reason to encourage people to add one. And the current state is a bit unclear, so I suggest adding this on the end of that 2nd bullet:

> Individual CharProcs streams shall not include a Resources entry.

Inheritance of Resources dictionaries in Form XObjects in Table 93 is a bit unclear, so break it into two pieces:

The 2nd para (starting “In a PDF whose version is 1.1”) is telling people how to make files against a 25-year old specification and does not seem appropriate in this standard. I suggest removing it, and replacing with a note along the lines of:

> NOTE: PDF files whose version is 1.1 or earlier followed different rules. A software developer wishing their PDF processor to offer maximum compatibility might need to review appropriate specifications.

The 3rd para of the Resources Value cell in Table 93 is also confusing; it’s defining post PDF 1.1 behaviour by comparison with the obsolete v1.1 structures. I suggest deleting the entire paragraph. Bullet 3 in 7.8.3 states clearly that a Resources dictionary is required in a Form XObject (at least if the Form needs any resources). So I’d replace the current “Optional but strongly recommended” at the start of the cell, which contradicts 7.8.3, with Required. I could suggest "Required if the Form requires any resources" instead, but the overhead of needing to add an empty Resources dictionary is pretty low.

Coming back to Type 3 fonts, this time in the Resources row of Table 110, replace “Optional but should be used” with “Usually required”. And then replace the last sentence of that cell with 

> 

> If any glyph descriptions refer to named resources then this Resources entry is required, otherwise it is optional.
> 
> NOTE Before PDF 2.0 202X the Resources dictionary was optional in a Type 3 font dictionary. Software developers might wish to make their PDF processors compatible with older PDF versions by looking up names in the resource dictionary of the page on which the font is used if no Resources entry is present in the Type 3 font dictionary.

Finally in that table cell, replace “required by the glyph descriptions” with “referenced by the glyph descriptions”.

Delete the last sentence of bullet d in the list immediately below table 110.

And finally, just to rock the boat on everything above:

The fourth bullet in 7.8.3 is a bit problematic because it implicitly endorses converting a pre PDF 2.0 file to a PDF 2.0 file without bothering to enforce all of the PDF 2.0 rules. It basically says “I know we said Resources is required in a Form XObject or a Type 3 font, but you can break that rule if you prefer”. If we want to allow that because we believe that doing anything else would be too great a drag on PDF 2.0 adoption, then so be it, but we would need to go back to optional Resources in at least those two places.

If we want to stay with making them clearly required then I suggest making the last bullet into a note, with appropriate tweaks to the wording.

-end-

One of the primary sources of confusion appears to be the fourth bullet in 7.8.3, describing behaviour according to previous versions of PDF. That bullet does not describe the behaviour of PDF 2.0 writers, but appears to be setting requirements on PDF 2.0 readers for files that do not conform to PDF 2.0 (“resources … shall be inherited …”). I suggest replacing that bullet with a sightly re-phrased note. In rephrasing I’ve removed the reference to Type 3 fonts because the proposal for bullet 2 already describes the same behaviour.

Bullet 3 explicitly lists annotation appearances and patterns. In PDF 2.0 (2020) patterns are required to have explicitly associated resources, and that’s true at least back to PDF 1.4. Appearance streams are explicitly form XObjects, so the requirement for forms to have explicitly associated resources also applies to them in PDF 2.0. In earlier versions the explicit description of annotation streams as form XObjects is still present, but of course forms did not have to have explicitly associated resources. As a result I’ve also added annotation appearance streams into the new note.

> NOTE 3   PDF files written obeying earlier versions of PDF **could** have omitted the Resources entry in form XObjects and **annotation appearance streams** used on a page. **Those earlier versions state that** resources that are referenced from those forms and streams are inherited from the resource dictionary of the page on which they are used.

I don't think things can get any more ratified or official than that! The fact that ISO no longer has appropriate pathways to correct highly technical documents is an issue with their choice of publishing model. This is also why the PDF Association provides the full set of all ratified solutions ("ISO approved") for free at https://pdf-issues.pdfa.org/. Content at this URL is actively maintained and, of course, you can always save the URL content to PDF for posterity (it has @media CSS for this purpose).

Note that this URL _also_ includes solutions that have been agreed by the PDF TWG, but are _not_ yet reviewed by ISO experts. There is a small risk that such solutions _might_ change during the ISO review process, if this process continues. Historically only minor wording changes to 2 errata were updated when ISO experts previously reviewed with the intent of the solution unchanged. I think there is a bit of confusion about HTO parameter values in an ExtGstate dictionary and the HTO value that is part of the graphics state and is subject to inheritance by nested constructions.

HTO in an ExtGState dictionary:
- when an ExtGState dictionary is 'processed' because of a gs operator, it specifies changes to the current graphics state.  For HTO this means that the HTO parameter values, which are expressed in local coordinates, must be transformed to device coordinates - only at the time this gs operator is executed.

HTO in the graphics state:
- this HTO value is always in device coordinates and since inheriting them in nested constructions does not change the graphics state, the physical location of the HTO on the device is not influenced at all

By consequence there needs not be any HTO computations or transformations when rendering subsequent graphical objects, when changing CTM or processing nested forms or images.  Only at the time of changing the HTO with a ExtGState 'command'.

> The understanding at the National Archives and Records Administration is that there are three ways to scan a document into the PDF format. 

Actually, there are MANY ways to scan a document into a PDF.   But they can be broken down into three categories.

- Image only.   Where the scanned images are turned into PDF pages without modification (modulo format and/or compression transcoding) and no-OCR is performed.
- Image + Hidden Text.  Builds on "image only" by adding text (most likely from an OCR process) to the PDF page (either above or below the image in the Z-order of the graphics objects)
- Converted content (aka "Formatted Text and Graphics") - A completely different method where the scanned image is analyzed and individual portions are reconstructed into "native" PDF graphics objects - text, vectors, rasters.

However, each of these has various "sub-categories" based on various techniques for improving compression ratios, searchability, etc.   For example, there is the use of MRC to segment an image into areas that can be compressed using the optimal techniques or the use of "Searchable Vectors".

> Yes, we have seen federal agency data which appear to have all three methods in the same file!

Yes, that is perfectly reasonable and not uncommon!   Remember that each page of a PDF is "separate", which is why even things like page sizes are per-page and not per-document.   Combining pages/documents is one of the top three "edits" performed on PDFs.

>Is there a way to determine programatically on a page by page basis which method was used for any given scan?

The content of the page is easily evaluated through various heuristics to determine their characteristics.  However, since many operations can be done post-scan, possibly by later processes, it doesn't necessary reflect on the original scanning process - just on what you have at that moment.
Note: this is not a PDF file format specification issue related to ISO 32000-2:2020

I think the "Image + Hidden Text" category indeed needs some help. The "Image Only" category is pretty self-descriptive, and for the "Converted content" the current `AFRelationship` mechanism is enough to reveal its relationship with the source image data.

The status quo of "Image + Hidden Text" approach is not good enough for accessibility though. Imagine a screen reader that shipped built-in OCR functionalities processes an "Image + Hidden Text" PDF file, it will reveal to the user that there's two pieces of information on the page, one is the "Hidden Text" data, while the other is the text OCR-ed on-the-fly from the image. The two pieces information will interfere with each other, but the AT cannot unify them with confidence since it has no knowledge at all of the former OCR process. It would be nice if there's standard practice that identify the "Hidden Text" so AT could behave better accordingly.

I think this issue now reduces down to whether PDF requires, prohibits, recommends, stays silent, or has any informative notes on the use/need or default value for `charset` parameters with textual MIME media types.

Since RFC2046 specifically describes the `charset` parameter I would assume it is therefore permitted in PDF from the current wording Table 44. RFC2046 also clearly states the default value as `US-ASCII` (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2046#section-4.1.2) but then RFC6657 has gone and changed this recommendation (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6657#section-3). I don't believe therefore we can change PDF to switch to RFC6657 since then the charset of existing PDF without an explicit charset parameter would also be changed.

So maybe the best solution is an informative note acknowledging RFC6657, but stating that for backwards compatibility reasons the default charset used in PDF remains "US-ASCII" as stated in RFC2046. And if new files want a UTF-8 default like RFC6657 recommends, then they will have to add it explicitly.

> I don't believe therefore we can change PDF to switch to RFC6657 since then the charset of existing PDF without an explicit charset parameter would also be changed.

Just to play devil's advocate: is it really that problematic to adopt the UTF-8 default from RFC 6657 going forward? Given that all valid US-ASCII data decodes to the same thing under UTF-8, I don't think existing (properly encoded!) files would be affected. If anything, we'd be making a bunch of currently invalid files valid.

I believe the potential concern would rather be with older processors assuming that something is ASCII when it's really UTF-8, but that (to me) feels like much less of a problem than invalidating existing _data_ out there. 

Anyway, I don't want to bikeshed this too much, and I'm OK with just adding a note to acknowledge RFC 6657, but I wouldn't object to just changing the default either. :)

Re-opening this Errata since the previous resolution did not fully address the PDF _syntactic requirements_ of what **Subtype** can or cannot contain. The previous resolution agreed that:
1. the RFC reference should remain unchanged (to RFC 2046), and 
2. any parameters (such as `charset=`) are not required by PDF processors. (And noting that there are **_NO_** processor requirements anywhere in 32K related to **Subtype**)

No disagreements there.

Point (2) above seems to presume that parameters therefore might be present in **Subtype** (suitably encoded into a PDF name object) but several validators reject such PDFs (primarily due to the presence of a SEMI-COLON AFAICT). The ISO 32K phrasing "_The value of this entry shall conform to the MIME media type names defined in Internet RFC 2046..._" uses the phrase "media type name" which does not occur in RFC 2046... 

[RFC 2046 Section 2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2046.html#page-4) clearly states that:
```
The definition of a top-level media type consists of:
    (1)   a name and a description of the type, including
          criteria for whether a particular type would qualify
          under that type,
    (2)   the names and definitions of parameters, if any, which
          are defined for all subtypes of that type (including
          whether such parameters are required or optional),
     ...
```
where `name` as used in RFC 2046 is a primitive lexical construct occurring in both type _and_ parameters (and subtype ("description" here) as mentioned elsewhere in RFC 2046 (and clearly nothing to do with PDF names). Thus a more accurate wording for ISO 32000-2 would be to simply use "media type" and delete "name" since that is an incorrect and confusing term of art from RFC 2046.

Thus “text”, “text/plain”, “text/foo”, “text/plain; charset=utf-8” and “text/plain; charset=utf-8; foo=bar; bar=foo” when encoded as PDF names would all pass the "_The value of this entry shall conform to the MIME media type ~~names~~ defined in Internet RFC 2046..._" requirement.

So proposed solution is to delete "name".

N entry in 3D nodes dictionary (Table 323) specifies node ID, to which these nodes properties (transformation matrix, opacity, etc) should be applied.

The format of node ID depends on the embedded 3D model formal and is different for U3D and PRC, as specified now in the definition of N entry. However, this definition assumes the presence of the 3D stream (Table 311), which does not exist in case of 3D model embedded into PDF as a RichMedia annotation.

In case of RichMedia the 3D model is embedded not as a 3D stream, but as an asset referenced from the RichMediaContent dictionary (Table 341). The only available mechanism today to determine the Subtype of an asset (=file format of the embedded 3D model) is a Subtype entry in the embedded file dictionary, which is optional at the moment. If this Subtype entry is not present in the embedded 3D asset, the only other mechanism available to distinguish between U3D and PRC is to read the header of the embedded file and use magic number technique.

One possible way to fix this issue would be:

  *   require MIME type defined (via Subtype entry of the embedded file) for all assets referenced by the RichMediaContent dictionary (this would be useful not only for RichMedia 3D annotations, but also for Audio and Video ones). In case of embedded U3D and PRC this is related to #155<https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/155>
  *   update the definition of N entry in Table 323 to use either Subtype entry in the 3D steam dictionary or a Subtype entry of the embedded file dictionary for the embedded 3D asset to determine the format of the 3D model

> PDF TWG agree that this might be re-considered as an enhancement in a future change to ISO 32000

To clarify this in light of a previous comment in the thread:

> WG8 is making other changes to ISO/TS 32003 (AES-GCM) so there as an opportunity for this to be resolved in that TS. Passing to the PLs to think through a general requirement.

The reason why we put the ball back in 32k's court is that ISO/TS 32003, _being an extension itself_, cannot meaningfully change the rules for how extensions can be "discovered" by general-purpose PDF processors. If ISO/TS 32003 would contain provisions describing an alternative mechanism to signal its presence, then a PDF processor wouldn't be able to make use of that mechanism unless it was designed with ISO/TS 32003 in mind, and then we're back at square one. Catch-22.

So, long story short: this really needs to be addressed in (a future version of) the core PDF standard, but it may be too big to process as an erratum. For the time being, extensions that augment PDF's encryption capabilities (e.g. ISO/TS 32003) will have to make do with the non-string entries in the extension dictionary.

First, it is worth looking at the history here...

From the Implementation Notes in the old PDF Spec
>The behavior of Acrobat has changed in the situation where a check box or radio button field have multiple children that have the same export value. In Acrobat 4.0, such buttons always turned off and on in unison. In Acrobat 5.0, the behavior of radio buttons was changed to mimic HTML so that turning on a radio button always turned off its siblings regardless of export value. In Acrobat 6.0, the RadiosInUnison flag allows the document author to choose between these behaviors.

And here is the text from the description of `/Opt` in PDF 1.5, where it `RadiosInUnison` was introduced
>When this entry is present, the names used to represent the on state in the AP dictionary
of each annotation are computer-generated numbers equivalent to the numerical position
(starting with 0) of the annotation in the Kids array. This allows distinguishing between
the annotations even if two or more of them have the same value in the Opt array.
For example, two radio buttons may have the same on state, but if the RadiosInUnison
flag is not set, only one of them at a time can be checked by the user.

And here is some additional useful info about Opt's history
>Opt array of text (Optional)This key is used when the value of the field cannot be represented
in PDFDoc encoding. There are as many entries in the array as there are widget
annotations in one radio button or checkbox field (i.e. they all have the
same name). The elements in Opt are text strings, where the ith string represents
the on state of the ith widget annotation. When the Opt array is
present, the names used to represent the “on” state in each AP dictionary are
computer generated numbers (starting with “0” for the first annotation of the
field).
Opt is also used when two or more annotations have the same “on” value. In
this case, Opt will include two or more entries that are equal. Since each annotation
has a different computer-generated number to represent its “on”
state, this allows checking a single annotation at a time while permitting duplicate
on states.

I can see why you’re asking the question, but I’m afraid that this is not the right place to ask it. This repository is specifically for errata in ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0) and its subset standards. 

Under 32000-2 your sample is invalid because the annotation is of Subtype FreeText and the Rect array has not got zero-sized dimensions. That means that AP (an appearance stream) is required and it’s not present.

So a reader processing the file as if it were PDF 2.0 is effectively free to do whatever it thinks is appropriate because it’s a non-conforming file. Acrobat has a tendency to not report errors because that would often not be a good fit for its business case.

But it would be more appropriate to treat this file as PDF 1.7, given that it claims to be 1.7.

Going back to the latest PDF 1.7 (ISO 32000-1), AP is optional. But a FreeText annotation can only use the keys listed in Table 164 (entries common to all annotation dictionaries) and table 174 (additional entries applicable to a free text annotation). IC is not present in either location. I agree that this is bizarre, when LE _is_ present, and this would be a good catch for an errata if we were developing errata for PDF 1.7.

As discussed during the last PDF TWG, @MPBailey, @lrosenthol and myself took this offline and discussed in detail. Our conclusion is as follows (for general PDF!):

* Table 66 is really a history lesson of what ICC versions were current when past PDF specs were first released.
* we CANNOT delete Table 66 as this will renumber most Tables in 32K, but we can replace its content or leave as "Table intentionally blank"
* ICC profiles all use major and minor version numbers in their profile header - the industry already uses terms such as v2.x, v4.x and v5.x (iccMAX) profiles. Don't confuse ICC profile header versions with ICC spec versions as these were different in the early days!
* we are NOT discussing v5 (iccMAX) profiles for PDF - that is later discussion for ISO TC 130 WG 2. 
* ICC profiles with the same major version numbers are compatible (as so stated in all ICC specs)
* thus PDF only needs to refer to the latest v2 and latest v4 specs, since these will include everything needed for all minor versions under that major version
* for v4 we recommend changing 32K-2 to an UNDATED revision of ISO 15076-1, since we know a dated revision is in progress (ISO 15076-1:202x)
* for v2, we need to refer "Specification ICC.1:2001-04 File Format for Color Profiles (v2.4.0)" dated April 2001 which we believe is the latest v2.x.x spec. I have reached out to the ICC for them to make this appropriately available via a "nicely referenceable" means... 
* we also checked the various ISO subsets PDF/X, PDF/VT, PDF/A, and PDF/R for other mentions of ICC version, ICC specs, ISO 15076, etc. Some minor maintenance is required for some of these and appropriate communication to the relevant WGs is in progress. Obviously subsets can further restrict things if they see fit.

There are various spots in ISO 32000-2:2020 to tidy up: the Normative Refs, the T&D for ICC profile, the Intro, Table 66, etc. 

Since we have Table 66 needing a replacement (so as not to renumber every other table) I propose to replace it with a Table that lists the ICC profile header major version and the appropriate normatively reference documents, with a statement referencing that table along the lines of "ICC profiles in PDF shall have ICC profile header major versions as shown in Table 66" (TBD wordsmith).
