ISO TC 130 JWG7 TPM has overridden JWG7 and insisted that ICC.1 is to be revised as a _dated revision_ of ISO 15076-1 which includes new tags and capabilities (ICC.1 v4.4) as well as the necessary errata that PDF wanted to incorporate (against ICC.1 v4.x). Specifically, the CICP tag introduced in v4.4 must not be supported by PDF processors as it potentially impacts rendered output - this ICC tag must be treated as a private tag and ignored by PDF processors!

As a result, this change MUST be reverted so that ISO 15076-1:2010 remains as the normatively referenced ISO document, even though it will not be available electronically once ISO 15076-1:2025 is published by ISO. But the errata corrections in ISO 15076-1:2025 / ICC.1 v4.4 should be understood since they reflect the reality of ICC.1 v4.x color profiles.

@lrosenthol I totally agree with your statements - but I am having trouble identifying exactly which "shall" statements in 32K are being violated...

Seems pretty clear to me with 7.3.10 (32K-2)

```
Any object in a PDF file may be labelled as an indirect object. This gives the object a unique object identifier by which other objects can refer to it (for example, as an element of an array or as the value of a dictionary entry). 
```
This sets it up that an indirect object is a standard object (as described in 7.3.2-7.3.9) which has a unique object identifier associated (by which other objects can refer to it).

This is followed by a clear normative statement:
```
The definition of an indirect object in a PDF file shall consist of its object number and generation number (separated by white-space), followed by the value of the object bracketed between the keywords obj and endobj.
```
So we see here that an indirect object **shall** consist of the object number + generation number + the **value of the object** (bracketed by obj/endobj).

So your example:
```
10 0 obj
/d /e /f 
endobj
```

cannot be valid, because the syntax of `/d /e /f` is not the syntax for any valid object as defined in 7.3.2-7.3.9.

3.44, T&D for 'object' says "basic data structure from which PDF files are constructed and includes these 9 types: array, boolean, dictionary, integer, name, null, real, stream and string". The same is stated in the 1st para of 7.3.1.

Neither of those explicitly say "one of", but I don't think it's necessary, because "/d /e /f" does not match any one of those object types.

Can I ask what triggered this question?

The question arose from SafeDocs when developing formal grammars of the PDF COS syntax for indirect references when used in array elements: whether the indirect reference always resolves to a single PDF object or could potentially be multiple PDF objects concatenated together (so more like a #include or macro expansion that an object reference). 

I think the answer is obvious and we'd all agree, but cannot see where we actually concretely state it using normative language.

A related question is whether an indirect reference can be decomposed into 2 indirect references (each to an integer) followed by the keyword R: so `10 0 R 0 R` which might then result in `99 0 R` if object 10 was just the integer 99:

```
10 0 obj
99
endobj
```
Again I think the answer is obvious (no!) and we'd all agree, but cannot see where we actually concretely state it using normative language.

This is what happens when people experienced in writing parsers for programming languages and compilers read our spec and say "_where does it state you cannot do that?_"🤣 - Is a COS parser LALR(1), LL(1), LALR(2),  something else? Is there no backtracking? Etc.

> A related question is whether an indirect reference can be decomposed into 2 indirect references (each to an integer) followed by the keyword R: so 10 0 R 0 R which might then result in 99 0 R if object 10 was just the integer 99:

I think we can resolve that one by simply making a statement that object dereferencing is not part of parsing.

That said, I don't see how we can address this entire class of issues without putting together a formal grammar that at least nails down what constitutes valid PDF object _syntax_, i.e. a full definition of everything between an `x y obj` header and `endobj`). Note the emphasis on _syntax_: things like "making sure stream data is decodable" wouldn't be in scope. I also don't think we have to agree on specific parser types as long as the production rules of the language are unambiguous.

I don't think such a grammar is all that difficult to write down. Actually, didn't we already have one somewhere?

I agree that this text (7.3.10 Indirect objects) answers the original question. The data between obj and endobj must be the value of an object. The syntax for object values is defined in 7.3 (including the syntax for references in 7.3.10). The latter is made explicit in 7.3.1 General:
```
    Each object type, their method of creation and their proper referencing as indirect objects is described
    in 7.3.2, "Boolean objects" through 7.3.10, "Indirect objects".
```
The above is a long way of saying "the following subsections define the syntax for objects".

As to the question of whether the numbers in an indirect references are allowed to be references themselves (e.g. "1 2 R 3 R"), let's look at what 7.3.10 Indirect objects says:
```
    references shall consist of the object number, the generation number, and the keyword R (with white-
    space separating each part):
```
It may not be absolutely explicit, but it's pretty clear from the context that what is described here is the syntax of a reference and that the numbers mentioned are not themselves considered to be PDF objects that happen to be numbers in the sense of 7.3.3 Numeric objects. >At the most fundamental level, a PDF file is a sequence of bytes. These bytes can be grouped into tokens according to the syntax rules described in subclauses 7.2.2, “Representation” through 7.2.4, “Comments”. One or more tokens are assembled to form higher-level syntactic entities, principally objects, which are the basic data values from which a PDF file is constructed.

I was trying to provide my reasoning in support of your own conclusion, @lrosenthol. I don't know what you're trying to get at, to be honest. I can assure you, however, that I am aware of the distinction between parsing and lexical analysis.

The first para of 7.12.1 says:

> The extensions dictionary, all developer extensions dictionaries, as well as their entries, shall be direct objects (i.e., this information shall be nested directly within the catalog dictionary with no indirect objects used).

And then the rows in Table 48 and Table 49 all say "shall be a direct object".

That does seem almost designed to make it difficult to update a document, although all it means is that the processor must read and rewrite the Extensions dictionary, which is unlikely to be excessively complex, especially if Table 49 is taken as an exclusive list of possible entries in a developer extensions dictionary.

I'm trying to remember why we built it like that.

I wasn't around when those additions were proposed, but I can think of one reason: you want to limit unnecessary dereferencing operations to avoid having to go and dig up the extensions dictionary from some object stream that (for all you know) might be encrypted/compressed/... using an algorithm that the processor doesn't know. Related discussion in #110.

I'm not taking any particular position here, but that sounds like a plausible justification.


Realistically, removing an extension will almost certainly involve more invasive changes anyhow, and adding an extension to an existing document will require the processor to "just deal with" whatever the original PDF producer did to the extensions dictionary. Also, rewriting the catalog is common in many workflows. If we would recommend that the extensions make use of indirect references, would it really make processor code all that much simpler?

Well, whether "negative" means `<0` or `≤0` can be somewhat regional. Some people would call these "strictly negative" and "negative", while others would say "negative" and "nonpositive".

I'm not sure if ISO has guidance on  this specific issue, but if we want to be absolutely unambiguous, we should say "The value shall be a number less than or equal to zero" (EDIT: assuming we want to allow descent=0, that is).

The current wording of the OpenType technology is even less strict (https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/os2#uswindescent):

> the usWinDescent value treats distances below the baseline as positive values; thus, usWinDescent is usually a positive value, while sTypoDescender and hhea.descender are usually negative.

I think the main idea is that the **Descent** value should be negative if the font glyphs go below the baseline. So this is not just the absolute distance, but the directional one, where "below" means negative.

As a side note, some implementations do use **Ascent** and **Descent** to calculate the visual highlight of the selected text. While this is definitely implementation dependent (PDF Spec does not mandate how to visualize the text selection), having the correct values of these two fields that match the corresponding properties of the embedded font program is highly recommended.

32000-2 uses "non-negative" for "0 or greater" (plus one of "nonnegative"); I could not find any instances of "non-positive" for "0 or less".

There are some statements that clearly imply 'negative' does not include zero, such as "may be either positive or negative but shall not be zero." There are also a number of instances where things would break if "negative" were interpreted as "0 or less". Let's not go there.

So I'd suggest that the text for Descent be replaced by "shall be zero or a negative number".

BTW - the nearest valid value to zero for Descent is not currently -1 because it's a number rather than an integer, so it's -0.000...0001. Close enough to zero for all practical purposes, which is why I'd be very relaxed about allowing 0.

Hi everyone, I've drafted some text.


## PDF/UA-2

Proposed note(s) for PDF/UA, in 8.9.2.3.13 (the clause on widget annotations, in case the numbering changes)

> NOTE 2: When used as part of a document workflow that makes use of signature profiles like PAdES-B-LTA, widget annotations associated with document timestamp signatures are often artifacts in this sense. In such workflows, the number of timestamps that will be added over time can typically not be predicted in advance. Since modifying the structure tree in incremental updates after signing complicates signature validation, it is important that invisible widgets be exempt from any tagging requirements otherwise imposed by this document.
> 
> NOTE 3: Invisible artifact widgets can nevertheless have their Print flag set, e.g. in cases where compliance with ISO 19005-4 (PDF/A-4) is required.

Obviously, NOTE 3 would be unnecessary if ISO 19005-4 were to be revised. But I think it's a good addition if we decide not to amend ISO 19005-4, since having to set Print on an otherwise invisible widget (that's also an artifact for UA purposes) is counterintuitive.

Wordsmith away!

## PDF/A-4

Here's the change I'd like to see in PDF/A-4, _if_ making that technical change is on the table at all.

In 6.3.2, change

> Except for annotation dictionaries whose Subtype value is Popup, all annotation dictionaries shall contain the F key. If present, the F key’s Print flag bit shall be set to 1 and its Hidden, Invisible, ToggleNoView, and NoView flag bits shall be set to 0.

to

> Except for annotation dictionaries whose Subtype value is Popup, and those where the value of the **Rect** key consists of an array where the value at index 0 is equal to the value at index 2 and the value at index 1 is equal to the value at index 3, all annotation dictionaries shall contain the F key. If present, the F key’s Print flag bit shall be set to 1 and its Hidden, Invisible, ToggleNoView, and NoView flag bits shall be set to 0.

I'd perhaps even go as far as to say that the Hidden flag _should_ be set on this type of zero-size annotation, but that's a separate discussion.

In my view, given the current state of adoption, these changes would be acceptable since they don't constrain any existing documents, and only require PDF/A-4 processors to accept more documents. Others may disagree, though, and I understand the reluctance towards making changes to a standard like PDF/A-4.


---------------------------

## Workaround in PDF 1.7

As a final comment on the status quo for PDF 1.7: after some experimentation, there's a somewhat hacky workaround that does clear the bar for all subsets. You can add the document timestamps without tagging them if you set the Print flag while making sure the bounding box (even if it has no area) doesn't intersect the crop box. Clearly this isn't particularly intuitive and also violates the intention behind the Print flag, but it's technically valid.

For this we should first determine what the difference of transport as a binary vs. transport as a text file means.

If transport as a text file merely means not allowing certain byte sequences in the output, it would be a special case of a binary transport. In this case the whole list item could be dropped.

If transport as a text file also means replacing any kind of line breaks by a single type (e.g. in SMTP CRLF) or expanding TABs by a number of spaces, this kind of "transport as text file" has to be forbidden for PDFs as it invalidates cross references and byte range offsets!

@mkl-public I suspect the text/binary transport distinction is mostly historical?

Pre-2000s-era e-mail systems would sometimes offer the choice of 7-bit or 8-bit-safe routing paths, and the FTP protocol _(also much less commonly used these days)_ has a binary/ASCII transfer mode selection when uploading or downloading files.
* Line endings _would be preserved regardless of mode_ in both of those systems, but transport of messages or files containing any character byte values of 128-255 _(0x80 to 0xFF)_ required special care.

Any future extremely-low-bandwidth applications that might naively suggest the use of 7-bit transport in the future _(e.g. sending e-mail attachments to an early outpost on Mars or near Jupiter)_ will probably be better implemented in other ways that won't need to impact the PDF _(i.e. with some sort of data compression built in to the transport protocol)_ specifications.

---

I doubt _'transport'_ would normally be defined to include regeneration or editing, so any replacing of line breaks or tab expansion would be more of a _'transformation'_.

Regardless, 'binary transport only' seems to be a fine rule for new PDFs in 2026* _(especially given the points that @MatthiasValvekens made about XREF offsets back in 2022)_.
* *It's probably been the norm since 2016, or perhaps even 2006.

- directly using the **null** keyword [7.3.9]
- an indirect reference to an object that is just the **null** keyword (your 1st object 10 example above)
- when the indirect reference refers to a "_nonextistent object_" [7.3.9]

ISO 32000 is a file format specification to define what valid PDFs must ("shall"!) be. So as soon as a PDF violates a mandated "shall" requirement (such as 2 keys in a dictionary with the same name) then how that PDF is to be interpreted is beyond the scope of ISO 32000. Note also the use of the term "key" so this requirement is clearly _not_ inclusive of the value of the key as described by T&D 3.16 for "dictionary object". And there is no conceptual 'hierarchy' of "shall" requirements - all requirements need to be met.

So because your example dict has 2 `/Foo` keys it fails a mandated requirement for PDF and thus is not a valid PDF. End of story. 😀

PS. Although not a formally defined term, we also try to use the term "entry" to describe a key/value pair, but that not be consistent everywhere.

What I get from this discussion is that @pesco argues `<< /Foo null /Foo null >>` **does not violate PDF specification** because processors when reading the dictionary should ignore first `/Foo null` and then read second `/Foo null` (and again ignore it 😊). If we apply rule A first and rule B after then we must say it's equivalent to `<< >>` and not violates PDF specification. But writers of PDF specification probably never think about this in this way. Probably they assume both have the same weight and both rules A and B should be applied to the syntax of the dictionary. Here is a complex table describing all possibilities

|          | A equal B | A then B | B then A<sup>2<sup> |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| `<< /Foo null /Foo null >>` | ❔<sup>1<sup> | ✔️ (same as `<< >>`) | ❌ |
| `<< /Foo (bar) /Foo null >>` | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `<< /Foo null /Foo (bar) >>` | ❔<sup>1<sup> | ✔️ (same as `<< /Foo (bar) >>`) | ❌ |
| `<< /Foo (bar) /Foo (foo) >>` | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

Notes to table:

1. Questionable because we (as a human) are thinking both rules apply at the same time but machines must apply in some order. And it depends on the PDF processor what happens first
2. In case **B than A** It depends on the fact how the PDF processor reads the dictionary. There are several options. For examples:
   - It may read all PDF objects in the dictionary and then validates if all keys are distinguished. This is more memory intensive but works.
   - It can read two PDF objects (key `/Foo` + value `(bar)`) and add them to the internal map. Again read the pair of PDF objects (`/Foo` + `null`). As the value is a Null object it may not process this pair (to speed up the reading process).
   - various others...

I worked on several low-level PDF object processors and the implementations are different. Some tokenize file content first and then process. Some processing byte to byte. Other processors may have syntax checks at the beginning some do not. And so on... Regarding what I learn for almost 20 years in PDF is that PDF specifications do not want to dictate how PDF processors will process. It's similar to state/federal laws. Laws are general rules we should follow but someone needs to explain the rules. And PDF Association is trying to explain these misconceptions they may rise.

**My opinion: In all cases, these files are not ISO-32000 compliant and it's on PDF processors if/how they deal with these situations.** As I know programmers, they use some type of map and do not take too much care about what happens in these situations. Map somehow deals with that (may not add, raise an exception, overwrite, ...). 😄

First, the addition of that bullet point is new in PDF 2.0, but reflects the reality of how most implementations already worked before. So the text of the bullet point itself is recent-ish.


As for the table:

> When ByteRange is present, the value shall be a hexadecimal string

This implies that (at least historically) there were at some point signatures that didn't involve **ByteRange**. My guess was that that had something to do with object-based signatures, and  the PDF 1.5 reference seems to back this up (emphasis mine):

> The signature value. When ByteRange is specified, the value is a hexadecimal string (see “Hexadecimal Strings” on page 32) representing the value of the byte range digest. **If ByteRange is not specified, the value is an object digest of the signature dictionary, excluding the Contents entry**.


Allow me to speculate a little (trusting @lrosenthol to correct me where I got the history wrong):

Object digests were never a thing in ISO-standardised PDF (not even ISO 32000-1) for interop reasons. From what I remember (and I might be wrong), object digests were intended to only apply to part of the object graph, so I think it's theoretically possible to upgrade an old document with such an object-based signature to PDF 2.0 without breaking anything. I suppose the non-ISO keys would simply be treated as class 3 names.


Is this a far-fetched objection? Absolutely. I certainly haven't come across anything like this myself. But I imagine the wording with "hexadecimal" was chosen for a reason, so I would hold off on changing the normative text until we know why the "hexadecimal string" condition is there. Nonetheless, I agree that the bullet point could use some clarification either way, so I'll propose an informative note in the meantime, to be inserted below the bullet list in 7.6.2:

> NOTE 1: For the signature types defined in this document, the value of the **Contents** entry is always a hexadecimal string.

PS: bookkeeping remark: there's another note all the way down in subclause 7.6.2 that now needs a number.

Object-based signatures never went to ISO because we never got them to work properly and so we removed them from the ISO version.  It's one of the two or three things we didn't bring over for similar reasons.

As for the issue at hand, I don't see any reason to change this - the text is correct as is.

I totally agree that the text is correct in a normative sense. However, read outside of its historical context, the standard as written _does_ kind of suggest that there are situations where the Contents entry is not a hex string. It just so happens that those situations never arise if one sticks to the features defined in ISO 32000-x when creating signatures.

If that confuses those of us who aren't already familiar with the way PDF signing works in current practice, I don't think a note would hurt.

I'll admit to being confused as the words implied a nuance I simply couldn't see elsewhere in 32K. But now I understand why.
A minor reword with a historical (non-detailed) informative note would help.

To summarize a proposed solution:

* change the last bullet in 7.6.2 to follow the structure of the earlier bullets:
> the value of the **Contents** key in a Signature dictionary

* add an informative NOTE after this bullet (not exactly sure what to say! My choice of words below is trying to infer that this also applied to 32K-1:2008):
> NOTE ISO 32000 has always required that the value of the **Contents** key in a Signature dictionary is a hexadecimal string (see Table 255).

That's the thing, I don't believe this is correct as written:

>  ISO 32000 has always required that the value of the Contents key in a Signature dictionary is a hexadecimal string (see Table 255).

While it's true that **Contents** must be a hex string if you use any signature mechanism _defined within ISO 32000-x_, the wording in the standard has always left the door open for other choices. Presumably that's for historical reasons (object-based signatures), but in principle a developer extension could use the **Contents** key in its own signature scheme that didn't involve **ByteRange**s and have it not be a hex string without violating 32k. Sure, the vast majority of implementations will never see anything other than **ByteRange**-based signatures, and will make assumptions along those lines, but I personally don't feel the need to change the spec to reflect that.

(Technical side note: with ByteRange-based digests there are pragmatic reasons why hex strings are preferable, the main one being that you don't have to put escapes in them so their length is more predictable. That reasoning doesn't apply to non-ByteRange-based signatures like the object-based ones that got removed way back when.)


EDIT: to show that usage of non-ByteRange-based signatures isn't _that_ far-fetched: you could imagine a signature scheme where the signed payload is an embedded file, and the signature needs to be computed exactly over the bytes of the embedded file (without involving any of the surrounding PDF data) for operational reasons, e.g. because the existing signing pipeline doesn't understand PDF. I'm pretty sure _someone_ out there has implemented this in some form. That person would've been within their rights to repurpose **Contents** to store their signature value with a regular `(...)`-string if they wanted to.

-----

Alternative suggestion: leave the bullet point as-is, and have the note say something like

> NOTE For the signature schemes enumerated in ISO 32000-1 and in this document, the value of the Contents key in a Signature dictionary is always a hexadecimal string (see Table 255).

Thoughts?

Interesting... Can't we side-step the whole encoding issue and mandate that the keys shall be sorted as byte strings in lexicographic order? That doesn't require any encoding. In pseudo-code-ish:

```
data ByteString = (Byte:ByteString) | Nil

Nil ≤ _ -> True
(_:_) ≤ Nil -> False
(x:xs) ≤ (y:ys) -> x < y || (x == y && xs ≤ ys)
```

This is completely unambiguous and avoids the whole quagmire of having to even _think_ about encodings for name trees that are defined as having binary entries (the `IDTree` for structure element IDs comes to mind). Leaving the encoding up in the air is bad, because then a general-purpose processor can't make any assumptions on the order, which makes it hard (if not impossible) to efficiently search the tree. Might as well use a list and search it linearly, then.

I suspect (hope?) that the scheme I cooked up above agrees with what most implementations would do given >99.9% of real-world inputs for name tree keys anyhow.

In the interest of avoiding going into the weeds on what it means to "define" something, and to avoid beating the "what is validation" dead horse: here's my 2 cents on the original question.

 - For better or worse, there's no prohibition on "garbage" data in between PDF objects, so if the would-be object has no xref pointing to it, I 'd argue that nothing is invalidated.
 - If there is a pointer in the xref table to the piece of data under scrutiny, I think it necessarily has to be a well-formed object, regardless of whether the object is used anywhere in the DOM. (=> full disclosure: I didn't check the actual wording in the spec yet, but that feels like something we should clarify if it's not in there already)
- I personally also subscribe to the converse position: any data that doesn't have an xref pointing to it is functionally not a PDF object, but there's definitely no language in the standard to back that up. It's also not really relevant to this discussion.

Basically, I'd argue that any data that can be accessed from the xref table is part of the PDF object model and should therefore abide by the provisions of the standard, to the extent that a processor that supports all the relevant filters (*) should be able to decode it. Whether an object is actually used/required/... is (IMHO) besides the point.

The question then becomes: do all "referenceable" stream objects that use (standard) filters have to contain data that is valid according to the definition of those filters? I think so.

(*) Remaining wrinkle: custom filters, crypt filters and whatnot are in principle permissible. _If_ this discussion leads to a proposed spec change, then the added text should be clearly scoped to only apply to those filters that are actually defined in the standard. Otherwise it's a breaking change.

I feel this discussion highlights some unstated (or at best very poorly stated) "philosophies" about how current PDF standards need to be read and interpreted which those of us involved in ISO committees have come to understand and agree over many years (and for many and various reasons - some historic, some reasonable, and maybe some not so good anymore), but those outside the ISO committees won't necessarily know or appreciate. We should be trying to make the PDF standards as easy to understand as possible but only within the scope for which they are intended, so that we maximize a common understanding and thus interoperability:

* parts of the PDF specification are 25+ years old and have not been reworked to follow formal ISO-ese, but when read through an ISO lens those sections could be potentially confusing. 
* PDF standards are first and foremost file format specifications, not software specifications 
* the vast majority of requirements are file format requirements with far fewer processor requirements. It may not always be clear which is which and we should try to rectify such issues.
* the PDF standard only defines valid PDF files as a set of data object definitions reached by following a set of requirements - it does not define error conditions per-se
* requirements are not hierarchical unless explicitly stated as such. 
* error handling and recovery (as done by software) are beyond the scope of all ISO PDF standards
* assumptions about specific software design choices, algorithms, etc. are avoided as much as possible.
* explanatory information is generally limited to a discussion of the (valid) file format, not how software works. 
* ISO standards are not textbooks or tutorials so the reader needs to understand that lots of implementation questions will likely be unanswered by the file format spec
* ISO specs never provide advice on permissiveness or other "real world" issues faced by PDF software
* ... probably others ...

So I think we could do a better job of explaining these kinds of things to the wider (non-ISO) audience in clause 1 Scope and setting reasonable expectations for the new reader as to what they will and will not find in PDF ISO standards.

And, unfortunately, for the things they won't find in the ISO standards we don't have much else to offer at this time...

In fact, I think we're confusing things if we merge these, since one is part of Logical Structure (**O** with values _NSO_ or _UserProperties_) and the other is part of Tagged PDF.  It is a common mistake to treat these as interchangeable, but they are not.  **O** is open-ended in Logical Structure with no known values and when used in a Tagged PDF, a set of known values within that open-ended set is defined and reserved.

I think you are misreading this section.  What we are saying is that the defined attribute owners in Tagged PDF have reserved attribute keys and values.  The _Layout_ set of attributes are reserved to that owner (but we are trying to be clear that there is no intent to reserve these values outside of _Layout_.  So, if you have an owner of _List_ and you have the attribute **BorderColor**, then you are effectively saying nothing (or a strict validator might reject this).  It isn't saying that the layout attributes have the same meanings and definitions.

If the same attribute key occurs within the same structure tree node or beneath but within a different attribute object with a different owner, then they have no interaction.

I agree with what @mrbhardy wrote, but there are two points I would like to clarify.

The first one is perhaps a little obvious, but when conceptualising attributes as key-value pairs, I like to think of them as `(Owner, Attribute name) <> Value` pairs. In other words, the owner is part of the key in the pairing. I'd call it a namespacing scheme, but that term is already quite overloaded as-is ;). With this perspective, the separation between different owners is also immediately obvious.


This "model" (if you can even call it that) is also useful to explain attribute inheritance, IMO:

> > so that must mean inheritance is solely a property of the attribute name (i.e. the key name) - which can be anything, but let's keep to the standard structure attributes identified by specific standard owners
>
> No


I get the feeling that the misunderstanding is about conflating two processor requirements that don't really interact.

Let's single out this piece of text quoted by @petervwyatt above:

>  14.7.6 "When an array of attribute objects is provided, the value of the O and NS keys may be repeated across attribute objects. If a given attribute is specified more than once, the later (in array order) entry shall take precedence."

This is not about inheritance, but rather about how to resolve conflicts when two or more attribute dictionaries with the same owner appear inside (the **A** entry of) a single structure element. The inheritance rules are orthogonal to that: once all the `(Owner, Attribute name) <> Value` pairs for a given structure element are known (after applying conflict resolution rules as necessary), these tuples are inherited down the structure tree according to the rules set forth in the spec for those particular attributes.

I hope that made sense.

>When the PDF reader searches for an object, if an entry is not found in any given standard cross-reference section, the search shall proceed to a cross-reference stream specified by the **XRefStm** entry before looking in the previous cross-reference section (the **Prev** entry in the trailer).
>NOTE [...]

So you look for an object entry first in the newest cross reference table section. If it isn't there, you look into the **XRefStm** attached to that section. And if the object entry is not there either, you continue with the previous section, then the **XRefStm** of that section, and so on.

I don't remember discussing this specific instance of it, but we did discuss a related question at ISO some time last year: does ISO 32002 support entail being able to process _certificates_ signed with Ed25519?

I don't recall the finer details, but the general consensus was that that was out of scope. Here are some reasons (not all of which were discussed in that meeting, FWIW):

 - Many PDF implementations delegate certificate chain-of-trust validation to external tools, and those external libraries could very well support a different set of cryptographic primitives than the PDF processor itself.
 - Moreover, ISO 32000-x is completely silent on the issue of certificate validation (with the possible exception of the clause on seed values, and perhaps some PAdES-related content, but that's a different story). It makes sense to keep it that way.
 - The chain of trust is in itself independent of the PDF and not something controlled by the author/signer or even by the issuer of their certificate! In principle, a certificate/signature/public key can have any number of chains of trust, but putting those together and choosing an appropriate one is the validator's responsibility. In other words, the signer is strictly speaking not in any position to make claims about which algorithms the validator has to support in order for trust validation to succeed. (Granted, this objection is probably academic in 99% of actual document signing use cases, but I don't think it can be dismissed offhand.)

Long story short, I believe these arguments still hold water in the situation you describe. As such, I don't think including the ISO 32001 extension would be _mandatory_ per se. But I think an argument can be made that including it anyway is beneficial in many situations. That certainly wouldn't violate any of the provisions in the extension documents as far as I'm aware :).

<strike>
Given it still matters and the topic is open, I would like to partially hijack this issue to suggest that as part of any resolution here, we do something about the "trailing apostrophe problem", which with uncanny timing I wrote an article on at https://bfo.com/blog/2023/01/17/odds_and_ends_dates_timezones_and_apostrophes/ recently.

Briefly:

* PDF 1.6 and earlier format dates like`D:20210313144715+01'00'`
* PDF 1.7 and ISO32000 format dates like`D:20210313144715+01'00`

Unfortunately the older syntax is both a) generated and b) required for correct parsing in "a large PDF product" - as such it remains with us many years after it was supposed to have changed. To demonstrate, [here is a PDF](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/10958260/with-apostrophe.pdf)
which has creation and modified dates at midnight UTC, but in the Indian timezone of +05:30 - the creation date has a trailing apostrophe (old-syntax), and the modification date does not (new syntax).

To reflect reality I'd propose that the trailing apostrophe on dates is noted as optional: anyone parsing these has to handle both syntaxes, and anyone generating them has to use the older syntax or risk questions from customers in India, Adelaide or other timezones with a non-zero minute offset.

Hmm, I think you're reading a little too far into RFC 3161 to make those inferences. Perhaps unfortunately, the steps of the validation algorithm in RFC 3161, Appendix B are formulated as if they were normative requirements on the timestamp tokens, but actually they're validator requirements. (To be even more pedantic: since Appendix B is an example annex, it's even debatable whether its contents are normative at all, but that's beside the point.)

In other words, when the text says "The date/time indicated by the TSA MUST be within the validity period of the signer's certificate.", the intended meaning in that context is probably more like "The validator _shall verify that_ the date/time indicated by the TSA is contained within the validity period of the signer's certificate.".


In practice, TSA certificates do expire (and can be revoked as well). For example, ETSI standards even outside the PDF context discuss at length what to do to establish trust in potentially expired timestamp records.

ETSI TS 119 102-1 seems to be the relevant document, but it's neither a normative reference for ISO 32000-2 nor for the ETSI EN 31 referenced by ISO 32000-2.

Expiry of a TimeStampToken (and therefore of a DTS) depends on validation policy. If the chain model is used, TimeStampTokens won't expire with their signing certificate (still subject to further requirements of the validation policy). If the shell model is used, they will expire with their signing certificate.

Therefore, ISO 32000-2 reads ""A timestamp token present either in a signature timestamp attribute or in a document timestamp dictionary MAY expire due to the expiry of its certificate [...]" rather than ""A timestamp token present either in a signature timestamp attribute or in a document timestamp dictionary WILL expire due to the expiry of its certificate [...]".

> ETSI TS 119 102-1 seems to be the relevant document

Ironically, that reference is also a bit outdated. I believe ETSI EN 319 102-1 is the most recently updated one. But you're right, this entire discussion is mostly out of scope for ISO 32000-2, and arguably also for RFC 3161, so I don't think there's a contradiction.

However, the passage from ISO 32k you cite was more or less copied from (a previous version of) the PAdES spec, if I recall correctly (@lrosenthol can probably be more precise).

>  If the chain model is used, TimeStampTokens won't expire with their signing certificate (still subject to further requirements of the validation policy). If the shell model is used, they will expire with their signing certificate.

Granted, my experience with the chain model is limited, but I'm not sure this is accurate... My understanding is that in the chain model, one still needs to _establish_ that a signature was produced within the validity window of the signer's certificate before treating it as valid. Either way, since time stamp tokens are also signatures, that means there are (roughly) two cases:

 - The TSA certificate can still be validated at the current time => OK
 - The TSA certificate is no longer valid/has been revoked/whatever => we need some other piece of evidence to prove that the timestamp was generated during the validity window (e.g. another timestamp, some assertion from a trusted archive, etc...)

AFAIK the difference between the chain and shell model would mostly show up in the validation of the TSA cert in this scenario, not the actual timestamp validation.

The verification time doesn't matter for the chain model, therefore signatures (and TimeStampTokens) don't expire when using the chain model.

Note that national law for at least one country specified usage of the chain model for validating signatures.

Again, I'm far from an expert on how the chain model is used in practice (I'm aware that it's mandatory in Germany), but that sounds like an oversimplification to me. For example, EN 319 102-1 still contains provisions specific to the chain model in its section on LTA validation (e.g. in the section on the "validation time sliding process"). None of that would be necessary if validation time simply didn't matter _at all_ in the chain model, no? Or is there something I'm misunderstanding?

If I'm wrong about this (which is certainly possible), could you perhaps provide a reference stating that timestamps are valid indefinitely in the chain model? I'd like to learn why that's the case.


Either way, since RFC 3161 doesn't really normatively specify a particular validation model, I still don't think there's any contradiction to fix in ISO 32000-2, or is there? :)

As defined in 7.2.4, a comment is everything after the `%`.   So while not explicitly defined, a "comment line" would be a line that starts with a `%`.   @petervwyatt definitely worth adding that definition or clarifying.

On the xref sections and startxref, any data preceding those keywords would be ignored - so, sure, in theory you could have other stuff on that line...

> On the xref sections and startxref, any data preceding those keywords would be ignored - so, sure, in theory you could have other stuff on that line...

The problem with that is that it would be impossible in the general case for a PDF reader to correctly interpret, e.g.:

```
startxref
The byte offset is 123. However, this line also contains the numbers 456 and 789.
%%EOF
```

(Although if the wording is changed, it might be worth clarifying whether the `startxref` and byte offset lines can end in a comment.)

Subclause 7.2.4 Comments is very clear that comments start with a `%` and go until (but not including!) the EOL - they are not "lines" per-se in that they have to be preceded with a starting EOL:
> Any occurrence of the PERCENT SIGN (25h) outside a string or inside a content stream (see 7.8.2, "Content streams") introduces a comment. The comment consists of all characters after the PERCENT SIGN and up to but not including the end-of-the-line marker. A PDF processor should ignore comments. PDF processors shall treat comments as single white-space characters for the purposes of lexical conversion (see 7.2, "Lexical conventions"). That is, a comment separates the token preceding it from the one following it.

I believe the confusion is from the use of the phrase "comment line" since that might be interpreted to infer a preceding EOL. However in the specific case for the binary marker comment line this is a **correct inference**:

* The phrase "_comment line_" only occurs once in PDF 2.0 in subclause 7.5.2 File Header:
> If a PDF file contains binary data, as most do (see 7.2, "Lexical conventions"), the header line shall be immediately followed by a comment line containing at least four binary characters–that is, characters whose codes are 128 or greater.

* Subclause 7.5.2 File header also enforces that the file header ends with an EOL so it is indeed a "file header line":
> The file header shall consist of `%PDF–1.n` or `%PDF–2.n` followed by a single EOL marker, where ‘n’ is a single digit number between 0 (30h) and 9 (39h).

The requirement also explicitly states "immediately" so nothing can precede it - altho' this should possibly allow for whitespace. Together this means the header + binary comment line of a compliant PDF needs to look like this:
`%PDF-x.y<EOL>%<b1><b2><b3><b4> ... <EOL>`

I think the only improvement to the text in 7.5.2 would be to use the correct term "file header" and possibly also repeat the "... followed by a single EOL marker" - otherwise the text is technically correct. And to account for whitespace.

As to the more generic problem of the word "line" in describing PDF syntax - that is more problematic and is already covered by Issue #112.

> The requirement also explicitly states "immediately" so nothing can precede it - altho' this should possibly allow for whitespace.

The *comment line* is what must immediately follow the header line. This does not necessarily imply that the *comment* contained within the *comment line* must immediately follow the header line. The intuitive reading is that a *comment line* contains a *comment* and nothing other than that *comment*, but nothing defines this explicitly.

That is, in
```
%PDF-2.0
Hello, world! %¡¡¡¡
```
line 2 contains a *comment* with at least four binary characters, and line 2 immediately follows the *header line* (line 1). But is line 2 a *comment line*?

> This does not necessarily imply that the comment contained within the comment line must immediately follow the header line.

"_Comment line_" is not a formal T&D nor is it an informal term defined anywhere (in italics) - in fact this phrase is used only once in the entire PDF spec. 

However the definition of a "comment" **IS** formally defined in 7.2.4 with the statement "Any occurrence of the PERCENT SIGN (25h) outside a string or inside a content stream (see 7.8.2, "Content streams") introduces a comment.". This clearly states that the `%` starts a comment. Furthermore, the formal definition of a comment **excludes** the EOL so there is no such thing as a "comment line".

So your example is not a "comment line" but a "line including a comment" and thus is not "immediately following".

If we really wanted to get this pedantic we might change to be:
> If a PDF file contains binary data, as most do (see 7.2, "Lexical conventions"), the file header line shall be immediately followed by a line containing only a comment that starts with at least four binary characters immediately after the PERCENT SIGN – that is, characters whose codes are 128 or greater.

If you are placing comments in Object streams, you've kind of missed the point of the purpose of object streams.

The purpose of object streams is to compress collections of objects. the more similar the objects are to each other, the more compressible the stream is.  Conversely, adding dissimilar content to the object stream reduces the compression savings. Comments won't be visible because the entire stream will be compressed so they would just be useless bloat within the object stream.

Content streams (7.8.2) are stream objects (7.3.8), but not all stream objects are content streams.
A 25h that is within a non-content-stream stream object's  stream and endstream delimiters is not a token delimiter (see table 2), it's just data.

Conversely, adding dissimilar content to the object stream reduces the compression savings. Comments won't be visible because the entire stream will be compressed so they would just be useless bloat within the object stream.

My purpose isn't to suggest that putting comments in an object stream would be a good idea, it's to clarify the boundaries of what a conforming PDF processor must be prepared to accept.

> A 25h that is within a non-content-stream stream object's stream and endstream delimiters is not a token delimiter (see table 2), it's just data.

> Technically this is an error and you'd be right to fail such PDFs, but your customers and other implementations will likely silently recover.

Alright, so should Note 7 be read as permitting PDF readers to delimit the objects at the byte offsets, *without* permitting conforming PDF files to contain a sequence of byte offsets for which this segmentation would change the results of parsing, relative to a simple parse of the entire sequence of objects? (E.g., segmenting `123 % 456` into `123 % ` and `456` would turn one object into two.)

Yes - it also means that `123456` is technically valid and can be processed as `123` and `456` with appropriate byte offsets for 2 objects from the first line of the object stream (and not as `123456` and `456`). However, given the 2017 edition this is probably not advisable to write.

I'm afraid I don't quite understand what you mean: is this pattern inadvisable, or is it forbidden? Is a PDF processor conforming to ISO 32000-2:2020 required to accept this pattern and correctly produce `123` and `456`?

If so, Note 7 feels like a bit of an understatement: an object stream doesn't really contain a "sequence of indirect objects" that would make an array if you surrounded it with `[` `]`, but instead a sequence of substrings delimited by the byte offsets instead of by the ordinary token boundaries.

It is **NOT** forbidden as this is not stated - only _potentially_ inadvisable because the 2017 edition stated a requirement that was never intended (missed during reviews), so any SW that has not been maintained up to the 2020 edition will work differently. Existing PDFs created against the 2017 edition will work with SW supporting either edition. 

And objects streams are, after the "_**N** pairs of integers_", definitely a sequence of indirect objects. See 7.3.10 for definition of an indirect object. Within every indirect object in the object stream the standard PDF lexical delimiter rules apply - this is the same lexical rules as if each object were an indirect object in a conventional PDF body section: the object ends just prior to the **endobj** token. What the requirements effectively state are that the byte offsets into the object stream of indirect objects are precise, non-overlapping, and obeyed by all processors - hence why I said above "_object stream is segmented BEFORE parsing - it is NOT segmented as a result of parsing._"

@petervwyatt well it certainly causes us problems: we repair the file by presuming the line-feed is missing, so our repair moves the comment to _inside_ the stream. If what follows is binary data, it's corrupted as a result. But you wouldn't see any problems if the comment was on an uncompressed token stream, eg a page, where such a comment is valid.

I'm attaching [corrupted.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22066911/corrupted.pdf) which demonstrates this; I took 10 bytes from object 6, added a ten byte comment after the "stream" in object 7 and modifed the XRef table to match. It fails in our API and several viewers.

Real-world PDF writers will always have bugs and oddities (I've heard that even Acrobat has created wrong offsets in xref tables), real-world PDFs will always have weird things as a result, and real-world PDF readers will always try to come up with a best-effort guess.

As an aside, reading back on this thread, I'm not a big fan of the proposed solution of singling out content and object streams in 7.2.4. In my view, it would be cleaner to say something generally along the lines of "During lexical conversion and tokenization of a PDF file, bytes occurring within strings, streams, and comments are never interpreted as tokens [as in the start of 7.2.3]." Then 7.5.7 and 7.8 can go back and invoke 7.2 and 7.3 for how to interpret their decoded bytes using the "PDF syntax rules", separately from the primary tokenization of the PDF file.

In fact, 7.8.2 already makes this clear with "A content stream, after decoding with any specified filters, shall be interpreted according to the PDF syntax rules described in 7.2, 'Lexical conventions'." For object streams, 7.5.7 could use similar language.

That is, within the syntactic interpretation of the *PDF file*, percent signs within streams are always just raw bytes, not introducing a comment. But within the entirely separate interpretation of the *stream contents* of object and content streams, they do have a particular meaning. Optionally, 7.2.1 could include a note that the "PDF syntax rules" are used not only when interpreting a PDF file, but also when interpreting the contents of object and content streams.

Don't get me wrong: I believe comments after the "stream" keyword are definitely invalid according to ISO 32000, with PDF/A standards making this limitation explicit. I'm sure strategies to cope with/recover such PDFs will vary greatly across implementations but these are invalid PDFs and thus out-of-scope from the spec PoV. 

(PS. in my tests, I did not have a SPACE after the "stream" keyword before the "%" sign - so apologies that the fragment I typed above was not like that. i.e. the "%" needs to be detected as the token delimiter immediately after the "stream" keyword: `stream%comment`).

I think one confusion in the current wording is that "whitespace" can be inferred to include comments (since it is stated "_PDF processors shall treat comments as single white-space characters for the purposes of lexical conversion_") whereas in several places PDF should state that comments are explicitly not allowed (with after the "stream" keyword being one of them).  

It's possibly better to differentiate "proper" whitespace from comments everywhere in the spec, and state that comments are ignored. There is no need to treat comments as whitespace, since the EOL is already explicitly defined as _not_ being part of the comment so ignoring the comment means its EOL always becomes the next byte(s) - and EOL is already formally defined as whitespace. Adding informative notes to various places (esp. in relation to keywords and file sections) stating where comments are also not allowed I think will help since things are so spread out. Of course implementations can always be more flexible.

(This note is for anyone who is writing parser for pdf format and thinking that content streams can be parsed into a tree structure because of those paired operators.)
The 0th content stream of the 0th page of the pdf specification itself (`ISO_32000-2_sponsored-ec2.pdf`) starts with this:
```
/Artifact<</Type/Page>> BDC
/Span<</Lang (en-US)>> BDC
q
/GS0 gs 0 0 595.25 842 re W* n
BT
/F0 11 Tf 379.9 691.45 Td
( )Tj
ET
EMC
EMC
Q
/Span<</Lang (en-US)/MCID 1>> BDC
...
```
If you maintain a stack of "expected closing operators", it will end up like this:

1. encounter `BDC` instruction: `[EMC]`
2. encounter `BDC` instruction: `[EMC, EMC]`
3. encounter `q` instruction: `[EMC, EMC, Q]`
4. encounter `BT` instruction: `[EMC, EMC, Q, ET]`
5. encounter `ET` instruction: `[EMC, EMC, Q]`
6. encounter `EMC` instruction: `error, not properly nested`

A workaround is to (relax the constraint in the specification and) maintain two stacks: all paired operators except `q` and `Q` use one, `q` and `Q` alone use the other.

I just double-checked this (as I guess everybody would do it):

Furthermore, this clarification, the ISO approved resolution, did not come into being before 2023, and then only has been provided for ISO 32000-2. So many PDF generating tools have been implemented without awareness for it and you have to be prepared to be confronted with PDFs without proper nesting.
Also be aware that `ISO_32000-2_sponsored-ec2.pdf` is only claiming to be PDF-1.7. Thus, it may well have been created by a tool based on ISO 32000-1 alone.

However there is one issue that could be considered either a bug in Adobe Reader or an omission in the standard. If you navigate the document (in presentation mode) and reach the end of the second page, you have to press right twice to get to page three. The same happens if you go backwards from page 3 to 2 and to 1. Only one press should be needed to move to the next page in sequence. However the PDF spec does not specify (in 12.4.4.2 at least) what should happen when the user is on a navigation node that has no `next` entry and navigates forwards (and equivalent for backwards navigation). IMHO the correct behaviour should be that if the `next` entry is missing, the PDF viewer should navigate to the following page.

The PDF creator could possibly create a fake navigation node with a page change action but that is extra works and this is such a common case that it should work out of the box.

This cause highlights a more general failing with the documentation of how these arrays, indexed by MCIDs, should work. 

Some explanation of how these nulls arise: 

The MCID numbers of the content items in a content stream can be arbitrary integers, they need not form a 'complete integer interval' such as {0,1,2,3,4,5}; they can be any set, such as {0,2,4}, or even (in theory) {0,2,4,652}.

This is somewhat strange but it is the reality to be dealt with.  But it is not covered in 14.7.5.4 or, I believe, anywhere else.

I did my check on those content streams and found no marked-content sequence other than those actually indexed in their `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values. So in my case [it was presumably a deliberated denormalization](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1721239796) (ie, a violation of the recommendation in NOTE of 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items): "Because marked-content identifiers serve as indices into an array in the structural parent tree, their assigned values need to be as small as possible to conserve space in the array.") — I wouldn't be surprised if a sizable part of @petervwyatt's PDFs fell under this abominable case.

Deliberated denormalizations aside, `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values are prone to entropic decay by their very own nature: they were clearly conceived to pack a tight bunch of references in the smallest space possible, on the assumption of careful processing to prevent them from falling apart; hence, *beside missing to state the use of `null` array elements (**file format requirement**)*, IMHO, *ISO PDF fails also to explicitly state* (other than the timid NOTE in 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items)) *the processing constraints (**processor requirement**) which should be honored by implementers to keep things in good shape*.

My proposal is to clearly state the **algorithm behind MCID assignment** in subclause 14.7.5.2 (Marked-content sequences as content items):
> When a marked-content sequence is assigned an MCID, it shall be the lowest available. For its determination, the processor scans the parent tree array associated to the content stream in which the sequence resides, looking for a free index (that is, a `*` element); if none is found, the next index shall be used (for example, if a 7-element array has no `*` element, the next index is 7, as the existing range is 0-6, inclusive). When an assigned MCID becomes unused (either because its marked-content sequence is deleted from the content stream or its entry in the property list of the marked-content sequence is removed), the corresponding element in the parent tree array shall be set to `*`; if it is the last element, the array shall be shrunk instead.

(where `*` is a distinctive value, as suggested by @car222222)

This algorithm deterministically prescibes which MCID shall be used in each and every case, ensuring the most compact `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values possible without remapping the existing MCIDs. *The assumption here is that the indexes left free by ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items* (@car222222's point) *can be told apart from the indexes of orphaned content items* (@bdoubrov's point), so the proposal by @car222222 to mark orphaned content items with a distinctive value is definitely crucial for the purpose.

NOTE: *Because of backward compatibility, **`null` elements must be assumed as associated to orphaned content items*** (otherwise, editing legacy PDFs, MCIDs of orphaned content items could be inadvertently assigned to new marked-content sequences, ending up with duplicated MCIDs!). As a consequence, **it's array elements of ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items to have a distinctive value to be assigned to**, while orphaned content items must be assigned `null` value — this is the opposite of @car222222 proposal, but I'm confident he will be merciful ;)

DEFINITIONS

This comment uses terms previously adopted within this thread:
- **orphaned** means an MCID whose associated marked-content sequence reference was detached from the structure tree (that is, either the reference or any of its ancestor structure elements in the structure tree was removed from the `K` entry of the corresponding parent structure node (either structure element or structure root))
- **nonexistent/unused** means an MCID which is not associated to any marked-content sequence in the content stream (possibly because it was removed from its marked-content sequence or the marked-content sequence was deleted altogether)

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE

Implementers could be recommended to make available **maintenance procedures to normalize legacy PDFs**:
- basic maintenance: analyze marked-content sequences in content streams and update the elements of `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` arrays with the distinctive value for ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items. For example, if the original structure is:
`[ null null 3743 0 R null null 3487 0 R null null null ]`
the normalized one would be (supposing `*` as distinctive value for ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items):
`[ * * 3743 0 R null * 3487 0 R * * null ]`
(remaining `null` elements represent actual orphaned content items)
- advanced maintenance: remap marked-content sequences in content streams with tight zero-based sequences of MCIDs and update the `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` arrays accordingly. For example, the normalized structure of the original one (see example above) would be:
`[ 3743 0 R null 3487 0 R null ]`
(array elements indexed to ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items are purged)

My feeling is that trading indexes (efficiency) for keys (flexibility) would be a lazy game without significant benefits and with certain drawbacks. In real-world applications, how would a dictionary of structural parents behave over time (editing session after editing session) compared to a (canonically generated and managed) array? Sure, the array could fragment with discarded MCIDs, or possibly expand when all discarded MCIDs are reused (as enforced by my algorithm proposal); the dictionary could shrink and expand, but its memory footprint would be often larger both in serialized and deserialized forms than its counterpart. Dictionaries would be somewhat more comfortable to juggle, but where is the solid gain of them as structural parents instead of current arrays? Trying to figure out a rationale behind that, page 39 of Case 2 seems to give a possible clue: *marked-content sequences nested in form XObjects* (see EXAMPLE 5 in subclause 14.7.5.2 (Marked-content sequences as content items)). Since form XObjects are inherently reusable, one might think that the MCIDs assigned to them couldn't be assigned elsewhere in the same file because of possible collisions. But subclause 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items) clearly states that *each content stream (page object or other kind) has its own set of zero-based MCIDs* (emphasis is mine):
> For a content stream containing marked-content sequences that are content items, the value shall be an array of indirect references to the sequences' parent structure elements. The array element corresponding to each sequence shall be found by using the *sequence's marked-content identifier as a zero-based index into the array*.
> [...]
> Because a marked-content sequence is not an object in its own right, its parent tree key shall be found in the *StructParents entry of the page object or other content stream in which the sequence resides*. The value retrieved from the parent tree shall not be a reference to the parent structure element itself but to *an array of such references — one for each marked-content sequence contained within that content stream*.

So: an MCID is a ZERO-based index into an array of references to parent structure elements, ONE FOR EACH marked-content sequence contained WITHIN THAT content stream. Because of such definition, no collision is possible, isn't it? In turn, *the only plausible reason for global MCID counter vanishes miserably... (that wouldn't be decisive, anyway, since the overwhelming majority of `null` elements existing in those files are unrelated to form XObjects)*

My goal is not to improve anything in these provisions, I just want to make sure that we are in synch with PDF/A and PDF/X.

Background to my proposal is that we in the PDF/A TWG agreed that RGB are not primaries in the context of TransferFunctions in HT5: https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/13

There in fact is a clarifying NOTE in PDF/A that limits primaries to CMYK, see Boris' [statement](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdfa-twg/issues/13#issuecomment-1453133070) as a minute to our discussions.

If we want to limit this in PDF/A but not in PDF we can't just use a NOTE there, it would have to be normative.

I'm not going to take a position on whether limiting TransferFunctions in halftones to only CMYK (and spots) would be useful or not because I just don't know. I do know of physical printers which require to be fed with RGB colour values, and some that actually 'print' in RGB, although I don't recall if any of those require halftoned data (obviously the ones that print in contone do not!).

But 32000-2 discusses RGB "process colours" in a variety of places, such as the bullet after note 4 in 8.6.6.5 (DeviceN colour spaces), backed up by the ColorSpace and Components rows of Table 71. This is made even more explicit in the 1st para of 10.2 (Raster output native colour).

Looking specifically at TransferFunctions, the first bullet in 10.5 (Transfer functions) explicitly discusses transfer functions for an RGB device.

And the last para of 10.6.2 (Halftone screens) discusses applying halftones for additive output spaces, including RGB.

So I'd argue against making any changes in 32000-2, at least without significantly wider discussion.

I have no problems with applying that rule in PDF/A.

ISO 32000-2:2020 clause 3 "Terms & Definitions" has the precise definition of "deprecated" meant for PDF - see subclause 3.15.

So the "_(Required, deprecated in PDF 2.0)_" means that from up to and including PDF 1.7 the entry was required, but from PDF 2.0 the entry is no longer required and is officially deprecated (i.e. "should not be written and should not be read" - where "should" is a special ISO word meaning "recommended"). 

There are also various issues with **Length** in extant data, including its value being in _bytes_ (not bits, as it is defined); having a value that disagrees with other keys (e.g. algorithm), having some other value altogether, being required to be present but its value is effectively ignored (since things work with wrong values), etc. so what writers generate and what implementations appear to do is not an indication of what the spec is stating as valid for valid PDF. Please report all implementation issues to specific vendors.
See also #184

> Also, I don't recall ever seeing a DA string that couldn't be encoded in 7bit ASCII (where PDDocEncoding and UTF-8 overlap), so I don't see why it needs to be a "byte" string.

`byte string` is about the **interpretation** (ie, semantics) of a string; even if its **representation** (ie, syntax) overlaps other subtypes (like in ASCII-encodeable data), *its interpretation doesn't change — and should command over syntax:* in a `byte string` entry (like `DA`) whose assigned value is a literal string starting, ad absurdum, with UTF-16BE BOM (FE FF), the BOM bytes should be interpreted, according to its semantics (a series of bytes whose encoding is unknown (7.9.2.4)), simply as bytes[0] (FE) and bytes[1] (FF) in the series, without special meaning (ie, it is NOT a `text string` even if it *looks like* that!). @petervwyatt, can you confirm this, please?

> Eh. Put another way, clause 7.3.4 differentiates between Literal strings and Hexadecimal strings. To me, indicating that a string is a "byte string" strongly implies the use of a Hexadecimal string for storing that data. ~~As @mkl-public stated, "string literals are highly questionable", as~~ [*] `DA` entries are serialized content stream chunks which by their very nature are `byte string`s (even if they use only ASCII characters, their context (content stream) implies both ASCII PDF tokens *and* arbitrary bytes (in particular, glyph selectors mapping to font-specific encodings) — they can *accidentally* contain just ASCII characters, BUT their lexical domain goes beyond that).

Unfortunately, to my understanding, PDF leaves too much leeway in this respect (literal/hexadecimal forms are essentially at developer's discretion): IMHO, associating syntax and semantics in unambiguous ways (literal form for `text string` (and `ASCII string`), hexadecimal form for `byte string`) would have been much cleaner.

[*] As @MatthiasValvekens noted, I mistook string literal *tokens* for literal strings.

> To me, indicating that a string is a "byte string" strongly implies the use of a Hexadecimal string for storing that data.

I beg to differ here. For better or worse, both the Literal and hex forms can be used (and are used!) to represent all manner of binary data unambiguously. Whether said binary data is to be decoded/interpreted as text is a separate issue, and context-dependent.

In fact, I'd go as far as to say that we probably shouldn't have _any_ string usages in the spec that aren't explicitly classified as binary or textual. The fact that this isn't the case is a bug IMHO 😉

At the end of the day, **DA** represents data that will be spliced into a binary stream as-is, so it should be binary. There are quite a few other string usages classified as "byte string" where the hex form is nonetheless not the most popular representation used in the wild.

(Side note: @stechio I don't necessarily disagree with your broader point, but I believe @mkl-public was referring to string literals being used as tokens inside the **DA**, as opposed to the preferred representation for the **DA** string itself.)

* Dates are always ASCII strings, never "text strings", so as never to be Unicode with BOMs or BCP-47 escapes- see Figure 7. Dates can however be either in literal (with or without `#` hex codes) or hex forms as NOTE 1 in 7.9.4 describes.

Since Table 35 ("PDF data types") is a declarative collection whose type names are referenced throughout the spec (the ubiquitous "Type" column of the tables describing specialized dictionaries), IMHO its definitions should be formally impeccable (extremely precise and uniform).

> * Dates are always ASCII strings, never "text strings", so as never to be Unicode with BOMs or BCP-47 escapes- see Figure 7.

THAT was *precisely* my thought! I had always assumed dates were `ASCII string` (it had been so for a long time, anyway), until I stumbled upon real-world PDF files containing dates formatted as `text string` [sic]... perplexed, I re-read the specification and discovered, to my bewilderment, that *the "Dates" section had changed the definition of its base type:*
- PDF 1.6, 3.8.3, "Dates":
`A date is a string of the form`
- PDF 1.7, 7.9.4, "Dates":
`A date shall be a text string of the form`
- PDF 2.0, 7.9.4, "Dates":
`A date shall be a text string value containing no white-space, of the form`

I double-checked the specs because it looked (and still does!) REALLY strange (after all, dates are *naturally* `ASCII string`, as they convey specially-formatted data, NOT informal human-readable content), but I had to accept that, if it was specifically reformulated and vetted by a standards commission, it should have been definitely authoritative...

BTW, here it is a sample (allegedly created by Adobe InDesign 15.0 for Windows and published on the UN website) containing UTF-16BE-encoded dates as values of `LastModified` entries of page-piece data dictionaries: https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/26261VNR_Report_Finland_2020.pdf

            /LastModified (D:20200529092447Z)
            /NumberofPages 1
            /OriginalDocumentID (xmp.did:0a6a5a8b-8ff9-4f40-83cd-096168779463)
            /DocumentID (xmp.did:570b4e15-239e-e241-9856-7675d6e127ad)
            /PageWidthList << /0 595.276 >>
            /PageUIDList << /0 20155 >>
            >>
        >>
    [...]
>>
```
where `D:20200529092447Z` was encoded this way (the hexadecimal representation here is just for our convenience):
`FEFF0044003A00320030003200300030003500320039003000390032003400340037005A`

NOTE: this sample declares itself as PDF 1.6, so it is non-conformant per-se (BTW, its page-piece data dictionaries are malformed too, missing their `Private` entries), nonetheless *the definition of dates as `text string` in the ISO PDF  specs needs to be fixed.*

Therefore:
1. the description of the following entry in Table 35 ("PDF data types") should be kept unchanged:
   - date:
   `Date (ASCII string)`

2. the definition of `date` type (PDF 1.7 and 2.0, 7.9.4, "Dates") should be amended as indicated:
`A date shall be an ASCII string [...]`
(in place of wrong `A date shall be a text string [...]`)

> * a "string" can be any type of string as illustrated in Figure 7. A "text string" is a specialised subset of "string". Anything defined as a "string" can be a "text string", but not vice-versa.

Again, THAT was *precisely* my thought! I had always assumed `string` data type was just string object (it had been so for a long time, anyway), so I re-read the specification and discovered, to my bewilderment, that *the `string` entry in Table 35 had changed the definition of its base type:*
- PDF 1.6, TABLE 3.31 (PDF data types), 3.8, "Common Data Structures":
`String object`
- PDF 2.0 (1.7), Table 35 (34) (PDF data types), 7.9.1, "General" - "Common Data Structures":
`Any string that is not a text string.`

Terminologically, `string` should be *any* type of string (as you argued), yet the way it is referenced in dictionary entries throughout the spec seems more appropriate to the restrictive acceptation stated in PDF 2.0 ("Any string that is not a text string"). - `string` should retain its pre-ISO (PDF 1.6) description (`String object`), which implies your statement ("a `string` can be any type of string")

I also want to propose a different solution, perhaps a more extreme change:

The only mandatory operator in `/DA` is the `Tf` operator, which takes a font and a font size. The font size can be 0, which means "auto-sized" (as per the 3rd last paragraph 12.7.4.3). In practice, this means the only required value is the font itself.

Most of them seem to already be doing that even when `/DA` is present, so I believe in practice it would not change much (in a good way), but I might be wrong.

FontFlags are part of a font descriptor.   A font descriptor is connected to a specific instance of a font - which itself may be either embedded or referenced.  But the descriptor is to THAT INSTANCE.

So if the descriptor is for an embedded font, then the flags (and all the other fields of the descriptor) are for that specific embedded (full or subset) font program.  If it is for a referenced (non-embedded) font, then it applies to the source material found by the PDF Writer at the time of PDF creation.

Proposed solution to clarify that it is instance-specific (i.e. a font object):

*  9.8.1, 3rd para first, sentence: "_A font descriptor is a dictionary whose entries specify various font attributes._" --> "_A font descriptor is a dictionary whose entries specify various font attributes specific to an instance of a font._" 

* 9.8.2, 1st para, 1st sentence: "_The value of the **Flags** entry in a font descriptor shall be an unsigned 32-bit integer containing flags specifying various characteristics of the font_." --> "_The value of the **Flags** entry in a font descriptor shall be an unsigned 32-bit integer containing flags specifying various characteristics of the instance of the font_." 

And/or we could do informatively via a NOTE such as at the very end of 9.8.1 - something like (thanks @lrosenthol!):

* NOTE: if the font descriptor is for an embedded font, then all fields of the descriptor are for that specific embedded (full or subset) font program. If it is for a referenced (non-embedded) font, then it applies to the source material found by the PDF Writer at the time of PDF creation.

I am speaking generally here - **not** specifically to the wording this issue highlights: ISO doesn't define such things, but in PDF standards we have 2 different types of requirements: "file format" and "processor". 

* "File format" means what has to happen within a file for it to be a valid PDF - if it is not done then the file is _invalid_ and usually falls outside the scope of ISO 32000. Files are just piles of passive bytes - they don't "do" anything.
* "Processor" requirements relate to what (all?) software needs to do. Software is active - it does something when given data accordingly. And verb-like word is always a processor requirement.

Generally speaking, we always try to define **file format** rules ahead of processor rules.

So the word "required" is _normally_ used to indicate a file format rule - e.g. some key or value is required, optional, or has some relationship to other data in the file.
The word "use" would imply a processor requirement as would other verbs ("ignore", "paint", etc.)

Of course this is how we have come to understand things today and not every sentence in all 1,000 pages will have been originally written with that understanding (hence my opening statement) - but does that help at all?

I ran into this problem when reading the spec as well.
my 2 cents is that, I see a few different consistent resolutions:

1. disallowing multiple OBJRs from referencing the same XObj
    - we basically have to replace & negate the note:
      >  "If the referenced object is rendered on multiple pages, each rendering requires a separate object reference."
    - in the case you want to do multiple reference, you'll have to convert your OBJRs to MCRs 
    and tag the "Do" operators at each instance

2. allowing and requiring the removal of StructParent in the Obj itself in this case (potentially a bit hacky)
    - the situation must be that the XObj is tagged via the Do operator in each including stream, and has an MCID in each
    - forward lookup from structure tree will go directly to the Obj via the OBJR in the leaf
      - works the same as single OBJR
    - backward lookup from the content will find that StructParent does not exist, and use instead the StructParents entry of the "owning stream" (this assumes the pdf processor somehow has a context stack to look up)
      - this proceeds as normal using the MCID given by the tagged 'Do' operator

3. allowing and requiring StructParent (singular) to be an Array in this case
    - this will provide enough information solve the multiple reference problem, 
    but will require additional logic to distinguish the instances
      - i.e. will have to look at all the potential linked OBJRs and match to the current context (i.e. via Pg?)
    - but may introduce unintended additional complexity, as all lookups will have potentially to take it into account
      - maybe fine if it's restricted to the XObjects special case? (i.e. not allowed for Pages)

Notes:
- MCRs won't work for Annotations, since those are not referenced in the streams,
but it's unclear reusing annotations is a valid use case, much less tagging them if reused.
- Separately (unrelated to OBJR):
We may want to add additional clarification/constraints on the requirement of fields such as Pg, Stm, StmOwn in the MCR to support unambiguous lookup in cases of multiple reference
