The PDF/A standards (ISO 19005 series) make explicit requirements ("shall" statements) from such recommendations regarding EOLs and white space that tighten the more flexible wording in the "general PDF" spec (ISO 32000). If in doubt, referring to PDF/A can definitely help.

In ISO speak, "should" is an official "recommendation" as defined by [ISO Directives Part 2, 3.3.4](https://www.iso.org/sites/directives/current/part2/index.xhtml#_idTextAnchor032) where things are "_deemed to be particularly suitable without necessarily mentioning or excluding others_".  

Nowadays, we try to write the PDF spec from more of an explicit, validatable file format perspective, rather than a processor (s/w) perspective. The concern is that changing words now in the PDF spec does not "fix" extant data that was written to much earlier specs, which may have been interpreted differently. But we also don't want to have readers rejecting large swathes of old PDFs because of a tightening of rules. So, with due care and attention(!!!), if you read the latest ISO 32000-2 with "should" as "shall" for "general PDF writers", then things will likely be the most portable across implementations. But "general PDF readers" need to be more flexible due to 30 years of history with earlier, less rigorous, and possibly ambiguous specs.

PS. This is also why ISO 32000 no longer uses the terms "conforming writer", "conforming reader", etc. "Conformance" is only for the subsets...

PPS. Historically the PDF spec was not created under the ISO Directives, so there are likely many places in the spec where "shall" or "should" statements are intended but not used, and the more casual original wording from the Adobe legacy references is used. So don't really on everything using these exact terms! However, I believe (hope!) that all _unintentional_ (i.e., casual) uses of the magic ISO terms "shall" and "should" should have been removed by now... (see what I did there? 😊)

> In ISO speak, "should" is an official "recommendation" as defined by [ISO Directives Part 2, 3.3.4](https://www.iso.org/sites/directives/current/part2/index.xhtml#_idTextAnchor032) where things are "_deemed to be particularly suitable without necessarily mentioning or excluding others_".

Experimentally I found that Acrobat Reader's implementation of spline interpolation seems to closely match Ghostscript's implementation.  I asked the new "Gemini CLI" to inspect the Ghostscript source code and to identify the type of spline interpolation used there.  According to Gemini, Ghostscript (and thus probably also Adobe Reader) uses Catmull-Rom splines:

> Based on the implementation in the Ghostscript C code, the specific version of Catmull-Rom splines used is a cardinal spline with a tension parameter a of -0.5.
>
> While "Catmull-Rom spline" often refers to the uniform variant where the tension is 0, the formula used here is a generalization. The parameter a = -0.5 is a specific choice that controls the "tightness" of the curve. This particular value is what the Ghostscript implementation uses for rendering Type 0 functions in PDFs.

For the multi-dimensional version, apparently a tensor product Catmull-Rom spline is used.

And whether the link target is correct or not (as far as a human is concerned) is orthogonal, as @DuffJohnson mentions. The author needs to explicitly make/define the cross-reference as active/actionable for the user via a PDF feature, such as a Link annot. @romantoda 
> Does the presence of a link annotation and/or Ref entry imply the actionability? Or is this about semantics, and therefore, the check is supposed to be human?

(TL;DR) This is about semantics, and the check is supposed to be human.

The presence of a `Link` annotation does not imply "actionably points". For example, you could have a document that is a collection of unrelated cartoons, one per page. The content and semantics of each cartoon does not point to the next cartoon, but the author could link each cartoon to the next one for user convenience.

The presence of `Ref` entries also does not imply "actionably points". UA-2 has an example of this in 8.2.5.25 List:
> If a list is continued in a subsequent list, or continues from a previous list, a Ref entry should be present and,
if present, it shall reference all list segments.

In this example, a Ref entry does not imply "actionably point". If a single List is broken into 8 non-contiguous parts, the refererence from part 3 referring to part 7 (among all the other parts) does not imply that part 3 "actionably points" to part 7.

---

@DuffJohnson 
> IMO, "actionably" here means simply that the PDF includes features that allow end users to change their view in the document. 

@petervwyatt 
> The author needs to explicitly make/define the cross-reference as active/actionable for the user via a PDF feature, such as a Link annot.

The sentence says, "[w]here _**content**_ actionably points to other content" (emphasis added), not "where _**a PDF feature**_ points to other content". It certainly does not mean `Link` annotations. If it did, that meaning would lead either to a tautology or a contradiction. Consider if the sentence had been written with "has a `Link` annotation" instead of "actionably points to other content":

> Where content \[has a `Link` annotation\], ..., such content shall use one or both of the following mechanisms:
> - a `Link` annotation;
> - a `Ref` entry.

This would mean that either the `Link` annotation requires a `Link` annotation (tautological), or the one mechanism is a `Ref` entry, and thus the `Link` annotation both exists and doesn't exist (a contradiction).

---

In general, UA-2 uses "interactive" and "non-interactive" to describe situations where references to other content respectively either have a `Link` annotation or don't have a `Link` annotation. For example, 8.2.5.20 Link and Reference:
> The Reference structure type may be used for both interactive links using link annotations and may also be
used for non-interactive content where a reference is present.
> EXAMPLE 4 An example of a non-interactive reference is a callout to a table in a document from within a paragraph.

---

This Example 4 is great for highlighting how "actionably points" is a human requirement. If the callout is in the last sentence of the paragraph and the table immediately follows, the callout is not actionable because the reader needs to take no action to read the table next.

If the paragraph is in a completely different part of the document, the callout still might "actionably point" to the table. For example, if the sentence says, "The raw data for the results for this step of the analysis is in Table 9 of Appendix Q", I would argue that does not "actionably point" the reader to go read the table of raw data.

On the other hand, if the sentence says, "Look at Table 4 and notice how...", one could argue that the callout is "actionably pointing" the reader to the table. Even when the content does actionably point to other content, UA-2 does not require a `Link` annotation -- UA-2 does not require interactivity.

@willkil - To be 100% clear, ISO 32000-1:2008 and ISO 32000-2:2020 both _explicitly state_ that a Link SE is an association between one or more Link annotations - see Table 338 and 368 respectively, and similar wording in 14.8.4.4.2 / 14.8.4.7.2 respectively. Whether anything is actually functional is solely a condition of the PDF processor (unfortunately, a few popular PDF apps do not support all forms of destination! 😒), not of the file. Whether the Link SE's Link annotation associated target(s) are "semantically correct" is a human check. 

That means if you have a Link SE, it **MUST** have at least one Link annot. A Link SE without any Link annot is bad PDF. But the reverse may not be true - nothing says all Link annots have to be associated with Link SEs (since that is all about the semantics - maybe something is an artifact). And whether the _target_ of the Link annot is valid is also not discussed (it could be a non-existent destination (e.g. deleted page) or a dead URL) - these would be semantic checks but can obviously change over time. And whether that Link annot actually _actively works_ is a function of the particular PDF software being used.

I didn't explain my thinking - I meant that (i) this is largely core 32K stuff, not PDF/UA (which does layer a bit more on top), and (b) "actionability" is a s/w processor thing vs "targets" which can be a file format thing, so terminology is important for file validation vs human check vs. application behaviour (out of scope).  (PS. I admit my wording in other comments further above should have used the word "targets" rather than anything implying an action or behaviour).

I think there is a misunderstanding that "intra-document" in UA-2 is equivalent to "intra-PDF-file", but this is not necessarily the same thing. The NOTE in UA-2 8.2.5.20 says "_External vs intra-document linkage is a semantic concept..._" so UA-2 8.8 title should really be "Intra-semantic-document destinations" which makes a lot more sense for this requiring human checks.  A single PDF file can have multiple "semantic documents", or it could be a partial "semantic document" in the context of something larger (such as referencing other chapters across multiple PDFs using Embedded Go-To actions). 

So I agree with you that most of this needs human checks, with validation largely reduced to PDF file validity -- but importantly, including core rules from 32K. For Roman's original question about "actionability", I think it then reduces to whether syntactically valid "targets" (e.g., SDs) should _also_ be validated as existing or not. Hmm, if "actionability" is a s/w processor thing, then I have been misinterpreting "actionably point". I interpreted "actionably point" as an author-to-consuming-user thing. Basically, does the author expect _the user consuming the document_ to take action (click, flip pages, etc.) in order to visit the target? If the author (to include remediators, etc.) expects that, then either a Link annot with SD destination or a Ref entry is necessary. Thus, it's a human check to decide whether to include the Link annot, Ref entries, both, _or neither_.

It's also certainly a human check to decide whether an existing target is correct or incorrect, but I do not think that is an accessibility consideration. It is a quality consideration. The wrong target is merely equally poor quality for all.

You raise an interesting point regarding a missing target. I would expect that to be a 32K-2 error, and one that UA-2 validators should check for. 32K-2 12.3.2.3 Structure destinations says, "the first entry in the array [of an SD] shall be an indirect reference to a structure element dictionary". And 7.3.9 Null object says, "An indirect object reference ... to a nonexistent object shall be treated the same as a null object." But the null object is not "an indirect reference to a structure element dictionary", so isn't the SD shall statement violated?

I think there is definitely an _author intention_ of the behaviour, but there is no _guarantee_ of anything since the consuming S/W environment cannot be guaranteed so I don't think an author should _expect_ anything (esp. given the level of support for PDF 2.0-aware AT and with SDs being new in PDF 2.0 - so SDs won't work in even the very best PDF/UA-1 conforming processor). Authors can hope tho 😊. So there's not much difference between our PoVs...

Note also the last para in 32K-2 12.3.2.3 Structure destinations that says "_...  the indirect reference to the structure element dictionary shall be replaced by a byte string representing a structure element **ID**_" so PDF 2.0 SDs support more than just indirect references to SE dicts. There is also the question of whether the referenced SE is in the structure tree or "orphaned" but the way 32K is written, the deterministic algorithm described will _always_ result in a page even in extreme (i.e. badly formed) circumstances so it actually doesn't matter what the array element is.

## Draft Changes for Review — Clarify `compressed_iso_spline`, Curve Type Suppression, and IsoNURBS Calling Context

NOTE: these have NOT been validated by checking implementations, but appear sensible.

**Section:** §7.9.21.9 (CompressedCurve general), §7.9.21.9.2 (PRC_HCG_Line),
§7.9.21.9.3 (PRC_HCG_Circle); secondary: §7.9.21.5.14.3 (IsoNURBSTrimCrv)
**Tables:** Table 234 (PRC_HCG_Line), Table 235 (PRC_HCG_Circle),
Table 236 (ParticularCircle), Table 237 (GeneralCircle), Table 239 (PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve)
**Change type:** Normative clarification, definition relocation, naming correction,
calling-context exposition, editorial fix
**Verification:** Confirmed by cross-referencing Table 218 (IsoNURBSTrimCrv)

---

### Background and Root Cause Analysis

**Title:** Clarification of Contextual Flag Evaluation and Elimination of Ghost Data Rows in IsoNURBSTrimCrv

**Applies to:** ISO 14739-1 (PRC Specification), §7.9.21.5.14 (IsoNURBSTrimCrv), §7.9.21.9.1 (Context Flags), and §7.9.21.9.3 (PRC_HCG_Line).

**Summary of Proposed Changes:**
This change request corrects a structural error in the baseline specification regarding how implicit iso-parametric trim lines are evaluated. Reviewer validation confirmed that when an iso-boundary is not a circle, no PRC_HCG_Line structure exists in the bitstream; its geometry is purely implicit and derived from topology (LoopVertexN).

Consequently, this CR:

- Removes the erroneous compressed_line row from Table 218 (IsoNURBSTrimCrv).
- Restricts the scope of the compressed_iso_spline context flag exclusively to circles and composite curves.
- Purges dead conditional logic from Table 234 (PRC_HCG_Line).

**Root Cause of the Initial Error**
The baseline specification suffered from a conceptual mix-up between implicit topological edges and explicit geometric curves.

Table 218 (IsoNURBSTrimCrv) originally contained a conditional branch for cases where iso_boundary is FALSE and is_a_circle is FALSE, indicating an iso-parametric straight line. The specification erroneously assumed that a PRC_HCG_Line structure was still written to the bitstream here, allocating a compressed_line data row and intending for compressed_iso_spline = TRUE to suppress its start/end coordinates.

In reality, the bitstream allocates exactly zero bits for a line in this configuration. The curve's endpoints are already perfectly defined by the topological bounding vertices (LoopVertexN). Because no PRC_HCG_Line is ever serialized or read in this context, the compressed_iso_spline flag is never passed to a line structure. This resulted in two critical specification defects:

Table 218 instructs parsers to read a non-existent compressed_line structure, creating a fatal parsing offset mismatch.

Table 234 (PRC_HCG_Line) contains dead logic attempting to evaluate a compressed_iso_spline context that can mathematically never be reached.

**This resolves the question: "If you can't read the type, how do you know if you have a circle or a line?"**

The answer is: when `compressed_iso_spline = TRUE`, you already know the curve type
before entering the curve reading routine — Table 218 (`IsoNURBSTrimCrv`) made the
type determination via the `is_a_circle` flag. The `type` token in `PRC_HCG_Circle`
is not a type-discovery field in this context; it is a redundant confirmation that is
suppressed to save bitstream space. The calling code dispatches directly to the
appropriate reading routine. `PRC_HCG_Line` answers the same question by a different
mechanism: because `is_a_circle = FALSE`, the reader already knows the next structure
is a `PRC_HCG_Line` before reading it.

**Why `PRC_HCG_Line` is affected by `compressed_iso_spline`:** The two curves that
appear as iso-parametric NURBS boundaries are circles and straight lines. Both can be
trim curves of a `PRC_HCG_IsoNURBS` face. When either is read in that context,
`compressed_iso_spline = TRUE` and `start_end_data` is suppressed, because the
start/end trim points of iso-parametric NURBS boundary curves are implicit in the
NURBS surface's parametric domain and do not need to be stored separately.

Yes, strictly speaking the referenced ISO directive section itself does _not_ forbid the use of "might" in question here: That section merely forbids the _use of “might” instead of “may” in **this context**_, and _this context_ consists of the _verbal forms that shall be used to express permission_. The "might" in question, though, is not about permitting anything, just about reminding that some situation is possible (and the whole clause is about stressing that this possible situation makes no difference).
Nonetheless, it surely can make one's life easier to not use "might" at all and so prevent any discussion about whether or not any occurrence of "might" is subject to the directive section above or not.

A similar issue happens in `7.3.8 Stream objects`. The same requirement is stated again with weaker strength after the stronger one.
In `7.3.8.1 General` (**should**): `There should be an end-of-line marker after the data and before endstream`
In `7.3.8.2 Stream extent` (**may**): `Streams shall also not contain too much data, with the exception that there may be an extra end-of-line marker in the PDF file before the keyword endstream.`

And the definition of `/F` conflicts with that: `If this entry is present, the bytes between stream and endstream shall be ignored. However, the Length entry should still specify the number of those bytes (usually, there are no bytes and Length is 0)`. To be precise: the `/Length` entry should still specify the number of bytes (excluding the extra end-of-line marker), usually, there are no bytes before the extra end-of-line marker and Length is 0.

ISO CS editors will scrub all uses of "might" and many other words regardless of what the ISO Directives actually might (pun intended!) be argued to allow.

According to the ISO 32000-2 Terms and definitions, a part of ISO 32000 is called "deprecated" if it "should not be written into a PDF 2.0 document, and should be ignored by a PDF processor" (ISO 32000-2 section 3.1.5).

Thus, in this context we probably should not try to "deprecate SHA1 with PDF 1.7" because the term "deprecate" in ISO 32000-2 is defined to refer to PDF 2.0.

My personal opinion on this:

I think the list of algorithms in ISO 32000-2 (table 260) should be considered an indication of which algorithms a validating PDF processor should at least be able to _process_, not a list of which algorithms - and parameters - it should consider _secure_ and applicable for secure signatures. For assessing algorithm strengths, a validating PDF processor should rely on the latest agreed information on algorithm security, e.g. SOG-IS, ECCG, ETSI, or NIST publications.

Also there may be very good reasons for a validator to accept SHA1 based PDF signatures; if a PDF with such a signature is known to have existed in its current form since e.g. 2007 (when SHA1 still was generally accepted), there is no reason not to validate the signature positively if it's cryptographically sound.

Similarly, a signing PDF processor should make use of the latest agreed information on algorithm security, too, when selecting an algorithm to use for signing.

Furthermore, if we discourage the use of SHA1 in ISO 32000-2 and so create the impression that we want to maintain a list of secure algorithms here, we should take a look at other algorithms (with parameters) in that table, too. For example the "RSA - Up to 1024-bit (PDF 1.3)" entry might then be perceived to imply that RSA with a key size of up to 1024 bits is a secure choice for signatures.

Thus, deprecation or discouragement of SHA1 for security reasons for me is not really necessary in ISO 32000-2. Instead I'd favor adding a note to indicate that assessment of the algorithm strengths is not the focus of this document.

Maybe even generically wording such a note since the essence of the statement is timeless and will likely apply to today's best crypto at some point in the future! i.e. the PDF specification needs to continue to define how to process any extant PDF with "old" crypto in perpetuity and does not make any statements about appropriateness of algorithms.

The C&P TWG observes that ISO 32000-2 is focused on PDF 2.0 and, therefore, cannot be changed in respect to earlier PDF versions.

One proposed option around this would be a PDF/Association publishing to recommend against the use of SHA-1 (and other weak algorithms) also in PDF-1.x. This option is to be discussed.

`As permitted by ISO 32000-2:—, 12.8, a PDF/A-4 conforming file may contain at most one user rights signature, at most one certification signature, any number of approval signatures and any number of document timestamp signatures.`

> This wording doesn't match 12.8 of ISO 32000-2. The problem is the "or". For instance, this wording prohibits one certificatation signature with one approval signature.

Most likely the authors here meant an _inclusive or_, not an _exclusive or_ (like in "either ... or").

Admittedly, though, natural language usage of "or" often means the exclusive variant. Thus, while not being a bug that needs a fix, one could consider this to be correct but in need of clarification,

> Also, 6.5.1 omits document timestamp signatures. Are these really forbidden in PDF/A-4?

There are different ways to view the relationship of timestamps and signatures. One option is to see timestamps as a special case of signatures, another is to see them as related but different. The language and display style used by a well known implementation seems to imply the former option but the ISO PDF specification (and also legal contexts like EU eIDAS) lean to the latter option.

Thus, when interpreting ISO 19005-4, you should not include timestamp whenever signatures are mentioned. In the case at hand, see 19005-4 section 6.5.3: "Document timestamp (DTS) dictionaries, as defined in ISO 32000-2:2020, 12.8.5, may be independently used for a proof of existence of a PDF/A-4 conforming file. In such a case, it does not matter whether the PDF document contains a signature as described in 6.5.2."
In ISO, "or" is inclusive indeed. Any permutation allowed.  Anyway, it's "certification signature", not "certifying signature". Fixed my proposal.

ISO-ese:

"should" = [recommendation](https://www.iso.org/sites/directives/current/part2/index.xhtml#_idTextAnchor085)
"may" = [permission](https://www.iso.org/sites/directives/current/part2/index.xhtml#_idTextAnchor088)
"can" = [possibility](https://www.iso.org/sites/directives/current/part2/index.xhtml#_idTextAnchor091)

3. Every change involves work for many people - spec editors, approval by working group, implementers (who have to ascertain if the change is functional or not).
4. Why is the text different for approval/timestamp? Historical reasons, probably - "approval" was the first type of signature.

Change involves Work+Risk. If the value of the change doesn't outweigh the work+risk, in my opinion is should be left out. That's just my opinion, I'm not the editor of 32K. And I really don't want to deter you from your revision process, but just be aware that each change comes with a cost.

In discussion with key stakeholders, it was noted that the industry adoption/usage of PDF/A-3 versus PDF/A-2 differs in the types of files that can be embedded. Technically, PDF/A-3 does NOT have to have any embedded files and thus is otherwise equivalent to PDF/A-2, but the archival and preservation communities effectively treat anything that is PDF/A-3 as needing additional analysis/metadata to achieve reliable long-term preservation (i.e. inspect each embedded file). In fact, many archives prohibit PDF/A-3 based on this assumption, when it is not what the ISO specs mandate.

So requiring PDF/A-4f to always have at least one embedded file avoids the unnecessary "over-specification" of PDF/A-4 conformance levels when "plain" PDF/A-4 is more appropriate (vast majority of files when no conformance level specified). It effectively reserves PDF/A-4f for non-trivial embedded files. 

PS. This is the inverse of the previous "under-specification" with Level B conformance in PDF/A-{1,2}, where archival files that are Level A or Level U were "dumbed down" to Basic. You often see advice from some archives that only accept Level B!

PS. Are you reading the 2020 edition or the latest Dated Revision draft from ISO? The DR mandates "_... at least one file specification dictionary ..._" now so an empty **EmbeddedFiles** name tree is no longer enough.

## Verification requested — confirmed, and we hit this in practice

@mvrhel asked whether I could verify this one. I can, and the evidence is stronger than agreement:
**our decoder cannot read real files using the currently specified type, and already carries the
proposed one.**

`number_of_connex` is read in nanoPRC as a plain 32-bit unsigned integer. The
`NumberOfBitsThenUnsignedInteger` reading is still present in our source immediately above it,
commented out, from when we tried it:

```c
/* Number of bits then unsigned integer for this count */
//data->number_of_connex = prc_bitread_number_of_bits_then_unsigned_int(ctx, bit_state);

data->number_of_connex = prc_bitread_uint32(ctx, bit_state);
```

So this is not a reading of the text — it is what we had to do to parse real-world uncompressed
`PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepData`. **The change to `UnsignedInteger` is correct.**

### Why it matters more than a type-name tidy-up

Unlike some of the neighbouring corrections, this one is a genuine **wire-format** difference, not an
interpretation difference. `NumberOfBitsThenUnsignedInteger` writes a bit-count prefix ahead of the
value; `UnsignedInteger` does not. A decoder implemented literally from the current text consumes
those prefix bits that are not there, desynchronises at that point, and everything after
`number_of_connex` in the body is misread. It fails silently rather than loudly, because the
misparsed count is usually still a plausible small number.

That makes this worth applying rather than leaving as an editorial nicety.

**Credit** for identifying it belongs to the proposer; this is corroboration from an independent
implementation, offered because it was asked for.

## Verification requested — confirmed, and the change is wire-compatible

@mvrhel asked whether I could verify this one too. Confirmed, with one point worth adding about the
risk of making the change.

**What we currently do.** nanoPRC follows the specification as written and reads both fields as
signed 32-bit integers — and flagged its own doubt in an inline comment at the time:

```c
data->number_of_elements = prc_bitread_int32(ctx, bit_state); /* Unsigned int ?? */
...
data->number_of_supplemental_doubles = prc_bitread_int32(ctx, bit_state);
```

So we independently arrived at the same question this issue asks, from the other direction — by
implementing the text and finding it read oddly.

**Both are already treated as unsigned in effect.** Each is immediately guarded with a `> 0` test
before it is used to size an allocation, so a negative value is already handled as impossible rather
than meaningful. There is no code path in which a negative element count does anything useful.

### The change is safe to apply

`Integer` and `UnsignedInteger` occupy the **same 32 bits on the wire** here; only the interpretation
of the top bit differs. So changing the declared type:

- cannot invalidate or re-interpret any existing file, since no conforming producer can have written a
  genuinely negative count;
- changes no decoder's bit positions, unlike #652 where the correction is a real format change;
- removes a nonsensical case (a negative array length) that an implementer otherwise has to decide
  what to do about.

**We agree with the change to `UnsignedInteger` for both `number_of_elements` and
`number_of_supplemental_doubles`.** Credit belongs to the proposer; this is corroboration from an
independent implementation, offered because it was asked for.

**CR-29.** This change is identified as CR-29 in the reports and correspondence it arises
from; please quote that identifier in any reply so the two stay tied together.

**Location:** `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/surface.yaml`. Text quoted from `main` at
`e308145`, read 18 September 2026.

## Defect

The amendment made under this issue added a `has_transform` Boolean to fifteen of the sixteen
transform-bearing surface entities and gated the transformation behind it. All fifteen nevertheless
still declare `transform` as `required: true` with no `require_conditions`.

An attribute that is present only when a Boolean is TRUE is not unconditionally required. A
generator or reader taking the definitions literally will write or expect the transformation in
every case, which is the condition this issue was opened to remove.

The correct form is already present in the same definitions, on the curve side, in
`PRC_TYPE_CRV_Circle`.

The sixteenth entity, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Plane`, is **not** part of this request. Its `description`
states the exception outright - "There is no *has_transform* Boolean for this type; it is considered
always to be TRUE" - so it is correct as written and no change is proposed to it.

## Proposed change

One replacement, applied to fifteen entities. The current text is byte-identical in all fifteen, so
a single pair is given; it is to be applied to each of the entities listed below.

Current text, in each of the fifteen:

```yaml
  - name: transform
    data_type:
      kind: Transformation
    required: true
    description: Position surface into model space
```

Replace, in each of the fifteen, with:

```yaml
  - name: transform
    data_type:
      kind: Transformation
    description: Position surface into model space
    required: false
    require_conditions: "if *has_transform* is TRUE"
```

The fifteen entities, being every transform-bearing surface except `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Plane`:

`PRC_TYPE_SURF_Blend01`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Blend02`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Blend03`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Cone`,
`PRC_TYPE_SURF_Cylinder`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Cylindrical`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Extrusion`,
`PRC_TYPE_SURF_FromCurves`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Offset`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Pipe`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Revolution`,
`PRC_TYPE_SURF_Ruled`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Sphere`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Torus`, `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Transform`.

## Effect if accepted

Each of the fifteen has its transformation made conditional upon the `has_transform` Boolean this
issue already added. The `has_transform` attributes themselves are unchanged, no `description`
string changes, and `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Plane` and `PRC_TYPE_SURF_NURBS` are untouched.

## Note on an earlier characterisation

An earlier report of this defect identified `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Pipe` as inconsistent with the other
surfaces, and a later one said the correction applied to all sixteen. Both are withdrawn by their
author. No surface states the condition correctly, so Pipe is not an exception; and Plane already
documents its own exception, so it is not part of the fix. The correct count is fifteen.

**CR-29, supplementary.** The change requested above is incomplete as filed, and this widens it.
The fifteen YAML replacements stand exactly as written; what follows adds a third document that
has to move with them.

## There is a third version, and it is the normative one

The request above treats this as a discrepancy between two things: the amended clause, which gates
the transformation behind a `has_transform` Boolean on fifteen surfaces, and `surface.yaml`, which
carries that Boolean but still declares `transform` as `required: true`.

There is a third, and it is the published document. **`has_transform` does not appear on the surface
side of it at all.**

Verified against ISO/CD 14739-1.4:2026, the 11 June 2026 draft. Exactly five entities declare a
`has_transform` Boolean in the whole document, and not one of them is a surface:

```
PRC_TYPE_ASM_ProductOccurrence
PRC_TYPE_CRV_Circle
PRC_TYPE_CRV_Intersection
PRC_TYPE_CRV_Line
PRC_TYPE_CRV_PolyLine
```

(The texture side carries a similarly-named but distinct `has_transformation`, which is not this
field and is not counted above.)

Every transform-bearing surface table declares `transform` as `Transformation (Required)`
unconditionally, with no Boolean in front of it, and `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Plane` reads exactly like the
other fifteen rather than differently.

A second implementation reports the same finding against N808, ISO/CD 14739-1.3:2025 of 17 October
2025. So the position is unchanged across two consecutive published drafts, and this is not a case
of a correction that has landed in the document and not yet in the definitions.

## The three versions, and why that matters

| | `has_transform` on surfaces | `transform` | `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Plane` |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| ISO/CD 14739-1.4:2026, published | **absent entirely** | Required, unconditional | same as the other fifteen |
| the amended clause | present on fifteen | gated | documented exception, always TRUE |
| `surface.yaml` at `e308145` | present on fifteen | **still `required: true`** | documented exception |

**An implementer working from the published CD reads no Boolean anywhere on the surface side, and is
not wrong to do so.** That is the sentence that turns this from a tidy-up into a defect. A reader
built faithfully from the normative document and a reader built from the amended clause disagree
about the bit layout of every transform-bearing surface in every file, and the normative document is
the one an implementer is entitled to rely on.

## What this changes in the request

Nothing in the fifteen YAML replacements. They are correct as filed and the quoted block was
re-checked today: it occurs **exactly fifteen times** in `surface.yaml` at `e308145`, byte-identical,
consistent with the entity list given above.

What it adds is that fixing them alone leaves two of the three versions disagreeing. For this issue
to close, all three have to say the same thing:

1. **`surface.yaml`** -- the fifteen replacements above, making `transform` conditional on
   `has_transform`.
2. **The clause text** -- already amended, and consistent.
3. **The normative document** -- carries neither the Boolean nor the Plane exception, and needs both
   before the next publication. Otherwise the next CD ships saying what the amendment was opened to
   correct.

Item 3 is the one this comment exists to add. It may be a publication-sequencing matter rather than
a drafting one, and if the amendment is already queued for the next CD then this is satisfied and
nothing further is needed -- but it should be confirmed rather than assumed, because the published
document has not moved across two drafts while the definitions have.

## Note on evidence

The 1.4:2026 measurement is ours, made by searching the published draft for every occurrence of the
identifier and reading each in context. The 1.3:2025 measurement is a second implementation's,
reported to us and repeated here as their result rather than ours. The two agree.

Differences between the seed value definitions in ISO 32000-1 (table 234) and Adobe PDF Reference 1.7 (table 8.83) with Errata:

| Key | ISO 32000-1 | Adobe PDF Reference 1.7 w/Errata |
|-|-|-|
| **Filter** | ... If **Ff** indicates that this is an optional constraint, this handler _**may**_ be used if it is available. If it is not available, a different handler _may_ be used instead. | ... If **Ff** indicates that this is an optional constraint, this handler _**should**_ be used if it is available. If it is not available, a different handler *can* be used instead. |
| **SubFilter** | ... The first name in the array that matches an encoding supported by the signature handler _**shall**_ be the encoding that is actually used for signing. If **SubFilter** is specified and the **Ff** entry indicates that this entry is a required constraint, then the first matching encodings _shall_ be used when signing; otherwise, signing _shall_ not take place. If **Ff** indicates that this is an optional constraint, then the first matching encoding _**shall**_ be used if it is available. If none is available, a different encoding _may_ be used. | ... The first name in the array that matches an encoding supported by the signature handler _**should**_ be the encoding that is actually used for signing. If **SubFilter** is specified and the **Ff** entry indicates that this entry is a required constraint, then the first matching encodings _must_ be used when signing; otherwise, signing _must_ not take place. If **Ff** indicates that this is an optional constraint, then the first matching encoding _**should**_ be used if it is available. If it is not available, a different encoding _can_ be used. | 
| **V** | A value of 2 specifies that it _shall_ be able to recognize all seed value dictionary entries specified. | A value of 2 specifies that it _must_ be able to recognize all seed value dictionary entries specified _**in PDF 1.7 and earlier**_. |
| **AddRevInfo** | ... A flag indicating whether revocation checking **_shall_** be carried out. If **AddRevInfo** is true, the conforming processor **_shall_** perform the following additional tasks when signing the signature field: ... If **AddRevInfo** is true and the Ff entry indicates this is a required constraint, then the preceding tasks _shall_ be performed. | ... A flag indicating whether revocation checking **_should_** be carried out. If **AddRevInfo** is true, the viewer application performs the following additional tasks when signing the signature field: ... If **AddRevInfo** is true and the Ff entry indicates this is a required constraint, then the tasks described above _must_ be performed. ... |

This table only includes those entries in which not merely normal ISOfication happened but actually the meaning changed. But even in those cases I think the meaning changed because of incorrect ISOfication:

* For a optional **Filter** constraint ISO 32000-1 only says *this handler may be used* while Reference 1.7 says *this handler should be used*. An _optional_ constraint should be considered a recommendation. Thus, *should* makes more sense here.
* For a optional **SubFilter** constraint ISO 32000-1 says *the first matching encoding shall be used* while Reference 1.7 only says *the first matching encoding should be used*. An _optional_ constraint should be considered a recommendation. Thus, *should* makes more sense here.
* In **V** ISO 32000-1 has dropped the *in PDF 1.7 and earlier* characterization. This probably is where the issue at hand started.

## CR-10 — Clarify `ContentCompressedAnaFace` and `AnaFaceTrimLoop` Sentinel-Based Encoding

**Section:** §7.9.21.7.3
**Tables:** Table 231 — `ContentCompressedAnaFace`, Table 232 — `AnaFaceTrimLoop`
**Change type:** Normative clarification, structural annotation, pseudocode insertion, editorial correction
**Verification:** Implementor pseudocode confirmed working (@socrat74 )

### Background

Multiple independent readers have identified this area as the least parseable section of
the compressed brep specification. The root cause is that Table 232 (`AnaFaceTrimLoop`)
presents `curve_is_not_already_stored` and `type` as named fields of the loop structure,
when they are in fact the first two fields of a sentinel `RefOrCompressedCurve` entry
that terminates the curves sequence. This misrepresentation gives rise to two directly
related confusions:

1. **How many curves are in a loop?** The `curves` array in Table 232 has no explicit
   count field. The array boundary is determined by reading `RefOrCompressedCurve`
   entries until a sentinel is encountered (a `RefOrCompressedCurve` where
   `curve_is_not_already_stored = TRUE` and `type` is `PRC_HCG_NewLoop` or
   `PRC_HCG_EndLoop`). This mechanism is not described anywhere in the current tables
   or prose.

2. **How many loops are in a face?** The `trim_loop` array in Table 231 also has no
   explicit count. It is terminated by the same sentinel mechanism: the sentinel's `type`
   value distinguishes "another loop follows" (`PRC_HCG_NewLoop`) from "all loops
   complete" (`PRC_HCG_EndLoop`). The current Table 231 description states the last loop
   "is of type `PRC_HCG_EndLoop`" as if `type` were a field of the loop itself, which
   it is not.

Additional editorial issues identified:

- Table 231 `trim_loop` description contains the typo `HPC_HCG_TOPO_NewLoop` —
  should be `PRC_HCG_NewLoop`.
- Table 232 states `curve_is_not_already_stored` is "always TRUE" — this is only
  true for the sentinel entry; for actual curve entries the flag may be either TRUE
  or FALSE (see Table 233).

### CR-10f — Insert Reading Algorithm in New §7.9.21.7.3.3

**INSERT** new subsection §7.9.21.7.3.3 immediately after the `AnaFaceTrimLoop` table

---

**7.9.21.7.3.3 Reading Algorithm for `ContentCompressedAnaFace` Trim Loops**

The following algorithm defines the normative reading order for the trimming loop data
of a `ContentCompressedAnaFace`. Implementors shall follow this algorithm; the column
descriptions in Tables 231 and 232 are informative summaries of it.

Conventions used below:

- `ReadBoolean()` — reads one bit from the bitstream
- `ReadCompressedEntityType()` — reads a `CompressedEntityType` token
- `ReadCompressedCurve(type)` — reads a compressed curve of the given type (§7.9.21.9)
- `ReadCurveReference()` — reads an `UnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber` index of
  `number_of_bits_to_store_reference` bits (§7.9.20)
- `PRC_HCG_NewLoop`, `PRC_HCG_EndLoop` — `CompressedEntityType` sentinel values

```
PROCEDURE ReadContentCompressedAnaFaceTrimData(surface_type : CompressedEntityType):
-- surface_type is the CompressedEntityType token already read from the enclosing
-- PRC_HCG_Ano* face structure (e.g. PRC_HCG_AnaTorus, PRC_HCG_AnaCylinder, etc.)
-- before this procedure is called.

  is_trimmed ← ReadBoolean()

  all_loops_are_vertex_loops ← TRUE   -- assumed until disproved below

  IF is_trimmed = TRUE THEN

    loopType ← PRC_HCG_NewLoop

    WHILE loopType = PRC_HCG_NewLoop DO

      loop_surface_orientation ← ReadBoolean()

      curve_count_this_loop ← 0

      -- Read curves for this loop until a sentinel is encountered
      REPEAT

        -- Each iteration reads one RefOrCompressedCurve entry (Table 233)
        curve_is_not_already_stored ← ReadBoolean()

        IF curve_is_not_already_stored = TRUE THEN

          loopType ← ReadCompressedEntityType()

          IF loopType = PRC_HCG_NewLoop OR loopType = PRC_HCG_EndLoop THEN
            -- Sentinel entry: signals end of curves for this loop.
            -- loopType controls the outer WHILE condition.
            EXIT REPEAT
          END IF

          -- loopType holds the curve type; read and add to loop.
          ReadCompressedCurve(loopType)

          -- Check vertex-loop condition: a vertex loop has exactly one curve
          -- and that curve is a degenerate PRC_HCG_Line.
          IF loopType ≠ PRC_HCG_Line THEN
            all_loops_are_vertex_loops ← FALSE
          END IF

        ELSE

          -- curve_is_not_already_stored = FALSE: curve already in cache.
          ReadCurveReference()
          all_loops_are_vertex_loops ← FALSE
          -- A referenced curve cannot be a degenerate line in this context.

        END IF

        curve_count_this_loop ← curve_count_this_loop + 1

      UNTIL FALSE  -- exits only via EXIT REPEAT above

      IF curve_count_this_loop ≠ 1 THEN
        all_loops_are_vertex_loops ← FALSE
        -- A vertex loop contains exactly one curve.
      END IF

      -- Store the completed loop.

    END WHILE
    -- loopType = PRC_HCG_EndLoop; all loops have been read.

    -- Read point_on_torus if all three conditions are met.
    -- There is no stored flag; the reader evaluates these conditions directly.
    IF surface_type = PRC_HCG_AnaTorus AND all_loops_are_vertex_loops = TRUE THEN
      point_on_torus ← ReadCompressedPoint()
    END IF

  END IF

END PROCEDURE
```

**Key behaviours implementors shall observe:**

1. The `curves` sequence within each loop has no explicit length. The end of the
   sequence is detected by reading a `RefOrCompressedCurve` entry where
   `curve_is_not_already_stored = TRUE` and the subsequent `CompressedEntityType`
   token is `PRC_HCG_NewLoop` or `PRC_HCG_EndLoop`. That entry is consumed but not
   added to the loop.

2. The `trim_loop` array has no explicit count. The end of the array is detected when
   the sentinel `type` value is `PRC_HCG_EndLoop` rather than `PRC_HCG_NewLoop`.

3. The `loopType` variable serves a dual purpose: within the inner loop it holds the
   curve type of the most recently read non-sentinel `RefOrCompressedCurve` entry;
   on exit from the inner loop it holds the sentinel type (`PRC_HCG_NewLoop` or
   `PRC_HCG_EndLoop`) that controls the outer while-loop.

4. A valid face with `is_trimmed = TRUE` shall have at least one loop; the first
   `RefOrCompressedCurve` entry read after `loop_surface_orientation` may itself be
   a sentinel (representing an empty loop), though writers should not produce empty loops.

5. `all_loops_are_vertex_loops` is a reader-derived boolean, not a stored field.
   It is initialised to TRUE before the loop-reading phase and set to FALSE if any
   loop contains more than one curve, any curve that is not `PRC_HCG_Line`, or any
   curve retrieved by reference rather than read inline.

6. `surface_type` is a parameter passed into the reading procedure from the enclosing
   face structure (e.g. `PRC_HCG_AnaTorus`, Table 212). It is the `CompressedEntityType`
   token read immediately before `ContentCompressedFace` in the enclosing table.
   It is not stored within `ContentCompressedAnaFace`.

7. `point_on_torus` has no preceding Boolean flag. Its presence is determined entirely
   by the evaluated conditions. A reader must not attempt to read it unless
   `surface_type = PRC_HCG_AnaTorus` AND `all_loops_are_vertex_loops = TRUE`
   AND `is_trimmed = TRUE`. Reading it unconditionally or testing only a single
   condition will misalign the bitstream for all subsequent faces.

8. The degenerate-line check for vertex loops is tolerance-based: start and end
   vertices of the `PRC_HCG_Line` curve are identical within the compressed brep
   tolerance (`brep_data_compressed_tolerance`, §7.9.21.1). Implementors shall
   not rely on exact bitwise equality.

I ran into the same question writing a `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress` reader. Tracing real CAD-exported PRC geometry sections bit-by-bit, here's what the encoding appears to be — and I think it answers "where do I find the size of the `curves` array?": **there is no size.** Both the per-loop `curves` array (Table 232) and the loop array itself (`ContentCompressedAnaFace.trim_loop`, Table 231) are **unbounded streams terminated by an in-band control code**, not length-prefixed arrays.

### The mechanism

Entries in a loop are read one at a time. Each entry starts with the `curve_is_not_already_stored` Boolean (the same field in Table 233 `RefOrCompressedCurve` and in the Table 232 row):

- **`curve_is_not_already_stored == FALSE`** → an `UnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber` index (width `number_of_bits_to_store_reference`) into the already-stored-curve array. Continue.
- **`curve_is_not_already_stored == TRUE`** → read a `CompressedEntityType` (§9.16 — a `bIsACurve` Boolean then a 2/4-bit code):
  - `bIsACurve == TRUE` → the code is a curve type (`PRC_HCG_Line` / `Circle` / `BsplineHermiteCurve` / …) and an inline curve body follows. Continue.
  - `bIsACurve == FALSE` → the 4-bit code is **not a surface** here but a **loop-control code** (the first two values of Table 204): **`0 = PRC_HCG_NewLoop`** and **`1 = PRC_HCG_EndLoop`**. This terminates the current loop's `curves`:
    - `PRC_HCG_NewLoop` → begin the next `AnaFaceTrimLoop` (read its `loop_surface_orientation`, repeat).
    - `PRC_HCG_EndLoop` → end of all loops on this face.

In other words `PRC_HCG_NewLoop`/`PRC_HCG_EndLoop` are written *in place of a curve* via `WriteCompressedEntityType(code, bIsACurve=false)`, and that single mechanism delimits both the per-loop curve list and the loop array. This is consistent with Table 232 listing a trailing `curve_is_not_already_stored` Boolean followed by a `type` `CompressedEntityType` of `PRC_HCG_NewLoop`/`PRC_HCG_EndLoop`: the "terminator" is just an ordinary entry whose `CompressedEntityType` is a control code rather than a curve.

```
# ContentCompressedAnaFace (Table 231)
read is_trimmed
if is_trimmed:
    while True:
        read loop_surface_orientation              # AnaFaceTrimLoop (Table 232)
        while True:                                 # curves
            read curve_is_not_already_stored
            if not curve_is_not_already_stored:
                read index (UIntVBN, number_of_bits_to_store_reference bits)   # referenced curve
                continue
            (is_curve, code) = read CompressedEntityType                       # §9.16
            if is_curve:
                read inline curve body (Line / Circle / Hermite / …)
                continue
            break                                   # non-curve code: NewLoop(0) or EndLoop(1)
        if code == PRC_HCG_EndLoop:  # 1
            break
        # else PRC_HCG_NewLoop (0): continue to the next loop
```

### What I've actually verified vs. inferred

- **Verified bit-exact** on several small CAD PRCs (smallest is a 112-byte `BrepDataCompress`): the body framing (`ContentBody` → `brep_data_compressed_tolerance` → `number_of_bits_to_store_reference` → vertex/edge reference counts → `single_connex` → `CompressedShell` `single_face`/`number_of_faces`) and the face dispatch (`CompressedEntityType` → `PRC_HCG_*` surface), and the loop reader above correctly consuming a mix of *referenced* and *inline* trim curves on an `AnaPlane` face.
- **Inferred** (from Table 232 + Table 204 + §9.16, not yet observed reaching a clean terminator): the `NewLoop`/`EndLoop` termination, because I haven't yet pinned the inline-curve *bodies* bit-exact — specifically `PRC_HCG_BsplineHermiteCurve` (see #583) and the iso trim-curve form (see #582) — so my reader drifts inside a curve body before it reaches the terminator. The array-*sizing* question, though, looks settled: it's a control-code-terminated stream, with no count to find.

Related: this also lines up with #705 — `is_an_iso_face` is independent of the surface type (an `AnaPlane` can have `is_an_iso_face == TRUE` and thus a `ContentCompressedIsoFace`).

Happy to be corrected if a reference writer does it differently.

Yes, and we would argue fairly strongly for it — with one amendment to CR-10f.

**Why incorporating matters rather than just closing the issue.** The question asked here was where to find the size of the `curves` array. The answer — that there is no size, and the array is terminated by an in-band sentinel — appears nowhere in Tables 231/232 or their prose. If the issue closes without CR-10 the defect survives: the next implementer reads the same tables and asks the same question. Four independent implementations now agree on the mechanism (@socrat74's pseudocode, @ralovich's working `prc-rs`, @t3dr0's CR, and our own bit-level trace posted above), so this is about recording a settled answer, not adjudicating one.

**CR-10a, b, d, e and g we would take as drafted.**

CR-10c is worth calling out as the highest-value single line in the set. Table 232 currently says `curve_is_not_already_stored` is "always TRUE". That is true only of the *sentinel* entry, and a reader implementing it literally mis-parses every referenced curve in every loop. It is not an
ambiguity, it is a statement that produces a wrong reader.

CR-10g is likewise structural rather than editorial, which is easy to miss. `point_on_torus` presence changes bit consumption, so a reader and a writer disagreeing about it desynchronises the stream loudly rather than producing a slightly wrong torus. A field whose presence is derived from three conditions that are not fields of the table it appears in needs exactly the kind of pinning CR-10g gives it.

## The amendment: CR-10f item 5 should be a writer constraint, not only a reader rule

CR-10f sets `all_loops_are_vertex_loops` to FALSE when a curve is retrieved by reference. That is the right call for decidability — a reader genuinely cannot tell whether a referenced curve is degenerate, because its vertices live in another face's data — but as drafted it reads as a
reader-side inference, and its correctness is assumed rather than established.

The failure mode if the assumption is wrong is not subtle. A writer that emits a degenerate vertex loop *by reference* would write `point_on_torus`; a reader following CR-10f would decide the loops are not all vertex loops, skip the field, and desynchronise from that point on.

We can say the shape is not hypothetical. Instrumenting our own derivation across our corpus, of the AnaTorus faces that reach the ana-face path, **12 loops consist entirely of referenced curves** — exactly the case the rule adjudicates. We cannot tell whether any of them is degenerate, and neither can any other reader.

So we would ask for it to be stated as a constraint on writers as well, along the lines of:

> A vertex loop shall be written inline. A curve retrieved by reference shall not constitute a 
> vertex loop.

That converts a reader-side assumption into something readers may rely on, and it costs nothing if no writer was doing it anyway.

## One data point to set expectations

`point_on_torus` appears to have no public instance. Across our corpus we dispatch **96 AnaTorus faces in 18 files** and the field is read **zero** times — of the 40 that reach the ana-face path, 26 are untrimmed and none of the remaining 14 has all-vertex loops (their loops fail on curve count: twelve are all-reference as above, five contain a circle).

That is not an argument against incorporating CR-10 — the specification should be complete and precise regardless of how rare a construct is. It is an argument for not treating the exact presence conditions as field-proven until a conforming writer produces a file that exercises them.
We have asked for one; if anyone reading this has such a file, it would settle both the presence conditions and the referenced-curve question above.

*(Separately: we supplied a `point_on_torus` sample earlier in this thread and @socrat74 reports it decodes with a reserved `PRC_HCG_Ellipse` as its first trim curve. We have not localised that and are not asserting whose reader is at fault — with no public instance of this path, neither is validated on it. Please do not treat that file as a reference.)*

# PRC Specification Change Requests
**Reference specification:** PRC-Spec-Revision-14Nov2025
## CR-6 — Clarify `number_vertex_references` and `number_edge_references` in Table 199

**Section:** §7.9.21.1  
**Table:** Table 199 — `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress`  
**Change type:** Normative clarification — tautological descriptions replaced; dual-cache indexing scheme documented  
**Verification:** Confirmed by @socrat74 and @mvrhel 

### Background

`number_vertex_references` and `number_edge_references` are currently described only by
repeating their own field names in both the table and the section prose. Implementor
testing confirms that these fields do **not** represent the total count of compressed
vertices or edges. They represent the size of the **iso-cache** partition only. The total
compressed vertex (or edge) stream is divided into two logically separate caches:

- **iso-cache:** entities referenced from iso-parametric faces; size = `number_vertex_references` (or `number_edge_references`)
- **ana-cache:** entities referenced from analytic faces; size = total stream count − iso-cache size

Index resolution: for an iso-entity use `cache[point_index]`; for an ana-entity use
`ana_cache[point_index − number_vertex_references]`. The same offset arithmetic applies
to edge references using `number_edge_references`.

### CR-6a — Table 199, row `number_vertex_references`, column Data Description

**BEFORE:**
> (Required) number_vertex_references

**AFTER:**
> (Required) Number of iso-vertices in the compressed brep — the count of vertices
> referenced from iso-faces, forming the iso-vertex cache. This value partitions the
> total compressed vertex population into two sequential caches: iso-vertices occupy
> indices `[0, number_vertex_references − 1]` and ana-vertices occupy the remainder.
> When resolving a `point_index` reference: if the vertex is an iso-vertex, retrieve
> from the iso-vertex cache at `point_index`; if the vertex is an ana-vertex, retrieve
> from the ana-vertex cache at `point_index − number_vertex_references`. See 7.9.21.10.

### CR-6b — Table 199, row `number_edge_references`, column Data Description

**BEFORE:**
> (Required) number_edge_references

**AFTER:**
> (Required) Number of iso-edges in the compressed brep — the count of edges referenced
> from iso-faces, forming the iso-edge cache. This value partitions the total compressed
> edge population into two sequential caches: iso-edges occupy indices
> `[0, number_edge_references − 1]` and ana-edges occupy the remainder.
> When resolving a curve reference: if the edge is an iso-edge, retrieve from the
> iso-edge cache at the stored index; if the edge is an ana-edge, retrieve from the
> ana-edge cache at `stored_index − number_edge_references`. See 7.9.21.9.

### CR-6c — §7.9.21.1 prose, bullet for `number_vertex_references`

**BEFORE:**
> `number_vertex_references` represents the number of referenced vertices in the brep;
> see 7.9.21.10

**AFTER:**
> `number_vertex_references` represents the number of iso-vertices in the compressed
> brep — the size of the iso-vertex cache. The total compressed vertex stream is
> partitioned into an iso-vertex cache of this size followed by an ana-vertex cache for
> the remainder; `point_index` values below this threshold index into the iso-vertex
> cache, and values at or above this threshold index into the ana-vertex cache with the
> threshold subtracted. See 7.9.21.10.

### CR-6d — §7.9.21.1 prose, bullet for `number_edge_references`

**BEFORE:**
> `number_edge_references` represents the number of referenced edges in the brep;
> see 7.9.21.9

**AFTER:**
> `number_edge_references` represents the number of iso-edges in the compressed brep —
> the size of the iso-edge cache. The total compressed edge stream is partitioned by the
> same dual-cache scheme as vertices: iso-edges occupy the lower index range and
> ana-edges occupy the upper range, with `number_edge_references` as the threshold and
> offset. See 7.9.21.9.

### CR-6e — §7.9.21.1, normative note to insert after the bullet list, before Table 199

**INSERT:**

> **NOTE — Dual-cache indexing for compressed vertices and edges.** The compressed brep
> maintains two logically separate caches for each of vertices and edges, distinguished
> by their geometric origin:
>
> - The **iso-cache** holds entities (vertices or edges) that are referenced from
>   iso-parametric faces.
> - The **ana-cache** holds entities referenced from analytic faces.
>
> `number_vertex_references` and `number_edge_references` define the boundary between
> these caches within the single serialised stream. A reader encountering more compressed
> vertices or edges than `number_vertex_references` or `number_edge_references`
> respectively shall not treat the excess as an error: the total count spans both caches.
> Index resolution shall apply the threshold-and-offset rule described in the table above.
> Implementations that treat `number_vertex_references` as the total vertex count will
> fail to index all the ana-vertex references.

## CR-13 — Correct `CompressedPoint` Fallback Encoding and Formalise `WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber`

**Section:** §7.9.21.11 (`CompressedPoint`)
**Tables:** Table 242 (`CompressedPoint`), Table 183 (`PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex`)
**Secondary:** §9 (Bit manipulation procedures — new §9.18 insertion point)
**Change type:** Normative correction (erroneous data type), prose replacement,
procedure formalisation, naming consistency, editorial typo fix
**Verification:** Confirmed by implementor testing (uNbBits 31, 32 observed);
confirmed by §9.14 signature constraint "uBitNumber shall be less than 31";
confirmed by @socrat74

---

### Background and Root Cause Analysis

`CompressedPoint` stores a 3D point using a variable-precision scheme. A 6-bit
`uNbBits` field determines which of two encoding paths is taken:

**Path A — `uNbBits ≤ 30` (variable-bit integer encoding):**
Each coordinate is written via `WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber` (§9.14), encoding
it as one sign bit + `(uNbBits − 1)` bits for the quantised absolute value. The
reader reconstructs: `coord = integer_value × dTol`, where
`dTol = brep_data_compressed_tolerance / 100`. Three such calls for x, y, z constitute
`WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber`, a procedure already drafted for §9.

**Path B — `uNbBits > 30` (raw double fallback):**
The §9.14 signature states "uBitNumber **shall be less than 31**", confirming
`WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber` is not called in this path. Instead, each
coordinate is written using `WriteDouble` (§9.17). Implementor testing confirms that
for uNbBits 31 and 32, three `WriteDouble`/`ReadDouble` values (x, y, z) are present
in the bitstream — no type token, no `BaseTopology`, no tolerance field.

**The spec's claim that the fallback stores `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex` is incorrect.**
`PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex` (Table 183) is a full topology structure comprising:
a `UnsignedInteger` type token, a `BaseTopology` (with has_base, optional attributes,
name, and id), a `Vector3D` vertex position, and a `has_tolerance`/`tolerance` pair.
None of this structure appears in the bitstream for `uNbBits > 30`. The confusion
likely arose because `UniqueVertex` internally stores a `Vector3D` (3 doubles), and
the fallback path also writes 3 doubles — but the surrounding structure is entirely
absent.

**`WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber` has been drafted** for inclusion in §9 but is
not yet present in the Nov 2025 revision. It encapsulates three sequential calls to
`WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber` for x, y, z with shared `uNbBits` and `dTol`.
Its formalisation into §9 resolves the current state where `Point3DWithVariableBitNumber`
is used as a data type in multiple tables (242, 223, and compressed curve tables) with
no corresponding procedure definition.

**Three naming variants** of this type exist in the current document, all referring to
the same concept:

| Variant | Occurrences | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `Point3DWithVariableBitNumber` | 4 | Canonical — consistent with §9 naming convention |
| `Point3DwithVariableBitNumber` | 4 | Inconsistent casing (lower `w`) |
| `Point3DWithVarBitNumber` | 2 | Abbreviated form — does not match procedure name |

All non-canonical variants should be unified to `Point3DWithVariableBitNumber`.

### CR-13e — Insert New Subsection §7.9.21.11.1 — CompressedPoint Read/Write Algorithm

**7.9.21.11.1 Read/Write Algorithm for CompressedPoint**

The following algorithms define the normative encoding and decoding of a
`CompressedPoint`. `brep_data_compressed_tolerance` is the tolerance field of the
enclosing `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress` structure (Table 199, §7.9.21.1).

```
PROCEDURE WriteCompressedPoint(x, y, z : Double;
                                brep_data_compressed_tolerance : Double):

  dTol ← brep_data_compressed_tolerance / 100
  uMaxCoordinate ← MAX(|x|, |y|, |z|) / dTol + 1
  uNbBits ← GetNumberOfBitsToStore(uMaxCoordinate) + 1

  -- uNbBits is always written as a 6-bit unsigned integer (values 0–63)
  WriteUnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber(uNbBits, 6)

  IF uNbBits > 30 THEN
    -- Fallback: uNbBits exceeds WriteDoubleWithVariableBitNumber constraint.
    -- Write each coordinate as a full PRC double (§9.17).
    WriteDouble(x)
    WriteDouble(y)
    WriteDouble(z)
  ELSE
    -- Compressed path via WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber (§9.18).
    WritePoint3DWithVariableBitNumber(x, y, z, dTol, uNbBits)
  END IF

END PROCEDURE


PROCEDURE ReadCompressedPoint(brep_data_compressed_tolerance : Double)
                               → (x, y, z : Double):

  dTol ← brep_data_compressed_tolerance / 100

  -- Read the 6-bit uNbBits field
  uNbBits ← ReadUnsignedIntegerWithVariableBitNumber(6)

  IF uNbBits > 30 THEN
    -- Fallback path: read three raw PRC doubles (§9.17).
    -- No type token. No topology structure.
    x ← ReadDouble()
    y ← ReadDouble()
    z ← ReadDouble()
  ELSE
    -- Compressed path via ReadPoint3DWithVariableBitNumber (§9.18 inverse).
    (x, y, z) ← ReadPoint3DWithVariableBitNumber(dTol, uNbBits)
  END IF

  RETURN (x, y, z)

END PROCEDURE
```

**Key behaviours implementors shall observe:**

1. All values of `uNbBits > 30` (i.e. 31 through 63) are equivalent: all take the
   `ReadDouble` fallback path. The specific stored value carries no further meaning.
2. `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_UniqueVertex` (Table 183) is never written or read as part of
   `CompressedPoint`. The two structures are unrelated despite both containing
   3-coordinate point data.
3. `dTol` is `brep_data_compressed_tolerance / 100`, not
   `brep_data_compressed_tolerance` directly.

Looking into the history of this a little further, it seems that the Parent entry in widget annotation dictionaries was only introduced in version 1.7. This raises the question:

- in the table 191 entry for Parent, should "(Required ...; optional otherwise)"   be changed to "(Required ...; optional otherwise; PDF 1.7)"

To me, the most obvious solution would be for the wording of the standard to reflect the reality that most widget annotation dictionaries are intentionally merged with a field dictionary. For the remainder, nobody can tell whether they are or are not - it depends whether you interpret the Parent entry as belonging to the widget or to an unnamed field.

So, why not just delete the Parent entry from table 191 and stipulate that the content of a widget annotation dictionary shall be merged with a field dictionary?

>So, why not just delete the Parent entry from table 191 and stipulate that the content of a widget annotation dictionary shall be merged with a field dictionary?

Because that would throw away a PDF feature which is in use. Why would anyone want to do that?

> Because that would throw away a PDF feature which is in use. 

Which feature would it throw away? If you look at a real widget dictionary, how do you tell whether the Parent entry is a table 191 Parent or a table 226 Parent?

To expand on my previous reply, let us look at the section 12.7.5.2.4 (Radio buttons) example:


```
10 0 obj                        %Radio button field
    <</FT /Btn
      /Ff …                     %…Radio flag = 16, Pushbutton = 17 …
      /T (Credit card)
      /V /cardbrand1
      /Kids [11 0 R 12 0 R]
    >>
endobj

...

12 0 obj                        % Second radio button
    <</Type /Annot
      /Subtype /Widget
      /Rect [100 100 120 120]
      /Parent 10 0 R
      /AS /Off
      /AP <</N <</cardbrand2 8 0 R
                 /Off 9 0 R
               >>
         >>
    >>
endobj
```

How can we tell whether the object 12 Parent entry is a table 191 Parent or a table 226 Parent? We can't tell by looking at object 12, and we can't tell by looking at the Kids entry of object 10, since under one interpretation object 12 is an actual widget annotations while under the second interpretation object 12 contains a field dictionary that according to section 12.7.4.2 (Field names) shall be considered a widget annotation. 

How can having two different interpretations for a single actual object add an additional feature that can be lost by selecting one of the interpretations? To my mind, having two alternate interpretations only  adds at best unnecessary complexity and confusion and at worst subtle inconsistencies in how different programs process the object depending on which interpretation each chooses.

> Which feature would it throw away? 

If you stipulate that the widget annotation dictionary always shall be merged with its parent field dictionary you make all implementations invalid that currently create two dictionaries.

Beside this it wouldn't help you with your example from 12.7.5.2.4 . There you have one field dictionary (10 0 obj) with two widget annotations as kids (12 0 obj is *not* a field dictionary as it has no **FT** key). What would you want to merge here? In general I believe you're over-thinking this, but - specifically - this is a table 191 parent because that object is *not* a combined widget/field - it is a widget only. It does not have the required `FT` key to make it compliant with table 226. 

If was a combined field? In that case, it doesn't matter because both in interpretations lead to the same result, assuming everything else is structured correctly. There's a note to this effect in 12.5.6.19

> This presents no ambiguity, since the contents of the two kinds of dictionaries do not conflict.

The main issue is there are two ways of determining the "truth": traverse down from the form through the fields to determine which fields exist, or traverse up from the page widgets to determine the fields that apply to each widget. If those two views don't align, the results depend on how the software has repaired the PDF.

However if those views do align and the structure is internally consistent then everything does work and there's no ambiguity. It certainly could have been done better, but the time to propose breaking changes to how this works was 20 years ago.

> To me, the most obvious solution would be for the wording of the standard to reflect the reality that most widget annotation dictionaries are intentionally merged with a field dictionary. 

Disagree. "Most" is subjective - and it's an implementation decision. Both approaches are valid.

> in the table 191 entry for Parent, should "(Required ...; optional otherwise)" be changed to "(Required ...; optional otherwise; PDF 1.7)"

The main underlying issue here is an issue in ISO 32000-1. There are the trees of dictionaries spanned by the **Kids** arrays starting with the document's root fields. These dictionaries can be field dictionaries (without or with merged widgets) or pure widgets (not merged into fields). But there is no clear criterion telling us for an arbitrary such dictionary whether it is a field or a pure widget.

One can consider all of those dictionaries to be field dictionaries.

Or one can apply restrictions. For example, the Field Names section can be interpreted to imply that non-terminal field dictionaries need to have **T** name entries.

In the context of your question, the observed Acrobat behavior is reasonable if Acrobat follows that very example restriction: In [signed-child.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24193109/signed-child.pdf) the dictionary in object 3 has no name. Thus, it cannot be a non-terminal field. Thus, it cannot have fields in **Kids**. Thus, its kid dictionary in object 4 cannot be a field dictionary. Thus, the field-ish entries in dictionary 4 (like its **V** value) must be ignored.

Beware, though, if you add a **T** name to object 3, Acrobat will change its behavior but not to what you expect. This most likely is due to Acrobat applying more restrictions to signature fields than can be derived from the spec alone to prevent certain types of misuse of signature fields.

Remember that Arlington is just a data model of the PDF DOM, not an implementation: it is about syntactical correctness that encodes basic data integrity relationships as defined by ISO 32000-2. It is not about functional correctness, functional behavior, or content/data validation. It is also a work in progress...

The question for RTL documents is whether a file-format change is needed, or processor advice. I'm very much of the opinion this should be processor advice, for several reasons.

Text in PDF "naturally" progresses left-to-right, owing to the advance for each glyph being a postive number - the "Width" array is defined as specifying the "glyph width for the character code", which is directionless: a negative width doesn't make sense, and wouldn't be allowed in PDF/A or PDF/UA anyway as the value has to match the value in the font, which is always positive.

So that's why a run of RTL text is typically drawn onto the page reversed, starting from left to right. There is a facility within PDF to specify text direction for a run of glyphs - specifically the `/ReversedChars BMC` marked content sequence defined in 14.8.2.5.3, which can be wrapped around the span - but this has no effect on layout. And `/ActualText` can be specified as well.

However: a processor can still process arabic (for example) very well by identifying the intrinsic direction for each glyph based on the Unicode value.. Just to call one out, Acrobat does this already - select a block or arabic text and the selection proceeds right-to-left, with the text extracted in logical order. To my surprise it even converted the shaped-forms of the glyphs back to the nominal forms in the U+600 range when copying! This happens with, or without a `/ReversedChars BMC` wrapping the text, and doesn't require a language code on the document.

So I think processor guidance to this effect is a great idea, but I wouldn't support file format changes suggesting glyphs have to be added in logical order on the page: you could do this with lots of negative kerning between glyphs, but this would very likely break most text extraction tools so would be a huge own goal. And as the described behaviour of Acrobat shows, it's not necessary.

Other points:

**Re: requiring that order of real content like tables etc. is in logical order**, i.e. right-to-left for RTL languages, I completely agree - and fortunately this is already a requirement for PDF/UA, which states content SHALL be in logical order.

**Re: the WritingMode attribute**; this is an interesting one. From the spec, it "Indicates the directions of layout progression inside Block Level Structure Elements". It does **not** indicate direction for glyphs within an inline span - that's inferred from the glyphs. So for your example showing the use of WritingMode in the word document you attached, WritingMode there has no effect: the two elements it applies to have no internal blocks.

In fact, because layout in PDF is fixed (unlike HTML) and because content already has to be laid out in logical order for PDF/UA, it's a fairly useless attribute: within a list item, *logically* the list bullet will always come first; whether it's *physically* on the page to the left or right of the content isn't controlled by WritingMode, it's fixed when the application puts the content onto the file.

It is unfortunate that the default value of the "WritingMode" attribute is set to "LrTb" - ideally it would be "auto, depends on the language, defaults to LrTb if no language is set". Maybe we should change this.

Thank you very much for this detailed and thoughtful explanation.
Your points are extremely helpful, and I fully agree with several of the clarifications you made—especially regarding glyph widths and the fact that PDF’s rendering model is intrinsically LTR.

However, the issue I am raising is specifically about assistive technology behavior, not visual layout or extraction in Acrobat.

Acrobat indeed performs excellent internal bidi and logical-order reconstruction when copying or visually selecting text.
The problem, however, is that: •	Screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, Narrator)
	•	PDF viewers (Edge, Chrome, Firefox, Foxit)
	•	Accessibility APIs on Windows, macOS, and Linux do not replicate Acrobat’s internal heuristics.
They rely strictly on the logical structure, reading order, and the character sequence in the content stream.

So while Acrobat succeeds, the wider accessibility ecosystem fails, even for PDFs that are “formally valid.”

In addition, Acrobat itself is not immune in authoring scenarios.
When exporting Arabic PDF/UA files through the official Acrobat add-in for Microsoft Word, the visual text is correct, but the logical structure tree contains reversed Unicode sequences.

This means that paragraphs, list items, labels, table cells, and spans may look visually correct, but inside the structure tree the characters appear in reverse order.
Acrobat’s accessibility tree then exposes these reversed strings to the operating system’s accessibility APIs, causing: •	NVDA to read reversed
	•	JAWS to read reversed
