I would like to summarize the proposed solution in a form that is low-impact, backward-compatible, and aligned with the consensus emerging in this discussion. The goal is to preserve enough bidirectional (bidi) semantics so that logical text can be reliably reconstructed for assistive technologies and text extraction, while avoiding disruptive changes to the PDF content model.

 

1) Introduce an explicit primary direction marker for glyph runs

 

Add a mechanism to express the base reading direction of a text run, analogous to HTML’s 'dir' attribute or Unicode bidi isolation/override controls. For example:

 

   /RTL BMC … EMC

   /LTR BMC … EMC

 

or using a property list:

 

   /Bidi << /BaseDir /RTL >> BDC … EMC

   /Bidi << /BaseDir /LTR >> BDC … EMC

 

Semantics:

This marker informs processors of the intended logical direction of the enclosed text for accessibility, extraction, and logical reconstruction—without imposing any requirements on visual layout or painting order.

 

2) Support bidi nesting levels via extended /ReversedChars semantics (preferred approach)

 

Extend the definition of /ReversedChars to allow reconstruction of nested bidi contexts:

 

   • Permit nested /ReversedChars spans.

   • Define that each nested level toggles the reversal, enabling embedding-level recovery.

   • Remove or relax the current restriction that the span cannot contain more than one space.

 

Rationale:

In mixed RTL/LTR content, especially where English quotes Arabic which quotes English, the original embedding levels cannot be recovered from glyph order alone because Unicode directional controls are not preserved in PDF. Nested /ReversedChars with defined toggling semantics provides a lightweight and deterministic way to restore those levels.

 

3) Clarify processing expectations for Tagged PDF and PDF/UA

 

For tagged PDF and PDF/UA conformance, processors should interpret /BaseDir or nested /ReversedChars semantics when constructing logical text for:

 

   • accessibility APIs,

   • reflow,

   • text extraction,

   • and screen-reader output.

 

This addresses the long-standing gap where text appears visually correct but is semantically unreadable for RTL users in the accessibility tree.

 

Conclusion:

 

This proposal preserves full backward compatibility, avoids changes to glyph painting behavior, and adds just enough semantic information for reliable bidi reconstruction—addressing the core issue identified in this discussion.

Why did you say that nesting extended /ReversedChars semantics is a preferred approach? 

I think nesting of `/ReversedChars` means more complexity and effort for all implementations to maintain a stack (so slow industry adoption), more complexity for reused Form XObjects (to make sure all referring instances have the correct number of nested `/ReversedChars` before every **Do** operator), difficulties when reusing partial content (as the stack is lost), and difficulties when editing PDFs when just some content streams are rewritten. And PDF software that doesn't support this enhancement will likely damage content when rewriting.

The advantage of a new marked content sequence tag is that it can be absolute (as you show above) so it can be understood in isolation (such as copying an isolated XObject to a new doc), and most existing PDF software will retain custom marked content sequences they don't understand so its (more) immune from being damaged. MCSes have always been designed to be extensible.

Let's use the "The title is AN INTRODUCTION TO C++ in Arabic." example you noted, lets say it all fits on one line, and the input was in a single string.

```
The title is AN INTRODUCTION TO C++ in Arabic.       <- the input
0000000000000111111111111111111122200000000000       <- the nesting levels

The title is C++ OT NOITCUDORTNI NA in Arabic        <- the visual layout
(The title is C++ OT NOITCUDORTNI NA in Arabic) Tj   <- how it might be stored in PDF (simplified!)
```
That's our starting position - what we have in the PDF is a String representing the visual layout. Our task is to convert that back to the original input so it can be passed to a screen reader.

We know the unicode value for each glyph - it's PDF/UA of course - so we can determine the strong direction for each glyph, and from there a level - 0 for LTR, 1 for RTL. If you do text extraction in any PDF tool (we tested Acrobat, Foxit, Chrome, Firefox and our own) that's how it works - ReversedChars is ignored, it's the strong direction of the character that matters. That's good! But it's not enough on it's own, because if we then reverse those sequences to try and reassemble the original input, it's incorrect
```
The title is C++ OT NOITCUDORTNI NA in Arabic        <- the input
000000000000000001111111111111111110000000000        <- the nesting level

The title is C++ AN INTRODUCTION TO in Arabic        <- the output (incorrect)
```
The ICU toolkit comes with a "reverse Bidi" and this is exactly the result you'll get with it if you remove any directional override characters from the input.

If we just look at the tagged PDF samples, there is a real mixed bag of approaches to how they're constructed:
* All of the samples add marked-content sequences to the structure tree in logical order.
* Only some of the samples write the marked-content sequences to the page in the same order they are in the tree - _logical structure order_ (ISO32000-1 14.8.2.3) or _logical content order_ (ISO32000-2 14.8.2.5) usually differs from _page content order_.
* Chrome puts the glyphs within a marked-content sequence on the page in logical order; everyone else uses visual order.
* Some tools write directional format characters to the stream, some do not.
* Some tools use ActualText to specify the text, some do not.
* Some tools create a ToUnicode with only "nominal" characters in the U+6xx range, others also use the presentation forms
* The only time /ReversedChars is used, it's used incorrectly.

So that's where we're at. I think this is the important bit:

> We agree that additional processor and creator guidance could be of huge value and would be open to the development of such content.

I have some ideas. Clearly there are many ways to create a PDF and we can't be too prescriptive. And I'm only thinking of tagged content for accessiblity: for any other reuse requirements like reflow, we'll need a way to determine Bidi nesting levels. Let's skip that for now.

For PDF creators:
1. The _logical content order_ must be correct - already specified in PDF/UA, just restating to underline the point!
2. Within a marked-content sequence, do not mix content with different "bidi nesting levels" (as defined in the Unicode Bidi algorithm).
3. If a marked-content sequence logical order does not match the physical order the glyphs are put on the page, then its entire text content shall be wrapped with `/ReversedChars BMC ... EMC`. Don't use this sequence for any other reason and do not apply it to a partial marked-content sequence. Such a marked-content sequence shall not span more than one line.

Most of the tagged PDF samples meet 1 and 2 already. None meet 3, but it's the correct thing to do according to 32000. Point 2 is the important one.

For PDF consumers:
1. Marked-content sequences must be extracted based only on _logical content order_ and not _page content order_.
2. Any arabic presentation forms are converted back to the nominal forms, and any U+0640 characters are ignored. If directional override characters exist they can be extracted, but as they're not spoken it doesn't matter for screen-readers.
3. (the strict option) - within a marked-content sequence, reverse any sequence wrapped in `/ReversedChars`, being sure to not to reverse the order of non-spacing marks so they continue to apply to the preceding character.

alternatively

3. (the pragmatic option) - If a marked-content-sequence contains R2L glyphs, ignore `/ReversedChars` and don't make any assumptions about the order of the glyphs in the stream: they should be extracted in visual order (i.e. taking into account kerning or text-matrix operations) and then reversed to put them into logical order. Again, with the strict option, be sure not to reverse the order of non-spacing marks.

I see point 1 as simply restating the requirement in PDF/UA - there is no requirement in 32000 or 14289 that the two orders SHALL agree, and the term "page content order" is not used in PDF/UA, which only requires that content is in the tree "in a logical reading order" and text "shall be tagged in logical reading order" (UA1), or that the "logical content order (14.8.2.5) ... shall be correct" (UA2). But if anyone wants a simple test, open [order-test.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25900628/order-test.pdf): extraction in logical order should read "logical order".

Point 2 should also be uncontroversial. Is the U+0640 "Tatweel" used for anything other than justificaiton in arabic?

The pragmatic option point 3 would mean all but one of the samples seen so far could be correctly derived back to their original input text for accessibilty. The strict option for point 3 agrees with the wording of ISO32000, but it means none of the samples seen so far could be derived properly.

That part of 7.3.3.1 now looks like:

PDF is no longer primarily a “portable desktop document” format. It is widely used as an internet-distributed document format and consumed by search engines, compliance tooling, digital preservation systems, and automated processing pipelines.

In these contexts, the inability to reliably identify and interpret internet-related content embedded in PDFs represents a significant interoperability and trust limitation.

This issue does not propose a specific technical solution or mandate changes to ISO 32000-2, but aims to highlight a structural gap and initiate discussion on whether a more internet-aware content representation would be beneficial.

Additional empirical confirmation (POC findings)

As a follow-up to the issue description, we have conducted a practical investigation using multiple PDF processing libraries and toolkits, including commercial and open-source solutions (e.g. Apryse SDK, pdf-lib, pdfjs-dist, Adobe PDF Services).

The following limitations were consistently observed across all tested tools:

1. Internet-related entities in PDF content are structurally invisible  
URLs, domain names, and email addresses embedded as plain text carry no semantic metadata and are indistinguishable from arbitrary text strings at the content level. Reliable extraction requires heuristic approaches such as regex matching or layout analysis, which are inherently fragile and context-dependent.

2. Hyperlink annotations are the only standardized mechanism — and they are insufficient  
Internet references are represented only via link annotations (/Link with /URI actions), which exist at the annotation layer rather than as part of the content stream. Many real-world PDFs contain visible URL text without corresponding link annotations, while link annotations may exist without visible text anchors.

3. Internal references dominate over external internet references  
Analysis of real-world PDFs shows that most link annotations represent internal cross-references (e.g. /GoTo actions), while externally visible URLs in content are often not implemented as clickable hyperlinks by authoring tools.

4. No native mechanism for inventory, validation, or governance  
There is no PDF-level structure to enumerate, validate, or govern internet-related entities. Building a reliable inventory requires combining annotation parsing, text extraction, pattern matching, and potentially OCR.

5. Tooling confirms the gap, not the solution  
Despite mature and capable PDF SDKs, none can overcome the fundamental limitation that internet-related entities are not first-class content objects in the PDF specification.

These findings suggest that the limitation described in this issue is not a tooling deficiency, but a structural characteristic of the current PDF content model.

Thank you for the thoughtful response — this distinction between generator behavior and the specification is exactly the point worth clarifying.

I agree that deficiencies in PDF generators play a role. However, the limitation described here is not limited to generators failing to create link annotations. The deeper issue is that the PDF content model provides no normative way to represent internet-related entities (such as domain names, URLs, or email addresses) as identifiable content elements independent of annotations.

Annotations are currently the only standardized mechanism, but they operate at an overlay/interaction layer rather than as part of the content stream itself. This means that even well-formed PDFs can legitimately contain internet-related information in content that is structurally indistinguishable from arbitrary text, without violating the specification.

Because the specification does not define a content-level concept for “internet-related entities”, generators have no interoperable target to emit, and consumers have no reliable structure to read. Any alternative marking today would be proprietary, heuristic, or viewer-specific.

The concern raised in this issue is therefore not that generators fail to do what the specification already defines, but that the specification itself does not provide a content-level construct that generators could consistently use.

At this stage, I am not proposing a specific mechanism or extension, nor asserting that the content model must be changed. The intent is to clarify whether the current model intentionally excludes such concepts, or whether this represents an area where guidance, clarification, or future exploration might be beneficial.

If it is helpful, I would be glad to narrow the discussion further to specific aspects of the content model that may be relevant, but my primary goal here is to establish whether this limitation is understood as a tooling issue alone, or as a structural characteristic of the current specification.

Yes, it is understood (and expected) that PDFs may legitimately contain completely untagged content, and **that this is expected to remain the case**. The intent here is explicitly not to forbid or constrain such use cases, nor to require tagging as a baseline.

The question we are trying to explore is narrower and optional in nature:

Given that Tagged PDF (ISO 32000-2, 14.8) and namespace mechanisms (14.7.4) already exist, is there a clearly understood and interoperable way to use these mechanisms to *optionally* express internet-related semantics at the structure/content level — when authors choose to do so?

In practice, what we observe today is that:
- **internet-related information often appears in content without annotations,**
- tagging is frequently absent or inconsistent,
- and there is little shared guidance on whether (or how) existing structure elements, roles, or namespaces could be used to convey internet-related semantics in a machine-readable way.

So the remaining question for us is not “should untagged content be disallowed” (it should not), but rather:
- whether the existing mechanisms are considered sufficient and merely under-documented for this use case, or
- whether additional clarification, examples, or guidance would be beneficial to support authors and tool vendors who *do* want to express such semantics.

At this stage, the goal is to better understand the intended design boundaries and existing capabilities, before discussing any new mechanisms.

Yes, Tagged PDF is clearly the intended extensibility mechanism for expressing semantic structure, and in theory it is flexible enough to accommodate internet-related semantics. I also fully agree that page breaks, content stream fragmentation, and mid-URL splits make naïve tagging approaches impractical, and that this quickly becomes a tooling challenge for both producers and consumers.

The point we are trying to surface is precisely the gap between theoretical capability and practical reality:

In real-world document flows, we routinely encounter PDFs that contain internet-related information in many forms — visible content, annotations, actions, metadata, bookmarks, embedded files, scripts — with highly inconsistent or entirely absent tagging. From an extraction and preservation perspective, this results in a fragmented and heuristic-heavy processing model, even when using mature tooling.

So the question we are exploring is not whether Tagged PDF *can* be extended in theory, nor whether untagged content should be restricted (it should not), but rather:

- whether there is sufficient shared guidance on ***when** and **how*** existing mechanisms are intended to be used for internet-related semantics,
- and whether optional clarification, examples, or profiles could help reduce ambiguity for tool vendors and content producers who want to do better.

In other words, the challenge we see is less about defining new capability, and more about bridging the gap between specification-level possibility and interoperable, scalable practice.

Hello everyone,

I would like to contribute to this discussion by sharing a recent experience that led me to reconsider the role of the PDF format. Historically, PDF established itself primarily as a standard for graphical consistency and print fidelity. Its core function has long been to ensure that what is designed on screen is reproduced identically, regardless of device or operating system. This visual stability has traditionally defined its purpose, almost its reason for existing.

A seemingly trivial exchange with my neighbor, however, shifted my perspective. He pointed out that my tree was particularly tall, which is true, and raised the possibility that, in the event of a storm, it might fall onto his house. An uncertain scenario, yet far from insignificant from a legal standpoint. He then asked a simple question: “Are you insured for that?”

The conventional response would have been predictable: contact the insurance company, review the contract, navigate the often complex structure of the insurer’s website, interpret technical clauses, and cross-check general and specific conditions. In other words, move through a fragmented informational environment that is frequently opaque and invariably time-consuming.

I chose a different approach. I neither contacted my insurer nor consulted my contract. I simply asked ChatGPT.

This apparently mundane action confronted me with a broader intuition: a silent transformation in our relationship to documents and information is underway.

What is changing here is not merely a usage pattern, but a cognitive architecture. The traditional web operates on a logic of visible navigation: pages, menus, hierarchies, links. The user must locate, select, and interpret. Conversational systems introduce a different logic: direct interrogation. Information is no longer navigated; it is queried. One no longer “searches through pages,” but instead questions a system that synthesizes, contextualizes, and reformulates.

Within this framework, PDF suddenly appears in a different light. Its global dominance makes it one of the largest reservoirs of structured knowledge: contracts, standards, reports, scientific publications, legal documents, technical manuals. Billions of documents originally designed for human reading are now becoming objects of machine interpretation.

The issue is therefore no longer purely graphical. It becomes epistemic.

A PDF is no longer just a visual container; it is increasingly an operational unit of meaning for AI systems. This shift opens substantial possibilities: simplified access to contractual clauses, extraction of relevant information, connection of dispersed knowledge, and reduction of the cognitive load associated with document navigation.

One can even imagine a near future where the interface itself nearly disappears. No longer screens crowded with options, but discreet, conversational, almost ambient mediation. Information that is not necessarily read, but quietly delivered: “Yes, François, you are insured against tree falls.”

This transition takes us far from the original intention behind PDF. Yet paradoxically, it builds upon its greatest structural strength: stability. Because PDF is already ubiquitous, any internal evolution can generate major systemic effects without requiring visible disruption for users.

A dominant standard that improves does not produce a perceptible revolution; it silently reshapes the infrastructure of the informational world.

Looking toward 2026 and beyond, the most significant evolution of PDF may therefore not be graphical, but semantic: the capacity to clearly expose the structure, status, and context of information in order to reduce interpretative ambiguity for AI systems.

In other words, moving from a format of representation to a format of intelligibility.

Perhaps this is where the next dimension of PDF will emerge.

The shift toward AI-driven document consumption is real, but PDF was never designed to be a “format of intelligibility.” Its core purpose has always been visual fidelity, ensuring the document looks the same everywhere.

Today, AI systems can extract meaning from PDFs, but they do so mostly through heuristics and reconstruction, not because the format exposes that meaning in a structured way.

So the key question isn’t whether PDF should become an intelligent format, but whether its existing semantic features (like Tagged PDF) can move from optional and rarely used, to something consistently implemented in real-world documents. That is where practical change would actually happen.

Well said, @jasonung-recover. This is a clear and grounded perspective that brings the discussion back to the real design intent of PDF.

The strength of your comment is that it separates vision from reality: AI may change how documents are consumed, but the PDF format itself was built for visual reliability, not semantic intelligence. Expecting it to behave like a natively structured, web-style or AI-optimized format overlooks its original purpose and constraints.

Your point about focusing on consistent use of existing semantic mechanisms, rather than redefining the entire format, is especially important. In practice, adoption and implementation discipline will likely matter far more than any new theoretical capability.

We are facing a fundamental challenge in the digital world:
**our documents are readable for humans—but largely meaningless for machines.**

PDFs, one of the most widely used formats globally, still lack a true semantic foundation. Links, references, and data points are often just visual elements—without structure, context, or long-term reliability.

Your current worked PDF examples use 1st-class names, not 2nd-class names for entries in existing dictionaries. As explained throughout ISO 32000 and in ISO 32000-2:2020, Annex E this is **NOT** OK. Vendor extensions always need to use registered prefixes to avoid collisions (think of the prefix as "namespacing" things). Once inside a prefixed dictionary then you can no longer need to include your developer extension prefix, since you are "namespaced" by the top entry. But it is critical you fix this to comply with PDF for entries in existing dictionaries!

Also your proposal does not address the fact that PDF Actions are _trees_ (see NOTE 1 below Table 196) and thus there can be mulitple URIs for anywhere an action is allowed. Furthermore, your definition and explanations only focus on page content and do not address other important PDF features authors may create and users may depend on, where _actionable_ URI/URN/URLs can exist - such as in outlines, annots, Catalog OpenAction, portfolios, etc. Each of these can be a tree and multiple nodes in a tree can be URI Actions (there is no restriction). Using URI Actions for outline items is a practice in several important document classes I am aware of. By associating your metadata with a URI action EVERY actionable URI/URN/URL in a PDF would have associated metadata. 

Your proposal also doesn't address non-actionable URI/URN/URLs that can also be in PDFs, such as XMP, JPEG EXIF/IPTC, non-actioned page content (very common in secure enclave documents where every URL by policy is "disarmed" (e.g. changes "https" to "hxxps" or similar), in some annotations (since most annotation subtypes don't support it - but that doesn't mean the URI is not there), embedded files, etc. I know some archival institutions already do deep URI/URL audits, but your proposal doesn't address this situation and is "less" than these current practices.

I hope we can find some time to discuss during the London PDF TWG.

@petervwyatt — many thanks for the detailed technical review and the invitation to discuss in London. All three points are well-taken; brief response on each below, with the substantive technical discussion deferred to the TWG session.

**Quick scope note before the three points.** SDL is a general element-level data binding mechanism with 25 standard DataTypes covering tables, charts, formulas, code, financial records, patent claims, and so on. The `/Link` DataType and the companion LinkMeta proposal address Issue #725 specifically, and that's clearly the lens of your review — fair enough, since this is #725. Two of your three points apply to that lens specifically; the first applies SDL-wide.

**1. First-class vs. second-class names (Annex E).** You're right, and this is on us to fix before anything else goes out. The current worked examples place entries on existing standard dictionaries (Catalog, Table 176, others) as first-class names — that does not comply with ISO 32000-2:2020 Annex E for vendor extensions. Corrective steps: register a developer prefix with the PDF Association, and revise the TechnicalSpec, the LinkMeta proposal, and all worked PoC PDFs accordingly. Keys *inside* the new prefixed dictionaries can remain unprefixed since they are namespaced by the parent. Editorial pass to follow in the next minor revisions.

Thank you for taking the time to review the material, @mkl-public — and also for the thoughtful comments.

Your point regarding COS syntax close to the actual URL is completely understandable, and we discussed this internally as well. For the simple hyperlink use case, embedding metadata directly near the URI action can indeed feel more natural and lightweight.

The reason we moved toward a more generalised SDL/DataDef approach is mainly architectural consistency across many different semantic object types. Hyperlinks are only one category. The same mechanism is intended to support tables, charts, formulas, code blocks, datasets, identifiers, references, and other machine-readable bindings. From that perspective, introducing a single reusable semantic binding mechanism seemed preferable to adding custom COS extensions separately to each PDF object type.

That said, we do not necessarily see these approaches as mutually exclusive. A lightweight COS-adjacent representation for simple link metadata could coexist with a more generic SDL/DataDef model for richer semantic bindings.

Your point regarding preservation of intentionally variable or dynamic content is also extremely important — and we fully agree.

The preservation layer is not intended to blindly archive every referenced resource. The idea is rather to support explicit provenance and preservation policies depending on context and intent. Some links represent immutable scholarly references where reproducibility is important; others intentionally point to evolving live systems ("current weather", stock prices, dashboards, APIs, etc.). In those cases, preserving a snapshot as an authoritative replacement would indeed be misleading.

One direction we are exploring is allowing preservation semantics to be explicitly declared, e.g.:

* live reference
* point-in-time snapshot
* archival preservation
* reproducible citation
* version-aware reference

So preservation would become policy-driven rather than automatic.

Regarding data consistency between visual content and parallel semantic data: we absolutely agree this is one of the central challenges.

Our assumption is not that SDL magically guarantees correctness. Rather, SDL attempts to make semantic bindings explicit, inspectable, and machine-verifiable instead of relying entirely on heuristics and inference from visual rendering alone.

The ZUGFeRD / Factur-X comparison was mainly intended to illustrate that the industry already accepts parallel machine-readable representations inside PDF ecosystems when there is sufficient value. But we agree with your observation that correctness validation then becomes essential.

This is one reason why provenance, binding definitions, checksums, signatures, and validation tooling play such an important role in the SDL concept. Long-term, we believe semantic consistency validation between visual and machine-readable representations would need to become part of authoring and conformance workflows — similar to accessibility validation or PDF/A validation today.

## SDL update — a general semantic data layer, with hyperlinks as the first demonstrator

Dear all,

Following the London discussion and the subsequent technical feedback, I would like to clarify the overall scope of the **Semantic Data Layer (SDL)** and explain how our implementation work relates to it.

**SDL is not limited to hyperlinks. Hyperlinks are our first showcase, not the boundary of the architecture.**

### 1. The overall objective

Our objective is a general semantic data layer for PDF that can bind machine-readable data to document objects and content.

This includes tables, charts, formulas, code, images, datasets, references, and other document object classes. The architecture should allow these objects to carry explicit meaning, structured values, relationships, provenance, and verification evidence.

The intended result is a document whose visual representation and machine-readable semantics are explicitly connected—not merely a document from which software attempts to reconstruct meaning through extraction heuristics.

SDL does not replace Tagged PDF, annotations, or existing PDF mechanisms. The challenge is to define a coherent semantic model and integrate it correctly with those mechanisms.

### 2. Why hyperlinks are the first showcase

Hyperlinks provide a concrete starting point because their identity, destination, preservation intent, and lifecycle can be demonstrated and tested.

The LinkMeta use case therefore serves two purposes:

- Deliver practical value for persistent references and link preservation.
- Exercise the general SDL architecture through a first object class.

A successful hyperlink demonstrator is an important milestone, but it does not establish that the complete semantic layer has been implemented.

The broader architecture must support other object classes without requiring a disconnected, ad hoc model for each one.

### 3. The common architectural questions

Across object classes, SDL needs consistent answers to several questions:

- **Identity and binding:** Which document object or content region does the semantic data describe?
- **Type and schema:** What does the object represent, and how are its values interpreted?
- **Relationships:** How does it connect to other objects, sources, or document versions?
- **Provenance:** Was the data authored, extracted, inferred, or subsequently enriched?
- **Consistency:** Does the machine-readable representation agree with the visible document?
- **Integrity and trust:** What has been verified, by whom, and what is actually covered by a signature?

For example, a chart may bind to its underlying dataset, a formula to its variables and units, and a table to typed values and their sources. These are different applications of the same architectural objective.

### 4. What LinkID contributes today

The LinkID implementation provides supporting infrastructure: resolver-based resource identity, destination checks, change history, controlled recovery, supported PDF hyperlink conversion, and integration work in Acrobat, Microsoft 365, and browsers.

These capabilities make the hyperlink showcase more concrete. They may also support identities and references used by other SDL object classes.

However, **LinkID platform capabilities are not, by themselves, proof of complete SDL object binding, interoperability, or conformance**. Those require separate implementation and validation.

### 5. How we propose to address the technical feedback

We take the feedback on existing PDF structures, COS syntax, action trees, dynamic resources, and parallel-data consistency seriously.

For hyperlinks, we want to evaluate a lightweight representation close to existing URI actions. This should remain compatible with the general SDL model rather than redefine SDL as a hyperlink-only extension.

Different consumers may need different representations: a PDF viewer handling a reference has different requirements from a data-processing application consuming a table or dataset. The architecture must address those requirements while avoiding ambiguous or contradictory copies of the same information.

Preservation must also remain explicit. Live references, point-in-time snapshots, archival preservation, reproducible citations, and version-aware references must not be treated as interchangeable.

### 6. Proposed next demonstrators and validation

Our next technical milestone should demonstrate **multiple object classes using a consistent semantic binding model**, with hyperlinks as the first completed use case.

The evidence should include:

- Example PDFs and documented bindings.
- Writer, reader, and validation results.
- Checks for agreement between semantic data and visible content.
- Explicit coverage and limitations for each object class.
- Independent producer and consumer testing.

Signature coverage, certification permissions, and PDF/A or PDF/UA conformance must remain separate validation questions. An incremental update alone does not prove them. Our current PDF conversion path rejects signed PDFs rather than claiming signature-preserving conversion.

The **LGEN** PDF developer prefix is registered. Separately, **`linkid:`** is an IANA-registered provisional URI scheme. Neither registration constitutes standardization or endorsement of SDL.

### Feedback requested

We would welcome feedback on:

1. How a reusable semantic binding model can best integrate with existing PDF structures.
2. Which additional object classes should accompany hyperlinks in the next interoperability demonstrator.
3. How consistency, provenance, and validation should be tested across those classes.

**Our goal remains the complete Semantic Data Layer. Hyperlinks are the first practical demonstration of that goal—not its final scope.**

Best regards,  
Christian Nyffenegger

@t3dr0 Ian, could you maybe comment on this?

Let me try to help with a small explanation:

1. `edge_status_array` is `CharacterArray` with "2 bits per character only" — it is written using WriteCharacterArray(pcArray, uCharArraySize, **2**, ...).
2. The spec says each element has flags |= 0x1 for right neighbour and |= 0x2 for left neighbour — i.e. it's a 2-bit bitfield per triangle, stored as a signed char (C char* may be signed).
3. The size of `edge_status_array` is 3 × length(`triangle_face_array`) — matching one entry per triangle edge (3 edges per triangle), not one per triangle.
4. Negative values arise because C char is signed on most platforms, and the Huffman decoder may sign-extend the 8-bit values.

In C and C++, char defaults to a signed char on many systems (such as x86/x64 MSVC and GCC) - I don't know about RUST.

During compilation/execution on the encoder side, an array populated as char* or evaluated using signed mechanics may contain values where the highest bit of its narrow 2-bit footprint is active (e.g., bit value 2 or 3).

When read out by a native Huffman decoder or bit-unpacking structure, if the system unpacks it into an 8-bit or 32-bit signed integer container without a strict bit-mask or custom clipping (& 0x03), the processor applies a sign extension.

Sign-extending a narrow value whose leading active bit is perceived as a sign bit results in values like -1 (which matches 0xFF or all-ones) or -2 (which matches 0xFE).

## CR-14 — Clarify `edge_status_array` Cardinality, Bit Semantics, Value Range, and Signed-Char Artefact in `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_COMPRESSED`
[Revised 26 June 2026]

**Sections:** §7.8.9.3 (Mesh Points and Triangles); §7.8.9 (Table 175)
**Tables:** Table 171 — Mesh Points and Triangles; Table 175 — Description of the
            Data Written to the File
**Change type:** Normative correction and clarification
**Status:** Confirmed — all normative claims below are directly verified against the
            nanoPRC reference implementation (CascadiaVoxel LLC, AGPLv3, https://github.com/mvrhel/nanoPRC), which is a
            working decoder of conforming PRC files.

---

### Background

Issue #727 reports two classes of ambiguity in `edge_status_array`. A reference C
implementation (`prc_decode_compressed_tess.c`) has since been made available and
resolves both classes definitively. Its conclusions are also independently corroborated
by implementor observation of multiple conforming PRC files.

---

### Resolution of Class A — Cardinality

**The array contains exactly T elements, one per triangle.**

The reference decoder indexes `edge_status_array` as:

```c
data->edge_status_array[triangle_count]   // triangle_count = 0, 1, 2, … T−1
```

where `triangle_count` is a sequential loop variable incremented once per decoded
triangle. No stride-3 indexing is used. The parser loads T consecutive values into the
array and the decoder consumes all T, each exactly once.

**Reconciliation with the observed 3× bitstream size.** Multiple implementors have
independently measured that the serialised `CharacterArray` for `edge_status_array`
contains `3T` bytes in the bitstream (i.e. `uCharArraySize = 3T` as written by
`WriteCharacterArray`). The reference decoder is consistent with this: it reads T
elements from what the parser has extracted, meaning the parser selects T of the 3T
serialised bytes. The precise rule by which the parser maps the 3T serialised bytes
onto T decoded values — whether it takes every third byte, or the first T of 3T
consecutive bytes, or some other scheme — is a property of the parser
(`prc_parse_tess.c`), which is not part of the evidence available to this CR. This
remains a **deferred item** (see below) requiring study of the encoder or parser source.

What is not deferred: the semantic content of each decoded element is one 2-bit bitfield
per triangle, as described below.

**The "3 × triangle count" claim in the previous draft of this CR was incorrect and is
withdrawn.**

---

### Resolution of Class B — Bit semantics, value range, and signed-char artefact

**Each element is a 2-bit bitfield encoding the presence of the right and left
neighbours of one triangle:**

```c
element & 0x01   non-zero  →  triangle has a right neighbour
element & 0x02   non-zero  →  triangle has a left neighbour
```
Valid unsigned values are therefore `{0, 1, 2, 3}`. The value `3` (`0x01 | 0x02`)
signifies that both neighbours are present; this is confirmed both by the reference
decoder and by independent implementor observation of conforming files.

**Negative values** (`−1`, `−2`) arise from signed-`char` storage of the 2-bit Huffman
symbols, as described in the previous draft. The mechanism is unchanged and correct:

| 2-bit pattern | Unsigned | Signed `char` (sign-extended) |
|---|---|---|
| `00b` | 0 | 0 |
| `01b` | 1 | +1 |
| `10b` | 2 | **−2** |
| `11b` | 3 | **−1** |

The values `−2` and `−1` carry the same semantics as `2` and `3` respectively.
Masking with `0x03` before testing recovers the correct unsigned interpretation
on all platforms.

---

### Additional correction: stack push order (new finding from reference implementation)

The reference decoder pushes the **right** edge first, then the **left** edge. The
code comment is explicit:

```c
/* The right is first pushed on the stack and then the left is pushed on the stack.
   This is different than described in the spec.
   Unless their stack is not a LIFO stack */
```

Since the traversal stack is LIFO, the left edge is therefore **processed first**. The
spec states that the left triangle is pushed first (implying it is processed last),
which is the opposite order. **The spec is wrong on this point.** The correct normative
statement is:

> When a triangle has both a right and a left unprocessed neighbour edge, the right
> edge shall be pushed onto the stack first and the left edge shall be pushed second.
> Since the stack is last-in-first-out, the left edge is popped and processed before
> the right edge.

This correction is independent of the `edge_status_array` question but is recorded
here as it was discovered during the same analysis.

---

### Deferred item — parser-level 3× mapping

The rule by which the parser converts the 3T serialised `CharacterArray` bytes into T
decoded `edge_status_array` values is not determinable from the decoder source alone.
The following evidence bounds what it must be:

- The decoder reads `edge_status_array[0]`, `[1]`, … `[T−1]` in strict sequence.
- Each value is a 2-bit field with values in `{0,1,2,3}`; value `3` is confirmed
  to occur in practice.
- The serialised array contains 3T bytes.
- The decoder produces correct results from the T-element array it receives.

A conforming parser must therefore produce exactly T values in this array. Whether the
remaining 2T serialised bytes encode additional information (e.g. entering-edge status,
which is always treated and therefore always 0) or are a Huffman encoding artefact
shall be documented in a follow-on CR once encoder source or a formal bitstream
description is available.

### CR-14d — Insert NOTE 1 after the revised paragraph

> **NOTE 1 — Array size and traversal role.** `edge_status_array` contains T elements, one per triangle. Its primary role in traversal is to control which forward edges are pushed onto the stack. When a triangle's element has value 0x00 (neither bit set), no edges are pushed and the traversal stack subsequently drains to empty. A stack-drain is the mechanism by which the decoder detects a ring or strip transition: it calls a seed-triangle builder that reads the next three entries from `points_is_reference_array` as a triple (consuming `points_is_reference_index` += 3 rather than += 1) to determine whether the transition seeds from zero, one, two, or three previously decoded vertices. The four seed types are:

    1. {0,0,0} — three new world-space points (full reboot or initial prologue)
    2. one entry = 1, two = 0 — one bridging reference, two new points
    3. two entries = 1, one = 0 — two bridging references (a previously decoded edge), one new apex
    4. {1,1,1} — three references (pure closure, no new geometry)

>The encoder controls ring and strip boundaries by setting edge_status_array[i] = 0 at the final triangle of each traversal strip.

> the left triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the right is pushed.

**AFTER:**

> If the current triangle has both a right and a left neighbour which are not treated,
> the right edge shall be pushed onto the traversal stack first, and the left edge
> shall be pushed second. Since the stack is last-in-first-out, the left edge is
> thereby popped and processed before the right edge.

> **NOTE — Correction.** Previous editions of this specification stated that the left
> edge was pushed first. This was incorrect; conforming encoders and decoders shall
> use the order stated above.

---
### CR-14g — Traversal phase structure (new note)

Insert a new note, just after 7.8.9.2 Mesh Traversal (existing section, after the two stack-rule bullet points)

> NOTE — Traversal phase structure. The stack rules above produce a three-phase structure that is directly observable in the point_is_a_reference and point_reference_array fields of §7.8.9.3:
(a) Prologue. The initial seed triangle and its immediate strip consist entirely of new vertices (point_is_a_reference = 0 throughout). This phase terminates when the traversal stack first drains to empty.
(b) Steady-state strip. Within a continuous strip, point_is_a_reference alternates between 0 (new apex) and 1 (reference apex), reflecting the zigzag structure of the triangle strip. References in point_reference_array advance sequentially through the previously decoded ring, consuming its vertices in creation order.
(c) Strip transition. When edge_status_array[i] is zero for triangle i, no forward edges are pushed and the stack drains. The decoder then reads the next three consecutive entries of point_is_a_reference as a single triple (advancing the index by 3, not 1) to determine the seed type for the next strip: all-zero (three new vertices), one reference and two new, two references and one new, or all-reference (pure closure). The type of transition encodes the topological relationship between the closing strip and the opening strip — for example, a washer or ring body transitions with two bridging references that form the base edge of the new seed triangle.
A conforming decoder that does not correctly interpret edge_status_array cannot detect phase (c) boundaries. It will misidentify the triple-consumption events as single-consumption events, permanently misaligning all subsequent point_array triple assignments and producing incorrect vertex positions for the remainder of the mesh.

Independent implementation feedback on CR-14, from a from-scratch (no-OCCT) `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_COMPRESSED`
reader plus a 19-file test harness. Two of CR-14's three claims are **confirmed independently**; for
the deferred 3-tuple sub-semantics we have **empirical evidence that it is not a fixed slot
permutation**, which we hope narrows the remaining question.

## Confirming CR-14a / CR-14d — cardinality is 3 × T

Confirmed. Reading the element count from `WriteCharacterArray`'s own stored count (rather than
assuming one element per triangle) yields exactly `3 × len(triangle_face_array)` on every conforming
file we have. Examples from our corpus:

| file | triangles T | `edge_status_array` length | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| (mesh A) | 492 | 1476 | 3.00 |
| (mesh B) | 40  | 120  | 3.00 |

A decoder that allocates `T` elements does indeed misparse everything after this field — we hit
exactly that during development. The "one 2-bit field per **edge** per triangle" model is correct.

## Confirming CR-14b / CR-14e — values, and the signed-char artefact

Confirmed, with a small clarification on where the negatives come from. If the 2-bit symbol is
decoded straight out of the Huffman alphabet (or read with an explicit `& 0x03`), the stored values
are strictly `{0,1,2,3}` and **no negatives ever appear** — the `-2 / -1` are purely a *consumer*
artefact of copying a 2-bit symbol into a signed `char` without masking, exactly as CR-14e states.
We can confirm that `2` (left) and `3` (both) genuinely occur in real data, so masking matters; a
value histogram from mesh A (1476 elements):

```
value:  0      1     2    3
count: 1006   171   32   267
```

Recommend the normative `& 0x03` + the `0x01`=right / `0x02`=left wording as written. Agree.

## The deferred item — the per-triangle 3-tuple → edge correspondence

We tried to pin this down empirically and believe the result is useful even though it is negative.

**Method.** We drive the §7.8.9.2 traversal directly from `edge_status_array`: for each triangle we
push a forward-edge gate **iff** its 2-bit slot is non-zero, sweeping the full space of
interpretations — every assignment of the three slots `[3i], [3i+1], [3i+2]` to (entering edge,
right-forward edge, left-forward edge), both stack push orders, with multi-component seed restart.
Each candidate is scored by the §7.8.9.7 oracle (`origin_array` = bounding-box centre, so a correct
reconstruction's bbox centre coincides with `origin_array`).

**Result.** **No fixed slot permutation reconstructs more than ~70 % of the triangles** on any test
mesh — the gate stack empties well before all `T` triangles are built. Moreover the *best-fitting*
fixed slot order **differs between files** (most commonly `(entering, right, left) = (slot0, slot1,
slot2)`, but other meshes prefer a different permutation), and none exceeds ≈0.68–0.70 coverage.

**Interpretation.** A static positional mapping of the 3-tuple to the three edges cannot be correct:
if it were, one permutation would reconstruct ~100 % on all meshes. The ~30 % of edges where
"push-if-non-zero" fails are the cases where the neighbour across that edge has already been realised
by the traversal — i.e. the per-edge flag's meaning depends on the **running traversal state**
(an EdgeBreaker-style merge/split operation), not on a fixed slot label. In other words, the open
question is really the **operation semantics** of the per-edge flags within the traversal of
§7.8.9.2 — how the right/left flags select among the C/L/E/R/S-type operations and when an edge
references an *existing* vertex — and not merely which slot names which edge.

This is consistent with CR-14's own statement that the sub-semantics "require reference-implementation
study," and we think it sharpens the request: the follow-on CR needs to specify the per-edge
**operation** rule (against running state), after which the slot↔edge labelling follows.

## Offer

We have a from-scratch decoder and a 19-file regression harness (the §7.8.9.7 origin-centre oracle).
We're happy to test any proposed operation-semantics formulation against that corpus and report
coverage / centre-error, or to share minimal annotated dumps (point/edge_status/triangle arrays for
a single-triangle, two-triangle, and fan mesh) if that would help the editing committee.

## Decompression Implementation Outline for Type: `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed`

The following provides a language-agnostic, formal pseudo-code specification for reconstructing triangular mesh geometry and restoring associated surface normal attributes from compressed bitstream data structures. The naming conventions, bit-mask constraints, and evaluation logic follow the structure of ISO 14739-1. Implementations require careful numerical precision and operation order. The pseudocode outline is just that; providing an example structure. Omission of error handling and data structure details is intentional.

---

### 1. Function: `Derive_Normal`

#### Description
This utility function calculates the orthogonal geometric surface normal vector for a given triangular topology defined by three coordinate vertices. The midpoint along the first edge is used to both define the position of the third vertex (during encoding) and compute the surface normal (during decoding). This uses the same midpoint-of-first-edge frame as the geometry reconstruction (O = (V1+V2)/2, cross of the two boundary spans) sharing a single convention.
 It establishes a localized vector space baseline by deriving the cross product between adjacent boundary spans.

#### Pseudo-code
```text
Function Derive_Normal(vertex_1, vertex_2, vertex_3)
    Input:
        vertex_1, vertex_2, vertex_3 : Vector3
    Output:
        normal_vector                : Vector3

    Let midpoint = (vertex_1 + vertex_2) × 0.5
    Let v1 = vertex_2 - vertex_1
    Let v2 = vertex_3 - midpoint
    
    Return CrossProduct(v2, v1)
EndFunction

```

---

### 2. Function: `Normal_Restoration`

#### Description

This procedure parses the `normal_bit_stream` to decode individual vertex or face normal attributes. It utilises an internal runtime historical cache to track previously established normal instances, determining whether an active coordinate must be uniquely computed via angular components or mapped from historical indices using variable-width bit decoding.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function Normal_Restoration(point_index, current_vertex_position_in_tri)
    Input:
        point_index                     : Integer
        current_vertex_position_in_tri  : Integer

    If MustRecalculateNormals is TRUE Then
        ExitFunction
    EndIf

    If normal_coordinate_type is equal to PRC_TESS_NORMAL_PER_FACE Then
        If current_vertex_position_in_tri > 0 Then
            ExitFunction
        EndIf
        Let normal_index_to_use = GetFaceNormalIndex(current_triangle_index)
    Else
        Let normal_index_to_use = GetElementNormalIndex(current_triangle_index, current_vertex_position_in_tri)
    EndIf

    If IsFirstTimeProcessingThisNormal(normal_index_to_use) is TRUE Then
        Let has_multiples = ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
    Else
        If has_multiples is TRUE Then
            Let normal_is_a_reference = ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
        Else
            AddNormalToCache(normal_index_to_use)
            ExitFunction
        EndIf
    EndIf
	   
    If normal_is_a_reference is TRUE Then
        Let max_index = Length(normal_indices) - 1
        Let nbits = BitCount(max_index)
        Let read_index = 0

        For bit_index = 0 To nbits - 1 Do
            Let bit_set = ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
            If bit_set is TRUE Then
                read_index = read_index + (1 LeftShift bit_index)
            EndIf
        EndFor

        Let ref_index = max_index - read_index
        Let existing_index = GetNormalIndexFromCache(ref_index)
        AddNormalToCache(existing_index)
    Else
        Next_Normal()
    EndIf
EndFunction

```

---

### 3. Function: `Next_Normal`

#### Description

Calculates a newly registered coordinate frame vector configuration from raw bitstream components. The local reference matrix ($X, Y, Z$) is adaptively chosen based on inner-product angular variance thresholds. To prevent platform-dependent floating-point truncation variances across different hardware layers, the angular displacements ($\theta, \phi$) are resolved into normalized radians using formal 4-term Taylor Series expansion approximations.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function Next_Normal()
    Output:
        the_new_normal : Vector3

    Let reversed_tri = ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
    Let reversed_x   = ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
    Let reversed_y   = ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)

    Let v1 = Normalize(tri[1] - tri[0])
    Let v2 = Normalize(tri[2] - tri[0])
    Let v3 = Normalize(tri[2] - tri[1])

    Let theta1 = AbsoluteValue(AbsoluteValue(ArcCos(InnerProduct(v1, v2))) - (Constant_PI / 2))
    Let theta2 = AbsoluteValue(AbsoluteValue(ArcCos(InnerProduct(v3, -v1))) - (Constant_PI / 2))
    Let theta3 = AbsoluteValue(AbsoluteValue(ArcCos(InnerProduct(-v2, -v3))) - (Constant_PI / 2))

    If (theta1 < theta2) And (theta1 < theta3) Then
        Let X_norm = v1
        Let Z_norm = CrossProduct(v1, v2)
    Else 
        If theta1 < theta3 Then  
            Let X_norm = v3
            Let Z_norm = CrossProduct(-v3, v1)
        Else
            Let X_norm = -v2
            Let Z_norm = CrossProduct(v2, v3)
        EndIf
    EndIf

    Z_norm = Normalize(Z_norm)
    
    If reversed_tri is TRUE Then
        Z_norm = -Z_norm
    EndIf

    Let Y_norm = CrossProduct(Normalize(Z_norm), X_norm)

    X_norm = Normalize(X_norm)
    Y_norm = Normalize(Y_norm)
    Z_norm = Normalize(Z_norm)

    If reversed_x is TRUE Then
        X_norm = -X_norm
    EndIf
    If reversed_y is TRUE Then
        Y_norm = -Y_norm
    EndIf

    Let bit_scale = (Constant_PI / 2) / ((2 RaisedTo params.normal_angle_bit_count) - 1)
    Let decoded_theta = params.normal_angle_array[normal_angle_index] * bit_scale
    Let decoded_phi   = params.normal_angle_array[normal_angle_index + 1] * bit_scale

    Let cos_theta = CosineTaylor4(decoded_theta)
    Let sin_theta = SineTaylor4(decoded_theta)
    Let cos_phi   = CosineTaylor4(decoded_phi)
    Let sin_phi   = SineTaylor4(decoded_phi)

    Let the_new_normal = (X_norm × (cos_theta × cos_phi)) + 
                         (Y_norm × (sin_theta × cos_phi)) + 
                         (Z_norm × sin_phi)
	
    Return the_new_normal
EndFunction

```
---

### 4. Function: `SineTaylor4`

#### Description

Approximates the sine of an angle near the origin using a 4-term Taylor series expansion. The polynomial evaluation is structured via Horner's Method to maximize intermediate numerical stability and eliminate platform-dependent power-function variations.

#### Constraints and Assumptions
- IEEE 754 Compliance: Floating-point operations must strictly adhere to IEEE 754 precision standards.
- Floating-Point Contraction: Floating-point contractions (such as hardware-level Fused Multiply-Add) shall be explicitly disabled to ensure identical rounding behaviour across platforms. Implementations should enforce `No_FP_Contraction`.
- Input Domain: Designed for localized spatial configurations where the input value is bounded by the interval [0, π/2].

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function SineTaylor4(x)
    Input:
        x   : Double-Precision Floating-Point (64-bit IEEE 754)
    Output:
        res : Double-Precision Floating-Point (64-bit IEEE 754)

    Let x2 = x × x
    
    Let c1 = 1.0 / 6.0
    Let c2 = 1.0 / 120.0
    Let c3 = 1.0 / 5040.0
    
    Let intermediate_1 = c2 - (x2 × c3)
    Let intermediate_2 = c1 - (x2 × intermediate_1)
    Let res = x × (1.0 - (x2 × intermediate_2))
    
    Return res
EndFunction
```
---
### 5. Function: `CosineTaylor4`

#### Description
Approximates the cosine of an angle near the origin using a 4-term Taylor series expansion. The polynomial evaluation is structured via Horner's Method to maximize intermediate numerical stability and eliminate platform-dependent power-function variations.

#### Constraints and Assumptions
- IEEE 754 Compliance: Floating-point operations must strictly adhere to IEEE 754 precision standards.
- Floating-Point Contraction: Floating-point contractions (such as hardware-level Fused Multiply-Add) shall be explicitly disabled to ensure identical rounding behaviour across platforms. Implementations should enforce `No_FP_Contraction`.
- Input Domain: Designed for localized spatial configurations where the input value is bounded by the interval [0, π/2].

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function CosineTaylor4(x)
    Input:
        x   : Double-Precision Floating-Point (64-bit IEEE 754)
    Output:
        res : Double-Precision Floating-Point (64-bit IEEE 754)

    Let x2 = x × x
    
    Let c1 = 1.0 / 2.0
    Let c2 = 1.0 / 24.0
    Let c3 = 1.0 / 720.0
    
    Let intermediate_1 = c2 - (x2 × c3)
    Let intermediate_2 = c1 - (x2 × intermediate_1)
    Let res = 1.0 - (x2 × intermediate_2)
    
    Return res
EndFunction
```

### 6. Function: `CheckIfNormalIsReversed`

#### Description

Evaluates the geometric alignment of the newly generated triangle face. If automated recalculation is inactive, it calculates the dot product between the explicitly calculated surface normal and the corresponding stored structural normal entry to assert orientation winding consistency.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function CheckIfNormalIsReversed()
    Output:
        is_reversed : Boolean

    If MustRecalculateNormals is TRUE Then
        Return ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
    Else
        Let calculated_normal = Derive_Normal(tri[0], tri[1], tri[2])
			
        If normal_coordinate_type is equal to PRC_TESS_NORMAL_PER_FACE Then
            Let stored_normal = FetchStoredNormal(GetFaceNormalIndex(current_triangle_index))
            Return InnerProduct(calculated_normal, stored_normal) < 0.0
        Else
            Return ReadBitFromStream(normal_bit_stream)
        EndIf
    EndIf
EndFunction

```

## 7. Function: `EvaluateAdjacentTri`

### Description

Determines which of the current triangle's two forward edges have unprocessed
neighbours, and pushes those edges onto the traversal stack for subsequent decoding.
The entering edge (the gate edge from which this triangle was decoded) is always
interior at this point and is not re-examined.

The neighbour flags are read from `edge_status_array[current_triangle_index]` as a
single 2-bit bitfield: bit 0 (`0x01`) = right neighbour present; bit 1 (`0x02`) = left
neighbour present. Both bits may be set simultaneously (value `0x03`).

**Stack discipline:** when both neighbours are present, the right edge is pushed onto
the stack first and the left edge is pushed second. Because the stack is LIFO the left
edge is therefore processed first. This order is the reverse of that stated in the
current specification text; the reference implementation is authoritative.

The right/left assignment of the two forward edges is made relative to the triangle
normal: if the normal is reversed, the initial right and left assignments are swapped
before further processing.

**Normative — interleaved decode.**
When normal_bit_stream is present (MustRecalculateNormals is FALSE), a conforming decoder shall evaluate EvaluateAdjacentTri for triangle i — including the CheckIfNormalIsReversed read from normal_bit_stream — before decoding triangle i + 1. The normal-reversal bit determines the left/right edge assignment (and therefore which edges are pushed and which existing vertex each later closure references), so connectivity cannot be reconstructed independently of the normal stream. Decoders that defer or skip the normal-stream reads will desynchronise the bit reader and fail to parse all subsequent triangles.

> NOTE: Normal-free reconstruction of topology. A decoder that does not need stored normals (e.g. one that recomputes them via Derive_Normal) may reconstruct identical topology without consuming normal_bit_stream, by replacing the edge_status-driven push with geometric edge-matching: offer both forward edges of every triangle and close an interior edge when two triangles meet on it. This yields the same vertex/triangle set; it does not reproduce the encoder's per-triangle traversal order, so it must not be used when bit-exact reproduction of that order is required.

### Inputs (module-level state)

- `current_triangle_index` — index of the triangle just decoded (0-based)
- `treated_index[3]` — the three vertex indices of the current triangle, in the
  canonical ascending-index order established during decoding:
  `treated_index[0] < treated_index[1]`; `treated_index[2]` is the apex
- `normal_was_reversed` — Boolean; TRUE if the triangle's stored normal was reversed
- `edge_status_array[current_triangle_index]` — 2-bit bitfield for this triangle;
  mask with `0x03` before use (see CR-14e)
- `traversal_stack` — the global LIFO edge stack
- `treated_edge_list` — the set of edges already fully processed (both sides interior)

### Pseudo-code
```text
Function EvaluateAdjacentTri()
# Step 1 — Establish initial left/right edge vertex assignments.
# Initial convention (before normal-reversal adjustment):
#   right edge connects treated_index[1] and treated_index[2],
#   with treated_index[0] as the far (basis) vertex.
#   left edge connects treated_index[0] and treated_index[2],
#   with treated_index[1] as the far (basis) vertex.

Let right_vtx_a  = treated_index[1]     # right edge endpoint
Let right_vtx_b  = treated_index[2]     # right edge endpoint
Let right_far    = treated_index[0]     # far vertex for right-edge basis frame

Let left_vtx_a   = treated_index[0]     # left edge endpoint
Let left_vtx_b   = treated_index[2]     # left edge endpoint
Let left_far     = treated_index[1]     # far vertex for left-edge basis frame

# Step 2 — If the stored normal was reversed, swap the right and left assignments.
If normal_was_reversed is TRUE Then
    Swap(right_vtx_a, left_vtx_a)
    Swap(right_vtx_b, left_vtx_b)
    Swap(right_far,   left_far)
EndIf

# Step 3 — Enforce ascending-index order on each edge's endpoint pair.
# (The basis frame computation requires the lower-index endpoint first.)
If right_vtx_a > right_vtx_b Then
    Swap(right_vtx_a, right_vtx_b)
EndIf

If left_vtx_a > left_vtx_b Then
    Swap(left_vtx_a, left_vtx_b)
EndIf

# Step 4 — Read the neighbour flags.
# Mask with 0x03 to handle signed-char artefact (see CR-14e).
Let status = edge_status_array[current_triangle_index] BitwiseAnd 0x03

Let has_right_neighbour = (status BitwiseAnd 0x01)   # non-zero if right present
Let has_left_neighbour  = (status BitwiseAnd 0x02)   # non-zero if left present

# Step 5 — Push edges onto the stack.
# IMPORTANT: right is pushed FIRST, left is pushed SECOND.
# Because the stack is LIFO, left will be popped (processed) first.
# This is the reverse of the order stated in the current spec text (see CR-14f).

If has_right_neighbour is non-zero Then
    Let right_edge = EdgeDefinition(
                         lower_index  = right_vtx_a,
                         higher_index = right_vtx_b,
                         far_index    = right_far)
    PushToStack(traversal_stack, right_edge)
Else
    MarkEdgeAsProcessed(treated_edge_list,
                        lower_index  = right_vtx_a,
                        higher_index = right_vtx_b)
EndIf

If has_left_neighbour is non-zero Then
    Let left_edge = EdgeDefinition(
                        lower_index  = left_vtx_a,
                        higher_index = left_vtx_b,
                        far_index    = left_far)
    PushToStack(traversal_stack, left_edge)
Else
    MarkEdgeAsProcessed(treated_edge_list,
                        lower_index  = left_vtx_a,
                        higher_index = left_vtx_b)
EndIf
EndFunction
```

### 8. Function: `MinimumNumPointsToProcess`

#### Description

Acts as a normative boundary check and validation constraint. It confirms that the remaining unique coordinate count and triangle sequence indices contain sufficient entries to fulfil the active decomposition operation.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function MinimumNumPointsToProcess(n_points, tri_index)
    Input:
        n_points  : Integer
        tri_index : Integer
    Output:
        is_valid  : Boolean

    Let cond1 = (NumberOfUniquePoints - CurrentPointIndex) >= UniquePointsRequired
    Let cond2 = (NumberOfPoints - CurPointIndex) >= n_points
    Let cond3 = tri_index < NumberOfTriangles
    
    Return (cond1 And cond2 And cond3)
```

### 9. Function: `GenerateNewTriangle`

#### Description

Generates a new, unattached root triangle when the topological neighbour stack is empty. Coordinates are derived via sequential predictive offset evaluation blocks (`P1_Predicted_Coords`, `P2_Predicted_Coords`, `P3_Predicted_Coords`) relative to the mesh origin, maintaining a canonical sorted ordering across local edge indices.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function GenerateNewTriangle()
    Let np = MinimumNumPointsToProcess(3, current_triangle_index)
    If np is FALSE Then
        RaiseException(PRC_ERROR_CORRUPT_BITSTREAM)
    EndIf

    Set tri[0] = FetchPoint(treated_index[0], P1_Predicted_Coords(origin))
    Set tri[1] = FetchPoint(treated_index[1], P2_Predicted_Coords(tri[0]))
    Set tri[2] = FetchPoint(treated_index[2], P3_Predicted_Coords(tri[0], tri[1]))

    If treated_index[0] > treated_index[1] Then
        Swap(tri[0], tri[1])
        Swap(treated_index[0], treated_index[1])
    EndIf
EndFunction

```

## 10. Function — `AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh`

#### Description
Constructs the next triangle on an existing boundary ("gate") edge popped from
traversal_stack by the main decompression loop. The gate edge supplies the entire local
context needed: its two endpoints and the far vertex of the already-committed triangle that
pushed it. The triangle's third vertex (the apex) is resolved in one of two ways: (a) as a
reference to an existing mesh point — the closure case, which in practice accounts for
roughly half of all triangles in a closed manifold — consuming a point-reference index and
no point_array triple; or (b) as a new point, identified by consuming the next
integer offset triple from point_array and evaluating it in the gate edge's local prediction
frame via ApexFromEdge.  The entering edge is implicitly retired; it is no longer a forward edge of any unprocessed triangle,
consequently it is never pushed again. Explicit marking is not required and is not performed.

#### Pseudo-code
```text
Function AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh(target_edge)
    Input:
        target_edge : EdgeDefinition   # popped from traversal_stack by the main loop

    # evaluation loop precondition
    If MinimumNumPointsToProcess(1, current_triangle_index) is FALSE Then
        RaiseException(PRC_ERROR_CORRUPT_BITSTREAM)
    EndIf

    # Gate-edge context. Endpoints are kept in ascending point-index order
    # (the treatment[] canonical order established when the edge was pushed).
    Let Va   = Point(target_edge.lower_index)     # endpoint with the lower point index
    Let Vb   = Point(target_edge.higher_index)    # endpoint with the higher point index
    Let Vfar = Point(target_edge.far_index)       # third vertex of the triangle that pushed this edge

    If NextPointIsReference() is TRUE Then
        # Closure: the apex is an existing mesh point; no point_array triple is consumed
        Let apex_index = NextPointReference()
    Else
        # New point: consume the next (ix, iy, iz) triple from point_array
        Let (ix, iy, iz) = NextPointOffsets()
        Let apex_index   = AppendPointToMesh(
                               ApexFromEdge(Va, Vb, Vfar, ix, iy, iz, point_tolerance))
    EndIf

    Set tri[0]           = Va
    Set tri[1]           = Vb
    Set tri[2]           = Point(apex_index)
    Set treated_index[0] = target_edge.lower_index
    Set treated_index[1] = target_edge.higher_index
    Set treated_index[2] = apex_index
EndFunction
```

---
### 11. Function: `ApexFromEdge` 

#### Description
Evaluates the predicted position of a newly decoded apex point in the local orthonormal frame of
the gate edge it is built upon. The frame uses the same midpoint-of-first-edge convention as
Derive_Normal and the seed predictors in GenerateNewTriangle — one convention shared by
position and normal reconstruction throughout: origin at the midpoint of the gate edge, X along
the edge, Z perpendicular to the plane spanned by the edge and the neighbouring triangle's far
vertex, Y completing the right-handed set. The decoded integer offsets (ix, iy, iz) are
quantisation-step multiples along these axes. If Y points toward the existing triangle's far vertex
(the committed surface interior), both Y and Z are negated.
This ensures Z consistently points away from the previously decoded surface, giving the apex a stable out-of-plane direction.
The function also includes a degenerate Z fallback. When Normalize(Z) fails (Z is zero-length,
meaning Vfar lies exactly on the gate edge), the function falls back to constructing an arbitrary orthonormal Y and Z.

#### Pseudo-code
```text
Function ApexFromEdge(Va, Vb, Vfar, ix, iy, iz, tol)

    Let O = (Va + Vb) × 0.5
    Let X = Normalize(Va − Vb)          # lower-index toward higher-index endpoint

    Let z_temp = Vfar − O
    Let Z = Normalize(CrossProduct(z_temp, X))

    If Z is degenerate (zero length) Then
        # Vfar is coplanar with the gate edge; construct an arbitrary orthonormal basis
        Let {Y, Z} = ArbitraryOrthonormalComplement(X)
    Else
        Let Y = Normalize(CrossProduct(Z, X))
    EndIf

    # Orientation test: ensure Y and Z point away from the committed surface
    Let w = O − Vfar
    If DotProduct(Y, w) > 0.0 Then
        Negate Y
        Negate Z
    EndIf

    Return O + (ix × tol × X) + (iy × tol × Y) + (iz × tol × Z)

EndFunction
```


### 12. Procedure: `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed` Triangle-Fan Decompression

#### Description

The main execution entry point for parsing and decompressing the highly compressed mesh block. It runs a sequential processing loop over the serialized T-fan data streams, synchronizing spatial coordinate extraction with topological adjacency tracking.

*Note: To resolve potential index race conditions and guarantee pointer safety across varying `normal_coordinate_type` modes, the loop evaluates orientation winding and edge-stack structures via `EvaluateAdjacentTri` completely before invoking individual vertex attribute `Normal_Restoration` routines.*

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Procedure PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed()
    Set current_triangle_index = 0
    ClearStack(traversal_stack)
    
    If Length(normal_bit_stream) is equal to 0 Then
        Set MustRecalculateNormals = TRUE
    Else
        Set MustRecalculateNormals = FALSE
    EndIf

    Repeat
        If IsFirstTriangleInFace(current_triangle_index) is TRUE Then
            InitializeFaceOutputStructures()
        EndIf
	  
        If IsStackEmpty(traversal_stack) is FALSE Then
            Let target_edge = FindFirstUntreatedEdge(traversal_stack)
        EndIf
 
        If IsStackEmpty(traversal_stack) is TRUE Or target_edge is Null Then 
            GenerateNewTriangle()
        Else
            AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh(target_edge)
        EndIf
	  
        If IsStackEmpty(traversal_stack) is FALSE Then
            FindAndSortUnusedEdges(sorted_edge_list)
        EndIf

        # Requirement 1: Evaluate mesh topology and adjacency maps first to lock index definitions
        EvaluateAdjacentTri()

        # Requirement 2: Execute attribute normal restoration vectors sequentially
        Normal_Restoration(GetPointIndex(0), 0)
        Normal_Restoration(GetPointIndex(1), 1)
        Normal_Restoration(GetPointIndex(2), 2)
	  
        Let face_is_reversed = CheckIfFaceIsReversed()
	  
        If face_is_reversed is FALSE Then
            Swap(triangle.z, triangle.y)
            CalculateGlobalFaceNormal()
        EndIf
		
        CommitTriangleToOutputMesh(current_triangle_index)
        current_triangle_index = current_triangle_index + 1
	
    Until MinimumNumPointsToProcess(1, current_triangle_index) is FALSE

    FinalizeFaceMeshOutput()
EndProcedure

```

Thank you @t3dr0 — this outline is exactly the operation-level formulation we hoped for, and we're glad to do the independent assessment. We checked it with our from-scratch (no-OCCT) reader against a small test set, using the §7.8.9.7 `origin_array` = bbox-centre relation as a correctness oracle. Summary: **the outline's structural model holds up**, we found **two reconciliation points** worth resolving before it becomes an annex, and we have a concrete note on the **geometry↔normals coupling** you introduced.


## What the test files confirm

Two of the outline's assumptions held on every mesh we looked at:

- **Closed fan/strip manifolds** — triangles per unique point is consistently ≈ 2.0 (Euler, as expected for a closed surface).
- **~Half of all triangles are closures** — the count of `point_is_reference` events is consistently ≈ half the triangle count. This is the important one: it confirms the `AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh` + `point_is_reference` design — roughly half the triangles add a new apex, the other half close onto an *existing* vertex and add no point. So a faithful decoder must thread those closures through the stack, not just append fans.

The `GenerateNewTriangle`-on-empty-stack restart (§7/§8) is also necessary and correct: a single seed plus a left-first fan covers only one stripe (we'd previously stalled at roughly two-thirds coverage for exactly this reason; the restart is the fix).

## Reconciliation point 1 — `edge_status_array` cardinality (vs CR-14)

`EvaluateAdjacentTri` reads `edge_status_array[current_triangle_index]` as **one value per triangle**, testing `& 0x01` (right) and `& 0x02` (left). But the bitstream stores **3 elements per triangle** — that was your own CR-14a/d (we independently confirmed the 3× ratio, and that values of `3` genuinely occur, not just `0/1/2`). The outline and CR-14 are inconsistent as written. It would help to state explicitly **which of the three stored elements** the single per-triangle status byte in `EvaluateAdjacentTri` corresponds to (entering edge vs the two forward edges), and why a stored element takes the value `3` if each is a single right-or-left bit.

## Reconciliation point 2 — geometry traversal is coupled to the normal bitstream

This is the one we'd most like clarified. In §5, the left/right edge assignment is swapped by `is_this_normal_reversed = CheckIfNormalIsReversed()`, and §4 shows that flag is read from `normal_bit_stream` (or derived from stored normals). So **the connectivity traversal cannot be reconstructed independently of the normal stream** — the order in which edges are pushed (and therefore which existing vertex each closure references) depends on per-triangle normal-reversal bits.

We can show this empirically. Implementing the outline **faithfully but normal-free** (treating `is_this_normal_reversed` as always false, since we recompute normals), coverage stalls at roughly two-thirds: it builds about half the triangles' worth of new apexes and then the stack starves, because the closure triangles can't be threaded without the reversal bits. By contrast, a purely **geometric edge-matching** traversal (push both forward edges, cancel an interior edge when two gates meet) reconstructs the full mesh on every file we tried — precisely because it sidesteps the reversal dependency.

So: either (a) the annex should state plainly that a conforming decoder must process `normal_bit_stream` *interleaved* with connectivity (the outline's §8 ordering note hints at this, but the hard dependency deserves to be normative), or (b) provide a normal-independent edge-selection rule. We'd favour documenting (a) and noting that geometric edge-matching is a valid normal-free alternative that yields identical topology.

## On the normals section (welcome addition)

- `Derive_Normal` uses the **same midpoint-of-first-edge frame** as the geometry reconstruction (`O = (V1+V2)/2`, cross of the two boundary spans). That internal consistency is good and worth calling out — the position frame and the normal frame share one convention.
- `Next_Normal`'s `CosineTaylor4`/`SineTaylor4` (the 4-term Taylor expansion "to prevent platform-dependent truncation") is a **conformance-precision hazard** as written: decoders using `libm` `cos`/`sin` will differ from a Taylor-4 implementation by more than typical `normal_angle_bit_count` quantisation near θ,φ → π/2. If bit-exactness of the angular reconstruction is intended to be normative, the series (its exact terms and evaluation order) needs to be specified, not "(not shown)". If it isn't normative, a tolerance should be stated and `libm` permitted.

## Minor

The apex local-frame for `AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh` is referenced only via `P1/P2/P3_Predicted_Coords` (named, not defined). For an annex it'd help to give the offset frame explicitly. For what it's worth, the frame that matches the `origin`-centre oracle for us is `O=(Va+Vc)/2`, `X=(Vc−Va)/|·|` (endpoints in ascending point-index order), `Z=unit((Vfar−O)×X)`, `Y=unit(Z×X)`, with the delta applied as `O + ix·tol·X + iy·tol·Y + iz·tol·Z` — i.e. the same midpoint frame as `Derive_Normal`.
