## 1. `edge_status_array` cardinality — reconciling `EvaluateAdjacentTri` with CR-14

The mismatch is just the array index: `EvaluateAdjacentTri` reads `edge_status_array[current_triangle_index]`, but CR-14 establishes the array has `3 × T` elements, so a per-triangle access has to be `edge_status_array[3 × current_triangle_index + k]` for some per-edge slot `k`. Minimal fix to the pseudocode:

```text
    # three consecutive elements per triangle (CR-14); mask per CR-14e
    Let es_base    = 3 × current_triangle_index
    Let right_elem = edge_status_array[es_base + RIGHT_SLOT] BitwiseAnd 0x03
    Let left_elem  = edge_status_array[es_base + LEFT_SLOT]  BitwiseAnd 0x03
    Let has_a_right_edge = right_elem BitwiseAnd 0x01
    Let has_a_left_edge  = left_elem  BitwiseAnd 0x02
```

On **why a stored element can be `3`** — this is the part we'd flag as still genuinely open, and we'd rather sharpen the question than assert a mapping we can't back with evidence. If each of the three per-triangle elements were a *single* edge's "has-a-neighbour" bit, it would be `0` or `1` only; the presence of `2` and `3` means each element carries the **full 2-bit `(right, left)` field**, not one bit. So the three elements are three *2-bit fields*, and the open question is what the three fields are *about*: the three edges each carrying their own `(right,left)` view (redundant, as @ralovich noted), or one operative field plus two that are context/back-edge. Our harness can't yet disambiguate this — driving the traversal by "push the forward edge iff its slot is non-zero," across **every** assignment of the three slots to (entering, right, left), tops out around two-thirds coverage and the best-fitting slot order **differs per file**. That's the signature of a rule that depends on running traversal state, not a fixed positional label.

Concretely, we'd suggest CR-14's deferred note stay deferred but be made precise:

> **NOTE (deferred).** Each of the three elements per triangle is a 2-bit `(right, left)` field (values `0..3` after masking with `0x03`). The mapping from the three array positions `[3i]`, `[3i+1]`, `[3i+2]` to the triangle's entering/second/third edges, and the rule by which `EvaluateAdjacentTri` selects the operative element(s), depend on the traversal state of §7.8.9.2 and are not yet specified normatively. A conforming description requires a reference encoder/decoder; see #727.

We remain happy to run any candidate slot/operation rule against our regression set and report coverage + centre-error.

## 2. Normal-stream interleaving — making the §10 ordering normative

We'd propose promoting the existing ordering note in `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D_Compressed()` from advisory to normative, because `EvaluateAdjacentTri` → `CheckIfNormalIsReversed` consumes `normal_bit_stream`, so the connectivity stack state depends on the normal bits being read in lock-step. Suggested normative text to add to the procedure prose:

> **Normative — interleaved decode.** When `normal_bit_stream` is present (`MustRecalculateNormals` is FALSE), a conforming decoder **shall** evaluate `EvaluateAdjacentTri` for triangle `i` — including the `CheckIfNormalIsReversed` read from `normal_bit_stream` — **before** decoding triangle `i + 1`. The normal-reversal bit determines the left/right edge assignment (and therefore which edges are pushed and which existing vertex each later closure references), so connectivity cannot be reconstructed independently of the normal stream. Decoders that defer or skip the normal-stream reads will desynchronise the bit reader and misparse all subsequent triangles.

And the normal-free alternative you agreed to note:

> **NOTE — normal-free reconstruction of topology.** A decoder that does not need stored normals (e.g. one that recomputes them via `Derive_Normal`) may reconstruct identical *topology* without consuming `normal_bit_stream`, by replacing the `edge_status`-driven push with geometric edge-matching: offer both forward edges of every triangle and close an interior edge when two triangles meet on it. This yields the same vertex/triangle set; it does **not** reproduce the encoder's per-triangle traversal order, so it must not be used when bit-exact reproduction of that order is required.

(That last clause matters: edge-matching gets the *mesh*, not the *order* — which is also why it sidesteps the normal dependency.)

Your 2026-06-09 `SineTaylor4`/`CosineTaylor4` (Horner form, `No_FP_Contraction`, IEEE-754 doubles) is exactly what was needed to make the angular reconstruction bit-reproducible, and we agree with **"shall be computed"** over "are computed" in 7.8.9.5. ## 4. `AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh` apex frame and `origin`

Here is the explicit frame that reproduces the §7.8.9.7 `origin`-centre relation for us, as a definition of the `P*_Predicted_Coords` blocks. Let `tol` be the decoded quantisation step and `(ix, iy, iz)` the integer offsets decoded for the new point:

    # ordered so that index(Va) < index(Vb)  (the treatment[] canonical order);

## Part 1 — `AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh` and `ApexFromEdge`

### Function: `AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh`

#### Description (proposed)

Constructs the next triangle on an existing boundary ("gate") edge popped from
`traversal_stack` by the main decompression loop. The gate edge supplies the entire local
context needed: its two endpoints and the far vertex of the already-committed triangle that
pushed it. The triangle's third vertex (the apex) is resolved in one of two ways: (a) as a
**reference** to an existing mesh point — the closure case, which in practice accounts for
roughly half of all triangles in a closed manifold — consuming a point-reference index and
**no** `point_array` triple; or (b) as a **new** point, materialized by consuming the next
integer offset triple from `point_array` and evaluating it in the gate edge's local prediction
frame via `ApexFromEdge`. The entering edge is then interior (both of its triangles exist) and
is marked processed; the two forward edges of the new triangle are subsequently evaluated by
`EvaluateAdjacentTri` exactly as in the current §10 ordering.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function AddPointToExistingTriangleMesh(target_edge)
    Input:
        target_edge : EdgeDefinition   # popped from traversal_stack by the main loop (§10)

    If MinimumNumPointsToProcess(1, current_triangle_index) is FALSE Then
        RaiseException(PRC_ERROR_CORRUPT_BITSTREAM)
    EndIf

    # Gate-edge context. Endpoints are kept in ascending point-index order
    # (the treatment[] canonical order established when the edge was pushed).
    Let Va   = Point(target_edge.lower_index)     # endpoint with the lower point index
    Let Vb   = Point(target_edge.higher_index)    # endpoint with the higher point index
    Let Vfar = Point(target_edge.far_index)       # third vertex of the triangle that pushed this edge

    If NextPointIsReference() is TRUE Then
        # Closure: the apex is an existing mesh point; no point_array triple is consumed
        Let apex_index = NextPointReference()
    Else
        # New point: consume the next (ix, iy, iz) triple from point_array
        Let (ix, iy, iz) = NextPointOffsets()
        Let apex_index   = AppendPointToMesh(
                               ApexFromEdge(Va, Vb, Vfar, ix, iy, iz, point_tolerance))
    EndIf

    Set tri[0]           = Va
    Set tri[1]           = Vb
    Set tri[2]           = Point(apex_index)
    Set treated_index[0] = target_edge.lower_index
    Set treated_index[1] = target_edge.higher_index
    Set treated_index[2] = apex_index

    MarkEdgeAsProcessed(target_edge)   # entering edge is now interior; it cannot be re-entered
EndFunction
```

No change is needed in §10 — the call site is already there, and `EvaluateAdjacentTri` /
`Normal_Restoration` then operate on the `tri[]` / `treated_index[]` state this function
establishes.

### Function: `ApexFromEdge`

#### Description (proposed)

Evaluates the predicted position of a newly decoded apex point in the local orthonormal frame of
the gate edge it is built upon. The frame uses the same midpoint-of-first-edge convention as
`Derive_Normal` and the seed predictors in `GenerateNewTriangle` — one convention shared by
position and normal reconstruction throughout: origin at the midpoint of the gate edge, X along
the edge, Z perpendicular to the plane spanned by the edge and the neighbouring triangle's far
vertex, Y completing the right-handed set. The decoded integer offsets `(ix, iy, iz)` are
quantisation-step multiples along these axes. This construction matches the frame described in
US patent 8,207,965 B2 (now expired), which @ralovich identified earlier in this thread; we
verified the correspondence independently. What the frame does **not** settle — see Part 2 — is
the traversal phase structure that determines which `(ix, iy, iz)` triple each apex receives.

#### Pseudo-code

```text
Function ApexFromEdge(Va, Vb, Vfar, ix, iy, iz, tol)
    Input:
        Va, Vb     : Vector3   # gate-edge endpoints, ascending point-index order: index(Va) < index(Vb)
        Vfar       : Vector3   # third vertex of the committed neighbour triangle on this edge
        ix, iy, iz : Integer   # decoded integer offsets for the new point (next point_array triple)
        tol        : Double    # point quantisation step (point_tolerance)
    Output:
        apex       : Vector3

    Let O = (Va + Vb) × 0.5
    Let X = Normalize(Va - Vb)                      # along the edge, from the higher-index endpoint toward the lower
    Let Z = Normalize(CrossProduct(Vfar - O, X))
    Let Y = Normalize(CrossProduct(Z, X))

    Return O + ((ix × tol) × X) + ((iy × tol) × Y) + ((iz × tol) × Z)
EndFunction
```

> **Correction to our 2026-06-09 sketch:** we previously wrote `X = Normalize(Vb − Va)`
> (lower→higher index) with all-positive offsets. Re-verifying against our shipped decoder and
> the patent frame, the configuration that validates is the opposite X direction, as written
> above (equivalently: keep X lower→higher and negate the `ix` and `iz` terms; Y is unaffected
> since Z is derived from X). Apologies for the slip.

### Unifying the seed predictors in `GenerateNewTriangle`

The `P1/P2/P3_Predicted_Coords` blocks are the degenerate cases of the same construction, with
offsets applied along the **world** axes (no edge yet defines a rotated frame):

```text
P1_Predicted_Coords(origin)          :  V0 = origin                    + (ix, iy, iz) × tol
P2_Predicted_Coords(tri[0])          :  V1 = tri[0]                    + (ix, iy, iz) × tol
P3_Predicted_Coords(tri[0], tri[1])  :  V2 = Midpoint(tri[0], tri[1])  + (ix, iy, iz) × tol
```

each consuming the next `point_array` triple in order. `P3`'s midpoint base is the same
`O = (V0+V1)/2` convention as `ApexFromEdge` and `Derive_Normal` — worth one sentence in the
annex, since this shared convention cost both our teams development time to rediscover.

## Part 2 — the traversal is legible in the streams: a concentric ring-strip zipper

We found an oracle class that does not depend on exact B-rep (most compressed-B-rep bodies are
blocked behind #582/#583): a **rotationally symmetric model** makes reconstruction quality
measurable with no ground truth at all — a correct decode places every vertex on one of a
handful of circles, so the cylindrical (r, z) profile collapses to the part's 2-D outline, and
any traversal error breaks the symmetry measurably. Our test file is a coin cell battery
(T = 3,716, single 173 entity, auth=15216). We'd encourage other implementors to look for
washers/bushings/caps in their corpora.

Reading this file's decoded field arrays as *sequences* rather than aggregates:

1. **`point_is_reference` rhythm:** an opening run of ~64 consecutive new-point events (one full
   ring laid out first), then almost perfect **new/reference alternation** (of 2,774 runs,
   1,389 + 1,385 have length 1). Alternating new/close is the signature of a zigzag triangle
   strip.
2. **`point_reference_array` is sequential:** reference values march upward (0, 2, 3, 4, 5, …) —
   closures consume the *previous ring's vertices in creation order*.
3. **Closure lag is quantised at ring circumferences:** lag = (new-vertex count at the closure) −
   (referenced index) concentrates at a few near-constant values — 113 (×470), 112 (×288), then
   153, 131, 133, 157… — the vertex counts of the part's circular rings.

Together: the encoder lays an initial ring/fan (the all-new prologue), then walks the surface
ring by ring, **zipping each new ring against the previous one with an alternating new/close
strip**, references consuming the old ring sequentially. This matches the Acrobat wireframe of
the part (faces fan-triangulated from rim hubs) and the patent's "stripe" language — but the
phase structure (prologue fan → per-ring zip → ring transition) is stated nowhere in the spec,
patent, or draft annex, and it is precisely what a conforming decoder needs. We verified it
directionally: a deterministic alternating continuation rule outperforms any same-side rule by
~20× on the symmetry metric; what it does not yet fix is the **ring transition**, where errors
accumulate — which is where `edge_status_array` and/or the stack discipline must carry the
information.

So we'd refine the CR-14 deferred note once more, and more concretely than our last attempt:

> **NOTE (deferred, sharpened).** The traversal of §7.8.9.2 has a phase structure: (a) an
> initial fan prologue of consecutive new points; (b) a steady-state alternating new/reference
> ring-zip, directly observable in `point_is_reference` / `point_reference_array`; and (c) a
> transition rule where a new ring or feature begins. (a) and (b) are now empirically
> characterised across conforming files; only (c) — and how `edge_status_array` encodes it —
> requires the reference implementation.

One structural finding worth recording for other implementors: per-step *geometric* probing
cannot recover the traversal even in principle, because `ApexFromEdge`'s Z axis is built from
the gate triangle itself — the out-of-plane apex offset is `|iz| × tol` for **every** candidate
gate, so all gate choices produce locally equally-plausible geometry. The order information is
carried only by `point_is_reference` / `point_reference_array` (and presumably
`edge_status_array`). This explains why several independent sweep efforts, ours included,
plateaued at partial coverage.

## nanoPRC implementation reveals the ring-transition process

@datalogics-pgallot's  open question was: *"what it does not yet fix is the ring transition, where errors accumulate — which is where `edge_status_array` and/or the stack discipline must carry the information."*

**The nanoPRC code answers this fully and precisely.** The ring transition is not a special mechanism — it is the natural consequence of three ordinary elements working together. Here is the complete picture.

---

### How the traversal state machine actually works

The decoder has two mutually exclusive operating modes on each iteration:

**Mode A — Stack non-empty (steady-state strip):** pop a gate edge, read one entry from `points_is_reference_array`, decode one apex (new or reference), build one triangle. This is the zigzag ring-zip the reviewer characterised.

**Mode B — Stack empty (transition event):** call `prc_handle_empty_stack_decode`, which reads the *next three* consecutive entries from `points_is_reference_array` and builds a new seed triangle from scratch. The loop then continues normally with Mode A from the new seed.

The transition from Mode A to Mode B is triggered by one thing only: **the traversal stack draining to empty.** The stack drains when `edge_status_array` bits instruct the decoder to push nothing — specifically when the current triangle has `edge_status & 0x03 == 0` (no right, no left neighbour unprocessed).

---

### The ring transition is fully specified by these two elements

**Element 1 — `edge_status_array` for the final triangle(s) of each ring.**
When the encoder sets `edge_status = 0` for the last triangle of a ring, the stack drains after that triangle is processed. The decoder detects this stack-empty and calls `prc_handle_empty_stack_decode`. The encoder controls ring boundaries exactly by placing `edge_status = 0` at the right triangle.

**Element 2 — The next three `points_is_reference_array` entries after the drain.**
`prc_handle_empty_stack_decode` reads `[i]`, `[i+1]`, `[i+2]` and dispatches to one of four seed-triangle builders:

| Pattern | Builder called | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `0,0,0` | `prc_compute_first_triangle` | Full reboot: three new world-space points. Used for the initial prologue and for disconnected components. |
| `1,0,0` or `0,1,0` or `0,0,1` | `prc_set_one_ref_treated_triangle` | One vertex bridges from the previous ring; two new points start the new strip. |
| `1,1,0` or `1,0,1` or `0,1,1` | `prc_set_two_ref_treated_triangle` | Two vertices bridge from the previous ring; one new apex. The base edge of the new seed triangle is a previously decoded edge. |
| `1,1,1` | `prc_set_three_ref_treated_triangle` | Pure closure: all three vertices are references. No new geometry; used to close fans or caps. |

For @datalogics-pgallot's coin-cell battery ring structure example, the ring transition will be the `1,1,0` or `0,0,1` cases: two vertices from the closing ring of the old strip form the base of the first triangle of the new strip, with one new apex to launch the next zigzag. This is what makes `point_reference_array` values march upward across ring boundaries — the references at transition points are the last vertices of the previous ring.

---

### The phase structure is now fully characterised

| Phase | Code path | `points_is_reference_array` consumption |
|---|---|---|
| **Prologue** (initial ring, all new) | `prc_compute_first_triangle` called once before the loop, then Mode A strip | 3 at startup, then 1 per triangle |
| **Steady-state ring-zip** | Mode A entirely | 1 per triangle (alternating 0/1 for new/reference) |
| **Ring transition** | Stack drain → `prc_handle_empty_stack_decode` | Reads next 3 entries to determine seed type; `points_is_reference_index += 3` |
| **New ring strip** | Mode A resumes from seed | 1 per triangle |

@datalogics-pgallot's finding that "a deterministic alternating continuation rule outperforms any same-side rule by ~20× on the symmetry metric but does not fix the ring transition" is now explained: the alternating rule correctly models Mode A (the zigzag strip), but Mode A and Mode B are syntactically *indistinguishable* from `points_is_reference_array` alone. The transition is signalled by the `edge_status_array = 0` on the final ring triangle, which drains the stack and causes `points_is_reference_index` to jump by 3 instead of 1. Without correctly decoding `edge_status_array`, a reader cannot know when the jump-by-3 occurs.

## Proposed change to §7.8.9.3

1. **Admit both cardinalities.** Replace "Each triangle has a flag" with wording allowing the array to
   carry **either one flag per triangle, or three flags per triangle (one per edge)**, and state that
   both forms are conforming.

2. **Name the discriminator, with its reliability condition.** The following wording was suggested by
   @datalogics-pgallot and we adopt it as drafted:

   > A reader determines which form is present by comparing the declared array length against the
   > tessellation's triangle count. Note that this comparison is only reliable where the triangle count
   > is itself known correctly; a reader that has partially decoded the tessellation should treat a
   > length matching neither form as evidence that its triangle count is wrong, rather than as a third
   > form.

   The caveat matters: without it the clause presents as safe a test that misleads a reader already in
   the failure mode this format exhibits.

3. **State the scope of the sizing.** The sizing is fixed within a tessellation. Note separately that
   it is *observed* to be fixed within a file, without requiring it — keeping the normative claim and
   the empirical one apart, so the clause survives a writer producing a mixed file.

4. **State what the per-edge form carries**, per the figures above, so no implementer treats the extra
   entries as padding and discards them.

## What we are no longer asking for

We originally intended to ask which cardinality is correct, assuming one was a defect. **We withdraw
that**, and CR-14a with it. A rule declaring either sizing non-conforming would retroactively
invalidate a large body of files that shipping readers handle today.

The reframing — state the rule per tessellation and record that both sizings are conforming, rather
than asking which is right — is @datalogics-pgallot's, not ours.

# CR-14f refinement: the push order, and whether it governs the seed triangle

The original CR-14f corrected the stack push order. A second implementation corroborates the
correction and, in doing so, exposed a second ambiguity in the same sentence that we had not seen.
This revises CR-14f to settle both.

---

## 1. The correction itself — now corroborated

**Location:** `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2553`, §7.8.9.2 "Mesh Traversal".

Current text:

> If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the left
> triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the right triangle is pushed on the stack.

This is the wrong way round for a LIFO stack. **Two independent implementations push the right edge
first and the left second**, so the left pops and is processed first — the opposite of the text, and
both arrived at it from files that decode correctly rather than from the specification.

In our case the source comment at that call site records the disagreement in the code itself, written
during implementation and predating this issue: *"The right is first pushed on the stack and then the
left is pushed on the stack. This is different than described in the spec. Unless their stack is not
a LIFO stack."*

## 2. The ambiguity that corroboration exposed

The second implementation reports that its **seed** path pushes in the other order — left first,
right second — matching the current text, while its steady-state traversal pushes right first, like
ours. So that decoder carries both orders: one for the first triangle and one for every triangle
after it.

They explicitly decline to offer this as evidence for the specification's version, on the grounds
that the function concerned is independently distrusted — it is the same one that carried a
`edge_status_array[3t]` indexing defect found this month. We agree it should not count as evidence
either way.

But it makes the real point: **the current sentence does not say whether it governs the seed
triangle**, and at least one implementation has quietly assumed it does not. That ambiguity is worth
closing regardless of which order is correct, because a decoder that seeds differently from its
steady state produces a different traversal from the same bytes.

## 3. What our implementation does, offered as a data point

nanoPRC makes **no distinction at all**. The first triangle is computed, then enters the same loop as
every other triangle: `prc_set_left_right_edge_indices` assigns the left and right edges from
`treated_index[0..2]` identically for the seed and for all successors, and the same right-then-left
push follows. There is no seed-specific path.

**One uniform rule, applied from the first triangle onward, decodes our corpus correctly.**

## 4. A question we cannot answer, and would rather ask

The second implementation frames this as "the seed triangle's **three** edges as against the
steady-state **two**", which is a reasonable reading: a seed has no entering edge, so all three of its
edges are candidates for traversal, where a later triangle has one edge already consumed.

Our implementation offers **two** forward edges for the seed, not three — the same left/right pair it
offers everywhere. It decodes correctly, so either the third edge is genuinely not offered by this
format, or it is reachable another way and our corpus does not exercise the difference.

We do not know which, and we would rather put the question than guess at it. The specification is
silent, and two implementations have resolved the silence differently: one by giving the seed a
different push order, one by giving it fewer edges.

## 5. CR-14f — proposed replacement

**BEFORE**

> If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the left
> triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the right triangle is pushed on the stack.

**AFTER**

> If the current triangle has both a right and a left neighbour which are not treated, the right edge
> shall be pushed onto the traversal stack first, and the left edge shall be pushed second. Since the
> stack is last-in-first-out, the left edge is thereby popped and processed before the right edge.
>
> This rule applies to every triangle, including the first triangle of a traversal. A conforming
> decoder shall not use a different push order for the seed triangle than for its successors.
>
> **NOTE — Correction.** Previous editions of this specification stated that the left edge was pushed
> first. This was incorrect; conforming encoders and decoders shall use the order stated above.

The second paragraph is the new material. It costs one sentence and removes a divergence that has
already occurred in practice.

## 6. What we are asking the working group to settle

The push order itself we regard as established — two implementations, arrived at independently, from
files that decode.

**The seed's edge count we do not.** If the intended model gives the seed triangle three traversable
edges rather than two, the replacement text above is incomplete and should say so explicitly, because
our implementation would then be relying on an accident. If it gives it two, the text above is
sufficient and our reading is right. Either answer is useful; the current silence is not.

## Correction to CR-14c — the per-writer clause is withdrawn

I have edited the CR-14a–d comment above to remove a clause from **CR-14c**. It previously ended:

and now ends at "conforming files." Nothing replaces the deleted clause. The per-file statement it

The clause was drawn from a 76-record sample in which the two sizings partitioned cleanly by

### The measurements

Across all 310 files of the public `prc-db` collection, 12,381 compressed tessellation entities
were walked: 7,382 sized `T`, 4,994 sized `3T`, none sized anything else. Of the 126 files
reached, 74 are entirely `T` and 52 entirely `3T`, and **none mixes the two**.

Crossing that against `unique_id_application`, at byte offset 27 of the header:

| `unique_id_application`               | files `T` | files `3T` |
|:--------------------------------------|----------:|-----------:|
| `1f5c7d43-dc4b11d4-a6f80050-04b60bca`  |         0 |         50 |
| null                                   |        74 |      **2** |

A null application id emits both sizings. In a corpus measured independently by
@datalogics-pgallot — 44,399 entities across 215 files — a single **non-null** application id
emits 88 files at `T` and seven at `3T`.

So both bodies of data contain a counterexample, and they run in opposite directions. Producer-
level consistency is not a claim either supports.

What survives, and is much better evidenced, is per-*file* consistency: no single file mixes the
two sizings, in zero of 215 files there and zero of 126 here. CR-14d already states that, as an
observation rather than a requirement, which is the right strength.

### A candidate predictor, offered only as a NOTE

The 9 September note on this thread said a replacement existed but wanted it checked against a
second population first. It has been, and it survived — which is why we are *still* not proposing
it as normative text.

In our data the minimal version word predicts the sizing without exception:

| `minimal_version_for_read` | files `T` | files `3T` | mixed |
|---------------------------:|----------:|-----------:|------:|
| 7094                       |         0 |         45 |     0 |
| 7095                       |         0 |          7 |     0 |
| 8137                       |        74 |          0 |     0 |

@datalogics-pgallot has tested the same rule against his 215 files, reports the same partition
with zero mixed files, and is adopting it in preference to his own.

The *authoring* version partitions neither corpus. Here, `authoring_version = 8137` carries 74
`T` files and 21 `3T` files; in his data it carries 88 `T` and 69 `3T`. Anyone reaching for a
version-based rule should be aware the two version words behave quite differently.

There is also a mechanism rather than only a correlation: one 97-file family in his data carries
twelve distinct `(minimal_version_for_read, authoring_version)` pairs — two minimal versions and
eight authoring versions from 7094 to 20225. That is what a compatibility floor declared per file
looks like, and it is not what a producer habit looks like.

Even so, it does not belong in normative text, because **a reader never needs it**. The array's
size is carried in the file and costs nothing to read. No conforming reader has to predict it,
and one that did would be strictly worse than one that did not. A predictor is of interest to a
*writer* choosing what to emit, and to anyone auditing a corpus — neither of which this clause
governs.

If it is wanted anywhere, the right place is an informative NOTE alongside CR-14d:

> NOTE  In files examined to date the sizing corresponds to the value of
> `minimal_version_for_read`, with `3T` in files declaring 7094 or 7095 and `T` in files declaring
> 8137. This is an observation about existing producers, not a requirement, and a reader shall
> determine the size from the file rather than from any version field.

We offer that without pressing for it. Having just had one partition fail after hardening it too
early, we would rather this one sat as a NOTE that nothing depends on.

### One caveat on our own figures

Our walker cannot skip past an uncompressed tessellation entry — entries are not length-prefixed,
so once one is met the bit cursor is lost — and 193 of the 310 files stop early for that reason.
Only 126 are reached. It undercounts; it does not misreport, and an earlier cut by a different
route reached 144 files with the same partition and the same absence of exceptions.

## The text at issue

`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2561`-`:2566`:

> To traverse the mesh structure.
>
> * If the current triangle has only one neighbour, this neighbour is pushed on the stack.
> * If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the left triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the right triangle is pushed on the stack.
>
> Once done with the current triangle, the stack is popped and it becomes the current triangle.

The structure is a stack that is pushed and popped, so it is last-in-first-out, and the second
bullet is the only place in the traversal where an order is observable: the first bullet pushes a
single neighbour, where order cannot matter. Everything below concerns that one sentence.

## Measurement

**Instrument.** A Release build of nanoPRC at commit `7bc8c1d`, carrying a checksum over each
mesh's emitted triangle-index array and an environment variable that swaps the two push calls.
Both arms run from the same binary, so nothing but the order differs.

**Denominator, reproducible.** The 145 files in the collection published by @ralovich
(https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db) that contain at least one compressed tessellation reaching
this traversal.

| | files |
|---|---|
| decode identically under both orders | 18 |
| decode differently | 127 |
| **abort partway under the order as written** | **91** |
| abort partway under the reversed order | **0** |
| decode *more* geometry under the order as written | **0** |
| complete under both orders but disagree on geometry | 36 |

The same run over a separate collection of 195 further files, held under licence, gives 95 aborts
and again none in the other direction. Combined: **186 of 340 files abort under the order as
written, and none aborts under the reversed order.**

The aborts are not a shading or winding difference. The decode returns an error and the containing
file fails to parse, so under the order as written those files are not readable at all.

**Worked example, from the public collection.** `PMI Analysis.stream-249`. Its first compressed
mesh decodes 16,412 triangles under the reversed order and 15,399 under the order as written --
1,013 triangles short -- and then the decoder fails and the remaining fourteen meshes in the file
are never reached.

Four more from the same collection, as meshes reached before the decode stops (reversed order
versus the order as written): `3D_PDF_iPhone_Replacement.stream-171` 5,228 vs 1;
`Alamo_DotProduct_PointFuse_PDF3D.stream-92` 2,808 vs 28; `tad50us12b-j.stream-90` 1,594 vs 19;
`unolinea-house-dwg.stream-79` 1,577 vs 1.

## A caution on choosing a fixture for this

We expected the 18 files that agree to be meshes of a single triangle, where there is no second
neighbour to order. They are not.
`TFM_DIEGO_ENRIQUE_ALVARADO_MARTIN.stream-306` is in the agreeing set and holds 192 single-triangle
meshes, one mesh of 46 triangles and one of 1,116, and produces a byte-identical index array under
both orders.

Mesh size is therefore not the discriminator. The discriminator is whether any single step finds
*both* neighbours untreated at once -- which is precisely the condition the second bullet governs.
A long fan or strip that exposes one neighbour per step traverses identically either way. So
"contains a multi-triangle mesh" is not sufficient to make a file a witness, and a fixture chosen
for triangle count alone may well not be one. That may be why this has been hard to reproduce on
small test files.

## Two candidate causes, which this measurement cannot separate

`:2559` defines the two labels only in its closing sentence:

> Left or right characteristic for the neighbour is determined using the triangle normal.

That says the labels are derived from the triangle normal but not how, and the worked example
earlier in the same paragraph fixes the arrangement of T0 to T3 without stating the rule that
produced it. Two readings are therefore consistent with everything measured above:

1. **The order in the second bullet is transposed.** The labels mean what an implementer would
   naturally take them to mean, and the sentence names them in the wrong sequence.
2. **The order is correct and the labels are under-specified.** In that case it is our labelling
   that is transposed relative to the intent, and the sentence is not implementable as written
   because the rule for assigning "left" and "right" is absent.

Both produce the same observable: an implementation that follows the text literally, with the
labelling an implementer would arrive at unaided, fails on 186 of 340 files. We cannot tell from
outside which of the two it is, and we are not asking the committee to accept reading 1 on our
word.

What the measurement does establish is narrower and, we think, sufficient to act on: of the two
possible combinations of label assignment and push order, one decodes these files and the other
does not, and the document as it stands does not tell a reader which combination to build.

## One observation from the document alone

Independently of any corpus, the paragraph at `:2559` gives a reader two hints about which
neighbour is treated first, and they do not agree with each other.

Its worked example reads, in order:

> Then, T1 is the right neighbor of T0. [...] T3 is the right neighboUr of T1. [...] T2 is the left neighboUr of T1.

So of the two neighbours of T1, the **left** one is numbered T2 and the **right** one is numbered
T3. If the numbering of T0 to T3 is the order in which they are treated, the left neighbour is
treated before the right -- which is what the reversed push order produces, and what the bullet as
written does not. But the prose introduces T3 before T2, which points the other way, and the
paragraph nowhere states that the numbering is the treatment order.

We put this as an observation rather than as an argument. It is weak on its own and we would not
file on it. It is worth recording because it is the one piece of evidence here that needs no files
at all, and because a reader working only from the document has three signals to reconcile -- the
numbering, the prose order, and the bullet -- of which at most two can be consistent. That is true
whichever way the committee decides the substantive question, and it is an argument for making the
rule explicit rather than leaving it to be inferred from an example.

## Proposed change

Either alternative closes it. **Alternative A** if the committee's answer is that the order is
transposed; **Alternative B** if the order is correct and the labels need pinning down. B is the
more thorough repair, because it also removes the need for a reader to infer the rule from the
worked example.

### Alternative A -- correct the order

**Current text** (`:2564`):

    * If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the left triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the right triangle is pushed on the stack.

**Replacement text**:

    * If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the right triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the left triangle is pushed on the stack. Because the stack is last-in-first-out, this causes the left neighbour to be treated first.

The final clause is included because the combination of a push order and a LIFO stack is what
determines the traversal, and stating the consequence makes the sentence checkable against an
implementation without the reader having to reason about the stack discipline separately.

### Alternative B -- define the labels, and state the consequence of the order

**Current text** (`:2559`, final sentence):

    Left or right characteristic for the neighbour is determined using the triangle normal.

**Replacement text**:

    The left or right characteristic of a neighbour is determined as follows. Let the current triangle's first edge be directed from its earlier-treated vertex to its later-treated vertex, and let N be the triangle normal as computed for this triangle. The neighbour across the edge that is counter-clockwise from the first edge when viewed from the direction of N is the left neighbour; the neighbour across the remaining edge is the right neighbour. This assignment, together with the push order given below and the last-in-first-out behaviour of the stack, fully determines the traversal and therefore the decoded positions of non-referenced vertices.

We offer the wording of Alternative B with less confidence than A, because it states a rule we have
inferred rather than one we can cite, and the committee may know the intended rule differs. If the
handedness in that paragraph is the opposite of the intent, then the same sentence with
"clockwise" substituted is the correction, and Alternative A becomes unnecessary. The point of
offering it is that *some* explicit rule is needed, not that ours is the right one.

## What this does not claim

The 36 files in the public collection, and 88 across both collections, that complete under both
orders but produce different geometry are **not** settled by this measurement. It shows that they
differ; it says nothing about which result is correct. Deciding those would need an independent
reading of the same files, which we have not done.

Nor does it bear on CR-14g, the sentence at `:2566` about popping the stack, which is unaffected
either way.

## Provenance

The measurement is nanoPRC's (CascadiaVoxel LLC, AGPLv3, https://github.com/mvrhel/nanoPRC). The
public half is reproducible from @ralovich's published collection; the second collection is held
under licence and cannot be redistributed, and is reported only as an aggregate that moves the
figures in the same direction. The probe used to take the measurement was temporary and is not in
any commit.

# Correction: our `origin_array` = bounding-box-center self-check is unsafe, and will report defects in correct decodes

In June I posted a self-verification recipe on this issue 

> The §7.8.9.7 check that pinned this down: `origin_array` equals the reconstructed mesh's
> **bounding-box center**, so an implementer can self-verify the frame by confirming the decoded
> bbox center coincides with `origin_array`.

That's not quite right, or rather not always right, `origin_array` is the reference point from which the first vertex's delta is measured. we've found that Writers in the wild populate it with **either** the bounding-box center of the compressed tessellation **or** the vertex centroid, and because it is only a reference point, both round-trip identically and both decode correctly. 

An implementer self-verifying an apex frame should therefore confirm that the declared origin coincides with either the decoded bounding-box center or the decoded vertex centroid. A mismatch against both is a real signal; a mismatch against one is not.

**#727: proposed changes for the compressed tessellation's coordinate systems and their arithmetic.**
These come from findings by Patrick Gallot (Datalogics) of 1 November, measured on large scanned
meshes from the collection @ralovich publishes, and checked against nanoPRC's decoder and encoder. For
a reader new to the thread: the compressed tessellation stores each new vertex as three integers in a
small coordinate system built from triangles already decoded, and each normal as two angles in another.
A reader that builds either system differently from the writer reconstructs the wrong mesh, and
reports no error.

Five changes are proposed. Current text is quoted from the TWG working source at `main` `6fb2ed9`,
`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc`. Code is cited at nanoPRC `main` `e1a53f7`.

## 1. 7.8.9.5 "Mesh Normal Construction": the second corner test (erratum)

The corner tests choose the corner of the triangle whose angle is nearest a right angle. Once the
first test has failed, corner 1 is known not to be that corner, so the second test has to compare
corners 2 and 3. As written it compares 1 and 3 again.

Current (`:2674`):

```
"Else if " (theta_1<theta_3) => vec(X) larr vec(V)_3 \ \ \ vec(Z) larr (-vec(V)_3 ^^ vec(V)_1)
```

Replacement:

```
"Else if " (theta_2<theta_3) => vec(X) larr vec(V)_3 \ \ \ vec(Z) larr (-vec(V)_3 ^^ vec(V)_1)
```

Only the condition changes; the assignments stay. nanoPRC's decoder makes this test
(`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c:194`). Datalogics found the difference on
`smallBMS-(3D-pdf).stream-13`, whose first compressed entity has a thin sliver as triangle 46. Two
decoders reading identical normal bits and identical angles for it choose different corners under the
two tests, and decode its normal as (0.608, −0.791, −0.069) under the text's test and as
(1.000, 0.00007, −0.0003) under the corrected one, which is nanoPRC's. That normal later decides
whether a triangle is reversed, and from there the traversal.

## 2. 7.8.9.3 "Mesh Points and Triangles": the direction of X

Current (eq-1, `:2584`):

```
vec(X) larr ((vec(V)_1-vec(V)_0))/(norm(vec(V)_1-vec(V)_0))
```

Replacement:

```
vec(X) larr ((vec(V)_0-vec(V)_1))/(norm(vec(V)_0-vec(V)_1))
```

With V₀ the earlier treated, as `:2599` defines it, X runs from V₁ to V₀ in nanoPRC's decoder
(`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c:1154`) and encoder (`src/prc_write_compress_tess.c:1802`). The
direction matters. Reversing X reverses Z through eq-2 and leaves Y as it was, so a reader following
eq-1 as written places every new vertex with its first and third coordinates negated: a mirror image
in the plane of the triangle. nanoPRC places the vertex at O + x·X + y·Y + z·Z, with no compensating
sign (`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c:332-352`). Files written by nanoPRC's encoder display
correctly in Acrobat. Datalogics' reader, which reproduces nanoPRC's decoder vertex for vertex on
whole parts of these files, and Datalogics' writer also take X from V₁ to V₀. That makes three
implementations against the equation as published.

## 3. 7.8.9.3: the orientation rule, on both routes, and the order of operations

The text gives the three axes but no rule for which way Y and Z point. Writers reverse both when Y
points towards the new vertex's side of the edge, and a reader that omits this step reconstructs
nothing usable. Datalogics found that the rule has to apply after the MakeOrthoRep() fallback too:
on `DotProduct-Tesla-CloudCompare-PDF3D.stream-79`, applying it on the ordinary route only first
departs from nanoPRC at vertex 10,950, an apex exactly in line with the edge, and applying it on both
routes moves that to vertex 20,036.

Three further points of order decide the result to the last bit, and the replacement states them: Z
is made unit before Y is computed from it; on the fallback route Y is recomputed from the X of
eq-1, not from the copy of X that MakeOrthoRep() makes unit again; and the new vertex is placed by
scaling each stored coordinate by the tolerance and then adding the three terms to O in the order X,
Y, Z. The reference MakeOrthoRep()
(`iso-prc/code/prc_pt.cpp:144-162`) is right as a general function. It is the apex coordinate system
that keeps its own X.

Current (`:2599`):

```
In the <<eq-1>>, stem:[V_0] and stem:[V_1] are taken so that stem:[V_0] has a treatment index less than stem:[V_1] (which means that stem:[V_0] has been treated before stem:[V_1]). A particular case occurs if the Z axis or Y are NULL (length less than FLT_EPSILON). FLT_EPSILON is the minimum positive floating point number of type float in accordance with the IEEE single-precision standard. In these cases, they are computed by the function MakeOrthoRep(), using the unit axis X as input. Then stem:[V_2] is expressed in this coordinate system, compressed the same way as before and updated in the working structure. Then the next triangle is traversed as explained in <<Mesh_Traversal>>.
```

Replacement:

```
In the <<eq-1>>, stem:[V_0] and stem:[V_1] are taken so that stem:[V_0] has a treatment index less than stem:[V_1] (which means that stem:[V_0] has been treated before stem:[V_1]). Z and Y are each made unit with Unitize() (see <<Basis_pseudo_code>>) as they are computed, so that the Z used in <<eq-3>> is already unit. A particular case occurs if the Z axis or Y are NULL (length less than FLT_EPSILON). FLT_EPSILON is the minimum positive floating point number of type float in accordance with the IEEE single-precision standard. In these cases, Z is computed by the function MakeOrthoRep(), using the unit axis X as input; Y is then computed as stem:[vec(Z) ^^ vec(X)] with the X of <<eq-1>>, not with the copy of X that MakeOrthoRep() makes unit, and made unit. X is not changed.

However the axes were obtained, they are then oriented: if stem:[vec(Y) * (vec(O) - vec(V)_3) > 0], Y and Z are both reversed. If the product is zero, they are not reversed. Then stem:[V_2] is expressed in this coordinate system, compressed the same way as before and updated in the working structure. The position that replaces stem:[V_2] in the working structure is computed from its three stored integers x, y and z: each is multiplied by the tolerance, each result multiplies its axis, and the three terms are added to O in the order X, Y, Z, as stem:[((vec(O) + x_t vec(X)) + y_t vec(Y)) + z_t vec(Z)], where stem:[x_t], stem:[y_t] and stem:[z_t] are x, y and z multiplied by the tolerance. A decoder reconstructs stem:[V_2] in the same way. Then the next triangle is traversed as explained in <<Mesh_Traversal>>.
```

The sentence defining FLT_EPSILON is kept word for word; it is outside this change. nanoPRC's
decoder does each step as stated (`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c:1151-1220`): Z made unit at
`:1168`, the fallback at `:1193-1210`, Y from the original X at `:1204`, and the orientation, strict,
at `:1215`, after both routes. It places the vertex as stated at `:332-352`. Its encoder repeats the
same steps so that its files decode (`src/prc_write_compress_tess.c:1787-1847`), and places the
vertex it reinjects in the same order (`:1755-1769`). Datalogics' decoder also makes Z unit before
computing Y from it, makes Y unit, and places the vertex in the same order.

The placement step is included because the NOTE of change 5 says that the order of operations is
specified; without it the text would promise one more thing than it delivers. The measurements
behind these changes show that last-bit differences matter in general. Neither implementation has
compared the two summation orders on a file, so the placement step records what both do rather than
a difference anyone has measured.

## 4. 7.8.9.1 "General": the precision, and what it is computed from

The clause already requires double precision of an encoder (`:2539`), and clause 10's
"Basis pseudo code" requires 64-bit arithmetic for its functions
(`iso-prc/sections/10-tessellation-compression.adoc:46`). Neither says that a decoder is bound in
the same way, nor what the calculations take as input. Datalogics' reader once ran its normal
stage on a single-precision copy of the vertices: every formula was right, and on a zero-area
triangle the reversal decision came out as the sign of the rounding.

Current (`:2539`, last sentence):

```
Double precision computations that are compliant with IEEE 754 shall be used for mesh compression calculations.
```

Replacement:

```
Double precision computations that are compliant with IEEE 754 shall be used for mesh compression and decompression calculations, with the functions given in <<Basis_pseudo_code>>. Every coordinate system, angle and test in the following subclauses shall be computed from the positions in the working structure: for an encoder, the approximated positions reinjected into it; for a decoder, the positions it has reconstructed. A single-precision copy of those positions shall not be used.
```

## 5. 7.8.9.1: a NOTE on why the arithmetic matters

Proposed new paragraph, after `:2543` (the paragraph defining treatment index):

```
NOTE: Each new point is expressed in a coordinate system built from points reconstructed before it, so reconstruction is a chain. A difference in the last bit of one coordinate changes every coordinate system built from it, and the difference grows along the chain. A decoder whose arithmetic differs from the encoder's only in rounding can therefore reconstruct a visibly wrong mesh with no error on either side. For this reason the precision, the inputs and the order of operations are specified in the following subclauses.
```

Datalogics measured the growth on the Tesla file: a difference of 5.7 × 10⁻¹⁴ at one vertex roughly
doubled at each vertex after it until the mesh was visibly wrong.

## What this does not propose

- **A general requirement for bit-exact results.** It would go further than anyone can test. The
  changes above cover every case the measurements found.
- **The derivation of `normal_was_reversed` for a triangle,** with its own zero case. The text does
  not define that derivation at all. It belongs with CR-14f, where a rule from Datalogics is to
  replace our Alternative B; that will follow in a separate comment.
- **A tie rule for the corner tests.** The reference `AngleBetween()` already clamps a cosine within
  10⁻¹² of ±1 (`iso-prc/code/prc_pt.cpp:137-140`), which scores such a corner as exactly π/2 away
  from a right angle. nanoPRC does the same (`src/prc_vector_util.c:171-178`).

**CR-14f, revised: which neighbour is left and which is right.** On 28 September we proposed CR-14f
in two alternatives: A, to reverse the push order at `:2564`, and B, to define left and right at
`:2559`, in wording we had inferred and offered with less confidence. Patrick Gallot (Datalogics) has
since found a rule that reproduces nanoPRC's decoder on large files from the collection @ralovich
publishes, and we have checked each of its steps against nanoPRC's code. With his agreement it
replaces our wording for B.

It also settles the choice between the two. The rule fixes which neighbour is left and which is
right, and with those names the push order that decodes these files is the one in A. So A and B are
no longer alternatives, and CR-14f is now the two changes below, made together. The names are the
ones the worked example at `:2559` already uses: with T0 = [V0 V1 V2], "T1 is the right neighbor of
T0. the edge between V1 and V2 is the first edge of T1". A text that exchanged the two names would
keep the push order as written and decode the same files; we propose the names the example already
uses, so that only the order changes.

Current text is quoted from the TWG working source at `main` `6fb2ed9`,
`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc`. Code is cited at nanoPRC `main` `e1a53f7`,
`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c`.

## 1. 7.8.9.2 "Mesh Traversal": the rule for left and right

Current (`:2559`, last sentence):

```
Left or right characteristic for the neighbour is determined using the triangle normal.
```

Replacement:

```
Left or right characteristic for the neighbour is determined as follows, for every triangle, including the first triangle of each chain. The vertices of the triangle are taken in order as t0, t1 and t2: for the first triangle of a chain, in the order in which they are read, with the first two exchanged if the first has the greater treatment index, as stated above; for any other triangle, the two vertices of the edge across which it was reached, in increasing treatment index, followed by its third vertex. The neighbour across the edge [t0 t2] is the left neighbour and the neighbour across the edge [t1 t2] is the right neighbour, unless the triangle is reversed, in which case the two are exchanged, each edge together with the vertex opposite it. Bit 0 of the triangle's edge_status is set if it has a right neighbour and bit 1 if it has a left neighbour, with left and right as determined here.

When must_recalculate_normals is TRUE, a triangle is reversed if its value of *normal_is_reversed* is TRUE. When must_recalculate_normals is FALSE, a triangle is reversed if stem:[((vec(P)_2 - (vec(P)_0 + vec(P)_1)/2) ^^ (vec(P)_1 - vec(P)_0)) * vec(N) < 0], where stem:[vec(P)_0], stem:[vec(P)_1] and stem:[vec(P)_2] are the positions of t0, t1 and t2 and stem:[vec(N)] is the normal stored for t0 in this triangle. If the product is zero, the triangle is not reversed. The positions are those reconstructed in the working structure, and the product is computed in double precision.
```

nanoPRC's decoder does each step as stated:

- the order of the vertices: a chain's first triangle as read, with the first two exchanged when the
  first has the greater treatment index (`:1327-1345`); any other triangle as the edge, in increasing
  treatment index, followed by the new vertex (`:3302-3304`);
- left across [t0 t2] and right across [t1 t2] (`:675-682`);
- the exchange of the whole of each side when the triangle is reversed (`:684-699`);
- each edge's two vertices put in increasing treatment index before either neighbour is visited, the
  opposite vertex left alone (`:705-733`);
- bit 0 for the right and bit 1 for the left, read after the exchange (`:735-753`);
- every triangle through the same routine, the first of each chain included (`:3068`);
- where normals are recalculated, the stored value (`:435`, `:1557`); where they are stored, the
  test above, strict, with N the normal at the triangle's first vertex (`:595-620`, with
  `:1491-1493`), or the face's single normal on a planar face (`:628-657`, `:1816`).

Datalogics routed the first triangle of each chain through this rule rather than a separate path, and
the part DRL-P0066.1 of `DRL_3DPDF.stream-403` (11,160 triangles) then agreed with nanoPRC on every
triangle and every one of its 8,325 vertices. On DRL-P0063.1 of the same file (90,712 triangles), a
chain starts on a triangle whose third vertex lies exactly on the midpoint of the first two, so the
product is exactly zero; with the comparison strict and the test computed on the reconstructed
positions in double precision, the part matches nanoPRC on every triangle. Computed on
single-precision copies of the same positions, the triangle is not degenerate, and the next triangle
came out reversed.

## 2. 7.8.9.2: the push order

Unchanged from Alternative A of 28 September.

Current (`:2564`):

```
* If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the left triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the right triangle is pushed on the stack.
```

Replacement:

```
* If the current triangle has both a left and a right neighbour which are not treated, the right triangle is first pushed on the stack. Then the left triangle is pushed on the stack. Because the stack is last-in-first-out, this causes the left neighbour to be treated first.
```

nanoPRC's decoder pushes the right neighbour and then the left (`:3112-3148`). The measurement of
28 September, above, stands: under the order as written, 91 of the 145 files of @ralovich's
collection that reach this step stop partway, and none does under this order.

## What this does not change

- **The sentence on popping the stack at `:2566`,** which is CR-14g.
- **The worked example at `:2559`.** Its first statement agrees with the rule. We have not checked
  the rest of it against a file, and propose no change to it.
- **The status of the rule.** As Datalogics put it, the rule is validated against what the writers
  of these files emit, not against any statement of intent: it says what files require.

**Correction to the frames comment above (5 November), changes 2 and 4.** Two points from Patrick Gallot
(Datalogics), both of which I agree with. Neither changes a conclusion.

**Change 2, the reason given.** The comment says that a reader following eq-1 as written "places every new vertex with
its first and third coordinates negated: a mirror image in the plane of the triangle." Negating two coordinates of a
right-handed system is not a mirror image. It is a half-turn about the Y axis through O: the vertex goes from
O + x·X + y·Y + z·Z to O − x·X + y·Y − z·Z. The replacement proposed for eq-1 is unchanged, and so is the consequence: a
wrong mesh, with no error.

**Change 4, the replacement text.** It requires double precision "with the functions given in Basis pseudo code", and
forbids single-precision copies of the positions. The reference `Length()` in those functions rounds the sum of squares
to `float` before taking the root (`iso-prc/code/prc_pt.cpp:96-114`), so a reader who takes "double precision" literally
would compute that length entirely in double and depart from the reference. nanoPRC's decoder and encoder follow the
reference here (`src/prc_vector_util.c:53-83`, used by `prc_vec_normalize` at `:116-129`; nanoPRC `main` `e32c194`), and
so does Datalogics' reader. The replacement should say so.

Proposed replacement for change 4, in place of the one above:

```
Double precision computations that are compliant with IEEE 754 shall be used for mesh compression and decompression calculations, with the functions given in <<Basis_pseudo_code>>, including the single-precision rounding in Length(). Every coordinate system, angle and test in the following subclauses shall be computed from the positions in the working structure: for an encoder, the approximated positions reinjected into it; for a decoder, the positions it has reconstructed. A single-precision copy of those positions shall not be used.
```

The only difference from the replacement above is the clause ", including the single-precision rounding in Length()".
The current text it replaces, and its location (`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2539`, TWG `main` at `6fb2ed9`),
are unchanged.

It depends.

If the extension is about adding new elements that are only reachable via second class names with the prefix of the extension, then you indeed don't need the extension dictionary to determine runtime behavior. At least as long as the owner of that prefix did a decent job, that is...

But if the extension is about something that does not bring along PDF names with the prefix, the situation might differ. E.g. consider extensions that define meanings for the standard security handler user access permissions bits marked "reserved" in 32K. There might be one hypothetical extension that defines bit 13 value 0 to mean that "a PDF MAC token is required to be present in all revisions of the document" while another extension defines bit 13 value 0 to mean that "a PDF document timestamp is required to be present in all revisions of the document". If a PDF processor supports both extensions, its runtime behavior will differ when finding a value 0 in that bit depending on the extension defined for the document; in particular when adding a revision it will add either a MAC or a timestamp. (Ok, it just might ignore the extensions declared and add both, but you probably see the effect I have in mind)

Yes, this example is somewhat artificial. But if extensions become more widely used, such collisions in extensions may occur and processors may have to base their runtime behavior on the declared extension.

Unfortunately the MDP level 2 is neither clearly defined nor coherently implemented.

According to ISO 32000-2:

> Permitted changes shall be filling in forms, instantiating page templates, and signing

Depending on whom you asked and when you asked, you'll get different explanations what "signing" means. In particular

* whether it means merely that existing, unsigned signature fields may be signed using the options provided by the field,
* or whether it means that also creating new signature fields and signing them is allowed.

Your requirement could be realized if the former interpretation was commonly accepted and implemented but it is not. Existing implementations show either behavior, sometimes even a mixture: Some tools only allow their user to sign existing signature fields for MDP level 2 but during validation accept signatures in newly created fields in MDP level 2 documents.

----

Concerning the originally intended behavior in ISO 32000-1, we'd have to wait for people involved in the ISOfication of the PDF spec to speak up.
Concerning the original Adobe intention you might want to read [this stack overflow answer](https://stackoverflow.com/a/16711745/1729265): According to the source referenced there adding signature fields to signed PDFs was not allowed at any MDP level, only for signed PDFs without MDP level, i.e. only signed with simple approval signatures.

C&P TWG asks for input by creators of PDF signing and signature validation software about their understanding of "signing" in MDP level 2. In particular whether they allow their users to sign MDP level 2 PDFs by adding new signature fields, and how they validate signatures if signature fields are added to MDP level 2 PDFs.

For reference checked what we have in iText for MDP level 2:

- Adding new signature fields is allowed when signing.
- Signature validation also permits such field additions and it is [explicitly documented in the code](https://github.com/itext/itext-java/blob/f0ef068cbbf86386997b430f2bc3982eb26df294/sign/src/main/java/com/itextpdf/signatures/validation/DocumentRevisionsValidator.java#L1450).

By default, PyHanko's validator forbids the creation of new visible signature fields after any certification signature (DocMDP level 3 is simply not supported, hence the lack of distinction between the levels). For pragmatic reasons, it does permit creating new visible fields if all prior signatures are approval signatures, since that's a very common scenario when putting multiple signatures on an otherwise non-interactive PDF document. Filling existing visible signature fields is also permitted at DocMDP level 2.

The rationale being that a document author that bothered to put in a certification signature presumably knew what they wanted re: the form structure.

Reference: https://github.com/MatthiasValvekens/pyHanko/blob/master/pkgs/pyhanko/src/pyhanko/sign/diff_analysis/rules/form_field_rules.py#L271-L274

Note: Restrictions around invisible signature fields are more lax.

Yes and no. Acrobat allows creating new fields at DocMDP level 2 (whether invisible or not), or at least it did when I last tested it several years ago.

I had a good reason to deviate from that de facto baseline for _visible_ signature fields (i.e. to disallow changes to the visual presentation of the page outside the author's intent), but for invisible ones I figured there wasn't really any harm in following the prior art from Acrobat. So it was part principle, part pragmatism.

C&P TWG determines that "signing" in DocMDP level 2 allows both for filling in existing signature fields and creating and filling new ones.
Thus, there is no way to guarantee that the next signature will be invisible.

1. The destination entry (`Dest`) is set to takes the user to Page 5 with `/Fit`.  So a user activating (and activating is defined in PDF through several mechanism, but let's say a click) is taken to Page 5 with the whole page on screen.  However, the user read the Outline Item text and quickly skims to to the corresponding "heading" on the page.
2. A non-sighted user is taken to the destination (i.e. what we refer to by Navigation).  But the Screen Reader doesn't know where to read, so it uses the `SE` entry to understand that it can start reading from that point.  This is not considered interactive navigation by the PDF spec, but is useful information that is actionable by a user agent.

So `SE` provides a useful function in PDF 1.x and 2.x.  Now, in 2.x, an author system can choose to use the structure destination that combines these two useful pieces of information and uses them both for interactive navigation.  So a PDF 2.0 authoring system can choose whether to use a classic Dest (easy to compute, can be added prior to structuring the document if so desired) or a Structure Destination.  In the case of a Structure Destination, for a PDF 2.0 processor, the `SE` is somewhat redundant in this case.  But in a PDF 2.0 file that uses a classic `Dest` and `SE` combo, things would still work just as they did in PDF 1.7 (hence no need or desire for deprecation).

More important, even when using the Structure Destination, an authoring system can choose to provide backwards compatibility.

# Proposed Editorial Changes to PRC Specification (Revision 14 Nov 2025)

**Subject:** Defects in §7.8.9.9 (`BinaryTextureData`) and Table 177 — ambiguous units
of `texture_binary_data_size` and incorrect derived array size formula.

---

## Change Request 1 — Clarify the description of `texture_binary_data_size` in Table 177

**Location:** §7.8.9.9, Table 177, description column for `texture_binary_data_size`

**Before:**

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `texture_binary_data_size` | `UnsignedInteger` | (Optional) texture_binary_data_size / 32 |

**After:**

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `texture_binary_data_size` | `UnsignedInteger` | (Optional) The number of 32-bit UnsignedIntegers in `texture_binary_data`. The total number of bits in `texture_binary_data` is therefore `texture_binary_data_size * 32`. The number of meaningful (non-padding) bits is `texture_binary_data_size * 32 - last_integer_used_bit_number`. |

---

## Change Request 2 — Correct the array size formula for `texture_binary_data` in Table 177

**Location:** §7.8.9.9, Table 177, Data Type and description columns for `texture_binary_data`

**Before:**

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `texture_binary_data` | `Array <bits(8)>[texture_binary_data_size / 8]` | (Optional) This size array is equal to `texture_binary_data_size` / 8. |

**After:**

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `texture_binary_data` | `Array <UnsignedInteger>[texture_binary_data_size]` | (Optional) An array of `texture_binary_data_size` 32-bit UnsignedIntegers, each written as 4 bytes via `MakePortable32BitsUnsigned` (see §9.2). The total bit content is `texture_binary_data_size * 32` bits, of which the last `last_integer_used_bit_number` bits are padding. |

---

## Change Request 3 — Correct the descriptive paragraph in §7.8.9.9

**Location:** §7.8.9.9, introductory paragraph

**Before:**

> Then `last_integer_used_bit_number` bits are added to this array so that `texture_binary_data_size`
> becomes a multiple of 32. Consequently, 0 ≤ `last_integer_used_bit_number` < 32. Then the unsigned
> integer array is written byte by byte: each unsigned integer leads to 4 bytes obtained from
> `MakePortable32BitsUnsigned`.

**After:**

> The bit field is padded with `last_integer_used_bit_number` zero bits so that its total length becomes
> a multiple of 32, where 0 ≤ `last_integer_used_bit_number` < 32. The padded bit field is then
> partitioned into 32-bit words and stored as an array of `UnsignedInteger`s, the count of which is
> recorded in `texture_binary_data_size`. Each unsigned integer is written as 4 bytes via
> `MakePortable32BitsUnsigned` (see §9.2).

---

## Change Request 4 — Give `last_integer_used_bit_number` a meaningful description in Table 177

**Location:** §7.8.9.9, Table 177, description column for `last_integer_used_bit_number`

**Before:**

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `last_integer_used_bit_number` | `UnsignedInteger` | (Optional) last_integer_used_bit_number |

**After:**

| Name | Data Type | Data Description |
|---|---|---|
| `last_integer_used_bit_number` | `UnsignedInteger` | (Optional) The number of padding bits appended to the bit field to bring its length to a multiple of 32. Satisfies 0 ≤ `last_integer_used_bit_number` < 32. The number of meaningful bits in `texture_binary_data` is `texture_binary_data_size * 32 - last_integer_used_bit_number`. |

(`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:732`):

> The number of 32-bit _UnsignedIntegers_ in *texture_binary_data*. The total number of bits in
> *texture_binary_data* is therefore *texture_binary_data_size* * 32. The number of meaningful
> (non-padding) bits is *texture_binary_data_size* * 32 - *last_integer_used_bit_number*.

That gives all three quantities an implementer needs — the unit (32-bit unsigned integers, not bytes
and not bits), the total bit count, and the meaningful bit count net of padding — and the companion
`texture_binary_data` row states the same relationship from the other direction.

We read the field on exactly those terms and have no discrepancy to report against real files.

**We agree this is closable.** This is corroboration of an answer already reached on the issue, not a
new finding; the credit belongs to the proposer.

## We would suggest this stays open — the length is still genuinely unstated

Checked against `pdf-association/3dpdf-twg`, `main` @ `ba2bdc1` (5 September 2026). We think the
triage recommendation to close is premature, and want to set out why rather than let it pass silently.

### The length is not merely under-described — the field carries no cardinality at all

In `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:561`, `normal_is_reversed` is declared as an
array whose `occurrence:` key is **present but empty**:

```yaml
  - name: normal_is_reversed
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence:
    required: false
    description: The number of normals is implicit, depending on the number of triangles and faces.
      Vertices have always as many normals as the number of faces to which they belong.
    require_conditions: "if *must_recalculate_normals* is TRUE)"
```

Every other array in this file carries an expression there. This one does not, and its description
declines to supply one in prose either — "the number of normals is implicit" is a statement that the
length is not being given.

The verbal rule that follows is also not obviously the cardinality a reader needs. "Vertices have
always as many normals as the number of faces to which they belong" describes a per-vertex-per-face
quantity; the array is consumed per **triangle**. Those are different counts, and the text does not
reconcile them.

### And the document contradicts itself about whether the field exists at all

§7.8.9.7, in the prose at `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2818`, says:

> * The *normal_is_reversed* field is reserved for future use.

A field that is reserved for future use does not also have a presence condition
(`if must_recalculate_normals is TRUE`) and an "implicit" length. Both statements cannot hold.

This matters beyond tidiness, because **the field is load-bearing in practice, not reserved.** It is
actively written and consumed by real encoders and decoders in the `must_recalculate_normals == TRUE`
case, where there is no external per-vertex normal source and the stored flags are the only thing
determining reconstructed normal orientation. We have a separate draft (our CR-22, not yet filed)
covering encoder-side guidance for deriving the value; it depends on this field being documented as
live rather than reserved.

### What we implement, offered as a data point rather than a proposal

Our reader takes the length to be **one flag per triangle**, specifically the length of
`triangle_face_array`, present only when `must_recalculate_normals` is TRUE, read as that many raw
bits rather than as a `CharacterArray`, and indexed by triangle index during traversal. That is
consistent across the real files we decode.

We offer this as evidence of what one implementation converged on in the absence of a stated rule —
**not** as a proposed normative cardinality. If other implementations read it differently, that
divergence is precisely the interoperability risk this issue exists to close, and it would be better
surfaced now than assumed away.

### Two editorial defects in the same declaration

Both visible only in the working source:

1. **Empty `occurrence:` key** (line 565) — either it should carry the cardinality expression, or the
   key should be removed and the length stated in prose.
2. **Unmatched parenthesis** — `require_conditions` reads `"if *must_recalculate_normals* is TRUE)"`
   with a closing parenthesis and no opening one.

### Summary

Closing this would leave three things unresolved: the array has no stated length, the prose calls a
live field reserved, and the two statements contradict each other. Any one of those is a reason to
keep it open; together they are the substance of the original report.

We recognise we may be missing context from the triage discussion — if "matches what we implement"
refers to a cardinality that has been agreed somewhere we have not seen, we would withdraw this and
would be glad to be pointed at it.

I recommend using a decoding strategy for *SingleWireBodyCompress* by mirroring the *BrepDataCompress* preamble fields, while substituting *curve_tolerance* wherever *brep_data_compressed_tolerance* is referenced. SingleWire objects explicitly store and use their own tolerance member (double) for curve precision. Note that *CompressedVertex* is excluded from the single-wire path. Never expect *CompressedVertex*, only use *CompressedPoint* data type for wire endpoint geometry. *CompressedPoint* uses a simpler coordinate-based structure compared to *CompressedVertex*. This is specified by the conditionals in Table 240: - start_vertex / end_vertex → "Optional; if curve_trimming_face is TRUE" (i.e. *BrepDataCompress* only) - start_point / end_point → "Optional; if curve_trimming_face is FALSE" (i.e. *SingleWireBodyCompress* only) *PRC_TYPE_TOPO_SingleWireBodyCompress* should also contain *number_of_bits_to_store_reference*, * PRC_TYPE_TOPO_SingleWireBodyCompress: Represents a mathematical wire frame body (open or closed curves moving through space without an underlying face or bounding sheet topology). As explicitly validated in Change Request 5 & 6, curve_trimming_face is always FALSE in a single wire context. Because a wire body contains no shared face topology, topological edges, or shared topological vertices (CompressedVertex), it consists entirely of a geometric curve bounded standalone by absolute coordinates (CompressedPoint).

"Text streams" as defined by 7.9.3 are only referenced from a few places (e.g. **RC**, **JS**, **RV**, etc. entries, covering only XFA rich text and JavaScript). A content stream is NOT a "text stream". Both XFA rich text and JS streams can contain Unicode sequences that need to be properly encoded/preserved so I believe the answer is yes, a "text stream" CAN start with the BoM for UTF-16BE and UTF-8 in PDF 2.0. If no BoM is present at the start of the text stream bytes then it would be interpreted as being **PDFDocEncoded** (which is not quite the same as ASCII). 

The other aspect of your question regarding text strings is the BCP 47 language escape codes, which can occur anywhere (e.g. mid-stream). I don't believe there is any _need_ for these, since neither JS nor XFA rich text defines support for such BCP 47 codes (AFAIK). But as to whether this would then invalidate the stream data, or is just meaningless and should be skipped over during processing, I am unsure... To answer your last question first, yes, INCITS 4-1986 (R2017) is intended to specifically identify US fixed 7-Bit ASCII. 

The PDF 2.0 2017 (first) edition used to reference "ANSI X3.4-1986, Information Systems - Coded Sets 7-Bit American National Standard Code for Information Interchange (7-bit ASCII), American National Standards Institute" but [that was withdrawn](https://standards.globalspec.com/std/902025/ansi-x3-4) and ISO required us to change to something else. Looking at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO/IEC_646, I think it was because ISO 646 "_... leaves 12 code points to be allocated by conforming national standards for additional letters of [Latin-based alphabets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin-script_alphabet) or other symbols._" and that is NOT what is needed - PDF needs everything locked down very precisely.
