Does a Java library for manipulating PDF files that uses Java strings for field names really have to scan the document for the preferred encoding for each component of the field name when adding a field name to the Fields array of a signature field lock dictionary?

Suppose such a library adds a field to a PDF document. It would have to scan all the signature field lock dictionaries to find out if such a field is already referenced to find out what encoding to use such that the field name in the signature field lock dictionaries matches the encoding of the name of the field. What if two different signature field lock dictionaries use different encodings (say, PDFDocEncoding and UTF-BE16)?

Suppose a PDF contains a field named "ä" where "ä" is encoded using PDFDocEncoding: (\344). A PDF library that uses Java strings is asked for a list of Java strings containing the names of the existing fields of the document. For one of the fields, It will return the Java string "ä". Then, that library is told to look up that field, using the name from the list returned earlier. The PDF library will have to traverse the field tree, comparing T entries to the components of the field name ("ä") passed as Java string, ie, it has to compare a Java string against text strings. J.3.3 specifies how to compare PDF strings, therefore the Java string needs to be converted to a PDF string to be able to apply J.3.3. Now, what encoding out of the three encodings available (PDFDocEncoding, UTF-16BE, and UTF-8) shall it use to construct the PDF string for J.3.3? If it chooses UTF-16BE (`<fe ff 00 e4>`) or UTF-8 (`<ef bb bf c3 a4>`), it won't find the field. The user will not be amused.

Therefore, Java PDF libraries usually convert field names from PDF documents (ie, text strings) to Java strings and then compare Java strings, ignoring J.3.3. (Here my question kicks in: shall language escape sequences be removed when converting text strings to Java strings?)

Is there really any PDF library out there which tries all available encodings (depending on the PDF version of the document) for all the components of the field name and then uses J.3.3 on all these PDF strings when trying to find a field?

Note that the Fields array in a signature field lock dictionary contains fully qualified field names. According to 12.7.4.2, fully qualified field names are constructed this way:

`For a field that is the child of another field, the fully qualified name shall be formed by appending the child field’s partial name to the parent’s fully qualified name, separated by a PERIOD (2Eh) [...]
`

How do you concatenate a UTF-16BE-encoded text string, a PERIOD (2Eh!), and a PDFDocEncoding-encoded text string? Suppose the top partial field name is `<fe ff 00 a4>` ("ä") and the child partial field name is `(b)` ("b"). Just concatenating the byte strings will result in `<fe ff 00 a4 2e 62>` which is nonsense. The partial field names and the PERIOD have to be converted to a common encoding: `<fe ff 00 a4 00 2e 00 62>` or `<ef bb bf c3 a4 2e 62>` or `<a4 2e 62>`.

When applying the signature field lock dictionary, we'll have to split the fully qualified field names from the Fields array to be able to compare them to the T entries of the field dictionaries according to J.3.3. But what encoding shall we use for the partial field names? That information has been lost. For instance, if we use partial field names `(\344)` and `(b)`, the field won't be found. Ditto for `<fe ff 00 a4>` and `<fe ff 00 62>`. Ditto for `<ef bb bf c3 a4>` and `<ef bb bf 62>`. Is there any software out there which tries all 3^n possibilities to encode the partial field names of a fully qualified field name that has n components? Ditto for constructing the fully qualified field name of all fields and comparing those to the elements of the Fields entry of the signature field lock dictionary. We'll have to try all three possible encodings.

> Annex J.3.3 in ISO 32000-2:2020 describes how to compare strings.

Annex J is about *XObject comparison*. *This annex describes how to generally compare two objects of stream type, though it is expected that such comparison will be used strictly for the purpose of determining uniqueness among a pair of XObjects.* 

Annex J.3.3, therefore, describes how to compare strings that are values (possibly nested ones) in the dictionaries of streams for the purpose of determining whether those streams should be considered the same.

In other contexts, in particular when comparing text strings serving as identifiers with each other, we surely want to compare across encodings.

Just for your understanding of ISO-ese: statements within informative clauses can be made normatively applicable through direct normative references to specific sections. ISO editors would normally comment on this within a doc, but across docs it's less frowned upon e.g. so "... shall be in accordance with ISO 123, Annex A.1.2" is fine. Maybe one should take a look at what "field locking" in the context of digital signatures in PDFs means.

Foremost it is part of the MDP (modification detection and prevention) scheme that indicates which changes to a document shall be allowed or disallowed by some digital signature in it. Thus, locking a field by a signature merely means that if during validation of that signature it is determined that the value of that field has been changed in some incremental update after signing, that signature shall be considered invalidated.

First, we need a precise definition of "signature". I think a signature is the incremental update (or initial version of the document for Adobe Acrobat's first signature applied to a document) containing the addition of the V entry. With this definition, a change to the V entry does **not** constitute a new signature but rather invalidates the existing signature. I think I remember some software that (decades ago) did not do an incremental update removing the V entry before signing a field again. For that software, an updated V entry constitutes a new signatures, which adds a whole new area of trouble.

For my definition of a signature, there can be only one P value in effect for one signature, viz, that in the incremental update that added the V entry (or, for Adobe Acrobat's first signature, the initial version of the document).

It does allow that but recommends against doing so:

_A_ byte range digest _shall be computed over a range of bytes in the PDF file, that shall be indicated by the **ByteRange** entry in the signature dictionary. This range should be the entire PDF file, including the signature dictionary but excluding the signature value itself (the **Contents** entry). In case of multiple digital signatures this range shall be the sequence of bytes starting from the "%PDF-" comment at the beginning of the PDF document to the end of the "%%EOF" comment, possibly followed by an optional EOL marker, terminating the incremental update that adds the digital signature dictionary to the document._

AFAIK most validators (including Acrobat) have only accepted signatures following that recommendation for many many years now. Thus, your hypothetic file usually would not be accepted... ;)

Historically, the first Adobe signing specs (e.g. "PDF Public-Key Digital Signature and Encryption Specification") specified **ByteRange** to contain exactly 4 integers describing the whole revision except the **Contents** value. When the signing spec was merged into the PDF spec, though, we find that more generic arbitrary number of integer pairs. Apparently Adobe wanted to leave the door open for supporting more exotic byte ranges.

We do not really have a high-level API for clearing signature fields. You would just remove the AcroForm field, as any other form field, or clear the `\V` value. So no special handling for this.

As for validation, our validator treats both incremental signature field removal and `\V` removal as disallowed modifications by default, even without `DocMDP`.

For clearing a signature, removing V (or the field) isn't enough. You also have to update the appearance stream, the permissions dictionary, and, depending on the signatures remaining, SigFlags. You also, and this is related to the issue at hand, may have to "unlock" other fields, see https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/760.

> For clearing a signature, removing V (or the field) isn't enough.

Essentially, "clearing a signature" is not well-defined. Only recently I have learned that "clearing a signed signature field" is mentioned in the spec at all, but I have not yet found any definitions or requirements specifically for doing so. Thus, different implementations will do so differently.

Nonetheless, it of course makes sense to update the appearance stream (in case of visible signatures, that is), the permissions dictionary (in case of a certification signature), the **SigFlags** (if the cleared signature field was the only signed one before), and fields identified to have been locked by the initial signing of the field. Additionally one may consider resetting the signature field's **Lock** dictionary to its state before initial signing. Also developer extensions added and used only for signing of that field may be removed. Similarly, DSS entries, in particular VRI entries, used for validating only that cleared signature could be dropped. And maybe one or two handful of other details, too.

That's an interesting question for certification signatures with P=1. After clearing such a signature, the DocMDP P=1 restriction will be gone. In most cases (ie, without UR/UR3), it will be possible to save the document non-incrementally after clearing the certification signature as a certification signature must be the first signature and there can be no other signatures due to P=1. After saving non-incrementally, the document looks like there never was a certification signature (if clearing is done correctly) and the violation of the DocMDP P=1 is undetectable. So, before clearing that certification signature, clearing it was forbidden, but after clearing that certification signature, clearing it was allowed.

And yes, Adobe Acrobat allows clearing a certification signature that has P=1. Here's a thought experiment to explain the change in P=1 semantics. As we all know, the size of a CMS signature payload embedded into a PDF is limited by the size of the ByteRange "hole" in the file.

On the other hand, keeping a signature "validatable" requires maintaining a timestamp chain with a potentially unbounded number of entries. A priori, nothing in CMS would prevent us from attaching a DSS-like structure to the _unsigned_ attributes of the signature, which could then be updated indefinitely by adding new layers of timestamps and validation material. This would not affect the integrity of the PDF signature at all. But the problem is that this process is unbounded: you can only repeat it so many times before your CMS payload exceeds the bounds of the ByteRange-excluded area!

So, the tradeoff was basically this:

 - We treat DocMDP level 1 as inviolable, and accept that these signatures therefore have a finite shelf life.
 - We accept "LTA maintenance" changes even at DocMDP level 1, which removes the shelf life limitation at the cost of complicating validation.

----------

PAdES went with option 2. For us, the situation is even worse now: the hypothetical CMS extension procedure I described above doesn't exist for PAdES, so in practice what that means is that even in the best case scenario, your signature will become impossible to validate in a self-contained manner as soon as the signature timestamp expires (and that's assuming the timestamp covers all validation data needed to check the status of the signer's certificate).
For something like a mortgage agreement, that's not good enough.

In that situation, the only way to keep the signature "alive" involves storing the timestamp chain/evidence record externally. And if that's on the table, why would you even bother with PDF signatures at all? Might as well just store the signature outside the PDF in the first place, then... ;)

I think this is where we fundamentally disagree about the purpose of PDF.

PDF for print is intended to be a static representation of the final output, as required by PDF/X. Once a document has reached the PDF stage, the expectation is that its appearance is fixed and reproducible.

Simply embedding the full variable font does not solve the real problem. Changing a variation axis (e.g. weight or width) can affect text metrics, requiring new line breaks, hyphenation, text reflow, and potentially even changes to page layout. At that point, you’re no longer making a simple edit—you are re-authoring the document.

In my opinion, PDF is not, and was never intended to be, a format for heavy editing. That is the role of the original authoring application. PDF’s strength is the reliable exchange and faithful reproduction of the final document, not preserving all editing capabilities.

You're side-stepping @pkleinheider's main technical objection: changing a variable font's parameters implies reflowing text. The vast majority of PDF readers can't do that today, and that makes sense: doing text shaping/paragraph layout requires context that may or may not be available to the reader (e.g. in the form of tags), but _is_ available to the author/writer. PDF is not HTML/ODT/DOCX: in those formats the paragraph layout is a viewer responsibility, unlike in PDF, where it falls on the writer.

In a hypothetical world where variable fonts were a feature in PDF, readers would need to do a hell of a lot more squeezing than what a writer needs to do today to instantiate a variable font. So you're not saving any time/effort there--quite the opposite.

Several reasons. Here are two:

- You point out yourself that a shaper is a nontrivial dependency to have, and may well make it impractical for e.g. a household printer to handle PDF input. Not to mention paragraph/page reflow, which is more complicated and heavily context-dependent.
- Text layout is equal parts art and science: it's not a deterministic process. Variable fonts would force the reader to be involved in layout, so printing/rendering the same variable-font text with the same parameters on different machines could produce wildly different results (even the page count could change!). We don't want that.

Agreeing with comments that simply embedding variable fonts alone doesn't offer advantages for a fully typeset, kerned, ligatured, sub-pixel accurate, author-defined page description language like PDF.

### The tie-break question is now measured — and it changes the proposal

The previous version of this issue presented CR-16a as a complete specification and did not say that
it left the equal-frequency tie-break undefined. It also offered to settle that by experiment. **We
have now run the experiment**, and it produced a clearer answer than expected — though not the one we
went looking for.

**Method.** We instrumented a decoder to dump, for every Huffman-coded array in a real file, the
producer's own stored leaf table together with the symbol frequencies implied by the decoded array.
Each array is then a labelled test case — *these frequencies produced this table* — with no vendor
cooperation needed. The corpus gave **86,986 arrays from 141 files across two independent producer
families**.

**Four results, in the order they matter.**

1. **The tree shape is confirmed at scale.** Kraft sum exactly 0.5, phantom on the root's 0-branch,
   and a complete tree once the leading bit is removed — each **86,986 / 86,986 (100.000%)**. Step 1's
   tree is also length-optimal for its frequencies in **81,102 / 81,102 (100.000%)**, so the greedy
   construction in CR-16a step 1 is right and the phantom merge is the only departure from it.

2. **The model is exact wherever nothing is ambiguous.** On the **43,306** arrays where no weight tie
   arises at any merge, reconstruction reproduces the stored code lengths exactly, 100.000%. That
   validates the frequency recovery and the phantom reading, and localises everything unexplained to
   the tie-break alone.

3. **The producers are deterministic.** **4,519** distinct frequency inputs occur more than once in
   the corpus; **none** disagrees with itself. So a rule exists — this is not an unstable sort.

4. **But no simple rule reproduces it.** **188 candidate rules** over five structurally different
   model families top out at **92.66%** and **91.93%** for the two families. The best model is
   positional (a maintained sorted array with merged nodes inserted before equal-weight entries)
   rather than any comparator key — which is what one expects from a list implementation detail
   rather than a designed rule.

**Why this argues for declaring it unspecified rather than naming it.** A conforming reader never
needs the rule: the complete code table is in the file, and the reader builds its tree from those
stored codes. The corpus confirms readers must be doing exactly that — the stored code values are not
the canonical assignment for their lengths in any of the 86,986 arrays. So the tie-break governs only
whether two encoders emit byte-identical output, never whether a file decodes correctly. Mandating one
producer's rule would make every existing producer non-conforming on a point no reader can observe.

**CR-16c** in the body proposes the one-paragraph statement plus a NOTE. We would rather the document
said "this is deliberately unspecified, and here is why it is safe" than either stayed silent or
guessed.

**What we did not establish.** We did not identify the actual rule either producer uses. We are not
claiming it is unknowable — 92% from a positional model is close — but the residual would change no
recommendation, so we stopped. If the group would prefer a named rule, the open question is whose
behaviour should become normative, and that is a decision rather than a measurement.

### What is good to go

**The tree shape itself.** It is measured byte-exactly against real files and isolated by splice
testing — swapping only the tree construction, holding every other byte constant, and observing a
major reader reject the standard-optimal variant and accept the phantom-wrapped one. That is causal
isolation rather than correlation, and it is the strongest evidence class we have offered on any of
these issues.

**The NOTE in CR-16b.** It records that a reader does not need the tree shape at all, since the codes
are stored explicitly, and that this is a writer-side requirement. That distinction is worth having in
the document — it tells an implementer whether the clause applies to them — and it is now the same
argument CR-16c rests on, measured across the whole corpus rather than asserted.

**CR-16c.** The evidence behind it is the strongest in this issue: every figure above is a census of
real producer output, not a sample, and the recommendation follows from the numbers rather than from
a judgement call about what implementers are likely to do.

**The gap itself needs no evidence.** A listing that calls an undefined function is a defect on its
face.

## Body updated again — one correction of ours, and independent corroboration

Two changes to the body since 4 September. The first corrects something in my own comment above, so
it goes first.

### The correction: two independent facts and a corollary, not three results

The comment above states that the tree shape was confirmed at scale by three properties — Kraft sum
exactly 0.5, every code beginning with bit 1, and a complete tree once the leading bit is removed —
"each 86,986 / 86,986 (100.000%)". The body said the same.

**Those three are not independent, and presenting them as three results overstates the evidence.** If
every code begins with bit 1, then stripping that bit maps each code of length `L` to one of length
`L−1`, which doubles the Kraft sum — so 0.5 becomes exactly 1.0 as a matter of arithmetic. The first
two force the third.

The honest reading is **two facts and a corollary**. The corollary was worth verifying and was
verified, but it is a consistency check on the other two rather than a third confirmation. The body
now presents it that way, with the rows labelled.

This does not change the conclusion — both independent facts are unanimous across two corpora — but a
reviewer counting three unanimous results would infer more independent evidence than exists, and that
is not a misunderstanding I want to leave in place. The catch is @datalogics-pgallot's.

### Independent corroboration, over a non-overlapping corpus

A second implementation has now parsed the same per-array leaf tables over **101,116 Huffman arrays in
212 files**, from a corpus that does not overlap ours:

| | ours | theirs |
|---|---|---|
| Kraft sum exactly 0.5 | 86,986 / 86,986 | **101,100 / 101,100 — 100.000%** |
| every real code begins with bit 1 | 86,986 / 86,986 | **100.000%** |
| *corollary:* stripping it gives a complete tree | 86,986 / 86,986 | **100.000%** |
| stored codes are not the canonical assignment | 0 / 86,986 canonical | **100.000%, no exceptions** |

Three things from that work are now in the body.

**The non-canonical result is stronger than I stated it.** I reported that no array's stored codes
match the canonical assignment for their lengths. They report that **not a single leaf in any array
coincides with its canonical code** — the partially-canonical count is zero across 101,101 arrays
carrying any code. That matters for CR-16c: the argument is that a reader never needs the tie-break
because it builds its tree from the stored codes, and the strongest form of it is that the stored
codes could not be reconstructed from lengths alone. They cannot, anywhere either of us has looked.

**One claim could not be checked, and the reason is the argument.** Their decoder does not reconstruct
trees from frequencies at all — it reads the stored table — so it had nothing to compare a
length-optimal tree against. That is precisely what CR-16c rests on: the construction is invisible to
a reader, so leaving the tie-break unspecified costs a reader nothing.

**An exclusion, stated rather than buried.** Sixteen arrays across six files were set aside there as
malformed, their declared maximum code length being impossible — zero with hundreds of leaves, or
values in the billions; one declares fourteen codes of length one, a Kraft sum of 7.0 where a prefix
code admits at most two. The same arrays fail every check, and all six files decode badly on grounds
unrelated to Huffman tables, so they read as decoder desynchronisation rather than producer output.
The headline is therefore **100.000% of well-formed arrays, with sixteen malformed arrays in six files
set aside and named**.

### What has not changed

**CR-16a, CR-16b and CR-16c are unchanged**, including CR-16c's proposed text in full. The tie-break
measurement stands as posted: deterministic per producer, not reproduced by any of 188 candidate
rules, best positional model around 92%.

If anything the recommendation is now better supported. Two independent implementations back it from
opposite directions — one measured that no simple rule reproduces real producer output, and the other
confirms its reader has never needed the rule, because it reads the stored codes. A specification
mandating a tie-break would make every existing producer non-conforming on a point neither reader can
observe.

Confirmed from a second implementation, on a different collection and from our reader side: over  **101,101 Huffman arrays in 209 files**, the Kraft sum of the stored leaves is exactly 1/2 on every array, every real code begins with bit 1 on every array, and stripping that bit leaves a complete tree on every array. The third of those follows arithmetically from the first two.

This is worth noting as independent: our reader guards Huffman tables at a Kraft bound of 1.0 rather than 0.5, explicitly because the 0.5 rested on this issue, so the measurement comes from an implementation that had declined to assume it.

One caution against over-reading a related figure: we also found 0 of 2,003,468 stored codes matching a canonical `(length, symbol)` assignment, but that is forced by the leading-bit result rather than independent of it, and should not be used to support the tie-break decision without re-generating the canonical codes with the phantom branch reserved.

## Correction from the submitter: (3a) should not be adopted as drafted

I filed this issue, and subsequent work has shown the *shape* of the fix I proposed is wrong. The
underlying observation stands and is now better supported; what needs changing is where the defect is
located and therefore what the remedy should be. Correcting it here before it reaches the draft.

### The proposed (CR-18a paragraph 3a) is a conditional whose predicate is always true

CR-18a asks for:

> **(3a)** Let `w ← O - V3`. If `Y · w > 0`, negate both `Y` and `Z`.

Given Formula (1) as implementations actually compute it (see below), write `Z_temp = a·X + b·P` with
`P` a unit vector orthogonal to the unit `X`. From (2), `Z ∝ Z_temp ∧ X = b·(P ∧ X)`; writing
`Q = P ∧ X` gives `Z = sign(b)·Q`, and from (3), `Y = Z ∧ X = sign(b)·(Q ∧ X) = −sign(b)·P`.

Since `w = O − V3 = −Z_temp`:

```
dot(Y, w) = −dot(Y, Z_temp) = −(−sign(b)·b) = |b| > 0
```

So the test holds for **every** configuration in which the basis is well defined. It is not a
discriminator between two cases; it is a tautology. An implementer following (3a) literally would
write a test, observe it never failing, and reasonably conclude their input was unusual.

This also resolves an internal inconsistency in my own issue body, which I should own: it reports the
step firing on "100% of grown triangles (15,077 of 15,077)" while the rationale claims that without it
the frame is correct "approximately half of all cases". The measurement was right; the rationale was
an assumption about what a conditional implies, and it was wrong.

### Measurement

Instrumenting the step and running a 310-file corpus gathered from the wild:

| | |
|---|---|
| apex-frame computations | 31,329,211 |
| took the negation | **31,314,935 (99.9544%)** |
| per-file range | 99.29% – 100.00% |
| files at exactly 100% | 60 of 129 |
| files below 99% | none |

(Denominator note: these are calls to the basis computation — roughly two per triangle, one per
candidate edge — not a triangle count.)

The residual 0.046% supports the algebra rather than qualifying it. The proof assumes `Y = Z ∧ X`
with `Z` proportional to `Z_temp ∧ X`; any non-firing case must be one where that construction did
not hold — precisely the null-axis case §7.8.9.3 already routes to `MakeOrthoRep()` ("A particular
case occurs if the Z axis or Y are NULL"), plus exact-zero dot products.

### Where the defect actually is: Formula (1)'s X

§7.8.9.3 prints:

> (1) `X ← (V1 − V0) / ‖V1 − V0‖`

Working decoders compute the **negation** of that — `X ← V0 − V1` — and only then does an orientation
step become necessary. Composing the two: with `X_work = −X_spec`, (2) gives `Z_work = −Z_spec` and
(3) gives `Y_work = +Y_spec`; the negation step then flips both, yielding `(−X_spec, −Y_spec, +Z_spec)`.

**The frame real files are encoded against is the frame of Formulas (1)–(3) rotated 180° about Z,
unconditionally.** My (3a) was one half of that rotation, expressed as a condition, bolted onto an
uncorrected (1).

### Suggested replacement — committee's choice of form

**Option A — correct Formula (1).** State the X axis as `X ← (V0 − V1) / ‖V0 − V1‖` and add the
compensating negation of `Y`, so the composed frame matches what files use. This puts the correction
where the divergence originates.

**Option B — leave (1)–(3) untouched and add a NOTE after (3):**

> **NOTE** — The axes given by Formulas (1) to (3) are related to the frame used by the encoder by a
> rotation of 180° about `Z`: the reconstruction uses `−X` and `−Y`, with `Z` unchanged. This applies
> unconditionally to every triangle for which the basis is well defined, and is not a test to be
> evaluated per triangle.

**I prefer Option A**, since Option B leaves the printed formulas describing a frame no implementation
uses. Option B is the smaller edit and carries no risk of partial application, which may matter given
that any shipping implementation has necessarily compensated somewhere already.

**Either way, (3a) as filed should not be adopted.**

### What is unchanged

The ablation evidence in the original issue stands: disabling the compensation causes hard decode
failure on three of four curated files and gross manifold corruption on the fourth. Omitting it is
fatal. That was the point of this issue and remains the point — only the diagnosis, and therefore the
remedy, has changed.

### Provenance

The algebra in §2 was worked through in correspondence with an independent implementer who
questioned whether our orientation step had been derived from the format or added to compensate for
the sign in Formula (1). It is the second, and the two questions turned out to be the same question.
The corpus measurement in §4 is ours.

Well, ByteRange has more than those two elements. Interestingly, the copy in 12.8.1 before Table 255 is (for the case of multiple signatures being present) stricter than the definition of ByteRange is Table 255 (see above):

```
[...] This range should be the entire PDF file,
including the signature dictionary but excluding the signature value itself (the Contents entry). In
case of multiple digital signatures this range shall be the sequence of bytes starting from the
"%PDF-" comment at the beginning of the PDF document to the end of the "%%EOF" comment,
possibly followed by an optional EOL marker, terminating the incremental update that adds the
digital signature dictionary to the document.
```

That is, the ByteRange of a non-ETSI signature SHOULD cover the entire PDF file if it is the only signature, but SHALL cover the entire PDF file if there are multiple signatures. Unfortunately, it is impossible to change a signature (with a ByteRange not covering the entire PDF file) that used to be valid because it was the only signature into one covering the entire PDF file when adding a second signature. If I modify its ByteRange, it (the first signature) becomes invalid due to a change message digest and if I do not modify its ByteRange it becomes invalid due to not covering the entire PDF file (at the time it was applied).

Another weird thing: suppose a PDF file has a single CR after %%EOF and has a valid ETSI signature (with a ByteRange including the CR). Now we append a LF. There's still a single EOL marker at the end. The signature becomes invalid because ByteRange no longer covers the entire PDF file (at the time of signing). Now we add another signature. The first signature becomes valid again as the size of the original document (at the time of signing) is computed from its ByteRange entry and we cannot find out whether the LF is part of the incremental update for the second signature or not.

So, there are cases where adding a second signature makes the first signature invalid (even without P=1) and there are cases where adding a second signature makes the first signature valid!

## Independently confirmed — good to go, and our formula is algebraically identical

We implement parabola evaluation and independently concluded the published type-0 formula was wrong.
Our source has carried this comment since before this issue was filed:

```c
/* Evaluate parabola at a single point using the modified spec formula (spec has an error) */
```

**The correction we derived is the same one proposed here.** Ours is written slightly differently, so
for the record, here it is beside the proposal:

| | proposed | nanoPRC |
|---|---|---|
| x | `param*param / sqrt(param*param + 16*f*f)` | `param2 / sqrt(16*f*f + param2)` |
| y | `2.0 * sqrt(x * f)` | `2.0 * f * sqrt(x / f)` |
| sign | negate y if `param < 0` | negate y if `input < 0` |

The `x` expressions are identical. The `y` expressions are algebraically equal for any
`focal_length > 0`, since `2f·√(x/f) = 2·√f·√x = 2·√(x·f)`. The sign handling matches. Two
implementations arriving at the same corrected evaluation from different starting points is about as
good as confirmation gets for a formula erratum.

We would suggest the specification adopt **`2.0 * sqrt(x * focal_length)`** as written in the
proposal, rather than our arrangement. It avoids dividing by `focal_length` and taking the square root
of a quotient, so it is better behaved as `focal_length` becomes small and needs no separate guard
against a zero focal length. We intend to adopt the proposed form ourselves for that reason.

For the analysis done of the PRC files I've collected, I agree with this. The contradiction is real and we also hit it from the writer
side: 4.2 uses one number for two jobs, and a file that satisfies the mandate is correctly refused under the same clause's reader requirement.

Our writer encodes **8137** in both `minimal_version_for_read` and `authoring_version`, and not the
mandated 10001, for exactly the reason the ticket gives. Our own bisection agrees with the ticket's
to the version: on a fully updated Acrobat DC 26.2.21931.0, **8137 opens and 8138 is refused.**

## Corpus evidence, 529 files

We swept the version fields across the 529 PRC files we hold — the public `ralovich/prc-db`
collection plus a SafeDocs-derived set. The fields are in the uncompressed header, so this needs no
decode and no reader.

**Not one file declares a `minimal_version_for_read` above 8137:**

| `minimal_version_for_read` | files | |
|---|---|---|
| 8137 | 351 | 66.4% |
| 7094 | 153 | 28.9% |
| 7095 | 25 | 4.7% |
| **above 8137** | **0** | **0%** |

The more useful cut is the pairing with `authoring_version`. **73 of the 529 were authored by tools
at a version above 8137 — up to 20225 — and every one of them declares a floor of 7094 or 7095**
(61 and 12 respectively). None declares 8137, and none comes close to 10001.

So writers that are demonstrably many versions newer than the mandate still encode a floor well
below it. In practice the ecosystem treats `minimal_version_for_read` as *the oldest reader that can
cope with this content*, never as *the edition I was written against*. 4.2 asks for the second
reading, and every file we hold declines it — including files produced after the mandate existed.

## What the reader's version number gates, and where that bites

The same number has a second job on the reader side, and this is the one with a decoding
consequence. A reader's `current_version` decides which `EPRCSchema_Block_Version` blocks it
executes — a block versioned *v* is executed when the reader's version is below *v* — and section 8
extension data is interleaved into the entity bitstream. Two readers that claim different versions
therefore consume different numbers of bits. They do not merely disagree about conformance; they
desync.

That makes the gap between the mandated 10001 and the measured 8137 a window worth sweeping, so we
swept it. Every `Block_Version` value across all 529 files — 86 of them declare at least one
versioned block, 67,011 encounters in total:

| value | blocks | files | reader at 8137 | reader at 10001 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7309 | 2,279 | 31 | skip | skip |
| 8016 | 2,279 | 31 | skip | skip |
| 15083 | 62,442 | 73 | execute | execute |
| 15216 | 11 | 8 | execute | execute |

**Not one block falls in `(8137, 10001]`.** Every value sits below both candidate thresholds or
above both, so across the whole corpus a reader at 8137 and a reader at 10001 behave identically. We
state that plainly because it bounds the practical urgency of this ticket: the contradiction is
real, but we cannot point at a file in the wild that is mis-decoded because of it.

**The exception is in this document.** The worked example at 8.4.4, *Adding a field to existing
entity* (`tab-Adding_a_field_to_existing_entity`, `sections/08-schema-defs.adoc:532` at `934f079`),
gates its versioned block on **9149** — "File version number 149th day of 2009" — which is inside
the window. A reader conforming to 4.2's mandate of 10001 skips the standard's own illustration of
the feature. A reader matching the deployed ceiling of 8137 executes it.

That seems to us the most economical statement of the defect: **the mandated version makes a
conforming reader skip this document's own example.**

Our schema interpreter therefore claims 8137 rather than 10001, with the constant overridable. We
would be glad to know what other implementations claim, because any two that differ across this
window diverge on a file carrying such a block — and none of us appears to have one to test against.

## One qualification, against our own practice

We write `minimal_version_for_read` equal to `authoring_version`. That matches 351 files exactly,
but it is **not** what those 73 newer writers do: they decouple the two, and on the reading above
that is the more correct behaviour.

Our 8137 is defensible for our content — 8.4.2 defines `PRC_TYPE_MISC_GeneralTransformation` at that
version and we emit it whenever a part carries a placement matrix, so declaring less would be wrong
in the other direction. But if #805 resolves toward "declare the lowest version that can read your
content", a fixed constant stops being adequate and we would have to derive it per file — and 4.2
attaches a second obligation to doing so. "If `minimal_version_for_read` is lower than
`authoring_version`, the PRC file writer shall write a schema description in the PRC file providing
the differences between the two versions." Writing the two fields equal is what currently exempts us
from that; decoupling them would oblige us to emit a schema, which we have never done. We mention
all of this because it bears on what the corrected text should require of a writer, not only on what
it should stop requiring.

## Method

Version fields read directly from the PRC header (Table 3/4); no section is decompressed and no
reader is involved, so those figures are independent of any decode disagreement. Acrobat bisection
performed by hand on DC 26.2.21931.0 by editing the two header words and reopening.

The `Block_Version` table is on a different footing and we would rather say so than let the two sit
together as if equally hard: it requires decompressing the globals and walking the schema blocks, so
it depends on our decode being right. Counts are of blocks encountered across the 529 files, and of
the distinct files in which each value appears — a file carrying two values is counted under both,
which is why the file column sums to more than the 68 files that carry any block at all.

## Option A is the urgent option, not the tidier one — and there is now direct evidence

A second implementation has measured the escape range independently, and its author,
@datalogics-pgallot, has sharpened the argument in a way that changes which option is urgent
rather than which is correct. We still recommend Option A. The reason we gave for it was the
weaker one.

### The consequence we understated

Our original framing set out an asymmetry of risk — a wrongly-adopted Option A renders real files
unreadable, a wrongly-adopted Option B merely documents a type nobody emits — and treated that as
a reason for caution. That is still true, but it misses the cost that Option B leaves in place.

Because no structure exists for `1100`, a reader that meets the code **cannot tell which failure
it is in**. It cannot distinguish a genuine reserved-type curve from its own loss of bit
alignment, and so cannot choose between resynchronising and reporting an unimplemented feature.
Those call for opposite responses. A reader told the code is malformed can treat it as the desync
signal it almost certainly is; a reader that believes it has met a valid-but-unimplemented type
carries on and emits garbage.

Option B does not remove that ambiguity — it only adds a type to it.

### The escape range, with its classes separated

The most useful change since this issue was opened is that the escape readings have been counted
as two things rather than one. Across the 310 files of the public `prc-db` collection,
@datalogics-pgallot reports that ten produce any escape decode at all, and they split:

| classification                               | count           |
|:---------------------------------------------|----------------:|
| bit-alignment failures (codes 12, 14, 15)     |              32 |
| `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` declined (code 13)   |  15, in 4 files |

Two files carry both classes in quantity — twelve and six, ten and seven — which is the spread a
garbage read produces. The files carrying only one or two of each are the sparse cases, and they
are correspondingly the hard ones to call.

Keeping the classes apart matters for the count quoted most in this thread. The number of escape
readings in that implementation fell from 46 to six over an interval in which unrelated B-rep and
tessellation defects were fixed and nobody touched the escape handling. Read as a single number,
that is suggestive. Read with the classes separated it is stronger: **a composite curve is
content.** It does not appear or disappear when unrelated desyncs are fixed. So whatever fixed
number of composite curves sits inside both the old 46 and the current six, subtracting it from
both ends makes the fall in the *alignment* component steeper than the raw figures show.

That reasoning assumes the older build read the same composite curves, which cannot be verified
without rebuilding it. We do not claim it as measured.

### Direct evidence from a second reader, on the two files in dispute

The two files in which escape codes are currently read are `ABM8-3D.stream-12` and
`PRC example.stream-9`. Our decoder reads both:

| file                    | compressed curves | `Line` | `Circle` | Hermite | escape codes |
|:------------------------|------------------:|-------:|---------:|--------:|-------------:|
| `ABM8-3D.stream-12`     |               692 |    510 |      182 |       0 |        **0** |
| `PRC example.stream-9`  |            18,266 | 11,821 |    5,972 |     473 |        **0** |

Zero escape codes in 18,958 compressed curves, in exactly the files where another reader finds
them. Both parse clean — no failures, no resyncs, no unknown tags — and in every geometry section
of both, the last entity read lands within a byte-padding tail of the section end, so the parse
runs to the end rather than stopping short. Our file-structure counts, four and seven, and the 278
`BrepDataCompress` bodies we count in `PRC example`, match the other implementation exactly. The
two readers agree about the container and disagree only inside it.

More directly still: @datalogics-pgallot supplied the five bit offsets at which his reader consumes
an escape code, counted from the start of each file structure's decompressed geometry section. We
instrumented our own reader to report the same quantity — the position of the first bit of each
`CompressedEntityType`, before any of it is consumed — and **not one of the five is an entity
boundary in our reading.** Three of the five are within nine bits of one of our boundaries, which
looks like small accumulating drift rather than a reader that has lost its place entirely; at the
other two we are 21 and 128 bits inside an entity we started earlier.

This is the evidence the issue was missing. Until now, the argument that escape readings indicate
desync rested on their co-occurrence with other damage in the same file, which is circumstantial.
Two readers disagreeing about *where an entity begins*, at the exact offsets in question, is not.

### One correction to the shortcut, and it matters for implementers

It is tempting to conclude that *any* escape-code reading proves a reader has lost alignment. That
holds for `1110` and `1111`, which ISO 14739 assigns no meaning at all, and for `1100`, which is
the subject of this issue.

**It does not hold for `1101`.** That is `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve`, which §7.9.21.9.1 "General"
lists among the four permitted compressed curve types and which §7.9.21.9.5
"PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve" and Table 239 fully specify. It is reachable only through the escape
prefix — §9.17's own listing writes it as `(3 << 2) + 1` — but reaching it is entirely legitimate.
A validity check written as "any four-bit type code means the stream is broken" will reject every
composite curve in a conforming file.

We mention it because we nearly implemented exactly that check ourselves, on the strength of the
shortcut, and caught it only against our own decoder.

### The zero-cost check that does survive

With `1101` excluded, a genuinely free validity test remains, and CR-23b's NOTE is the natural
place for it: `1110` and `1111` have no meaning in any version of this document, so reading either
is positive evidence that the bit cursor is no longer on an entity boundary. A reader can say so
instead of reporting an unknown feature.

We have implemented it on that basis, and one detail of doing so is worth passing on. Our first
attempt put the check in the curve-type dispatch, which was the wrong layer: the reader below it
resolves the whole four-bit escape prefix itself and rejects the unassigned codes there, so a
caller only ever sees an assigned type or a failure. The check was unreachable, and the ambiguity
this issue is about stayed in place undetected, because nothing in the corpus reaches it. If your
decoder resolves the prefix in one place and dispatches on the type in another, the check belongs
in the first.

### What would still settle it

Unchanged, and worth restating because it has been found by neither implementation: **a single
file containing a genuine `PRC_HCG_Ellipse`.** Its existence decides for Option B and gives the
field order directly. Its continued absence across two independent corpora decides for Option A.

One observation sharpens where to look. In one file, the escape is the *first* entity type read in
its section, with nothing before it that could have gone wrong. That is either alignment loss at
the section boundary or a genuine reserved type, and nothing in between — which makes files of
that shape the most informative candidates, in either direction.
This has already been applied to the PRC spec draft and so can be closed.

# Attestation on both CRs, from an independent implementation and a 529-file census

We support both change requests and have nothing to dispute in the issue as filed. Two things we
can add: our implementation reached both rules independently and before the issue existed, and we
have now measured them across our corpus.

## The implementation is independent evidence, because it predates the issue

Our uncompressed `PRC_TYPE_TESS_3D` reader has implemented exactly both proposed rules since the
texture-sampling work in June 2026, some months before #810 was filed. Neither rule was taken from
a specification sentence, because there is not one — both were derived from files, which is the
gap the issue exists to close.

- **The dimension.** We read `number_of_texture_coordinates` and then that many **doubles** into a
  flat array, treating it as `number_of_texture_coordinates / 2` UV pairs.
- **The index scale.** A corner's stored texture index is used as a **flat offset into those
  doubles** — it addresses `u` directly, with `v` at the next position — exactly as the point and
  normal indices in the same function are flat offsets pre-multiplied by three.

It is validated by **rendering**, not by round-trip. If the index scale were three rather than two,
the UVs would be wrong and the texture detail would be noise; it is not.

We note the issue's own provenance remark that the reference implementation applies the factor of
two with the comment *"Not sure about the texture indices though"*. That is the point worth making
plainly: two implementations arrived at the same factor of two from files alone, and neither had
normative support for it. That is a specification gap behaving exactly as a specification gap does
— everyone guesses, and this time everyone guessed the same.

## The census

529 PRC files; **64 carry an uncompressed entity with texture coordinates**, holding **9,175** such
entities. Measured at the single point every corner index passes through before any mesh filtering,
so the count is not bounded by a later filter.

**Does the count measure values?** If the element is a `(u, v)` pair and the count is in values, the
count is always even. An odd one falsifies it outright.

| | |
|---|---|
| entities with texture coordinates | 9,175 |
| ... whose count is **odd** | **0** |
| texture-coordinate values in total | 19,531,956 |
| ... implied UV pairs | 9,765,978 |

**Does the corner index address values or pairs?** If it addresses values, every index is even and
no index exceeds `number_of_texture_coordinates - 2`.

| | |
|---|---|
| corner texture indices seen | 21,335,610 |
| ... **odd** | **0** |
| entities whose largest index is out of range | **0** |

Both halves survive without exceptions.

### Where the corpus does *not* settle it, stated because it does not

**342 of the 9,175 entities have a largest index that would also fit a pair-indexed array**
(`max < count / 2`). For those, our corpus cannot distinguish the two readings — they are simply
small enough that both work. The reading is separated on the other **8,833**, and the even-index
result above holds on all 9,175, but the pair reading is not *impossible* corpus-wide and we are
not going to claim it is.

### By encoding signature, so the null is not one writer's habit

Keyed on the file header's version words and identifier class. **Producer strings are not used**: a
producer names the wrapper rather than the 3D writer, and SDK names appear in files that SDK did not
write, so a per-producer tally is wrong in both directions.

```
signature                 files entities   oddCnt      indices   oddIdx      OOR
v7094/8137 structured        45     7268        0     16061661        0        0
v8137/8137 structured         6     1033        0      3000819        0        0
v7094/15216 structured        3      777        0      1724841        0        0
v7094/15083 structured        2       81        0       537093        0        0
v8137/8137 random             6       12        0         6468        0        0
v7095/15216 structured        1        3        0         4692        0        0
v7095/8137 structured         1        1        0           36        0        0
TOTAL                        64     9175        0     21335610        0        0
```

Seven distinct signatures, all clean. The convention is not an artefact of one writer dominating the
sample.

## How that clean result was reached, because the first run was not clean

The first run of this census reported **83 odd corner indices and 8 out-of-range entities**, all in
one file. **Those were ours, not the file's.**

The file sets `must_recalculate_normals`, so no normal indices are stored, and `start_triangulated`
is declared *as if* they were. We converted a face's declared offset into the actual numbering with
a per-face stride ratio. That is correct only when every preceding face has the same stride as the
face being read. Exactly one normal index per corner is suppressed, so the correct conversion
subtracts the **number of preceding corners** and does not involve this face's stride at all. On an
entity whose faces mix textured and untextured, the ratio overshoots, and where it overshoots by an
odd number the read lands on the wrong half of a `(texture, point)` pair — so every "texture index"
it reports is a point index. That is the entire source of the 83.

Fixed 29 October. Across the same 529 files: **527 unchanged, 1 strictly better, 0 worse**, and the
82 clamped primitive runs in the whole corpus — a face asking to read past the end of its index
array, which is what a wrong offset produces — went to **0**.

So the figures above come from an instrument whose only disagreement with the proposed reading was a
defect in the instrument. We would rather say that than quote the clean number on its own.

## What the corpus can and cannot support

The 529 files are two unrelated samples: **310** from the public `ralovich/prc-db` collection, and
**219** distilled from a broad public-web crawl by filtering for 3D annotations. The result does not
depend on the half shared with the issue's filer — **44 of the 64 files and 7,195 of the 9,175
entities (78%) come from the web-crawl half**, which that collection does not contain.

The limit worth stating: engineering PDFs — drawings, TDPs, assembly documentation — are largely
never published, so no public crawl can reach the population where most PRC is written. This sample
is good evidence about what public files do. It is not evidence about files nobody publishes, and a
clean null here should not be read as one.

**CR-29 and CR-30: proposed solution against the working source.** The description gives its
proposed wording against the printed draft, by page. This comment gives the same two rules as
replacements of the TWG source, line by line, so that they can be applied as written. The rules are
unchanged. Since the description was filed, Datalogics has confirmed both from an implementation that
predates this issue and from a census with no exception: 1,980 textured entities in 20 files of the
public prc-db collection, and 7,195 in 44 files of the SafeDocs collection (comment of 30 October).

We implement `PRC_TYPE_SURF_Blend03` and measured this rather than taking it on trust. The test
needs no rendering and no reading of the clause: a `Blend03` is a fillet, so the centre is the curve
the other two are equidistant from. At each station, for each candidate centre `c`:

```
imbalance(c) = |d(c,a) - d(c,b)| / max(d(c,a), d(c,b))
```

Over all 44 `Blend03` surfaces we can reach — 4 in
[`3D_PDF_PROSTEP-Advanced_Maintenance_Manual.stream-124.prc`](https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db/blob/main/prcs/3D_PDF_PROSTEP-Advanced_Maintenance_Manual.stream-124.prc)
and 40 in
[`Release-to-Manufacturing_Prendergast.stream-6.prc`](https://github.com/ralovich/prc-db/blob/main/prcs/Release-to-Manufacturing_Prendergast.stream-6.prc),
both in `prc-db`; our surface counts for both match nanoPRC's:

| Candidate centre | Surfaces |
|---|---|
| `i*3+0` — Table 293 | 0 |
| `i*3+1` | 0 |
| `i*3+2` — this issue | **44** |

Slot 2 scores **exactly 0.0000**. Slots 0 and 1 reach 0.4304 and score *identically to each other in
all 44* — the signature of two symmetric rails, and the check that the metric is detecting fillet
geometry rather than preferring an answer.

This also makes the nominal evaluation self-consistent at the stations:
`P = centre + |rail_2 - centre| * normalize(rail_1 - centre)` lands on `rail_1` at `v = 0` only
under equidistance, which holds to 0.0000 here and fails by up to 43% under Table 293's order.

**Two limits.** The test is symmetric in the two non-centre slots, so it confirms the **centre** is
at `i*3+2` but does not distinguish `rail_1` from `rail_2`; we implement the order as proposed but
have not measured that half. And measured on the *interpolated* splines rather than at the stored
stations, our own surface loses the equidistance — a separate defect in our quintic Hermite
evaluation that we found while checking this. It affects both readings alike, so it does not bear on
the curve order, but it is the reason we are not claiming our `Blend03` output is validated.

**Confirmed from the writing side, with a rendered result.**

This issue describes the defect as it reaches a reader. It reaches a writer the same way, and the
consequence is a file that is structurally perfect and visibly wrong.

nanoPRC implemented the text literally. Its colour allocator returned a 1-biased **entry** index —
the Nth colour as *N*+1 — because "an index into the RGB array" reads as an index of colours. Every
other part of the file was correct: the array was written correctly, the material referenced a real
index, the bit count was exact, and the file reopened with no error anywhere.

A two-item test file, one item asking for red and one for blue, was written that way and opened in
Acrobat. Both items rendered **grey**. After changing the allocator to return *N*×3+1, the same
fixture, written by the same code path, renders **red and blue**. Nothing else changed.

So the reading given in the recommendation is the one conforming viewers implement, and it is now
confirmed by a writer that got it wrong and a viewer that showed it.

**One observation that may bear on how widespread this is.**

The defect is invisible in any file carrying a single colour. Under the entry-index reading the first
colour is index 1; under the double-index reading it is also index 1. Entry 0 therefore resolves
correctly by accident, and a writer can hold the wrong rule indefinitely without producing a single
visibly wrong file.

nanoPRC's allocator had been wrong since it was written. The error surfaced only when per-item
materials introduced a second colour into the same file. Before that, the one field that was already
being resolved wrongly was the emissive index of the default material, which pointed at black and
resolved to grey — a difference nobody was going to notice.

That suggests the population of affected writers is larger than the population of visibly affected
files, and that a writer's own round-trip testing will not find this: our reader divided by three
throughout, so reader and writer disagreed while every internal test passed.

**On the recommendation itself.**

Stating the rule once at the array, rather than on each of the six fields that address it, is the
right shape: the six agree today, and a rule repeated six times is a rule that can be amended five
times.

The proposed sentence is unambiguous for a reader. It would serve a writer equally if the obligation
were explicit in both directions, for example:

> Indices into this array are expressed in individual double values rather than in `RgbColor`
> entries. An index *i* identifies the colour at position (*i* − 1) / 3 in the array; a writer
> storing the colour at position *n* shall write the index 3*n* + 1.

That is a suggestion, not a defect in the recommendation. The rule as drafted is derivable in the
writing direction by anyone who reads it carefully, which — on the evidence of this issue — is the
assumption worth avoiding.

The fixtures, before and after, can be attached if they would be useful.

**A reader-side witness, from a third-party file.**

Our comment of 18 September showed the defect from the writing side. It reaches a reader just as quietly, and a public
file shows it.

`GS19090-002_3D.stream-70.prc` (prc-db) has a button whose style stores colour index 7. Adobe Acrobat draws the button
red. Read as the issue says, in doubles, 7 gives (7 − 1) / 3 = position 2, the file's third colour, which is red; read
as an index of `RgbColor` entries, it names a different colour. Nothing else in the file distinguishes the two
readings: every field is read with the same number of bits either way.

nanoPRC had the rule right everywhere but one lookup, the one that gives a face its style's plain colour, which took
the index as an entry index. Fixing that one lookup (CascadiaVoxel/nanoPRC #247) changed the colours of 217 of the 916
files we test with, 210 of them in prc-db, with no other effect on any file. A defect that costs no bits and raises no
error survives in an implementation that otherwise gets it right, which is the strongest argument for stating the rule
once, at the array, as the recommendation does.

**The markup Color code follows the same rule.** The inner code of a markup *Color* entity ("an index into the colour array stored in *FileStructureInternalGlobalData*", `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2426`, Table 150 at `:2229`) also counts the array's double values, three per colour: in the 37 public prc-db files that have coloured markup, every code we decode (74,623 coloured markup primitives) is a multiple of 3 and in range read that way, while 7,767 of them (10.4%) would be out of range read as an entry index, and Datalogics counts the same on its side (20,579 *Color* entities, all multiples of 3, 555 out of range as entries), so the recommendation for this issue should state the rule once, at the array, for the markup code too.

## The recommendation is better supported than when filed — and should be qualified, not applied as drafted

We filed this issue. Two new measurements since: one that strengthens it, and one that bounds where it
applies. Posting both rather than sitting on them.

**Summary: `rotation` is read as ONE `Vector2D` on a texture and as TWO on a curve, by the same
viewer.** The recommendation above is well supported for the context this issue was raised in — better
supported than when it was filed, since the reference viewer now agrees with the corpus. What is not
established is that it should be applied to the shared structure, because Table 88 is also reached
from curves, where the same viewer does the opposite.

Our suggestion is to qualify the recommendation rather than withdraw or apply it.

Both halves are measured, one of them on a third-party file:

| | what real writers write | what the reference viewer reads |
|---|---|---|
| **texture** transformation | one `Vector2D` — 23 corpus files | **one `Vector2D`** |
| **curve** transformation | no corpus file carries one | **two `Vector2D`** |

### What was measured

Two matched pairs of synthesised files, each pair identical except for the field under test, on two
different curve types. Each file is a plane whose
surface domain is `[0,20] x [0,20]`, trimmed to the square `[5,15] x [5,15]` by four
`PRC_TYPE_CRV_OnSurf` edges. Each edge's `uv_curve` is a 2D `PRC_TYPE_CRV_PolyLine` (`is_3d_flag`
FALSE, points written as `Vector2D`) carrying a `0x02` `PRC_TRANSFORMATION_Rotate` transformation — a
90 degree rotation, with the polyline points written pre-rotated so that both files describe the same
square. Neither file contains a tessellation section, so nothing can be drawn from a baked mesh.

| file | uv curve | `rotation` written as | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `uvxform-rotate` | 2D PolyLine | **one** `Vector2D` — x-axis as (cos, sin), y-axis derived | 3D data parsing error |
| `uvxform-rotate2` | 2D PolyLine | **two** `Vector2D` — x-axis and y-axis, as Table 88 declares | **renders correctly** |
| `uvxform-line` | 2D **Line** | **one** `Vector2D` | 3D data parsing error |
| `uvxform-line2` | 2D **Line** | **two** `Vector2D` | **renders correctly** |

The viewer consumes four doubles. If it consumed two, the two-vector files would carry four surplus
doubles and desync; they do not, they draw the figure.

**The `Line` pair is the stronger half, and it settles a question the PolyLine pair cannot.** A 2D
PolyLine carries explicit points, so a viewer that consumed the transformation at the right width and
then ignored it would still draw something sensible — `rotate2` alone therefore establishes the
*width* and not the *reading*. A 2D Line has no points of its own: `P(sv) = M·(sv,0) + T`, so its
entire geometry is the transformation. `uvxform-line2` is drawn in the right place, at the right
scale and the right orientation, measured against three fixed reference marks in the same file. The
four doubles are not merely consumed; they are consumed **as a rotation matrix's two columns** and
applied as one.

### The texture half, measured on a third-party file

`5571858.pdf` from the digital-corpora set is an architectural model by an unrelated authoring tool.
Its globals carry 22 texture definitions. Three of them — indices 10, 11 and 13 — have behaviour
`0x02`, and the rest are identity, so those three are the only ones that exercise `rotation` at all.
Two of the three are especially useful: they reuse pictures 4 and 8, which also appear untransformed
at indices 4 and 8, so the same image is applied twice in one file with the disputed field as the
only difference.

The file opens in the reference viewer and renders completely: roughly twenty distinct textures, each
on the right surface — a legible undistorted logo, square tile grids, level stone courses, a
different floor covering in each room.

**That is the measurement, and it does not depend on seeing the rotation.** Texture definitions 12
through 21 come *after* the rotated definition 10 in the array. Had the viewer consumed four doubles
there where the file wrote two, every later definition would have shifted — wrong pictures on wrong
surfaces, or none. That is exactly the desync the original filing reports from reading four. The
array survives intact, so the viewer read two doubles: one `Vector2D`, y-axis derived.

Bit accounting from our own parse agrees: those three definitions are 282 bits against 184 for the
identity ones, a difference of 98 bits, which is two doubles and not four.

### Why we think this is clean

The pair sits inside a larger set of 13 files that vary one aspect of the same transformation at a
time, and a single model accounts for all 13:

1. the 2D form is read on a 2D curve, so the `is_3d_flag` rule in 7.10 *is* implemented;
2. `rotation` is two `Vector2D`;
3. the per-entity permitted-flag tables are enforced.

Two of the 13 were **predictions written down before the files were opened** — a `0x01` translation
and a `0x08` uniform scale, both predicted to render, both of which did. Four further files write the
*3D* transformation form under `is_3d_flag = FALSE` and all four fail, each with exactly the surplus
the 2D reading predicts.

`uvxform-line2` was also a prediction rather than a sweep: `uvxform-line` had failed, the two-vector
reading said it was two doubles short, and writing those two doubles made it render. **Two different
curve types, tested independently, give the same answer.**

We also had two fixtures of our own that were simply non-conforming, and they are worth mentioning
because they cost us three rounds of wrong conclusions: they used `PRC_TRANSFORMATION_NonUniformScale`
and `PRC_TRANSFORMATION_NonOrtho` on a PolyLine, which 7.10.17 forbids
(`value_data.yaml:286` permits only Identity, Translate, Rotate and uniform Scale there). The viewer
was right to refuse them. Once they are set aside as our bugs rather than as data, the model above is
the only one left standing.

### What it does and does not do to the original argument

It does **not** touch the corpus measurement in the filing. Reading two doubles still realigns the
texture-definition array in those files, and still recovers roughly 23 textured files that reported
zero materials. That result is real and this measurement does not explain it away.

What it does is establish that the same structure is read as **four** doubles somewhere else. The
definitions contain exactly one 2D transformation structure — `misc_data.yaml:417` — so these are not
two different tables that happen to look alike. We checked that before writing this.

When this comment was first drafted we could not tell whether the reading was context-dependent or
whether one of the two measurements had another explanation. The texture measurement above narrows
it: **the reference implementation is context-dependent** — one `Vector2D` for a texture
transformation, two for a curve transformation, on files it did and did not author respectively.

Whether the *specification* should follow it there is the committee's call, and we want to be careful
not to smuggle that in. Two readings remain open:

* **The behaviour is correct and the table must say so.** Then the recommendation needs qualifying,
  because as drafted it makes the curve case non-conforming.
* **The curve behaviour is a viewer defect.** Then the recommendation is right exactly as written, and
  what we have found is a bug to report elsewhere rather than a reason to change the text.

We cannot choose between those, for one concrete reason: **no corpus file carries a 2D transformation
on a curve** — 529 files across two corpora, no `PRC_TYPE_CRV_OnSurf` at all, three with any coedge UV
curve. So there is no writer evidence for the curve column, only viewer evidence, and a viewer alone
should not move a clause.

What we would say either way: the two measurements behind this issue were never in conflict. They were
measuring different contexts, and both are right about the context they measured.

The structural argument in the original filing is unaffected either way, and we still think it is the
strongest part: `non_ortho_matrix` is declared identically to `rotation` and genuinely does carry two
vectors, while `rotation` is present only when `NonOrtho` is FALSE, which is exactly when the second
column is determined. That asymmetry is real whatever the wire format turns out to be. But it is an
argument about what the format *should* be, and the evidence above is about what it *is*.

### What this suggests for the recommendation

The change proposed above is correct for the texture context and should not be applied to the shared
structure unqualified. Two shapes would work; we have no strong preference and the committee will see
the drafting consequences better than we do.

1. **Qualify Table 88 itself** — state that `rotation` is written as a single `Vector2D` when the
   transformation is carried by a texture, and as two when carried by a curve. That records what is
   actually out there, at the cost of a structure whose field widths depend on its container.
2. **Split the structure** — leave Table 88 as the literal two-`Vector2D` form and give the texture
   transformation its own table with the single-`Vector2D` `rotation`. That is a larger edit but
   removes the conditional, and `PRC_TYPE_GRAPH_TextureTransformation` already has its own clause to
   hang it on.

Either way the writing direction should be explicit, for the reason given in #816's comment thread: a
rule that is merely derivable is one that gets derived wrongly and produces files nobody notices are
wrong.

One thing we have NOT established: what real writers put in a **curve** transformation. No file in
either corpus carries one — 529 files, no `PRC_TYPE_CRV_OnSurf` at all, and only three with any
coedge UV curve. So the curve column rests on the viewer alone, and if the committee knows of a
writer that emits them, that would be worth more than anything further we can synthesise.

### Fixtures

`uvxform-rotate` / `uvxform-rotate2` and `uvxform-line` / `uvxform-line2`, plus the rest of the set,
are available as `.prc` and as PDFs with a `/3D` annotation, all brep-only. Each carries three fixed
reference marks alongside the figure under test, so a wrong answer is distinguishable from a right one
by eye rather than only by whether the file opens. Happy to attach them here or send them on.

One caveat on reproducing them: `PRC_TYPE_CRV_OnSurf` also needs a `has_transform` Boolean that
Table 262 does not declare — the same defect as #658, on the curve side — and without it every file
in the set is refused before the rotation is ever reached. That is being filed separately, and it is
why this question took as long to reach as it did.

[uvxform-line.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32396732/uvxform-line.pdf)
[uvxform-line2.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32396734/uvxform-line2.pdf)
[uvxform-rotate.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32396733/uvxform-rotate.pdf)
[uvxform-rotate2.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32396735/uvxform-rotate2.pdf)

**A third-party witness for the texture case, and an independent reader that failed exactly as the issue predicts.**

This supports the recommendation as qualified in the comment of 18 September: one `Vector2D` where Table 88 is reached
from a texture transformation, with the curve case left open.

`3D_Schreibtisch_2010.stream-954.prc` (prc-db) has two texture transformations with the rotate bit set. Each stores one
`Vector2D`, and the file reads to its end only that way. nanoPRC read the table as written, two vectors, and refused the

recommendation's mat[0][1] = −mat[1][0], mat[1][1] = mat[0][0].

We hold no curve file that reaches Table 88 with the rotate bit set, so this says nothing about the curve case.

# Three additions: the defect is provable from the text alone, the fan/strip arm now has writer-side evidence, and there is a third defect in the same cluster

Three things since this was filed. The first sharpens the issue's own argument and needs no corpus
at all; the second settles the one arm of the recommendation that no implementation had evidence
for; the third is a defect in the same structure that this issue does not yet mention.

## 1. The contradiction is internal to the clause, six lines apart

This issue argues that `size_of_triangulateddata` cannot be both an array's length and the count of
point indices inside it. That is right, and there is a stronger way to say it that needs no file.

Two bullets in the same list (TWG working source at `6fb2ed9`,
`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc`):

> **:1972** — The *size_of_triangulateddata* field is the number of entries in the array
> *triangulateddata*.

> **:1978** — The *has_vertex_colors* field is a flag indicating if colours are stored directly in
> the vertices. Either there is no color for the vertices, or every vertex shall have a color.

For a face whose only primitive block is a triangle list, `triangulateddata` holds **one** entry —
the triangle count. So `size_of_triangulateddata` is **1**, and the derivation in §7.8.7.2 gives a
1,000-triangle face exactly **one** color, while line 1978 requires one per vertex.

This is not a reading that is merely wrong by some factor. It is a reading the clause contradicts
six lines above the requirement it breaks. The "factor of nine on a real file" in the issue body is
a symptom of it, and we would rather lead with the text than with our corpus.

## 2. The fan/strip arm: writer-side fixtures, with a viewer verdict

The recommendation tells a reader to count point indices — `3 × ntri` for a list, and the sum of the
point counts for a fan or strip. **The list arm is measured. The fan and strip arms were measured by
nobody**, in either direction, by any implementation.

### What the corpus says, and why that made a fixture the only route

Census over 529 PRC files from two collections — the public `ralovich/prc-db` set and a
SafeDocs-derived set — counting `TESS_Face` primitive-block kinds at the point the face header is
read, so a face is counted whether or not its blocks later decode:

| block kind | faces | files | with vertex colours | files |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| triangle list | 142,554 | 303 | **674** | 3 |
| triangle fan | 2,718 | 4 | **0** | 0 |
| triangle strip | 56,659 | 15 | **0** | 0 |
| one-normal | 2,497 | 7 | 0 | 0 |
| no block bit set | 19,381 | 7 | 0 | 0 |

217,081 faces in 313 carriers. A face may set several block bits, so the rows do not sum to the face
count.

Two things follow. **Fans and strips are not rare** — strips are about a quarter of all faces in the
corpus, across 15 files, so the reference viewer handles them at scale. And **not one fan or strip
face anywhere carries vertex colours.** The gap is the *combination*, which no corpus can close.

Separately: the 674 coloured faces, every one a plain triangle list, is the same figure the nanoPRC
maintainer reports. Two readers, two instruments, the same number. Our 529 files contain the
310-file `prc-db` collection, so this cross-checks the two **instruments** rather than widening the
evidence.

### The fixtures

## 4. A third defect in the same structure, not currently in this issue

**`is_segment_color` is listed on a `TessFace` and then excluded by its own description.** Table 143

— *"(Optional; not present when reading a `PRC_TYPE_TESS_Face`)"* — so a reader or writer working

Evidence for the requirement that the size of point_reference_array equal the number of non-zero elements of

- 24,587 are empty (no bit set); the size, still written, is 0.
- 1,562 have 1 to 3 references and are stored plain (the figure in the other issue on this field).
- 8,710 are stored compressed.

Checks of the instrument. The count of tessellations in each file equals the count recorded for it independently, in all 166 files, so
none was skipped. Pairing each size with the wrong array (shuffled) gives 17,383 differences in 34,859.

So the sentence "shall be equal to the number of non-zero elements" has no counter-example here, and the same sentence stated in the

# A second implementation's answer on CR-28: seven of the ten tested in Acrobat, 7 of 7 for the gate

CR-28 asks for a `has_transform` Boolean on ten curve entities that declare `transform`
unconditionally, following the form `PRC_TYPE_CRV_Circle` already uses. We have implemented and
shipped that reading on both sides of a reader/writer pair, and tested the half of it that no file
in any corpus can arbitrate. **Everything below supports the change as proposed.**

## First, the count, recounted independently

Parsing `definitions/base-entities/curve.yaml` at `6fb2ed9` gives **14 curve entities carrying a
transformation, 4 gating it and 10 bare**, and the named ten match CR-28's list exactly:

| gated | Circle, Intersection, Line, PolyLine |
| bare | Blend02Boundary, Composite, Ellipse, Equation, Helix01, Hyperbola, Offset, OnSurf, Parabola, Transform |

unrelated reason, and got the same answer. Two derivations from two sources.

filtered from the SafeDocs web crawl — finds **only two of CR-28's ten entities present at all**,
