## The result: six one-bit pairs, 6 of 6 in Acrobat

*(A seventh of the ten, `OnSurf`, is settled by three files rather than a pair and is covered
below; seven of CR-28's ten therefore carry viewer evidence.)*

Each pair is the same model written twice, differing by a single inserted `has_transform` bit.
That was verified at the bit level rather than assumed: decompressing both arms, exactly one
content section differs, the gated arm is the bare arm with one `1` bit inserted at the same
offset, and every bit after it is identical.

| entity | transform written BARE | transform GATED |
|---|---|---|
| Equation | tree populates, **nothing drawn** | renders — the two-turn helix its parameters specify |
| Helix01 *(sub_type 0)* | no nodes | renders — a three-turn helix |
| Hyperbola | tree populates, **nothing drawn** | renders |
| Parabola | tree populates, **nothing drawn** | renders |
| Offset | no nodes | renders — a circle |
| Composite | no nodes | renders — three sides of a rectangle |

Each gated arm draws the geometry its parameters specify, so these are not merely parse results.
The five earlier pairs carry a known-good reference body beside the subject, because a blank
viewport is not a measurement. The Equation pair is a single curve with nothing else in the file;
there the check is that the gated file draws exactly the curve its parameters specify.

**A caution worth more than the table.** Three of the six fail *silently*: Equation, Hyperbola and
Parabola build a Model Tree node and draw nothing, with no error and no dialog. **A populated Model Tree
means the file parsed far enough to build a node, not that the curve record was read** — and on a
wire body the curve is the only content, so an empty viewport has nothing else to blame. A survey
that counts refusals finds four of the seven (with `OnSurf`, below) and concludes the field is
type-dependent. It is not.

## The general rule comes from a type CR-28 does not touch

`PRC_TYPE_CRV_PolyLine` is one of the four the tables **already** gate. Written in its shipping
gated form it renders; the identical model with the Boolean removed populates a tree and draws
nothing. **PolyLine is not one of CR-28's ten and its table already has the Boolean**, so that

## We have adopted the proposal in full, on both sides

Our reader now consumes `has_transform` on all ten. Our writer emits it on every one of the ten
it is able to produce — **nine**; `Blend02Boundary` is the exception, and only because our writer
has no path to emit that entity at all — as of producer version 0.11.0. `Equation` was the last of
the nine: our writer emitted its transform bare, as its table declares, until 3 November, after it
had corrected the others from this same ticket. That is a small instance of the case for one
statement in place of ten table edits: ten edits can be applied to some types and missed on others. That is a
deliberate divergence from the published tables, taken on the evidence above. Both retain a documented switch back to the table-literal reading, kept so the A/B
stays reproducible and marked as the known-wrong arm.

We mention the adoption because it is a different kind of statement from the measurements: it is
one thing to report that a viewer wants the Boolean, and another to have changed a shipping
producer's output format on the strength of it.

## Where our evidence stops, stated plainly

* **Helix01 is sub_type 0 only.** The law-driven sub_type 1 shows no nodes **both** bare and gated,
  so a second and unrelated defect masks this question on that form entirely. Anyone reproducing
  the helix row must use the constant-radius sub_type; a law helix returns a null either way and
  would look like a refutation.
* **Transform is not ours to corroborate.** Our corpus carries none, and we have built no file for
  it. Our reader gates it, but following nanoPRC and the evidence already in CR-28, not any
  measurement of our own. (`Equation` was in the same position until the pair above; no corpus
  file of ours exercises it either.)
* **A writer and a reader from one house can be wrong together.** Our two implementations agreeing
  would prove nothing; that is why every fixture was taken to Acrobat, which is a third decoder
  that shares no code and no derivation with either.

## The convention holds for every surface type, not only for NURBS

The evidence above rested on two populations: nineteen files in a public corpus whose zero-loop
faces carry no boundary topology at all, and four files from a second implementation's corpus in
which all 2,040 zero-loop faces sit on `PRC_TYPE_SURF_NURBS`.

That second group left a question open, and we raised it ourselves rather than being asked: whether
"no loop means the whole surface over its parameterization domain" depends on the surface being
**intrinsically** bounded. A NURBS patch carries its extent in its control net. A plane does not --
a plane's extent exists nowhere in the file except its parameterization field. If the convention
were really about intrinsic bounds, a zero-loop plane would be the case where it broke.

**It does not break.** That second implementation has since built the matched set, one variable
across six surface types, `number_of_loops = 0` on every face and no tessellation section anywhere,
and reports that the reference viewer opens all six, populates the model tree and draws:

```
surface     extent comes from                     result
plane       neither parameter intrinsically       renders
NURBS       both, from the control net            renders
sphere      u periodic, v by definition           renders
torus       both periodic                         renders
cylinder    u only; v from the parameterization   renders
cone        u only, and it has an apex            renders
```

Stated here as their measurement, not ours. With the four production files already described, that
is **ten independent zero-loop files accepted across five surface types**, and the plane is the one
that matters: it is the case the intrinsic-bounds reading predicted would fail.

## What this changes in the request

Only the confidence, not the wording. The proposed text above already states the convention without
qualification --

> If the list is empty, the face is not bounded by loops and its extent is the parameter domain of
> the face.

-- and we would have had to narrow it had the plane behaved differently. It did not, so the sentence
can stand as drafted, and the editor is not being asked to generalise from one surface type.

The request therefore remains a pure clause problem: 7.9.12 says `number_of_loops` shall be one or
more, seventeen of thirty-four files in one corpus declare zero, four more in another do, and the
reference implementation renders all of them.

**CR-31, correction.** The second-implementation figure in the body undercounts, and one clause
attached to it does not survive the larger census. Neither change affects the proposed replacement
text, and the first moves in the argument's favour.

## What the reference viewer declines is narrower than "degenerate geometry"

The evidence above shows two files declining to draw: a sphere and a torus, each bounded by a single
one-point vertex loop. Read on its own, that set is consistent with a broader rule -- that the
reference implementation declines degenerate geometry as such -- and we did not include the fixture
that separates the two readings.

The second implementation has since supplied it. **A degenerate edge inside a real loop renders.**
A half-sphere bounded by two meridian edges plus two pole degenerate edges opens and draws. So the
distinguishing condition is not the presence of degenerate geometry in the face; it is that the
degenerate loop is the face's **only** boundary.

Stated here as their measurement rather than ours, alongside the earlier four-file set in which a
closed sphere bounded by a real seam-split loop renders and the same sphere bounded by a vertex loop
does not.

## Why the distinction is worth stating in the clause

Two reasons, and the second is the practical one.

It keeps the request honest about its own scope. As filed, this asks the committee to settle the
status of a face whose loops are all vertex loops. It does not ask them to say anything about
degenerate edges generally, and a reader of the ticket should not have to infer that from the
absence of a counter-example.

And it means **a writer that must cover a pole is not out of options**. If the rule were "degenerate
geometry is declined", a closed sphere would have no conforming representation that the reference
implementation draws. It is not, so the pole can be carried as a degenerate edge inside a real loop,
or -- as the dominant real writers do, measured across six sphere faces in three production files --
by splitting the sphere into patches bounded by two meridian arcs and one latitude arc, with the
pole as an ordinary vertex where the meridians meet. Neither route is closed off by this request,
and the clause should make that visible.

> loops** as extending over the whole of its parameter domain, and shall render it accordingly.

visible without reading the correspondence behind it.

## The one-variable pair

Two shapes, each written twice — once with the face bounded by a degenerate vertex loop, once with a real loop — and nothing else changed:

| Fixture | Boundary | Acrobat |

**It establishes** that the reference viewer does not draw a face bounded only by a correctly formed degenerate vertex loop, and that replacing it with a real loop makes the same shape render.

**It does not establish** that the viewer is wrong. - **"Renders" and "renders what we meant" are different claims.** The verdicts are the former.
  The real-loop files draw; whether they draw the intended shape is a separate question with its own evidence.
- **7.9.21.7.1 and its neighbours are *compressed*-face clauses** — 7.9.21.7.2 even states that the loop of an IsoFace cannot be degenerate, confining vertex loops to AnaFaces — while these fixtures are uncompressed B-rep. CR-32's own census found **none of 20,816 loops in 36 prc-db files is degenerate**. The construct is sanctioned by the specification and unexercised in the wild, so no implementer has interop
experience of it and nothing will surface the ambiguity naturally. That is exactly the condition in which a one-sentence statement is cheap and its absence is expensive.

Parsing that token will give an error at which point (as we know all too well) behaviour is undefined. However to answer your question, the only thing we need to know is whether "split the token into two and put the second half back in the token pipeline" is a plausible strategy for error recovery - because that's is the only way you could ever get `12.34` and `.56` as two tokens. I agree with @faceless2.

> Do consecutive numbers need whitespace or do +/-/. act as a delimiter?

No: The definition of delimiters is clear and does not includes those characters.

> Clause 7.2 Lexical conventions does not mention whether the leading PLUS +, MINUS -, or PERIOD . in numbers causes one number to end and another to start (i.e. act as numeric token separators), or if this is a syntax error.

Neither. Clause 7.2 defines whitespace, delimiters, regular characters, and tokens. Neither the prose nor Tables 1 or 2 in Clause 7.2 define any of PLUS `+`, MINUS `-`, or PERIOD `.` as whitespace or delimiters.

Clause 7.2.3 says, "All characters except the white-space characters and delimiters are referred to as regular characters." Thus, PLUS +, MINUS -, or PERIOD . are regular characters per Clause 7.2, the same as digits 0-9. Clause 7.2.3 further says, "A sequence of consecutive regular characters comprises a single token.".

Thus, each of `12.34.56` and `-12.34-56` is a single token and not a syntax error per Clause 7.2. Instead, Clause 7.3 implies that each one is a syntax error. Clause 7.3.1 says:

> PDF syntax includes nine basic types of objects: boolean values, integers, real numbers, strings, names, arrays, dictionaries, streams, and the null object.
> ...
> Each object type, their method of creation and their proper referencing as indirect objects is described in 7.3.2, "Boolean objects" through 7.3.10, "Indirect objects".

The tokens `12.34.56` and `-12.34-56` are not described by any of 7.3.2 through 7.3.10. In particular, 7.3.3 Numeric objects says, "A real value shall be written as one or more decimal digits with an optional sign and a leading, trailing, or embedded PERIOD (2Eh) (decimal point).", which clearly excludes tokens that contain multiple signs or multiple decimal points.

While it's clearly a syntax error, I agree (again) with @faceless2 that a processor may perform error recovery. The error handling can validly result in zero or more intermixed numbers and errors, of which two valid special cases have already been mentioned:
- Parsing the first possible number and ignoring the rest of the token.
- Parsing multiple numbers from the token.

> All(?) processors seem to handle PLUS +, MINUS -, or PERIOD . starting a number WITHOUT requiring any whitespace when the preceding char is an official delimiter (e.g. ), >, ])

As they should. That's expressly specified as valid.

The sample PDF from @faceless2 has a negative number for an RGB component, although this should get rounded into range if the spec is followed to the letter (potential compounding issue). Try doing this with path construction operands instead, remembering that all excess operands (depending on what the parser does!) will get popped off the stack at the end of every operator, so there _should_ be no flow-on effect on later operators...

It seems to me that there is very strong consensus that `+`/`-`/`.` do NOT act as consecutive number delimiters, yet some implementations clearly do. Therefore, 32K needs an explicit statement rather than relying on inference or back-engineering of technically incorrect implementations (since none disclose the PDF has syntax errors). This can be done informatively and gives everyone something explicit to point at:

> NOTE: PLUS, MINUS, and PERIOD characters never act as token delimiters for consecutive numeric (number or integer) tokens. Consecutive numeric tokens, such as may occur in some PDF arrays or as operators to some operands, always require whitespace.

I will then also add both valid and invalid examples to this note.

When that was drafted, "iso-edge cache" and "ana-edge cache" were our own coinage, and a fair

That objection no longer applies. Both caches are now named and defined in the clause itself -- the

replacement uses the clause's own terms, which was not true when it was written.

The premise in the Defect section stands: a compressed B-rep contains no `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Edge`

**CR-30: the first replacement is withdrawn.**

This ticket proposed that a `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` "shall not be used as a trimming curve of a compressed face". That
proposal rested on an argument from structure, and the ticket said that better knowledge should win over it. Datalogics
has since supplied that knowledge: a set of small test files, each a compressed cube differing from its neighbour in
one field, read in Adobe Acrobat. Acrobat draws a composite as a trim curve of a compressed analytic face, and draws it
correctly. So the first replacement is withdrawn, and so is the alternative recorded beside it, which had the right
permission but none of the rules the files go on to establish. The proposed solution that Datalogics is posting below
replaces both. The title now states that answer; it previously described only the defect.

What the files establish, in brief (the proposed solution has the arms and the text):

- a composite's own start and end are `CompressedVertex`, as for any trim curve in a face, but the start and end of
  each curve in its `curves` array are `CompressedPoint`;
- a curve inside a composite takes no place in the compressed B-rep's list of curves, so it shifts no later reference;
- a curve inside a composite may not itself be a reference.

nanoPRC (CascadiaVoxel/nanoPRC, `main` at `097ffe4`) takes the opposite reading on all three, which is the reading the
text leads to. It reads the inner curves' ends as vertices, and so refuses every file in the set that holds a
composite. With that one point changed in a scratch copy, it reads them, and gives each inner curve a place in the
list of curves, as Datalogics' own reader did. In the two files that differ only in the index of one referenced curve,
that numbering resolves the index Acrobat draws wrongly to the shared edge, and the index Acrobat draws correctly to
another curve. With the inner curves given no places, the two resolve the other way round: the correct file's index
names the shared edge, and the other's names the second trim curve of the cube's −Z face, which is the curve
Datalogics' description of that file predicts. That is a second reading of the bits, not a second rendering: nanoPRC
cannot yet draw a composite.

The half of this ticket's argument that concerned iso faces is not settled by the files, which test the trim loop of
an analytic face. The proposed solution lists it under "Not addressed".

## Two statements that disagree

The `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` subclause (`07-base-entities.adoc:4087`):

> The _PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve_ structure defines a compressed composite curve (see
> <<tab-entities-PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve>>). It must not be used on edges or coedges.

Read as the topology entities, this forbids nothing: `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_Edge` and `PRC_TYPE_TOPO_CoEdge` hold their curves through `PtrCurve`, whose `curve` is a `PRC_TYPE_CRV` (`topology.yaml:1645-1647`), so a `PRC_HCG_*` curve cannot be stored there at all. The sentence has content only if it means the trim curves of compressed faces, which the compressed B-rep clause treats as edges
(`number_edge_references` is "the number of iso-edges in the compressed brep — the size of the iso-edge cache", `:3273`).

On that reading the tables permit what the sentence forbids. A compressed face's trim curves are `RefOrCompressedCurve` (`topology.yaml:1274`, `:1279`, `:1340-1344`); a `RefOrCompressedCurve` that is not a reference holds a `CompressedCurve` (`:1373`); and "A compressed curve is one of _PRC_HCG_Line_,
_PRC_HCG_Circle_, _PRC_HCG_BsplineHermiteCurve_ or _PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve_" (`:3965`), with no exception for faces.

## Effect

- A reader can decode a composite in a face from the text, and knows how to read its sub-curves.
- Files Acrobat already reads stay conforming; no writer we know of is affected.
- `StartEndData` (`topology.yaml:1566-1596`) needs no change: its vertex and point fields are  conditioned on `curve_trimming_face`, so they follow changes 3 and 4.
- Unchanged: the bit stream, and the curve list (`:3965`) -- a composite's inner curves are compressed curves in the sense of that sentence, and a composite may still nest one.
- Table "RefOrCompressedCurve" (`topology.yaml:1358-1376`) is unchanged, and the composite's `curves` array still uses it; change 5 only restricts that use to stored entries. Its other uses are untouched: an iso face's first and second trim curves (`:1274`, `:1279`) and an analytic face's trim-loop curves (`:1340-1344`), each of which may still be a reference to an already-stored curve; and the loop sentinel  (`:1323`), which is always stored.
- Not addressed:
  - **Whether the composite itself may be referenced, and from where.** Arms E to G settle what the inner curves do; the composite occupies one place in the list of curves and arm F's index counts it, but no arm names the composite itself from a later face. ## What Acrobat does

Ten small files, each a compressed cube, each differing from its neighbour in one field.

**First, four arms on the endpoints.** Each differs from the control in one trim curve of one face:

| arm | first trim curve of one face | its sub-curves' endpoints | Adobe Acrobat |
|---|---|---|---|
| A [cubebc-control.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694627/cubebc-control.pdf) | an ordinary `PRC_HCG_Line` (control) | -- | renders |
| B  [comptrim-subject.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694687/comptrim-subject.pdf)  | a `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` | `CompressedVertex` | empty model tree |
| C [comptrim-points-subject.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694663/comptrim-points-subject.pdf) | a `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` | `CompressedPoint`, positions mis-scaled by the writer | renders, one corner displaced |
| D [comptrim-points-fixed.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694706/comptrim-points-fixed.pdf)  | a `PRC_HCG_CompositeCurve` | `CompressedPoint`, correct | renders the cube |

So Acrobat implements a composite as a face trim curve and draws it correctly. It also settles a point no clause states: the composite's **own** start and end are `CompressedVertex`, as for any trim curve in a face, but the start and end of **each curve in its `curves` array** are `CompressedPoint`. Writing them as vertices gives an empty model tree.

Two readers written independently of Acrobat agree on the bits of arm D once they take this reading:
Datalogics' reader, and nanoPRC (CascadiaVoxel/nanoPRC) with one change made for the test. Both read the composite's own start and end as new vertices at (15, 15, 15) and (−15, 15, 15), its two inner lines with `CompressedPoint` ends through (0, 15, 15), and every later **vertex** reference
with the same number as in arm A -- so the inner curves' points take no place among the vertices. That is the vertex array; the **curve** list is a separate question, and the next six arms answer it.

**Second, six arms on the curves array.** In these the `+X` face stops restating the edge it shares with the `+Z` face and names that face's copy instead, by its index in the compressed B-rep's list of curves. One face's surface is deliberately twice the size of the face, so that a trim loop which is not honoured leaves a visibly oversized patch rather than coinciding with the right answer:

| arm | what it does | Adobe Acrobat |
|---|---|---|
| E0 [refctl-ordinary-line.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694761/refctl-ordinary-line.pdf)  | the reference, with **no composite in the file** -- the control | renders the cube |
| E [ref-index-counts-inner.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694773/ref-index-counts-inner.pdf) | arm D's composite, index **counting** its two inner curves | renders, one face notched |
| F [ref-index-skips-inner.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694796/ref-index-skips-inner.pdf) | the same, index **not counting** them | renders the cube |
| G1 [split-loop-only.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34695038/split-loop-only.pdf) | the `+Z` loop in five curves, no composite -- ladder rung | renders the cube |
| G2 [inner-curves-stored.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34695057/inner-curves-stored.pdf) | G1 plus the composite on `+X`, **both** inner curves stored | renders the cube |
| G [ref-inner-curve-is-ref.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34694844/ref-inner-curve-is-ref.pdf)  | G2 with the first inner curve replaced by a **reference** | empty model tree |

E and F are the same length and differ in one five-bit index; G2 and G differ only in whether that first inner curve is stored or referenced. So:

- **an inner curve takes no place in the list of curves** (E against F, with E0 showing that a referenced trim curve is honoured at all, including one traversed in the opposite direction);
- **an inner curve may not be a reference** (G2 against G, with G1 and G2 showing that neither the five-curve loop nor the composite's new position accounts for the empty tree).

**The wire form is unchanged.** `topology.yaml:1566` declares the composite's `curves` as an `Array` of `inner_kind: RefOrCompressedCurve`, which is a `curve_is_not_already_stored` Boolean followed by either an index or a curve (`:1358-1376`), and the arms bear that out: every stored inner curve in arms D, G2 and the rest is written with that Boolean set to TRUE, and Acrobat draws them. What the arms add is two rules about how such an entry is used, neither of which the table states:

- a stored inner curve **takes no place in the list of curves** -- it is part of the composite, and only the composite itself occupies a place;
- an inner curve **shall not be a reference**: `curve_is_not_already_stored` shall be TRUE for every entry of `curves`.

Change 5 above states both in the table. Changes 2 to 4 state the endpoint rule, which is independent of them.

The text does not say this. Two sentences state the literal reading. "If a compressed line is part of a compressed face, the compressed line is represented by a pair of start/end vertices" (`:3974`), and
`curve_trimming_face` "is TRUE if this compressed line is part of a _PRC_TYPE_TOPO_BrepDataCompress_"
(`:3976`, and the same for circles at `:3995`). A sub-curve of a composite in a face is part of both, so read literally its endpoints would be vertices, which is arm B. nanoPRC as released takes that reading and refuses arm D.

**CR-22: the advice in the description is withdrawn, and a proposed solution replaces it.** The
description recommends that an encoder take `normal_is_reversed` for a growing triangle from the
triangle the traversal reached it from. That advice is wrong, and following it produces files whose
triangles decode with alternating winding. Two implementations found this independently, and this
comment replaces the advisory NOTE with a statement of what the field does and how an encoder sets
it. It also takes in a related draft of ours, CR-34, which was never filed: the clause still says
the field is "reserved for future use".

**What is withdrawn.**

* The advice to inherit the value from the parent triangle, in the proposed NOTE and the summary.
* The wrong-value rates (52% to 5.1% on a 227,000-triangle file; 100% to about 0% on four smaller
  files). They were measured in August against a proxy, the tilt of the reconstructed normal, and a
  direct check of decoded winding in October contradicts them. Our 26 October correction said these
  rates stand; they should not be relied on. The Acrobat results were already withdrawn on that date.

**What the field does.** When `must_recalculate_normals` is TRUE, a decoder has no stored normal to
compare with, and takes each triangle's winding from `normal_is_reversed` alone. In nanoPRC's
decoder, one value per triangle decides three things: whether the second and third vertices, in the
order the traversal produces them, are exchanged to give the triangle's winding (they are when the
value is FALSE); which way the triangle normal used for the local coordinate system points; and which
of the triangle's edges are taken as left and right for the next step of the traversal. The last two
move decoded positions, so a decoder cannot ignore the field.

**How real writers set it: per triangle.**

* Read that way, the third-party files decode with consistent winding. Over the 82 files of the
  public prc-db collection in which every compressed tessellation recalculates its normals
  (45,496,894 triangles), 40,345 of 18,102,851 shared edges, 0.223%, join two triangles that wind
  in opposite directions. That is an upper bound, since parts that coincide add to it; most files
  have none. `3D-PDF-Example_FEA_Flange.stream-14`, for example, has 23,552 triangles and no
  inconsistent edge, and its value changes between consecutive triangles at least 5,972 times, so it
  is not inherited along the traversal.
* nanoPRC's writer inherited the value until 17 October 2026. Its output decoded with every other
  triangle of a strip reversed, and about half the edges of a cube inconsistent. Since nanoPRC #202,
  it sets the value for each triangle from that triangle alone, and its output decodes with the
  winding of the source mesh, on the same cases.
* Datalogics' reader, measured on third-party files, agrees: no local rule reproduces the stored
  values, and inheritance from the parent triangle is refuted, so the files' writers set the value
  for each triangle. (Where normals are stored, the flag is not in the file, and that reader derives
  it for each triangle by the dot test.)

```
+
```

**Correction to the CR-22 comment above (5 November): `normal_is_reversed` has two roles, not three.** Patrick Gallot
(Datalogics) asked whether nanoPRC lets the field reach the local coordinate system of eq-1 to eq-3, as the comment says.
It does not, and the comment was wrong to say so.

In nanoPRC's decoder (`src/prc_decode_compressed_tess.c`, `main` `e32c194`), the axes of eq-1 to eq-3 are built from
V₀, V₁ and V₃ alone (`:1151-1220`), as the equations say, with no triangle normal. When normals are recalculated, the
decoder computes each triangle's normal from its vertices and negates it when the field is FALSE (`:437-440`), but that
normal is only the normal it outputs for the triangle (`:1546-1552`); no position is computed from it. Since FALSE also
exchanges the second and third vertices, that normal is simply the normal of the triangle as wound, and needs no rule of
its own. The field reaches positions in one way only: by deciding which edges are left and right (`:684-699`), and so
which edge, and which V₀, V₁ and V₃, the next coordinate system is built on.

So in "What the field does", the field decides two things, not three: the winding, and which edges are left and right.
The second is the one that moves decoded positions.

```
* The *normal_is_reversed* field is present when *must_recalculate_normals* is TRUE, with one value for each triangle. The same value decides which of the triangle's edges are its left and right edges for the traversal, as the test given in <<Mesh_Traversal>> does when normals are stored. A decoder shall apply it before reconstructing positions.
+
NOTE: An encoder sets *normal_is_reversed* for each triangle from that triangle alone, by comparing the order in which the traversal produces its vertices with the triangle's winding in the source mesh. A value copied from the triangle from which the traversal reached it gives the wrong winding for alternate triangles of a strip.
```

## `face_has_texture` confirmed — length 1

**The measurement.** Two files from one Quake III map, differing by exactly 39 bits in
`face_has_texture` and nothing else. Each carries the entity **twice** in one
`FileStructureTessellation`, both referenced by the tree, so a mis-sized read desyncs the second copy
instead of running off the end of the section:

| `face_has_texture` length | Acrobat |
|---|---|
| **1** | renders, both entities |
| `face_number` (40) | empty Model Tree |

The two-entity form is necessary. `face_has_texture` is the last field before `has_behaviors`, so in
a single-entity file a wrong length corrupts only the entity's own tail — we built that pair too, and
Acrobat renders **both** arms. The same pair also excludes a third reading the clause leaves open,
that the array is absent: at length 0 the length-1 file would over-read by one bit and fail exactly
as the 40-bit file does, and it renders. So the length is exactly 1 — not 0, not `face_number`.

The entity has 40 faces, 31 textured and 9 flat, so the array carries a genuine mix rather than a run
of TRUEs. We also have the `has_faces == TRUE` arm rendering with an explicit `face_has_texture[40]`.

Two corrections to my comment above; Neither changes its conclusions.

1. **`line_attribute_array` in the castle.** I was wrong in saying it "is not constrained to 1 either — Castle writes zero entries under the same flag.": `Castle_of_Bouvignes_Belgium_landscape.stream-48.prc` stores **one** entry there.  `line_attribute_array` is a `ShortArray`, which carries its own count, so its length does not depend on `has_faces` either way.
2. **The `face_has_texture` pair.** "Differing by exactly 39 bits" is the difference per entity. Each file carries the entity twice, so the two files differ by 78 bits in all.

The findings stand: `face_has_texture` has length 1 when `has_faces` is FALSE, and `is_face_planar` decodes only at `face_number`.

**Proposed solution (CR-45): the three arrays that have one element when `has_faces` is FALSE.** @ralovich's
report above gives the rule for `is_point_color_on_face` and `is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face`, and Datalogics'
comment of 9 October adds `face_has_texture` and excludes `is_face_planar`. This comment collects the evidence for all
four and proposes the text. The bit stream does not change; a reader that follows the text as written reads
`face_number` elements where these files store one, and reads the rest of the entity out of step.

Current text is quoted from the TWG working source at `main` `6fb2ed9`.

### Evidence

**`is_point_color_on_face`.** The castle in prc-db,
`Castle_of_Bouvignes_Belgium_landscape.stream-48.prc` (and its copy `output.prc`), stores `has_faces` FALSE, 65,804
faces and a single element. Read with one element, it reads to the end in Datalogics' reader and in nanoPRC's
(CascadiaVoxel/nanoPRC #225), and the two agree on the position of every field to the end of the entity. To see what
viewers do with both layouts, we wrote a unit cube as one compressed tessellation of 12 triangles in 6 faces, one colour per
face, four ways, with nothing else different:

| has_faces | elements | Adobe Acrobat | PDF-XChange Editor |
|---|---|---|---|
| TRUE | 6 | draws, all six colours right | draws with colour |
| TRUE | 1 | "3D parsing error" dialog | draws the cube without its face colours |
| FALSE | 6 | empty model tree | draws the cube without its face colours |
| FALSE | 1 | draws, all six colours right | draws with colour |

Both viewers read `face_number` elements when `has_faces` is TRUE and one when it is FALSE. "Always `face_number`"
would draw both six-element files, and "always one" both one-element files; neither viewer does either. The four files
are attached.

**`face_has_texture`.** Datalogics' pair, attached to the comment above: two files that differ only in this array, each
carrying the entity twice so that a wrong length desyncs the second copy. Acrobat renders the file with one element and
shows an empty model tree for the file with `face_number` (40).

**`is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face`.** The same pair. In both files the entity stores `has_faces` FALSE, 40 faces and
`is_multiple_line_attribute` TRUE, and both read only with one element of this array: with 40, nothing after it reads in
step. Since Acrobat renders the one-element file, it reads this array as one element as well.

**`is_face_planar` keeps `face_number` elements.** As Datalogics found above, 303 entities in two prc-db files store
`has_faces` FALSE with more than one face and carry this array, and they decode only at `face_number`. nanoPRC's reader
agrees. prc-db has since grown from 310 files to 606, and across all of them it is 518 entities in eight files; nanoPRC
reads all eight to the end at `face_number` and refuses all eight when this array is read with one element. The
evidence here is these files alone; there is no viewer verdict on this array.

No other file in prc-db, or in a private collection of 384 files, carries `is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face` or
`face_has_texture` with `has_faces` FALSE. One more file in prc-db stores `is_point_color_on_face` with `has_faces`
FALSE and more than one face: `isprsarchives-XXXVIII-5-W16-483-2011.stream-178.prc`, added to prc-db on 31 October,
with 2,080 faces and a single element. Like the castle, it reads to the end in nanoPRC's reader with one element, and
is refused with 2,080. Every other point-coloured compressed tessellation in either collection has a single face, where
the readings agree. So the three arrays rest on the files named here. (prc-db counts updated 9 November, on all
606 files.)

### Proposed change

Eight changes: one to the `has_faces` field, so that the rule is stated where a reader looks for it; the length of each of
the three arrays in both tables that give it; and the description of `face_has_texture`, which also says TRUE where
the table says FALSE.

**Change 1 of 8.** `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2801`

Current text:

```
* The *has_faces* field is TRUE if the entity is built using geometrical faces.
```

Replace with:

```
* The *has_faces* field is TRUE if the entity is built using geometrical faces. When it is FALSE, *is_point_color_on_face*, *is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face* and *face_has_texture* each have a single element, which applies to every face; *is_face_planar* still has *face_number* elements.
```

**Change 2 of 8.** `iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:2870`

Current text:

```
* The *face_has_texture* field is a Boolean array. It indicates which faces have texture when *no_texture* is TRUE and *all_faces_have_texture* is FALSE.
```

Replace with:

```
* The *face_has_texture* field is a Boolean array. It indicates which faces have texture when *no_texture* is FALSE and *all_faces_have_texture* is FALSE.
```

**Change 3 of 8.** "Mesh Texture Structure", `iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/tessellation.yaml:433-439`

Current text:

```
  - name: face_has_texture
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence: face_number
    required: true
    description: An array of Boolean values indicating if the corresponding face has texture. The size of this array corresponds to the number of faces stored in the mesh
```

Replace with:

```
  - name: face_has_texture
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence: "face_number if *has_faces* is TRUE, otherwise 1"
    required: true
    description: An array of Boolean values indicating if the corresponding face has texture. The size of this array is the number of faces stored in the mesh when *has_faces* is TRUE, and 1 when *has_faces* is FALSE
```

**Change 4 of 8.** "Mesh Attribute Structure", `tessellation.yaml:453-459`

Current text:

```
  - name: is_point_color_on_face
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence: face_number
    required:
    description: TRUE if corresponding face has point color. The size of this array corresponds to number of faces stored in the mesh.
```

Replace with:

```
  - name: is_point_color_on_face
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence: "face_number if *has_faces* is TRUE, otherwise 1"
    required:
    description: TRUE if corresponding face has point color. The size of this array is the number of faces stored in the mesh when *has_faces* is TRUE, and 1 when *has_faces* is FALSE.
```

**Change 5 of 8.** "Mesh Attribute Structure", `tessellation.yaml:470-474`. Besides the length, this corrects the
field's name, which carries a stray "a" here and nowhere else.

Current text:

```
  - name: is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face a
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence: face_number
```

Replace with:

```
  - name: is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face
    data_type:
      kind: Array
      inner_kind: Boolean
      occurrence: "face_number if *has_faces* is TRUE, otherwise 1"
```

**Changes 6 to 8 of 8.** "Description of the Data Written to the File", `tessellation.yaml:629`, `:648` and `:678`,
in the entries for `is_point_color_on_face` (`:625`), `is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face` (`:644`) and
`face_has_texture` (`:674`). In each, the current text:

```
      occurrence: face_number
```

Replace with:

```
      occurrence: "face_number if *has_faces* is TRUE, otherwise 1"
```

### Effect

* A reader can size all three arrays from the text, and reads the rest of the entity in step.
* Files written with `has_faces` TRUE read as before.
* The descriptions of `is_point_color_on_face` (`07-base-entities.adoc:2856`) and `is_multiple_line_attribute_on_face`
  (`:2862`) are left as they are; their "the corresponding face" and "the face" read correctly with change 1.
* **Unchanged:** field names (apart from the stray "a" in change 5), field order, data types and the bit stream; the length of `is_face_planar` and of every
  other array.
* **Not addressed:** what a single FALSE element means, which none of the evidence here tests.

A question on the premise here: does `sense_array` mean what Table 214 prints?

ISO 14739-1:2014 §8.9.21.5.14.1 says `sense_array`'s first two Booleans give the natural boundary the first trim curve lies on (FALSE FALSE Umin, FALSE TRUE Vmin, TRUE FALSE Umax, TRUE TRUE Vmax), and the third gives the order of the rest: FALSE runs Umin, Vmin, Umax (then Vmax), TRUE the reverse.

Across about 1,350 `PRC_HCG_IsoNurbs` faces in a corpus of real files, `sense_array` takes all eight values. We checked the reading on the 12 boundary trims whose two ends are both corners of the surface's parameter rectangle, so their side and direction are known from the geometry. The printed reading matches in none of the 12: in 4 the trim is on the side the bits name but runs the other way, and in 8 it is on another side. (3,120 more boundary trims end at no corner, so they can't be checked this way.)

Questions:

1. Which natural boundary do the first two bits name, and in which order are Umin/Vmin/Umax/Vmax meant?
2. Does the third bit reverse the order the four curves go round, the direction each curve runs, or both?
3. Is "the first curve" `Curves[0]` of Table 214's `Curves` array?

A worked example (a face with its `sense_array` and the four trims' sides and directions) would settle it. It matters for the change proposed here: an implementation that places iso-NURBS trims on the boundaries `sense_array` names, read as printed, draws them on the wrong side.

Thank you; this is a fair challenge, and the answer has two parts.

**What this issue proposes does not depend on the reading of `sense_array`.** The change is to the description of
`iso_boundary` (`iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:943`): when it is TRUE, no curve data follows. That
rests on the files read in step, not on which side the curve lies: nanoPRC reads nothing after a TRUE and stays in
step through all 4,501 `IsoNURBSTrimCrv` records in the 15 prc-db files that carry them, 1,566 of them TRUE, and the
Datalogics reader does the same. Whatever `sense_array` turns out to mean, those records hold no curve. The proposed
replacement does point to `sense_array` for where the curve lies, so if its meaning changes, that pointer stays right
and the meaning is fixed where `sense_array` is described.

**Your doubt about what `sense_array` means is, we think, well founded.** The description you test
(`iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3544-3553` at `78e64f0`, the same as the 2014 text) has not been checked
against geometry in this issue, and we have reason to think the files follow a different assignment. That evidence is
not ours to post: Datalogics is preparing an issue of its own on exactly this, with its own instrument and denominators, and we
would rather it came from them than second-hand. We will link it here once it is filed.

One thing worth checking on your side meanwhile, because it alone could put trims on the wrong side: the order in
which an iso-NURBS surface's compressed control net is rebuilt. The description of `CompressedControlPoints` builds the
first edge in one parameter direction and the storage order writes the other first; a reader that rebuilds the net in
the described order builds a different surface, which no longer meets its trim curves (not a transposed one: the prose reorders only the two edge chains, and the interior is still stored by row). If your 12 corner trims were placed on a
net rebuilt that way, some of the "other side" results may be that different surface rather than `sense_array`.

On your three questions, for what nanoPRC can say: it reads `sense_array` but does not yet place iso-NURBS trim curves
at all (the face is not tessellated), so it has no evidence on 1 or 2. On 3, we read "the first curve" as the first
trim curve in the order stored, which is how the record list is built; we have not seen anything that suggests
otherwise, but we have not tested it against geometry either.

The Datalogics issue on the sense_array assignment is #864. It states the assignment checked against this issue's twelve curves and
against both public collections.

* The value-rule rows are his reader's shipped behaviour. The kind-rule rows are modelled from the

**CR-38: the four references left out of range, now explained.** This updates the second of the three
caveats in the comment of 28 October. That caveat said the 4 out-of-range references the value rule
leaves in Datalogics' reader were in files with other known defects in that reader, and were not
explained. Patrick Gallot (Datalogics) has since printed the full resolution context for each, and

|---|--:|--:|
| Miter-Saw-Assembly | 7 | 4 |
| 4341011 | 13,409 | 3,789 |
| 3409645 | 10,602 | 4,260 |
| 3409645 | 13,844 | 4,260 |

## Comment for #849 (CR-36a, signed steps in the indice arrays)

An independent count from the reader side, by Patrick Gallot (Datalogics), over the same 310-file
prc-db collection (309 decoded; reader pinned before the sweep). His reader sign-extends at the
element width in every branch it can reach, so it is a second implementation of the rule this
issue proposes:

| array | form | arrays (his / ours) | negative values (his / ours) |
|---|---|---|---|
| point_reference_array | Huffman | 8,448 / 8,448 | 3,883,122 / 3,883,122 |
| point_reference_array | plain | 1,562 / 1,562 | 88 / 88 |
| triangle_face_array | Huffman | 5,776 / 5,776 | 649,874 / 649,874 |
| triangle_face_array | plain | 28,682 / 28,682 | 0 / 0 |

44,468 arrays, every cell equal. His reader also found a negative first element 0 times across all
44,468, consistent with the first element being an absolute value.

The caveat is his and worth keeping: both readers were built from the same prose, so agreeing with
each other is not the same as both being right. What it does establish is that the behaviour this
issue describes is the one two independent readers already rely on, and that the sentence at
09-io-algorithms.adoc:116 contradicts both.

**CR-36a: further evidence, and the reader's side stated for both forms.** This adds three things to
the description. They come from a draft we sent Datalogics on 1 November as CR-44, which turned out to
duplicate this ticket and has been withdrawn. Nothing here changes the defect or the figures above.

**1. A second array, and a controlled Acrobat test.** The description's Acrobat failure (nanoPRC #156,
18 October) was in `point_reference_array`. On 1 November the same thing happened in
`triangle_face_array`, on a 2,048-face mesh written by nanoPRC with its optional arrays stored plain.
Three files, each changing one thing from a baseline that displays, all read back by nanoPRC with
4,032 triangles:

| what is stored plain | how a negative step is stored | Adobe Acrobat (1 November 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| the bit lengths of `point_array` (absolute, never negative) | (none occur) | displays |
| the bit lengths of `triangle_face_array` | 6-bit form, so -1 is 63 | hangs |
| the bit lengths of `triangle_face_array` | 8-bit form, so -1 is 0xFF | displays |

So the plain form needs the 8-bit representation in the face array as well as the point array, and
what Acrobat rejects is a negative step in the 6-bit form, not storing the array plain.

**2. A second count agrees with the table.** On 1 November a separate probe in nanoPRC's reader
counted, over the same 310 files, the elements after the first that lie in 32 to 63 and in 192 to
255, before any sign correction. Before the count it was run on three files whose contents were
known: a Huffman-compressed array with 1,144 negative steps (counted 1,144 in 32 to 63), the same
array stored plain in the 6-bit form (1,144 in 32 to 63), and stored plain in the 8-bit form (1,144
in 192 to 255). So it sees either form when it is present. Its totals match the table: 14,224
Huffman-compressed arrays with 4,532,996 elements in 32 to 63 and none in 192 to 255, and 30,244
plain arrays with 88 in 192 to 255 and none in 32 to 63.

**3. The reader's threshold for the plain form.** The proposed replacement tells a reader how to
restore the sign only for the Huffman form ("a reader shall sign-extend leaf values of 32 or more").
For the plain form it gives the stored value (-1 as 0xFF) but not the test. If the reader's side
should be stated for both, the last sentence but one of the replacement could read:

Current proposed text:

```
When the array is Huffman-compressed, each is a leaf value of 6 bits, so −1 is stored as 0x3F, and a reader shall sign-extend leaf values of 32 or more.
```

Alternative:

```
When the array is Huffman-compressed, each is a leaf value of 6 bits, so −1 is stored as 0x3F. A reader shall treat an element after the first as negative when it is 128 or more in a plain array, and when it is 32 or more in a Huffman-compressed array.
```

Every negative step in prc-db already meets the alternative (all 88 plain ones are 128 or more, all
4,532,996 Huffman ones are 32 to 63), so it changes no file.

evolution, from the formula rather than from the field's name

15 + 15 · 2π = 109.2 after one turn and 15 + 15 · 6π = 297.7 after three, to one decimal place.

(`:4756-4759`) is

    tmp_point.x = radius * cos( param );
    tmp_point.y = radius * sin( param );

which, in a right-handed frame (the *z*-axis, the *x*-axis, and *y* = *z* × *x*), turns from the *x*-axis towards the
*y*-axis: counter-clockwise seen from +*z*. That is the opposite of the description and of what Acrobat draws. I
checked the latter on the control and the FALSE file, with each one's camera moved onto the +*z* axis and the axis

says so. nanoPRC's evaluator computes the TRUE branch as written, with the model's own axes
(`src/prc_tessellation_exact_geom_curves.c:863-875`), so for the control it turns counter-clockwise. That is the same

- and exchange the two branches in both formulas, so that `cos( - param )` and `sin( - param )` go with TRUE.

**Agreed on all four points. Two things to add, and a question on the fourth.**

**Your formula changes reproduce Acrobat on the attached files.** With `transform_point( o, x, z, p )` defined as
*o* + *p.x* · *X* + *p.y* · (*Z* × *X*) + *p.z* · *Z*, and the branches exchanged so that TRUE takes `− param`,
the control turns clockwise seen from +*z* and the FALSE file counter-clockwise, as Acrobat draws them. Reading
`pitch` as the rise per unit of the parameter gives the control's 37.7 units over three turns. The Datalogics
reader evaluates type 0 helices this way. I will add `pitch` to the issue as a fourth field of the same kind and
fold your formula changes into recommendation 3.

**The definition of `transform_point` also needs *X* and *Z* to be orthogonal, and Acrobat makes them so.**
For type 0 they are, by construction: the *x*-axis runs from the axis to `start`, at right angles to it. For
type 1 they are the stored `unit_u` and `unit_z`, and Table 269 describes each component only by its own name
(`Unit_u[0]`, ...); nothing requires the two to be unit length or orthogonal. Taken as stored, a non-orthogonal
pair draws a sheared helix. Acrobat does not: a type 1 file whose `unit_u` is tilted to (0.5, 0, 0.866), still
unit length but at 30° to `unit_z`, draws the same curve as its control with `unit_u` = (1, 0, 0). So Acrobat
normalises `unit_z` and makes `unit_u` orthogonal to it. Suggested addition to 7.10.11.3, which keeps existing
files conforming: "`unit_z` is normalised, and `unit_u` is made orthogonal to it and normalised, before
use." A "shall be of unit length and orthogonal" would also do, but would make such files non-conforming
while Acrobat reads them.

**For type 1, Acrobat follows the formula as written, so the exchange should not be carried over.** The type 1
control stores `orientation` TRUE, and Acrobat draws it turning counter-clockwise seen from +*z* -- the
formula's TRUE branch, `cos/sin(+param)`, with *Y* = *Z* × *X*. Exchanging the branches by analogy with type 0
draws the mirror image, which Acrobat does not. So as Acrobat reads them, TRUE means clockwise for type 0 and
counter-clockwise for type 1, and the text should say which for each sub_type rather than leave one rule to be
inferred. The type 1 file with `orientation` FALSE turns the other way in Acrobat, so on type 1 the flag works
as the formula is written.

**On point 4, type 1 already offers a writer a way out.** A type 1 helix stores its *x*-axis explicitly as
`unit_u`, and its radius law may start at zero. So a conical helix that starts at its apex already has a form
that states its phase. Acrobat, for its part, does draw the type 0 case: on a file of ours with a +*z* axis,
`start` on the axis and a growing radius, it starts the spiral along +*y* -- consistent with an *x*-axis of
*axis* × *X*, though one axis direction cannot separate that from other rules. So forbidding the case would
make files Acrobat already reads non-conforming. Two resolutions follow: state the rule Acrobat uses, once a
tilted-axis file has named it, or forbid the case and direct such helices to type 1. What does Acrobat draw for
the helix of this kind in your collection?

A second, independent reading of the corner assignment in this issue, made with nanoPRC's reader (not with the Datalogics
fixtures), over prc-db (github.com/ralovich/prc-db, a collection of real-world PRC files gathered from public sources
across the internet and curated by @ralovich; the files are the work of many independent producers).

Method. For every PRC_HCG_IsoNURBS face in prc-db (1,304 faces in 15 files) the control net was decoded, the two corners of the
parameter rectangle that each trim curve joins were found from the loop's vertices (vertex j is shared by curves j and j+1), and the
side and direction of each curve were compared with what each reading predicts. A corner counts as met when the loop vertex is within
2 steps of the stored control net (a "quantum"); 20 steps gives the same result.

Result.
- The assignment in this issue (first two Booleans give the side; the last gives the direction): 3,700 of 3,700 curves are exact at
  2 quanta, and 4,080 of 4,080 at 20. None is reversed and none is on another side.
- The text as printed (iso-prc/sections/07-base-entities.adoc:3551, iso-prc/definitions/base-entities/topology.yaml:873): 0 of
  3,700 exact. 1,122 (30.3%) are reversed, and only for first bits 00 and 11; 2,578 (69.7%) are on another side.
- Control: with the three bits of every curve shuffled, 416 of 3,700 are exact, so the test can fail.

Limits. The total of 4,748 curves in this issue is not reproduced as a number (our coverage is 3,700 at the tighter setting and 4,080 at
the looser). Faces with a side shorter than 6 quanta (9) were left out, because at that size one corner cannot be told from its
neighbour. The 12 curves of #844 are from a collection we do not have, so they are not repeated here.
